docs.text: Whitney’s translation of the Atharvaveda, revised and edited by Charles Lanman, with a long commentary. Text read by machine (OCR) from the scanned pages (hosted by the Internet Archive, item in.ernet.dli.2015.263106) and set as a book; it has not been proofread and contains recognition errors. docs.title: A note on this edition
docs.text:
This is the text of Atharva-Veda Saṃhitā, translated with a critical and exegetical commentary (Harvard Oriental Series, vol. 7). It was made from the scan held by the Internet Archive (in.ernet.dli.2015.263106): the pages were read by machine and the text has not been proofread.

What is here. The text of the book, pages 13–628 of the scan, with the author's footnotes where the machine could tell them from the text. Left out: the title pages and the printed table of contents (the library makes its own), the index, whose references are to the pages of the printed book, advertisements and library stamps. This volume is the first half of the work (Books I to VII); the hymn headings within each book are taken from the printed translation, and the footnotes at the foot of the page are left in the running text.

How it was made. Each page of the scan was cleaned and read with the Tesseract engine (version 5), using a model trained on proofread letterpress English with transliterated Sanskrit. Running heads and page numbers were taken out, the lines of each paragraph joined, words broken at the end of a line rejoined, and footnotes linked to their marks; the chapters follow the book's own.

How good it is. On scans like this the machine gets roughly one or two characters in a hundred wrong, more in footnotes, in Sanskrit words with diacritics, in tables, and at drop capitals at the start of a chapter or poem. Words printed in Devanagari or another non-Latin script are not read: they are shown as [Skt.] or as the machine's guess. Where the text matters, check it against the scan.

Machine-read for Pustakālaya, November 2026.

docs.title: 1.1 Book I
docs.text: THE first book is made up mostly of hymns of 4 verses each, and no other ground of its existence as a book needs to be sought. It contains 3o such hymns, but also one (34) of 5 verses, two (11 and 29) of 6 verses, one (7) of 7, and one (3) of 9. There are conjectural reasons to be given in more than one of these cases for the exceptional length. Hymns of 4 verses are also found in books vi. and vil. (12 in vi, and 11 in vii.), also g in xix. The whole book has been translated by Weber, Jndische Studien, vol. iv. (1858), pages 393-430.

docs.title: 1. For the retention of sacred learning
docs.text:
LAtharvan. — vâcaspatyam. caturycam. ânustubham : 4. 49. virâd urobyhatr]

The hymn is found also near the beginning of Pâipp. i. MS. (iv. rz. I end) has the first two verses. It is called in Kaug. (7.8 ; 139. IO) Frigaptiya, from its second word; but it is further styled (as prescribed in 7. 8) briefly pârva ' first, and generally quoted by that name. It is used in the ceremony for production of wisdom " (medhâjanana: Io. 1), and in those for the welfare of a Vedic student (11. r) ; further, with various other passages, in that of entrance upon Vedic study (139. ro); and it is also referred to, in an obscure way (probably as representing the whole Veda of which it is the beginning), in a number of other rites with which it has no apparent connection (x2. 16;; I4. 1; 18. I9; 25. 45 32. 28); finally (13. I, note), it is reckoned as belonging to the varcasya gaga. And the comm. p. 5, end ] quotes it as vsed by a garâg sta (5. 3) in the puspâbhiseka of a king. The Vâit. takes no notice of it.

Translated : Weber, iv. 393; Griffith, i. I.

I. The thrice seven that go about, bearing all forms —let the lord of speech assign to me today their powers, [their] selves (zanṅ).

Ppp. reads pazyanti in a, and lfanvam aâṅyâdadhârn me for 9. MS. combines trisaptâs in a, and tanv) 'dyâ in . The sof our #iapta is prescribed in Prat. il. 98; vâcas p- is quoted under Prat. ii. 71.

Trisaptâs is plainly used as the designation of an indefinite number, = "dozens ' or escores.' Supposing crurâ to signify one's acquired sacred knowledge, portion of crati, it perhaps refers to the sounds or syllables of which this is made up. If, on the other hand, gruta (as in vi. 41. 1) means ' sense of hearing,' the 7risaptâs may be the healthy hearers, old and young (so R.). R. prefers to regard Zanvâs as gen. sing. : fan) me

= ‘to me; the comm. docs the same ; Weber understands accus. pl. Read in our edition ââ27 (an accentsign dropped out under -43).

As an example of the wisdom of the comm., it may be mentioned that he spends i a full quarto page and more on the explanation of frisaptâs. First, he conjectures : that it may mean (three or seven'; as the three worlds, the three gunas, the three highest gods ; or, the seven seers, the seven planets, the seven troops of Maruts, the seven worlds, the seven meters, or the like. Secondly, it may mean ' three sevens, as ¹ seven suns (for which is quoted TA. 1. 7. r) and seven priests and seven Adityas

(TA.iî. 13.3; RV.ix. 114.3), or seven rivers and seven worlds and seven quarters

(TB. i. 8. 38), or seven planets and seven seers and seven Marut-troops. Thirdly, it may signify simply thrice seven or twenty-one, as twelve months + five seasons + three worlds + one sun (TS. vil. 3. 105), or five maṅâbhâtas + five breaths + five jṅânen-

Jriyas + five karmendriyas + one antaṅṅarepa. At any rate, they are gods, who are to render aid. Discussed by Whitney, Feszgruss an Rotk, p. 94.

2. Come again, lord of speech, together with divine mind ; lord of good, make [it] stay (ni-ram) ; in me, in myself be what is heard.

Two of our mss. (H. O.) have râmaya in c. Ppp. begins with wâa nckha, and has i asogpare in c, which R. prefers. But MS. rather favors our text, reading, for c, d, ¹ vâsupate vf ramaya mâyy evâ tanvâm mâma ; and it begins a with paprehi. The ¹3 comm. explains crutam as upâdhyâyad vidhito ‘dha vedagâstrââikam; and adds a ⁴ because, though well learned, it is often forgotten. f 3. Just here stretch thou on, as it were the two tips of the bow with 5: the bow-string ; let the lord of speech make fast (ni-yam) ; in me, in myself, be what is heard. of Ppp. reads, in a, b, fanṅ ubhey ararni. With the verse is to be compared RV. x. i 166. 3. Prat. i. 82 prescribes the pada-reading of ârtntoiva, and iv. 3 quotes abht of tau. [That is, apparently (a), ' Do [for me] some stretching [or fastening], namely, gr ¹ of my sacred learning, as also in c. J

4. Called on is the lord of speech; on us let the lord of speech call;

may we be united with (sam-gam) what is heard ; let me not be parted with what is heard.

i Ppp. has, for b fŚ., wpaknṅto ‘han vâcaspatyn soursytena rââhasi samyrtena vr l : v7râdhasi— badly corrupt. For similar antitheses with pak, see AB. ii. 27 ; VS. ii. ro b, : 11a. In AA. (il. 7. 1) is a somewhat analogous formula for the retention of what is heard or studied (adkrta) : grutarm me mâ pra kastr anenâ dhitenâ 'horârrânt sar dadhâmi. The Anukr. notes the metrical irregularity of the second pâda.

docs.title: 2. Against injury and disease: with a reed
docs.text:
[Atharvan. — cândranasam ; pârjanyan. ungublan : 3-32 vir GunâMa gHyarrs]

The hymn is not found in the Pâipp. ms., but may have been among the contents of the missing first leaf. In the quotations of the Kâug. it is not distinguishable from the ee ; following hymn; but the comm is doubtless right in regarding it as intended at 14. 7. 1 ¹ Ee ee RE where it, with i. rg—21 and sundry other hymns, is called sâṅigrâmâZka or ' battle-hymn,' used in rites for putting an enemy to flight; and it (or vs. 1) is apparently designated by prathamasya (as first of the sâṅgramika hymns) in 14.12, where the avoidance of wounds by arrows is aimed at; it is also reckoned (14. 7, note) as belonging to the aparâjita gana; further, it is used, with i. 3, in a healing ceremony (2 5. 6) for assuaging wounds, etc. ; and, after hymn r has been employed in the #pâkar man, it and the other remaining hymns of the annvâka are to be muttered (139. rr). The comm. Ip. 16, top J, once more, quotes it from Naksatra error, for Cânti, says Bloomfield ] Kalpa 17, 18, as applied in a makâcanti called aparâjita.

Translated : Weber, iv.394; Griffith, i. 3 ; Bloomfield. 8, 233. — Discussed : Bloomfield, AJP. vil. 467 . or JAOS. xiii. p. cxiii ; Florenz, Bezsenberger's Bei trâge, xiv. r 78 ff.

I. We know the reed's father, Parjanya the much-nourishing; and we know well its mother, the earth of many aspects.

Vidma is quoted in Prat. iii. 16 as the example first occurring in the text of a lengthened final a.

z. O bow-string, bend about us ; make thyself a stone ; being hard, put very far away niggards [and] haters.

A bow-string is, by Kâug. 14. 13, one of the articles used in the rite. With b compare ii. 13. 4 b. Pâda â is RV.iii. 16. 5 d. Niggard' is taken as conventional rendering of 4râri. The comm. reads uâlus, RV.-wise.

3. When the kine, embracing the tree, sing the quivering dexterous (? r6hṅ) reed, keep away from us, O Indra, the shaft, the missile.

That is, apparently (a, b), ' when the gut-string on the wooden bow makes the reed-arrow whistle: cf. RV. vi. 67. ir c,d. The comm. explains yŚkum as urn bhâsamanarn (¹), and Jidyum as dyotamâanam, which is probably its etymological sense. [ Discussed, Bergaigne, Rel. vââ. i. 278 n., ii. 182.

4. As between both heaven and earth stands the bamboo (? kana), so let the reed-stalk (mâ#7ja) stand between both the disease and the flux (âsrâovâ).

The verse seems unconnected with the rest of the hymn, but to belong rather with hymn 3. The comm. glosses zjana with ven. For âsrâva, cf. ii. 3; vi. 44. 2 ; the comm. explains it here by mautrârisâara difficulty () of urinating' or painful urination' ' diabetes,' rather? ]. Bloomfield understands it to mean diarrheea," and bases upon this questionable interpretation his view of the meaning of the whole hymn, which he entitles « formula against diarrhoea."

docs.title: 3. Against obstruction of urine: with a reed
docs.text:
[Atharvan.— navarcam. parjanyamitrâdibakudevatyam. ânugtubhqm : I-35. patkyâpankri.]

Of this hymn, only vss. 7-8 are found in Pâipp. (in xix.), without the refrain. It is doubtless intended at Kâug. 25. 10, as used in a rite for regulating the flow of urine; vss. 89 are specified in 25. 12. The "reed " implies some primitive form of a fistula uwrinaria, the vastiyantra (one of the nâdiyantrayu:) of the later physicians — who, however, do not appear to have made frequent use of it.

Translated : Weber, iv. 395; Griffith, i. 4; Bloomfield, ro, 235. — Cf. Bergaigne- Henry, Manuel, p. 130.

I. We know the reed's father, Parjanya of hundredfold virility ; with that will I make weal (câm) for thy body; on the earth [be] thine outpouring, out of thee, with a splash !

The last pada is found also at TS. iii. 3. 102 ; 347 #i, again at xviii. 2. 22.

2. We know the reed's father, Mitra of hundredfold virility ; with that will etc. etc.

3. We know the reed's father, Varuna of etc. etc.

4. We know the reed's father, the moon of etc. etc.

5. We know the reed's father, the sun of etc. etc.

6. What in thine entrails, thy (two) groins (? gaviṅt), what in thy bladder has flowed together — so be thy urine released, out of thee, with a splash ! all of it.

The comm. reads in b (with two or three of SRP's mss., which follow him) sazgrâta. He explains the gavinyân as " two vessels (7âgr) located in the two sides, affording access to the receptacles of urine."

7. I split up thy urinator, like the weir of a tank —so be thy etc. etc.

The comm. (with the same mss. as above) has in b varâam. Ppp. reads vrtrar vegantyâ : yaniyak. |'I pierce or open up thy urethra'— with a metallic catheter, says the comm. J

8. Unfastened [be] thy bladder-orifice, like [that] of a water-holding sea— so be thy etc. etc.

Ppp. gives, for b, samudrasyo ¹adhir eva.

9. As the arrow flew forth, let loose from the bow — so be thy etc. etc.

Instead of parâeâpatar in a, we should expect parâcpârat, the equivalent of a present.

It is easy to reduce this hymn to the substance of four verses, the norm of the book, by striking out vss. 2—, as plainly secondary variations of vs. r, and combining vss. 7-8 (as in Ppp.) into one verse, with omission of the sense-disturbing refrain.

docs.title: 4. To the waters : for blessings
docs.text:
[Sindkudvipa.— aponaptriyâṇi, somâbdâivarâni. gâyatrâpi: 4. purastâdbyhari.]

The hymn is not found in Pâipp. It and the two that next follow are reckoned by Kang. (9. 1, 4) to both ¢ânti ganas, major (474at) and minor (laghu) ; also (7. 14) to the apârṅ: suktâni or water-hymns, applied in various ceremonies ; and by some (18. 25, note) to the salila gana, which Kâug. begins with hymns 5 and 6. The same three are Joined with others (19. r) in a healing rite for sick kine, and (41. 14) in a ceremony for good fortune. Again (25. 20), this hymn is used (with vi. 51) in a remedial rite, and (37. 1) in the interpretation of signs. Hymns 4-6 further appear in Vâit. (16. 10) as used in the aponaptriya rite of the agniytoma sacrifice, and 4. z alone with the setting down of the vasatrvarr water in the same sacrifice. The four verses are RV. i.23. 16-19; for other correspondences, see under the verses:; Translated : Weber, iv. 396 ; Griffith, i. 6. ¹

I. The mothers go on their ways, sisters of them that make sacrifice, i mixing milk with honey. d

2. They who are yonder at the sun, or together with whom is the sun — let them further our sacrifice.

The verse is found further, without variant, in VS. (vi. 24 e). f

3. The heavenly waters I call on, where our kine drink ; to the rivers (sindkn) is to be made oblation.

Cf. note to x. 9. 27, below. ]

4. Within the waters is ambrosia (amjta), in the waters is remedy; and by the praises (prâcasti) of the waters ye become vigorous (vâân) horses, ye become vigorous kine.

The second half-verse is here rendered strictly according to the accent, which forbids taking the nouns as vocatives ; SPP. reads in c, with all his mss. and the great majority of ours Śhâvarha (our two Bp. give bâav-); the accent is to be regarded as antithetical. RV. gives prâcastaye at end of b, and ends the verse with c, reading deva bhâvata vâjinak. Other texts have the verse : VS. (ix. 6a), TS. (i.7.7¹), and MS. (i. 11. 1) all lack a fourth pâda, and have at end of b grâcastiyu ; for c, VS. has âcvz bhâvata vâjinak, TS. dcvâ bhavatha vâjinah, and MS. âvâ bhavata vâjinaṇ.

docs.title: 5. To the waters : for blessings
docs.text:
ISindkudvipa.— (etc., as 4).

The first three verses occur, without variants, in Pâipp. xix. The whole hymn, with the first three verses of the one next following, are, also without variants, RV. x. 9. I-7 (vs. 5 is here put before 4; 6, 7 are also RV. i. 23. 20 a, b, c, 21) ; and they likewise occur in other texts : thus, 5. 1-3 in SV. (ii. 1187-1189), VS. (ai. 50—52 et al.), TS. (iv. I. 5 et al.), MS. (ii. 7. 5 et al.), and TA. (iv. 42. 4 et al.), everywhere with the same text for other references, see MGS., p. 147; as to 5. 4 and the verses of 6, see under the verses. Hymns 5 and 6 together are called cambhumayobke, Kâug. 9. 1 ; for their uses in connection with the preceding hymn, see under that hymn. Both appear also in the house-building ceremony (43. rz), and this one alone in the dargapurpamasa- or parvan-sacrifices (6. 17) ; while the schol. add it (42. 13, note) to the ceremony on the home-coming of the Vedic student. For the use in Vâit. with hymns 4 and 6, see under 1; with 6 (also under the name cambkumayobkt) it accompanies in the pagubandka (10. 19) the washing of articles employed ; and with it alone, in the agnicayana (28. 11), is the lump of earth sprinkled. The comm., finally, quotes the hymn from Naks. Kalpa 17, 18, as used in a mahâcanti called âdikya.

Translated : Weber, iv. 397 ; Griffith, i 7.

I. Since ye are kindly waters, do ye set us unto refreshment (777), unto sight of great joy.

2. What is your most propitious saver (râsa), of that make us share here, like zealous mothers.

3. We would satisfy you in order to that to the possession of which ye quicken, O waters, and generate us.

May not janâyatha, like English produce, here mean 'bring,' and so signify about the same thing as jfnvatha ?

4. Of the waters, having mastery of desirable things, ruling over human beings (carsant), I ask a remedy.

The verse follows in RV. our 6. 1. It is found, without variants, in TB. (ii. 5. 85) ¹ and TA. (iv. 42. 4) ; but MS. (iv. 9. 27) has a corrupt third pada, with much discordance among the mss., and adds a fourth.

docs.title: 6. To the waters : for blessings
docs.text:
[Sindhudvipa (Atharvâkrti).— (etc., as 4). g. patkyâpaṅkti.]

The hymn is not found in Pâipp., but perhaps stood at the beginning of its text, on the lost first leaf : see Bloomfield's introd. to the Kâug., p. xxxvii and ref's, esp. Weber, v.78 and xiii. 431 J]. Verses r—3 occur in RV., as noted under the preceding hymn, and 1 I—2 in other texts, as pointed out under the verses. For the use of the hymn, with its predecessor or its two predecessors, in Kâug. and Vâit., see above, under those hymns.

Verse 1 is also (Kâug. 9.7) directed to be repeated (with the gâyatrI or sâzvitrEverse)

at the beginning and end of ¢ânti rites, and to be recited part by part six times, with rinsing of the mouth, in the âramakorsava ceremony (140. 5). ² Translated : Weber, iv. 397 ; Griffith, i. S. â I. Be the divine waters weal for us in order to assistance, to drink; Ee weal [and] health flow they unto us.

The verse occurs further, without variants, in VS. (xxxvi. 12), TB. (i. 2. 1 et al.), TA.

(iv. 42.4), and Ap. (v. 4.1); in SV. (i.33) is repeated ¢â7z nas (instead of #pas) at beginning of b. The comm. explains aâkis7i by abkhiyajana ⁴ As to the prefixion of this verse to the whole text in a part of our mss., see p. cxvi.

2. Within the waters, Soma told me, are all remedies, and Agni (fire)

wealful for all.

Found also in TB. (ii. 5. 86), without variants, and in MS. (iv. ro. 4), with, for c, ¹ âpag ca vigvâcambhuval.

3. O waters, bestow a remedy, protection (vârâtha) for my body, and long to see the sun. : Only RV. hâs this verse. ¹ 4. Weal for us the waters of the plains, and weal be those of the marshes, weal for us the waters won by digging, and weal what are (4 brought in a vessel; propitious to us be those of the rain.

Pâdas a-d are nearly repeated in xix. 2. 2. 5 : The mss. sum up this anuvâka Lz. ] or chapter as of 6 hymns, 29 verses ; and their quoted Anukr. says ââyaprathama reo nava synr vidyâr: ie. the verses exceed by 9 the assumed norm of the chapters, which is zo. [Regarding vidyât, see end of notes

docs.title: 7. To Agni: for the discovery of sorcerers
docs.text:
[Câtana.— saptarcam. &nugtubkam : 3. trigtubh.] This hymn and the following occur in Paipp. iv., where the length of this one is more in place than here among the hymns of four verses. Both, with eight other hymns (mostly attributed by the Anukr. to Câtana as author), are called by Kâug. (8.25) câtanâni 'expellers,' and are used in a few places for exorcism and such purposes.

Translated : Weber, iv. 398 ; Ludwig, p. 523 ; Griffith, i.g ; Bloomfield, 64,237. — Ct. Bergaigne-Henry, Manuel, p. 131; also Whitney, Festgruss an Rok, p. 94 f.

I. Bring hither, O Agni, the sorcerer (yâtudhâna), the kimidin, speaking out (stu); for thou, O god, being revered, hast become slayer of the barbarian (dâsyn).

Stu is shown by its use also in 8. 1, 2 to have here the virtual meaning 'confess' ‘naming, i.e. confessing himself; cf. laudare ' praise,' but also "name,' ‘mention ']. The comm. does not see this, but stolidly renders it ' praise,' making the first line mean bring the god who praises my oblation or else who is praised by us, and make the yaârudhâna etc. go away"! He is never weary, when kimidin occurs, of repeating Yaska's (6. 1) silly etymology from k7m idânim ' what now ?' Ppp. reads for a stzvânaṣtânaya, and, for c, 6, tvan: ki devân: stuto kanta tasyo ‘ta babkṅvyatha.

2. O most exalted one (paramesthin), Jatavedas, self-controller, Agni, partake of (pra-ac) the sacrificial butter, of the sesame oil (); make the sorcerers cry out.

The translation ' sesame oil' follows our text, fâilâsya ; but the reading of all the mss., which SPP. follows, is z7ulâsya, and Ppp. has râlasya. The comm. explains the word as meaning situated in the sacrificial ladle," from fz ⁴ balance,' used for ⁴spoon,' because by the latter the butter is measured out — or, he adds, it signifies simply avadtyamaâna cut off (in the technical sense), since the root 27 means wnmâne mete out']. Ppp. further reads in c, 4d prâcânam yârudhânâd vilzpayak. The comm. first takes vi lâgaya from root 7, and makes it equal winâcaya? but he adds further a derivation from vi lap ' make 'em squeal,' as we should say ]. At end of a, the sa kitâ-mss., as usual, are divided between -s7kin and -57kâṅ ; SPP. chooses the former of. Prat. fi. r1 J. Ppp. has waginz in b.

3. Let the sorcerers cry out (vi-lap), let the devouring kimidins; then do you, O Agni together with Indra, welcome this our oblation.

Ppp. combines, as often, -?hânâ 'tri-, in a-b; and it reads yatṅâ for aha in c, and at the end ṅaryatâam. SPP. reads everywhere aririn, the theoretically correct form, but never found in the mss.

4. Let Agni first take hold ;. let Indra, having arms, push forth; let everyone that has a demon, coming, say “here am I."

Yâtumant ' having a familiar demon (yâtu)' is the equivalent of yârudhâna 'sorcerer,' litly ‘holding a demon. Ppp. has for a, b agnis purastad a yackharu pratka indro nudadas vâakumaâ ; and for â, ayam asmai teâya.

5. We would fain see thy heroism (vizyâ), O Jâtavedas ; proclaim to i us the sorcerers, O men-watcher ; let them all, burnt about by thee in front, come to this place, proclaiming themselves.

Ppp. reads in a vṅryâ; in c, -taptas ; in â, yântu. The change of meter makes the verse suspicious as original part of the hymn ; but the presence of all the verses in : Ppp., in the same order, puts the intrusion, if it be one, far back.

6. Take hold, O Jâtavedas ; thou wast born for our purpose ; becoming our messenger, O Agni, make the sorcerers cry out.

The comm. this time, utterly regardless of the obvious conection with v7 lapantu in 2d, and of the general sense of the hymn, glosses vi lâpaya only with vinâaya.

Ppp. has a totally different text: a rabhasva brâhmanâ jâtavedo hydi kâmaâya 4 ranâhaya : dṅto na agnir wt tistha yarudkâanâan ikâ "naya.

7. Do thou, O Agni, bring hither the sorcerers bound ; then let Indra with his thunderbolt crush in (apâ-wrage) their heads.

Api vrage (used almost always of the head) is perhaps more nearly cut open'; Ś Ppp. reads apa cṅrŚa vrgcatu. In b, âpa badâhâr would be a more acceptable reading.

The Prat. (ii. 27) quotes upabaddkṅâṅ as the first instance in the text of such treatment of final -7z. Our text, by an error of the printer, reads 547rena for vâj- in c.

docs.title: 8. To Agni and other gods: for the discovery of sorcerers
docs.text:
g ¹ [Câtana. — ânugubham : 4. bârkatagarbhâ trigtubh.] id The hymn, except vs. 4, is found in Paipp. iv. also next after our hymn 7, but in the verse-order I, 3, 2. For its use by Kâug. with 7, see under the latter.

Translated : Weber, iv. 401 ; Ludwig, p. 523; Griffith, i. i 1 ; Bloomfield, 65, 239. —

Ct. Bergaigne-Henry, Manuel, p. 132 ; Whitney, Festgruss an Roth, p. 94 f.

I. This oblation shall bring the sorcerers, as a stream does the foam; i whoever, woman [or] man, hath done this, here let that person speak out.

Ppp. has for c, 4 nidan stri pumân kar yagam bhuvatâm janak. |For stu, see

² i. 7.1, note. J

2. This man hath come, speaking out ; this man do ye welcome ; O

Brihaspati, taking [him] into thy control— O Agni and Soma, do ye (two)

pierce [him] through. : Ppp. has in a, b stuvâna gama tvar smo 'ta prati; in c, 6, vace krtâ 'gnṅomâṇ i : id dkatari. The comm. makes nonsense every time by insisting on rendering stz by He “praise ; here it is yusman stuvan.

3. Of the sorcerer, O soma-drinker, slay the progeny and conduct

[him hither]; of him, speaking out, make fall out (nispat) the upper eye and the lower.

The comm. fills out the ellipsis in b by making it mean (conduct our progeny de to obtain desired result"! and stxvânasya is bhityâ tvadvisayâan stutiv: kurvatap.

Ppp. reads zyastuvânasya. SPP's text as well as ours gives nz sz- (p. nâṅ: st-); the — ¹ a sa kitâ-mss., as everywhere, are divided between that and #7 sz; the latter is authora ized by the silence of the Prâticâkhya see p. 426 concerning the combination.

4. Wherever, O Agni, thou knowest the births of them, of the devourers that are in secret, O Jâtavedas, them do thou, increasing through worship (brâhman) — slay of them, O Agni, with hundredfold transfixion.

The irregular meter and broken connection of the second half-verse suggest possible corruption of the text : cf. âsurâṇâri catatarkân, TS. i. 5.76. The meter (11 + 11: 9 + 9 = 4o) is well enough described by the Anukr. if we may take Śârkatagarbka as meaning âwibârk- ' containing two pâdas of nine syllables." [ For -²â7kam, cf. Gram. Ś 995-1

docs.title: 9. For some one's advancement and success
docs.text:
[4 tharvan.— vasvâdinânâmantroktadevatyam. trââgtubham.)

Found also in Pâipp. i. Reckoned to the varcasya gana (Kâug. 13. I, note), and further used in various ceremonies : by itself, in that of the restoration of a king (16.27); with i. 35 and v. 28, in two ceremonies for fortune and for power (II. Ig; 52. 20) ; with seven others, employed by a teacher at the reception of a Vedic student (55.17). In Vâit. (3. I), vs. 3 accompanies an oblation to Agni in the par7an-sacrifices. And the comm. quotes its use in the Naks. Kalpa 17-19, in two sakâcânti ceremonies called d âirâvarr and barkhaspati ; and in Paricista 5.3, in the puspâabhiseka rite.

Translated : Weber, iv. 4or ; Ludwig, p. 456 ; Zimmer, p. 163 ; Griffith, i.12; Bloomfield, 116, 239.

I. In this man let the Vasus maintain good things (oâsz)— Indra, Pṅshan, Varuna, Mitra, Agni ; him let the Adityas and also the All-gods maintain in superior light.

Ppp. substitutes rvaszâa for p75â in b, and uta me deva for uttarasmin in 4. The Anukr. appears to sanction the metrical combination gâityo 'ta in c.

z. At his direction (gradi), O gods, be there light, sun, fire, or also gold ; be his rivals (sapâtna) inferior to him ; to the highest firmament (nâka) make this man ascend.

The translation implies in c the obviously called-for emendation of asmât to asmat the comm. first explains it as asmadtyar purusâr, and then, alternatively, as used for asmaâr by Vedic shortening of the vowel. Ppp. begins with asmân devâṅ pradigcâ; and its second half-verse is quite different : uztarena brakmaṇnâ vi bhâhi krpvâno anyârn adharan saparnan (4 = ii. 29. 3 9).

3. With what highest worship (brâhman), O Jâtavedas, thou didst bring together draughts (2âyas) for Indra, therewith, O Agni, do thou increase this man here ; set him in supremacy (crââstkya) over his fellows (sajarâ).

Ppp. reads wttarena in b, and its d is râyas posar: crâithyam dhehy asm. The verse is found also in TS. (iii. 5. 42), MS. (i.4. 3), and K. (v. 6). Both TS. and MS. read kavâsâ for brâhmaṇâ in b, and agne tvâm wtâ (for tvâm agna ikâ) in c; and MS. has -bharan in a, vardhayâ m&m in c, and ma for enam at the end ; and it I inserts mâdh=ye before cratsthye in d.

4. I take to myself their sacrifice and splendor (vârcas), their abundance of wealth and their intents (cirâ), O Agni ; be his rivals inferior to him ; to the highest firmament make this man ascend.

The second half-verse is the same with = c, 4 above, and the translation makes the same emendation as there. Doubtless viz7âni acquisitions ' should be read for cittâni in b; the comm. glosses with buddhim. The text is defaced in Ppp. ; but in d can be read wṅtame devâ jyortisi dhatutama (¹) meaning, presumably, dadhâtana.

docs.title: 10. For some one's release from Varuṇa's wrath
docs.text:
[A 2harvan. — âsuram, vârupam. trâ tubham : 3, 4. anugtubh (3. kakummati).] Ś Found in Pâipp. i. Used in Kâug. (25.37) to accompany lavation of the head in a ; healing ceremony (for dropsy, comm. and schol).

Translated : Weber, iv. 403 ; Ludwig, p. 445 ; Griffith, i. 13 ; BloomSeld, 11,241;

Weber, Sb. 1897, p. 599, cf. 594 ff. — Cf. Bergaigne-Henry, Manuel, p. 133.

I. This Asura bears rule over the gods; for the wills (vâga) of king

Varuṇa [come] true ; from him, prevailing by my worship (Śrâhman), from the fury of the formidable one (ugrâ) do I lead up this man.

⁴ Come true,' i.e. are realized or carried out : the more etymological sense of sazyâ.

Ppp. reads wââya for vac ki. The comm. explains câzadâna as exceedingly sharp;

having attained strength by favor of Varuna, gratified by praise etc." 7uzas pari in c, as the first example of its kind of combination, is quoted in Prat. ii. 66. The Anukr. . (ignores the first pada as a jagatr. . 2. Homage be to thy fury, O king Varuṇa ; for, O formidable one, thou dost note (ui ci) every malice (drugâhâ). A thousand others I impel ar (pra-sṅ) together ; a hundred autumns of thee shall this man live.

The obscure third pâda is understood by the comm., perhaps correctly, to mean «I buy off this man by furnishing Varuṇa a thousand others as substitutes." Two of our mss. (O. Op.) read ugrân: (or ugram) in b; Ppp. is defaced in a, b; as second half-oo verse it reads : cata sakhasraṅ pra suvâmy anyân ayam no jrvârn carado uyapaâye. ¹ Here, too, pââa a is an unacknowledged jagarr. Comra. cites, for c, AB. vil. 15. li 3- In that thou hast spoken with the tongue untruth, much wrong — from the king of true ordinances (-âhârman), from Varuna, I release thee. : I Read yâr tvâm uvâktha ânytam?] The comm. has in a the absurd reading ee wvakta, treating it as for zvaktha, which all the mss. give.
  1. I release thee out of the universal, the great flood (arṅavâ); speak,

O formidable one, unto [thy] fellows here, and reverence our incantation

(brâhmman).

¹ Universal (vââuâanara), i.e, perhaps, dangerous to all men; and the dropsy, 40 : Varuṇa's special infliction, is probably spoken of as (flood cf. RV. vii. 89.4. The

(doubtful) rendering of the second half-verse takes it as addressed, like the first, to the

²5 patient ; the comm. regards it as said to Varuna, which is not impossible. ] See Geld- 5 eŚ ner, ZDMG. li. 733.1 Ppp. reads auṅcarm at the beginning, and has a lacuna in place a of c, 4. Render apa-ci by ' regard?

docs.title: 11. For successful childbirth
docs.text:
[âtharvan. — jagycam. pâugyam. pânktam : 2. anuggubk i 3. 4:9. usHiggAVVRâ FO RUMIMarV anu ubk ; 4-6. patkyâpankti.]

Verses 2—4 occur together in Pâipp. i., 5 and 6 in xx., but at different points. In Kâug. (33. 1) it is quoted at the beginning of a long and intricate ceremony (filling the whole section) for safe delivery, the first of the str7karmâṇi or women's rites; its details have nothing to do with the text of the hymn, and cast no light upon the latter's difficulties. The Anukr. add to the author's name : ancna mantroktâan aryamaâadidevan nariukhaprasavayâ 'bhistuye ‘stam ca sarvâabhir aprarthayat.

Translated : Weber, iv. 404 ; Ludwig, p. 478 ; Griffith, i. 14 and 473 ; Bloomfield, 99,242.— Discussed : Roth, Ler den Atharva-veda, p. 5.

I. At this birth, O Ptshan, let Aryaman [as] efficient (vedkâs) invoker utter oâsat for thee ; let the woman, rightly engendered, be relaxed ; let her joints go apart in order to birth.

The translation of c implies emendation of the text to of sâsytânz. Roth formerly preferred sâsyzânr nary rtâprajarak 'let a timely child come forth, O woman '; Weber leaves sâsratâm as pl. with indefinite subject, and understands the two following words as a parenthesis : " be the woman properly constructed " ; Ludwig renders as if sâs7 172; Roth now (as in BR.) would emend only sâyzâm, and understand it of the 'ffow' of water preceding birth ; but that would be rather sr, and sy without a prefix in such a sense seems very unlikely ef., however, sârann Śpal, RV. iv.17.3) Rtâprajara might also be possessive, 'rightly engendering. The comm. takes sṅtâr as from sâti not s#rt, fem., nor S71, fem. : note accent and gender ¹, and meaning the ceremony at birth; vedhâs as = Dhâtar 'the creator; 7taprajati as = jroad-apatyâ ; and sisrarâm (to the plural form of which he finds no objection) as “may she be relieved (einihsy1â) of the pangs of birth.” The metrically irregular verse (9 + ro: ro + II = 40) is a paṅkti solely in virtue of the aggregate ] number of its syllables.

2. Four [are] the directions of the sky, four also of the earth : the gods sent together the foetus ; let them unclose her in order to birth.

Or tunclose it,' tâm, which SPP. reads in text and comm. (the latter omits the word itself in the paraphrase) with the minority of his mss., but against all of ours; Weber and Roth prefer 747. The word and its predecessor are quoted in the Prat. (ii. 30), as the earliest example in the text of a combination of 7 and 7 without inserted s; but the form of the quotation (samnâirayantââinâm) prevents our seeing whether its authors read 7âm or (4m ; the comm. gives f7m. In d, the comm. gives the false form ârṇavantu. The text in Ppp. is confused, but does not appear to intend any variants from our reading.

3. Let Pishan (?) unclose [her or it] ; we make the yâzi go apart ; do thou, sâgaṇâ, loosen ; do thou, bigkalâ, let go.

The translation implies a very venturesome emendation in a, pâ54 for s57 (all the authorities have the latter) : Pushan, referred to in vs. r as principal officiating deity, might well be called on to do in particular what all the gods were begged to do in vs. 2 ce, d. [But see Bloomfield's comment. ] The comm. gives three different etymologies for sâ5â: root s7 + suffix -sâ; root si + root san ; and su-ugas. S#gaṇnâ and bŚikala are possibly names of organs ; for the latter, Ppp. has puskale, probably an alteration to a more familiar word ; the comm. understands sâsanâ and bâ5kali (of course, equally possible) ; the former, from roots sz and san, is name of an accouching goddess ; the latter (for which are given three diverse but equally absurd etymologies) is another deity. The Anukr. apparently intends the verse to be read as 6 + 8: 7 4 8 = 29, ; instead of admitting the obvious resolution Ś2-ân in c. The supplying of gârbham as omitted at the beginning would make a good azuszubh. . 4. Not as it were stuck (â4ata) in the flesh, not in the fat, not as it were in the marrows, let the spotted slimy (?) afterbirth come down, for the dog to eat ; let the afterbirth descend.

SPP. reads in a pfvasi, with the comm. and a small minority of his mss. ; three of ours (H. O. Op.) have pâbasi. Ppp. has a very different text (preserved in the aâgarz copy, though lost in the original text) : nâi ¹va saâvasu na parvasu na kerhesu (kegesu)

na nakhesu ca; then our c, d, without variant ; then zâi "va pause (mânse ?) na proasi nâi 'va kastyo; vanâ yutam ; then our e ; and with this ends the hymn as given in book i. The comm. reads in a mâṅnsena for mâṅse nâ, and resorts to various devices to get rid of the difficulty thus caused ; two of our mss. (O. Op.), and one or two of i SPP's, give the same. Some of our mss. are very awkward about combining jar&yn . and âztave, in part omitting the v, or (I.) reading htt PGS. (i.16. 2) has the verse, but in different order : first our c, 4, without variant ; then our a, b, in the form 777 va maâṅsena proari na kasming canâ "yaram ; then our e. But for its support of (évalam, we might be tempted to emend to Śâvalam ; the comm. has the worthless explanation jalasyo 'paristhitacârvâlavat ântarâvayavâasambadâdham. Further may be compared

HGS. ii. 3. 1. I MP., at ii. iI. 19, 20, has the verse with variants.

5. I split apart thy urinator, apart the yâni, apart the [two] groins, ¹ apart both the mother and the child, apart the boy from the afterbirth;

let the afterbirth descend. : Ppp. (xx.) has for a, b ²7 te cr tami ragariṅ o yoni vi gaveRyân; for 8, vi garbhar:

ca jarâyujak ; and TS. (iii. 3. ror) presents a version nearly accordant with this, but

¹ with fakarâm, gavinyaṅ, and (at the end) jarâyu ca : neither has our refrain.

6. As the wind, as the mind, as fly the birds, so do thou, O ten months' t [child], fly along with the afterbirth ; let the afterbirth descend. ¹ : Ppp. has the version yathâ vâto yarhṅ dagha yarhâ sasadroyajanta : evâ te garbha ejatn nir âitu dagamasyo bahir jarâynupâ saka. For 'do thou fly' might be given ' do a thou fall, the verb having both meanings. Ten (lunar) months : cf. Weber's second naksatra-essay, p. 313, Abk. der Berliner Akad., 1861.1 Ct. RV. Vv. 78.8. I ¹ : This anuvâka 2.) has 5 hymns, 25 verses ; and the old Anukramayi, as quoted, says paṅca pare ru (apparently the widyar quoted at the end of az. 1 belongs rather a here than there).

docs.title: 12. Against various ailments (as results of lightning ?)
docs.text:
a BhrgUaṅgiras.— yaksmanâcanadevartikam. jâgatam : 4. anugtubk.

rgvars yaks 7 J — ee Found also in Pâipp. i. It is reckoned (Kâug. 26. I, note) as belonging, with many other hymns, to a lakmanâgana or takman-destroying gana, and is used (26.1) to accompany the drinking of yarious things in a healing ceremony (comm. says, against disease arising from hurtful changes of wind, bile, or phlegm), and also (38. 1) in one against bad weather (durdina), or (Keg.) for the prevention of rain. The third verse further is added to the Mrgâara hymns in connection with lavation in another healing rite (27. 34).

Translated : Weber, iv. 405; Griffith, i. r5 ; Bloomfield, JAOS. xiii. p. cxiii ff. (= PAOS. May 1886) ; AJP. vii. 469 ff. ; SBE. xiii. 7, 246. — Bloomfield regards it as addressed to ⁴lightning, conceived as the cause of fever, headache, and cough." See his elaborate comment. Weber made it relate to fever, puerperal or infantile (on account of jarâyujâ, 1 a).

I. First born of the afterbirth, the ruddy (usrâya) bull, born of wind and cloud (?), goes thundering with rain; may he be merciful to our body, going straight on, breaking ; he who, one force, hath stridden out threefold.

The translation implies emendation in b to vz27547â7âs or 7s, as suggested by 3c; it is proposed by Weber, and adopted by Bloomfield, being a fairly plausible way of d getting out of a decided difficulty. Weber renders, however, "with glowing windbreath "; R., “with scorching wind" (emending to -Śârajjâs). The comm. reads vâtavrajas (a couple of SPP's mss., which usually follow him, do the same), and d explains it as "going swiftly like the wind," or, alternatively, " having a collection of winds. The (bull is to him the sun, and he forces this interpretation through the whole hymn. Neither he nor Kâug. nor the latter's scholia see anywhere any intimation of lightning ; yet this is perhaps most plausibly to be suspected in the obscurities of the expression (so R. also). The first words in a are viewed as signifying ‘just escaped from its foetal envelop (in the cloud).' Ppp. is wholly defaced in the second half-verse; in the first it offers no variants, merely combining yas pratṅ- in a, and reading -bkraja st- in bh. Emendation in d to yâsyazt' kam would improve both meter and sense. 7reâhâ in d must be read as three syllables (as in RV.) to make the verse a i full jagarz. [At OB. vi. 59 b, vâta-âkrajâs is suggested—by R.? q

2. Thee, lurking (77) in each limb with burning (gocâs), we, paying homage, would worship (vââ%) with oblation ; we would worship with oblation the hooks, the grapples, [him] who, a seizer, hath seized this man's joints.

Or yâs, at beginning of d, is abbreviation for 'when he ' or with which he.' [ Render, rather, 'hath seized his (accentless) joints." The patient is in plain sight of the exorcist. Emphatic pronoun is therefore needless ; so ena vs. 3. ] Some of our mss., by a frequent blunder, read in a gâ7y-. The prolongation of the final of asya in â is noted by the comment to Prat. iv. 79. Ppp, has a very different (and corrupt) text : .. câriyâno yo grhita parasya grbhtii : aṅko tan aṅko havisâ yajami kai (rite manasa yo jajana. The definition of this verse and the next as (7757u5h seems to have been lost from the Anukr., which reads simply âoizzyâ before antyâ'n ust bh.

3. Release thou him from headache and from cough — whoever hath entered each joint of him; the blast (? gâgmza) that is cloud-born and that is wind-born, let it attach itself to forest-trees (vânaspâri) and mountains.

Ppp. has syjarâm for sacatâam in 9. The comm. takes kâsâs in a as nomin., explaining it as krtkanthamadhyavarti prasiddhal clesmarogavicesah s vâtajâs to him is kâusihyâd vâyor ulpannaṅ. |For (orsati, see Knauer, Jnâogermanische Forschun- : : gen, Anseiger, vil. 225 ; Bloomfield, AJP. xvii. 416 ; B6htlingk, Berichte der sâchsischen

Ges., 1897, xlix. 50, who takes it as ' a stiff neck with head awry.

4. Weal [be] to my upper member (gâ?ra), weal be to my lower, weal . to my four limbs ; weal be to my body.

Ppp. has a quite different text: in a, b, 72 both times for me, and parâya for avai râya; for c, car te prṣ|tidhyo majjabhyakṅ ca in â, tava for mama : the address to a second person is decidedly to be preferred. This is found also in the corresponding : verse in VS. (xxiii. 44) and TS. (v. 2. 122), with readings in part agreeirg further with ²4 those of Ppp. : câr te pârebhyo gârrebhyal câm asto âoarecbhyak : câm asthâbhyo I majjâbkyaṅ gâm v astu tanvâ) tâva: but TS. has for â cân u te tanṅve bhuval.

docs.title: 13. Deterrent homage to lightning
docs.text:
= [Bhrgraṅgiras.—vâidyntam. ânugubham : 3. 4:p. virâd jagati; gq. trigtupparâ Śyhatigartha : pankti.]. : The hymn occurs in Pâipp. xix., and vs. r also in xv. It is used by Kâug. (38. 8, 9)

in a charm against lightning, with vil. 11 ; and it also appears (139.8), with i. 26 and

vii. 11 and several other hymns, in the ceremony of introduction to Vedic study.

Translated : Weber, iv. 406 ; Griffith, i. 16.

I. Homage be to thy lightning, homage to thy thunder; homage be He to thy bolt (âgman), with which thou hurlest at the impious one (4774). i d The version of this verse in Ppp. xix. is like ours ; in xv., 4 reads yena âṅrar pradi- Ś6 Jjassasi (pratyasyasi?). The first half-verse is found also in VS. (xxxvi. 21 a, b).

The irregular combination ââgâge (p. duṅedâge) is noted by Prat. ii.6o. The comm. ge regards Parjanya as addressed, but then proceeds to give another interpretation of the be verse, based on the absurd assumption that namas = annam, which appears also in Hl numerous other places. To him, also, 4man is a meghanâman. In our edition, an accentmark is omitted over the cma- of âcmane. a z. Homage to thee, child of the height (Śrauât), whence thou gatherest (sam-7k) heat (tâpas) ; be merciful to ourselves ; do kindness (nâyas)

to our offspring (lokâ). : Ppp. has caṅ: nas for mâyas in d. The first half-verse forms in VS. (xxxvi. 21 Cc, d) ¹ one verse with our I a, b; but VS. has for a nâmas te bhagavann astu and J for b fe yâtak svâh samthase ' from whence thou strivest after the sky,' which indicates ihat a ¹4 our reading is corrupt. [Pischel discusses pravât (= stream ') at length, Ved. Stud.

i. 63-76, see 68. â 3. Child of the height, be homage to thee; homage we pay to thy ed missile (kerf) and heat (t4pus); we know thy highest abode (Dkâmar) oe that is in secret; thou art set as navel within the [cloud-]Jocean.

. I The 72 in b is superfluous.] Ppp. rectifies the meter of a by omitting eva its â4 other pâdas are more or less corrupt : namas te hete tipugyai in b (which ends there); i gandharvo nama par- in c; nikitâsa nabhih at the end. The comm. takes tâpus as i adjective. The verse is scanned by the Anukr. as 12 + 12: IT + II = 46 syllables.

4. Thou whom all the gods did create, the bold one, [[the gods] I making an arrow for hurling — do thou, besung in the council (vidârṅa), ¹ be merciful to us; to thee as such be homage, O goddess.

Dk«rsuum in b might qualify 42m directly. The comm. supplies ke agane O thun- ¹ derbolt' as addressed. He reads sla in c. Ppp. reads for a, bya tuâ devâ ajanayanta vigvesân krpvanâ aganâya trisvâai; and for d mitrasya varupasya prasystar. The Anukr. seems to scan as ro + II: Io + 9 = 4o syllables. Read in c mrâaya and in â urâ tâsyâi ?— For widâtha, see discussions of Bloomfield, JAOS. xix.?17, and A Geldner, ZDMG. li. 757 ; and the literature cited by Foy, KZ. xxxiv. 226. ] 4

docs.title: 14. Imprecation of spinsterhood on a woman
docs.text:
[Bkygvarngiras.— vâruṇari vo 'ta yamyar: vâ. ânugubham :: r. kakummatr; 3. 4:p- vir â.]

Found in Pâipp. i. Used by Kâug. (36. 15-18) in an incantation against a woman; the details of it cast no light on those of the hymn ; and the comm. defines its purpose simply as striyaṅ purusasya va daurbhâgyakaraparn. d

Translated : Weber, iv. 408 ; Ludwig, p. 459 ; Zimmer, p. 314 (these misapprehend its character) ; Griffith, i. 17; Bloomfield, JAOS. xiii. p. cxv = PAOS. May, 1886; or AJP. vii. 473 ff.; or SBE. xiii. 107, 232.

I. Her portion (5kâga), splendor have I taken to myself, as from off a tree a garland ; like a mountain with great base, let her sit long with the Fathers.

Ppp. has for a aka: te bhagam â dade; its b is defaced ; in c it gives maṅâmulâi ³va. The comm. renders (haga by bhâagyarm, here and in the other verse, recognizing : no sexual meaning. Pizysu he renders in the later [2 c, d] to be specified houses of father, mother, etc.," and all the translators understand it in the same way ; but it is questionable whether the plural of gitar would ever be used in this sense ; and the repeated mention of Yama later indicates that there was at least a double meaning in ¹ the expression. Perhaps a girl remaining unmarried was called bride of Yama," i.e. as good as dead, and her stay at home compared to that in the other world. Cf. Antigone, 816, I shall be the bride of Acheron," 'Axâporr. vageiza. The Anukr. appears to ratify the abbreviated reading -(udâkâne 'va in c; it counts six syllables in d.

2. Let this girl, O king, be shaken down to thee [as] bride, O Yama; be she bound in her mother's house, also in her brother's, also in her father's.

Ppp. has yat for esa at the beginning. The comm. foolishly interprets 7âjaz as indicating Soma, because Soma is first husband of a bride (he quotes RV. x.85. 40: cf. AV. xiv. 2. 5 ff.), and takes yama as his epithet, as being her constrainer (niyamaka). For nidhṅ compare iii. I. 7; at TS. v.2. 53 it is used with pâz7su. ] Does not nâ-âkhṅ covertly suggest nidkuwvana, which, in its obscene sense, may be as old as the Veda?

3. She is thy housekeeper, O king ; we commit her to thee; she shall sit long with the Fathers, until the covering in of her head.

The translation of â implies the obvious emendation to sem opy ar, which SPP. even admits into his text, on the authority of the comm,, but against every known ms. ; Ppp., : : however, gives samopgyâ. The comm. explains it by sa7kvaganât bhâmâu sampatanâr, y and as equivalent to maranagaryantam (ll death ' ; that this last is the virtual sense is extremely probable. That uâp has not the sense shave ' in the compound (cf. ACS.

vi. ro. 2) is shown by the inappropriateness of the prefixes sa + a to that sense, and the frequency of the combination in the other sense. ] See Bloomfield, 255, 7 crrsnâh . kecam âpiat, ' till she shed the hair from her head] Ppp. has further inâm w pari;

dadkmasi in b. The comm. gives kulapa (for pas : our pada-text kulacpâk) in a. The resolution gâr-sy-ak in 4 would make the verse a full anustubh ; the Anukr. counts only ¹ 14 syllables in the second half.

4. With the incantation (brâhman) of Asita, of Kagyapa, and of Gaya,

I shut up (api-nak) thy portion (vulva ?), as sisters do what is within a : box (-kâ7a).

For the names, see Bloomfield, 255, and AJP. xvii. 403. ] &kaga perhaps has 4c 4 here a double meaning. Three of our mss. (E.I.H.) with one or two of SPP's, read in c antagkogâm, against Prat. ii. 62, which expressly prescribes 2. The comm. treats ana) and Foam as two independent words ; antâṅ kâce would be a not unacceptable

; emendation. The Anukr. appears to sanction the abbreviation -kocaz: 'va.

docs.title: 15. With an oblation : for confluence of wealth
docs.text:
VAtharvarn.— sâindhavam. &nugtubham : a. bhurikparhyâpaṅkti.] : Found in Pâipp. i. (in the verse-order 1, 4,3, 2). Used by Kâug. only in a general rite for prosperity (19. 4), to accompany a douche for persons bringing water from two ee navigable streams and partaking of a dish of mixed grain; it is also reckoned (19. I, Se note) to the pu57ika mantras, or hymns bringing prosperity. a Translated : Weber, iv. 409 ; Ludwig, p. 371 ; Griffith, i. rg. 7 3 y

I. Together, together let the rivers flow, together the winds, together the birds (patatrin); this my sacrifice let them enjoy of old ; I offer with a confluent (saṅsrâgyaâ) oblation. es The verse is nearly identical with xix. 1. I, and in less degree with ii. 26.3. From ² xix. I. 3 c it may be conjectured that we should read pradkas in c. If we do read

‘ Śradtvas, why not render it by ' continually '? ] Ppp. has not the second half-verse, : : but instead of it vs. 3 c, d. For b Ppp. gives saṅz vâtâa diya uta. The comm. accents ec sârz-sam in a. There is perhaps some technical meaning in saṅzsrâ"yâ ' confluent or L ⁴ for confluence ' which we do not appreciate, but it is also unknown to the comm., who explains the word only etymologically. The verse is an âstâragaRkti (strictly virâj:

8+ 38: 11 + II = 38), and its definition as such is perhaps dropped out of the Anukr. a text (which reads aâya Jeâtiyâ bhurik etc.).

2. Come straight hither to my call, hither ye confluents also ; increase HR g this man, ye songs; let every beast (pag) there is come hither ; let what ² ee wealth (ray?) there is stay (szkâ) with him. â ¹ The pada-mss. all give yâṅ in e. Ppp. has in a, b iar hayyâ upetane 'dar, and,

⁴ (for c, asya vardhayato rayim. The last pada is nearly RV. x. 19:3 d. [Render di 'with this man let etc. ] The omission of evâ in a would make the verse regular.

3. What fountains of the streams flow together, ever unexhausted, with all those confluences we make riches (âkâna) flow together for me.

Ppp. has in a, b ye nadibhyas samsravanty ucchâmas saram aksikâ. The comm. gives the verse twice, each time with a separate explanation.

4. What [fountains] of butter (sarpâs) flow together, and of milk, and 4 of water, with all those confluences we make riches flow together for me. Ś

Ppp. reads saṅsrâvâs for sarpisas in a. The comm. supplies first avgyavâs as omitted subject in the verse, but afterwards u7sâsas from vs. 3, which is of course right. i

docs.title: 16. Against demons : with an amulet of lead
docs.text:
3 [Câtana. — agnindram, vâruṇam, dadhatyam. ânugtubham : 4. kakummats.] i Found in Pâipp. i. Kâug. does not include the hymn among the câranâni (8. 25), ‘ but a Parig. (ib., note) reckons it to them (in accordance with the Anukr.). Kaug. ‘ (47-23) uses it once in a rite of sorcery (for the death of one's enemies : comm. ), and ; its commentator (47. 13, note) in another. ; Translated : Weber, iv. 409 ; Grill, 1, 75 ; Griffith, i. 20 ; Bloomfield, 65, 256.

I. What devourers, on the night of new moon, have arisen troopwise (?) — the fourth Agni is the demon-slayer ; he shall bless us.

Vrâjam in b is obscure ; 'troopwise ' is the conjecture of BR. ; the comm. reads 4 instead 547âjam, and absurdly explains it as bkrâjamânâm or -nasn ' shining," and ' qualifying either the night or the «hearty " man whom the demons have risen to injure Ppp. has fuzyas for turâyas in c; what is meant by it is not clear ; the comm. gives d three different explanations : fourth after the death of his three brothers and predecessors (quoting for these TS. ii. 6.6) ; as the house-fire apart from the three sacrificial ; or as the â7girasa fire, as distinguished from the sacrificial, the household, and that of battle — thus teaching us nothing but his own ignorance and perplexity. Grill follows Weber in understanding the word to mean powerful." For â, Ppp. has san nak paru tebhyak. ]

2. The lead Varuṇa blesses ; the lead Agni favors; Indra bestowed on me the lead; it, surely, is a dispeller of familiar demons.

Ppp. combines mai 'ndra g- in c, and has for d amzoâyas tu câram (for câtananmr). The comm. ascribes the mention of Varuṇa to the fact that river-foam is one of the articles declared (Kaug. 8. 18) equivalent to lead, and here intended by that name. { LCE. Bloomfield, JAOS. xv. r58.

3. This overpowers the vâskandha; this drives off (547k) the devourers ; with this I overpower all the races (jâ?â) that are the pigârt 's.

The first half-verse is nearly repeated below, as ii. 4. 3 a, b. The short a in the reduplication of sasake in c, though against the meter and in part against usage, is read by all the mss., and in the comment to Prât. iii. 13. Ppp. has in a wiskanâan: (but compare ii. 4.3, where -dkazz). The comm. explains the (more or less fully personified) disorder as a disturbance caused by raksas or picâca and obstructing motion (gaz- : pratibanâhaka) : cf. below ii. 4 and iii. 9.

4. If our cow thou slayest, if [our] horse, if [our] man (pârusa), we pierce thee there with lead, that thou be no slayer of our heroes.

Ppp. has for c sisena vidhyâmas toa.

The 5 hymns of this anuvâka 3. J, as of the next, have just the norm, zo verses, and the quotation from the old Anukr. (given at the end of hymn 21) is vâṅcakâv ato

'nyan. At the end of the present hymn is read vââgatyâ kuru, which is perhaps the statement as to the assumption of a norm.

The first prapârkaka ends here.

docs.title: 17. To stop the vessels of the body
docs.text:
; Brahman. — yogiddevatyam. ânugubham : I. bhuriy i 4-3-p- ârgi gâyatrr. Cd Found in Pâipp. xix. (in the verse-order 3, 4, I, 2). Used once by Kâug. (26. ro ct the quotation appears to belong to what follows it, not to what precedes), in a remedial rl rite, apparently for stopping the flow of blood (the comm. says, as result of a knife , : wound and the like, and also of disordered menses). i Translated : Weber, iv. 411; Ludwig, p. 508; Grill, 16,76; Griffith, i. 21 ; Bloomfield, 22, 257. — Cf. Hillebrandt, Veda-Chrestomathie, p. 46.

I. Yon women (yogâ2) that go, veins with red garments, like brother- 69 less sisters (jâmi)— let them stop (sz4â), with their splendor smitten.

Ppp. makes yositas and jâmayas change places, and has sarvâs (better) for kiras in b. The comm. takes yogâas as gen. sing., and hence naturally understands rajovaec kananâgyas to be meant in the verse ; he renders kiras by sirâs ; and he explains that TT brotherless sisters pir kule saṅtanakar mane pindadânâya ca tisthanti. The Anukr.

refuses to sanction the contraction -zare "va in c. iq 2. Stop, lower one! stop, upper one l do thou too stop, midmost one 7 if the smallest stops, shall stop forsooth the great tube (dkamâni). ee The accent of 57kari seems to show ca to be the equivalent of cez here. a 3. Of the hundred tubes, of the thousand veins, have stopped forsooth Ś these midmost ones; the ends have rested (ram) together. ¹ In 4, emendation to 4nzyâs 'the end ones ' would be an improvement ; but Ppp. ( also has antâs : sakam antâ 'raṅsata its c is corrupt (aszkâ nibadâhâmâava) ; and it a inserts ze after catasya in a. Ll 4. About you hath gone ((ram) a great gravelly sandbank (kant);

stop [and] be quiet, I pray (sâ kam).

¹ The comm. sees in âhant only the meaning bow," and interprets it "bent like a

Ś bow" : namely, a vessel containing the urine ; in sikalâs he sees an allusion to the

4 menses, or to gravel in the bladder. Kaug. (26. ro) speaks of sprinkling on dust and gravel as a means of stanching the flow of blood ; more probably, as Weber frst sug-

⁴ gested, a bag filled with sand was used : in neither case can the menses be had in view.

Ppp. reads siktamayt bunṅ sthirag carasthidam. The third pada is identical with

RV. i. 191.6 4; the comm. (as Sâyaṇa to the latter) fails to recognize the root 77; and he renders it prerayata, as if root ir were in question.

docs.title: 18. Against unlucky marks
docs.text:
[Dravipodas.— vâinâyakam. ânugiubham : r. uparigtâdvirâgbrhati; a. nicgjagarr;

3 wir âdastârapanktitrigubh.]

Verses 1—3 are found in Pâipp. xx. (but vs. 2 not with the others). Used by Kâus. (42.19) in a charm against unlucky signs in a woman. ¹

Translated : Weber, iv. 411 ; Ludwig, p. 498 ; Geldner, I%â. Stud. i. 314 ; Griffith, i.22 ; Bloomfield, 109, 260. — It may be mentioned that Geldner takes the whole hymn as relating to a domestic cat. i

I. Out we drive (nir-sâ) the pallid sign, out the niggard; then, whatever things are excellent (bkadrâ), those we lead together (?) for our progeny.

The translation implies in d the very venturesome emendation of ârâtim to sâm the former appears wholly impracticable, and has perhaps stumbled into d from b; Geldner conjectures instead oz. Ppp. is defaced, and gives no help. The comm. reads laksmam, and explains lalâmyam as accus. sing. masc. : lalame bhavar: tila-; kasthanagatam ; to yâni in c he supplies cânâni making c a separate sentence and supplying bhavantu J. It would also be possible to make the cesura after prajâyaâi, and read nâcayâmasi (so R.). In our edition, dele the accent-mark under (- of ¹âni in c.

2. Savitar has driven out the trouble (? âraṅi) in her feet; out have Varuṇa, Mitra, Aryaman [driven] [that] in her hands; out hath Anumati, bestowing (7) upon us; the gods have driven this woman forward unto good fortune. All the mss. give in a szvisak, which SPP. very properly retains, though the comm. and Ppp. have saz (see my Skt. Gr.e, § 151 a) ; 'sâvigak (p. as-) would be an improve- ¹ ment, and may be understood. For c, d, Ppp. has yad âdityâmavwatr rar ana pr pasuvâ Ś savitâ sâubkagâya. The comm. gives two etymological guesses at araniṇz (which is his reading, instead of -zim), both worthless, and describes raranâ as accented on the final. The separation of this verse from the others in Ppp. indicates that it probably has nothing to do with marks." It is rather unusual for the Anukr. to take notice of d the occurrence of a zâ5tubk pada in a jagatr verse. ld, no less than c, is (4517254, pronounce âzvâsaviuṇ. J

3. Whatever in thy self, in thy body, is frightful, or what in hair or in mien — all that do we smite away with [our] words; let god Savitar advance (sd) thee.

⁴ God Savitar' or ' the heavenly impeller,' everywhere equivalent. Ppp. begins yar } 17 "tman tanvâ ghoram, and has for c, 4 far te vidvan upabâadhayesark pra tvâ suvâ savita sanbhagâya. The metrical description of the verse (11 + II : Io + 10 = 42) by the Anukr. is unusual and questionable.

4. The antelope-footed, the bull-toothed, the kine-repelling, the outblowing, the licked-out, the pallid — these we make disappear from us.

Designations either of the unlucky signs or of the women marked with them — probably the former. The comm. prefers the latter, except for the two last, which he blunderingly takes from the stems -74ya and -mya, and makes them qualify zṅ ma : : understood. He explains gogedha (p. goosedhâ) as "going like a cow," and viltgha : : as a lock on the edge of the forehead, licked as it were the wrong way "— or what is ¹ called a "cowlick" Skt. .7kapaksa ]. Both editions give at the beginning r4yag-, instead of the true reading gyap-, which the comm. (with three of SPP's mss.) has;

the mss. bungle all the occurrences of this word. In part of our edition the 7 is broken off from vṅsadaitr. v

docs.title: 19. Against enemies
docs.text:
[Brakman.— 3âvaryam. ânugubham : 2. purastâdbr halt i 3. parkyâpaṅkti.] ⁴ The hymn is found also in Pâipp. i. With the two that follow it (and others), it is reckoned by Kâvug. (14. 7) among the sz7gramikani or battle-hymns, or, likewise (ib., g note) to the agarâjira ('unconquered ') gana ; without them, but with vi. 13, it is used , in several of the charms to ward off the effects of portents (104.3 ; 105.1; II3. 3). In

Vâit. (9. 21), vs. 3 appears alone in the câzturmaâsya or seasonal sacrifice, accompanying the release of the two purodâca baskets. 4 Translated : Weber, iv. 413 ; Griffith, i. 23 ; Bloomfeld, r2o, 26z.— Ct. Bergaigne-

; Henry, Manuel, p. 134. : I. Let not the piercers find us, nor let the penetraters find [us]; far from us make the volleys (arauyZ) fly, dispersing, O Indra. Ś Ppp. combines so '5ki- in b. The rendering of gara"ya follows the comm., here and to vs. 3 (carasaṅihati).

2. Dispersing from us let the shafts fly, those that are hurled and that are to be hurled; ye divine arrows of men (manugya-), pierce my Ś enemies. I ¹ : The comm. inserts an and " in c : ⁴divine and human arrows"; this is possible, ¹Ś but opposed by the accent. Ppp. has for c, 4: dev manugya rsayo 'mâtrân no vi

¹ vidâdkaru ; the comm. also reads vidkyatu.

3. Whether one of our own or whether a stranger, fellow or outsider, ¹ whoso assails (a54i-dâs) us—let Rudra with a volley pierce those my Ś enemies.

Ppp's version is somewhat different : yas samâno yo 'samâno 'mitro no jighṅâsati:

rudrag savyâ tan amitrân vi vidâkata. With a, b compare RV. vi. 75. 19 a, b : y6 ec nak soâ ârano yâ; ca nâtyo jghânsati (= SV. ii. 1222 a, b, which combines svâ 'razo);

the latter half of this verse is our 4 c, 4. Two or three of our mss. (P.M. O.p.m.) fol-

low RV. in omitting yâ after sus. Ap.iv. 16.1 has yo nak sapatno yo 'rage marto ee ¹bhidasari devak, with a wholly different second half. The comm. absurdly explains nistyas as nirgataviryo nikrstabalak gatruk.

i 4. Whatever rival (sapâtna), whatever non-rival, and whatever hater of shall curse us, him let all the gods damage (âk77v); incantation (5râhman) eo is my inner defense.

Ppp. has as first half-verse sabandhug ca ¹sabandhug ca yo na inârâ bkidâsati. i : The second half-verse is found, without variant, in RV. (and SV. : see under vs. 3). a The comm. explains sepatna well as jâatirâpak gatruk. SPP. follows the very bad : example of a part of his mss. by reading Jvâgan ck- (instead of -27 or -a7) in b ef. 1.33.2, if. 4.6, and see Prat. ii. to, 17, and especially r1.— The gada-text reads âvisân].

docs.title: 20. Against enemies and their weapons
docs.text:
LArharvan.— sâumyam. ânustubham : I. tregtubh.];

The first three verses are found in Paâipp. xix., and vs. 4 in ii. : see below. For the use of the hymn by Kâug. with rg and 21, see under 19. And vs. 1 is used alone (so the comm.) in the parvan-sacrifices (Kâug. 2. 39), on viewing the cooked oblation. ¹

Translated : Weber, iv. 413 ; Griffith, i. 24.

1. Let there be the ââârasyi, O god Soma; at this sacrifice, O Maruts, ( be gracious to us ; let not a portent find us, nor an imprecation ; let not i the wrong that is hateful find us.

The first pada is rendered on the assumption that the sâmar of this name, as described in PB. xv. 3.7, is intended ; it might be used of the person intended to be ¹ benefited : ‘let him be one not getting into a split (i.e. hole, or difficulty) ': this is the sense distinctly taught in PB. ; the comm. says na kadâcid api svastrisamzpanm g7aâ- : pnotu (madtyak catruk) ¹ The verse occurs in TB. (iii. 7. 5²2 : and repeated without change in Ap. ii. 20. 6), with Śkavata in a, mrâatâ (without the anomalous accent) in b, l and vzjâna in d. Ppp. begins with aâârasur bk-, adds ayam after soma in a, and has in d the easier reading p77 "pad duckunâ for vidad vyjinâ. The second halfverse I occurs again as v. 3.6 c, d. Though connected with vss, 2, 3 in Pâipp. also, this verse does not appear to have anything originally to do with them.

2. What missile (sé7ya) weapon of the malignant (aghâyâ) shall go up today, do ye, Mitra-and-Varuṇa, keep that off from us. ² The first half-verse in Ppp. is yo "dya sâinyo vadho jighâsark nam upâyarr which is nearly our vi. 99. 2 a, bh. The half-verse occurs also in PB. (i. 3.3 a, b) and ACS. : (v. 3.22 a, b), both of which have sâumyas ; PB. elides yo "âya ; ACS. gives at the end -rati. Aghâyanâm would be the proper accent (and this the comm. has), unless { the word were understood as feminine.

3. Both what [is] from here and what from yonder — keep off, O Varuna; the deadly weapon ; extend great protection (rârman) ; keep very far off the deadly weapon.

The pada text marks the pada-division in the first half-verse before instead of after the second yâz. Ppp. reads in b yâvayak. The second half-verse is found again at the end of the next hymn — which is perhaps an additional indication that this hymn properly ends here. The Anukr. ignores the metrical irregularity of the verse (9 + 8: 7 + 8 = 32). [Read in a 4 yâd, and in c yacka nak. ]

4. Verily a great ruler (câsâ) art thou, overpowerer of enemies, unsubdued, whose companion (sâk47) is not slain, is not scathed (jy) at any time.

This verse is the first in RV. x. 152, of which the remaining verses constitute the next hymn here ; in Ppp. it occurs with them in ii., far separated from the matter which in our text precedes it. RV. and Ppp. both read for b amitrakhâde ââtkutak ; and RV. accents in d jtyare kâââ. The comm. paraphrases (âsâs by (âsake niyantâ; he takes jiyâre as from root ji, which is of course equally possible.

docs.title: 21. Against enemies
docs.text:
i [Atharvan.— Findram. &nugtubkam.]

- As just pointed out (under 20. 4), this hymn and the last verse of the preceding make one hymn in RV. (x. 152) and in Pâipp. (ii.) ; the latter has a different verse-order (3, 2, I, 4), but no various readings. For other correspondences, see under the several verses. For the ritual use of the hymn with the two preceding, see under 19;

it is further reckoned (Kâug. 16. 8, note) to the abkaya (' free from fear or danger") ; gana. It is the first hymn applied (with vii. 55) in the svastyayana or ' for well-being '

ceremonies (3o. ), and is, according to the comm., referred to as such in 25. 36. Verse 2 is also used, with others, by Vait. (29. 5), in the agnicayana or building of the fire-altar. el Translated : Weber, iv. 414 ; Griffith, i. 25.

I. Giver of well-being, lord of the people (v5), Vrtra-slayer, remover of scorners, controlling, let the bull Indra go before us, soma-drinker, eo producing fearlessness. : i The comm. renders vimydhâs by viesena mardhayâta catrânâm, although he explains mFdhas in vss. 2, 3 by saṅzgrâmân ; the word is plainly a possessive com-

pound accent! no genitive J, expressing in form of epithet the action of 2 a and 3 a. ie RV. reads in a viâs pâtis. The verse occurs further in TB. (iii.7. 114) and TA. (x.I.9);

both have wâdâs, and, in 4, svastidâs for somapâs.

2. Smite away, O Indra, our scorners (mydk); put (yam) down them en that fight (p7za7y) [us]; make go to lowest darkness whoso vexes us. ¹ RV. reverses the order of c and d, and reads ââkaram ; and with it agree precisely 46 SV. (ii. 1218) and VS. (viii. 44 a et al.); while TS. (i. 6. 124) and MS. (iv. 12. 3) have e Ś for c adkaspadân: tâm wR kyâhi. Ct. MGS. ii. 15.6 h and p. 155.

3. Smite away the demon, away the scorners ; break apart Vrtra's g (two) jaws ; away, O Indra, Vrtra-slayer, the fury of the vexing enemy.

RV. and SV. (ii. 217) have the same text; TS. (i. 6. 125) reads câzrân for râksas, ¹ nuda for jaki, and bhamits for vrtrakhan. ee 4. Off, O Indra, the mind of the hater, off the deadly weapon of him that Hh would scathe; extend great protection ; keep very far off the deadly weapon. i RV. reads manyâs for makât in c, and yavayâ for yâu- in d. TS. (iii. 5.8, only a, b) Ś supplies in the first half-verse the missing verb, jak, putting it in place of vaâṅârm. i i Unless we resolve gârma into three syllables, the anustubh is defective by a syllable.

1Ad] nak after yacha ?

The 5 hymns of this anuvâka 4. ] again have zo verses, the norm : see at the coner clusion of the preceding anuvâka (after hymn 16).

docs.title: 22. Against yellowness (jaundice)
docs.text:
[Brakman,— sâuryam uta mantroktakarimadevatyam. Enugtubkam.] ; Found in Pâipp. i. Used by Kâug. (26. 14) in a remedial rite (against heart disease and jaundice [kâmala, Keg. ; kâmila, the comm.]).

Translated : Weber, iv. 415; A. Kuhn, KZ. xiii. 113 ; Griffith, i.26 ; Bloomfâeld, 7, 263. — Cf. also Zimmer, p. 388 ; Bloomfield, AIP. xii. 437; Bergaigne-Henry, Manuel, (f P- I34. Kuhn adduces analogous old Germanic charms. i

I. Let them (both) go up toward the sun, thy heart-burn (-gyozâ) and yellowness ; with the color of the red bull, with that we enclose (parî-âkâ) thee.

Ppp. reads in a udetam ; its c is yo rohitasya gor varnas, which construes better with d. The abbreviated writing k7âyor- for krdâyot- (see my Skt. Gr. § 232 a and Ś Roth, ZDMG. xlviil. ro2 J) betrays the pada-text into dividing kredyotâṅ (ct. tâd yâm, ( iv. 19.6 ; so even the RV. pada-text has jaratovisam from jaraddvâsam at v.8. 2). SPP. has properly in his text the unabbreviated form Śrââyo-. U'deayatâm in the i AV. Index Verborum is an erratum for #2 ayatâm : the comm. takes the form, doubtless wrongly, as 3d sing. mid. instead of 3d du. active. Kaâug. follows the indication of c, d, and of 3 a, b, by prescribing the use of products of a red cow, hair and skin etc., in the healing rite.

2. With red colors we enclose thee, in order to length of life ; that this man may be free from complaints (-râgas), also may become not yellow.

Ppp. has a different second half-verse : yazkâ tvam arapâ so atho 'hârite bhava. The third pada is iv. 13.4 d (or RV. x. 137. 5 d). The comm. explains rapas as = pâṇa.

3. They that have the red one for divinity, and the kine that are red — form after form, vigor (vâyas) after vigor, with them we enclose thee.

The translation implies the easy emendation in a to 7âkâṇidevatyâs, in accordance; . with the universal use of devazya elsewhere. The (red one' is perhaps the red star (or lunar asterism) Rohiṇi, our Aldebaran. Ppp. reads rokinir dewatyâ, and in b rokipir ura; in â it has vena rea.

4- In the parrots, in the zopaṇâkâs, we put thy yellowness ; likewise in the kâridyavas we deposit thy yellowness.

Not one of our mss. gives at the beginning the true reading câkesu, as found in RV. i. 50. 12 [ and Ppp. J (and TB. iii. 7. 622), but it is presented by the comm., and by three of SPP's authorities. RV. and TB. have me for fz both times, and accent kâriâraveésu. The names are understood by the comm. as those of birds : ropanakaâ = ṅâsthacuka, apparently a kind of parrot, and kâridrava = gopitanaka, apparently a yellow water-wagtail. Ppp. has in bprapanâkâca.;

docs.title: 23. Against leprosy : with a healing herb
docs.text:
[Atharvan (cvetalaksmavinâcanâyâ 'nenâ 'siknim ogadkim astâur).— vânaspatyam.

gnugtubham.)

Found in Pâipp. i., but defaced, so that for the most part comparison is impossible. Also, with vs. 3 of the next hymn, in TB. (ii. 4.42). Used by Kâug. (26. 22-24), in company with the next following hymn, in a remedial rite (against white leprosy, coetakustha, schol. and comm.).,

Translated : Weber, iv. 416 ; Ludwig, p. 506 ; Grill, 19, 77 ; Griffith, i. 27 ; Bloomfield, 16, 266 ; furthermore, vss. I, 2 by Bloomfield, AJP. xi. 32 5.— Cf. Bergaigne-Henry, Manuel p. 135.

I. Night-born art thou, O herb, O dark, black, land ] dusky one; : O colorer (rajant), do thou color this leprous spot and what is pale ( palitâ).

According to the comm., the herb addressed is the kZaridrâa (Curcuma longa).

R. writes : " The rajant is known to the lexicographers, and has later as principal name parpafi [an Oldenlandia dyeing red, OB.], Madana 46. 47, Dhanvantari (ms.) i. 27. In

Bhâvapr. i. 194 (where, according to my old and good ms., raṅjant is to be read instead,

! of -a7), it is noted that this remedy is fragrant, and comes out of the north. It has a i dark aspect. The species not to be determined, because the later identifications are 35-4 entirely untrustworthy." See Dhanvantari, Ananda-âgrama ed., p. 17.] The causative stem rajaya (the meter calls for 777) is found only here. ee 2. The leprous spot, what is pale, do thou cause to disappear from ¹ hence, the speckled ; let thine own color enter thee; make white things â (cuklâ) fly away. : TB. has na (naj ?) for toâ and agnutâm for viarâm in c, and in d cvetâni for if cuklâni. The comm. gives pythak for pyŚat in b, and has the usual support of a small 4 i minority of SPP's mss.

3. Dusky is thy hiding-place, dusky thy station (âstkâna); dusky art il thou, O herb; make the speckled disappear from hence. : TB. has the easier reading nââ4yanans: in a. The comm. again gives p7tkak in 4; ¹ he holds that the plant here addressed is the indigo (n7r). â 4. Of the bone-born leprous spot, and of the body-born that is in the skin, of that made by the spoiler (Śgi) — by incantation have I made ¹ the white (coverâ) mark disappear. i a ¹ Ppp. has in c âkâgyâ y TB. reads instead Śrtyâya the comm. explains â7ṣi as carr ntpaditz kyrtyâ. Ppp. has at the end anenacarn.

docs.title: 24. Against leprosy
docs.text:
⁴ [Brakman. — âsurioanaspatidevatyam. ânugiubham : a. nicytparkyâpankti.] ; Found in Pâipp. i., but not in connection with the preceding hymn. For the use of : 23 and 24 together by Kaâug., see under hymn 23. : Translated : Weber, iv. 417; Ludwig, p. 509 ; Grill, 19, 77 ; Griffith, i. 28 ; Bloomil Ś field, 16, 268.

I. The eagle (suparpâ) was born first ; of it thou wast the gall ; then

the Asura-woman, conquered by fight (dk), took shape as forest-trees. ¹ Ppp. reads at the end vazaspatik, which is more in accordance with the usual construction of râpaṅ: kr (mid) and the like. Ppp. has also jighânṅsita for yudkha jitâ in c. ( R. suggests the emendation : zed âsun instr.) jghatsitan ru-, 'that, attempted to be eaten by the Asuri, took on vegetable form' : i.e. became a healing plant. The comm.

still regards the indigo as addressed. He coolly explains ji by its opposite, jitavats. g All our mss, have in â the absurd accent câkre (emended in the edition to caṅre); ¹ SPP. reports the same only of two paâa-mss.

2. The Asura-woman first made this remedy for leprous spot, this effacer of leprous spot ; it has made the leprous spot disappear, has made i the skin uniform (sârâga).

Ppp. has again (as in 23.4) anenagat in c ; in d it reads surâpanm.

3. Uniform by name is thy mother ; uniform by name is thy father; ' uniform-making art thou, O herb; Iso] do thou make this uniform.

Found also, as noted above, in TB. (il. 4. 42), which has for c sar 7pa 'sy ogadie. Ppp. reads throughout surâp-. It inserts between this verse and the next: yat tanzjar yad agnijar citra kilâsa jajṅise : tad astu sukytas tanvo yatas toâ pi nayârmass. i

4. The swarthy, uniform-making one [is] brought up off the earth; I do thou accomplish this, we pray; make the forms right again.

All our mss. have at the beginning câmâ, and also very nearly all SPP's ; but the latter very properly admits gya- into his text, it being read by the comm. with a couple of mss. that follow him, and being found in Ppp. also. Ppp. once more has sur 7gpit corrupts b into pr 7hivyâbhyarbhavam, and gives sâdaya at end of c. The phrase idâm 7 s7 is quoted in Prat. iii. 4 and iv. 98, which prescribe the protraction and lingualization, and words of the verse are repeatedly cited in the commentary to other rules. i

docs.title: 25. Against fever (takmân)
docs.text:
IB ky gvaṅgiras.— yaksmanâcanâgnidâivatam. trâigtubham : 2,3. virâggarbkâ;

4. puro nus ubA.] i

Found in Pâipp. i. Used by Kâug. in a remedial rite (26. 25) against fever, in con-; = nection with heating an ax and dipping it in hot water to make a lotion ; and reckoned i (26. 1, note) to the fzkmanâcana gana.

Translated : Weber, iv. 419 ; Grohmann, Jad. Stud. ix. 384-6, 403, 406 ; Ludwig, ¹ p. 511 ; Zimmer, p. 384 and 381 ; Griffith, i. 29 ; Bloomfield, 3, 270; Henry, Journal Asiatigue, 9.x. 512. — Cf. Bergaigne-Henry, Manuel, p. 136. i

I. As Agni, entering, burned the waters, where the maintainers of duty (dkârma-) paid acts of homage, there they declare to be thy highest birth-place ; then do thou, O fever (fakmân), complaisant, avoid us.

The comm. explains pada a in accordance with the ceremonial act founded on its mechanical interpretation ; c [cf. RV. i. 163. 4 d shows that it is part of the heavenly waters that is intended. Saṅrvidvân (occurring nowhere else) he renders fully knowing thy cause, the fire (or Agni)" : the translation takes it as equivalent to the not uncommon saṅvidana. Adakat he quietly turns into a future : ⁴shall burn thee, O d fever"! Ppp. reads adukat instead, and in c combines to 772 "kuk. ] Cf. Grohmann's interpretation, Le., 403, 404.

2. If thou art flame (arcâs) or if heat (oc), or if thy-birth-place seeks the shavings (?), krââu by name art thou, O god of the yellow one; then do thou, O fever, complaisant, avoid us.

The pada-reading cakalyacest in b is assured by Prat. iii. 52, but the meaning is extremely obscure. Ppp. has the better reading câkalyesu among the shavings"; 4 Jjanitram rather requires a locative. The comm. guesses it as loc. of ¢zkalyes, from d cakalya explained as a "heap of shavings," and root is ' seek," and so an epithet of fre; ² BR. conjecture following the shaving, i.e. glimmering." Ppp. reads in a dkṅmas for ; : ocis. The name at the beginning of c is of quite uncertain form ; the ms. readings are :. hrâgu, hrâdru, krugu, kndu, rugu, krudbhu, rug, raghu krâghu ] ; SPP. adopts i in his text the same form as we, and, it is to be hoped, on the authority of his oral { reciters, which in such a case must be better than mss. ; Ppp. has (in both verses)

hugu, which is a word occurring also elsewhere, and meaning "ram" ; the comm. reads

Fâdhu, explaining it as = rohaka or purusacarire utpâdaka ' producing in the human body.' i Henry, Journal Asiatique, 9. X. 513, suggests that the problematic word may be connected with the Assyrian âuragu and the Hebrew kar 7g, and so go back to a proto-

Semitic ¥karâgu, 'gold' J. Halévy, however, Le., 9. xi. 320 ff., suggests that it may be ⁴ rather a Sanskritization of yMepts, 'greenish-yellow,' and compares the relations of . vaâidnrya, Prakrit velurya (veruliya) Grpt"hov. Cf. further, Barth, Reuue de I'kistoire 4 des religions, xxxix. 26. : 3. If heating (oṅâ) or if scorching (abkigokâ), or if thou art son of king Varuna, krââu by name etc. etc. : : Ppp. has for b the more sensible version ruârasya prâpṇoe yadi vârupoe (va 'runo?) si.

4. Homage to the cold fever, homage I pay to the fierce (77râ) heat er (cocis) ; to the one that befalls on every other day, on both days, to the ¹ third-day fever be homage.

i Ppp. reads in b durâya ;ruwâ vaya te, and in c ubkhayebhyag ca katas. The com- Ś pound wâkayadyus is noticed in Prat. iv. 21. [As for rhythmical fevers — tertian, quartan, etc., see Grohmann, le., 387, 388.

docs.title: 26. For protection from the wrath of the gods
docs.text:
[Brahkman.—indrâdibakudevatyam. gâyatram: a. 3-p. Sâmnî trigtubk ; 4. pâdanicyt ; (2, 4. ekâvasâna)].

Found in Paâipp. xix., but vss. 3-4 elsewhere than r—2. The hymn appears to be 7 called (so schol. and the comm.) apanodanâni ' thrusters away ' in Kâug. (14.14), and quoted and used as such in 25. 22 and (with iv. 33) in 42. 22; it is further applied ee (with 27 and vi. 3, 76) at the beginning of the svastyayana rites, on going to bed and fd getting up again (50. 4), and (with i. r3 and other hymns) in the rite of entrance on

Vedic study (139.8). gr Translated : Weber, iv. 420 ; Griffith, i. 31. Ś I. Far be that from us— may [your] missile (kerr) be, O gods; far the bolt (âgman) which ye hurl.

The last pâda is identical with RV. i. 172. 2 c ; the other two pâdas (for which Ppp.
