has no variants) sound in part like a misunderstood echo of the RV. text : are sâ vak i fo sudâanave mâruta rRjart (âruk. For c Ppp. has âre mantâm (or martam.; for maruiam ?) agastih: The comm. foolishly supplies an ⁴ O our enemies" in cj; agmâ he l Ś explains as yantrâdivinirmuktah pasânak. The Anukr. ignores the defectiveness of b. 4 2. Be yon Rati (liberality ') a companion (sâkki) for us ; a companion

[be] Indra, Bhaga, Savitar of wondrous favors.

Râtt seems to be made a personification here, as in iii. 8.2 and vii. 17. 4 below; the f comm. makes it equal to Mitra or Sârya. Ppp. has a very different text : sekke "va no râtir astu sakhe 'nâras sakhâ savitâ : sakhâ bhagas satyadṅarmâ ne stu ; which is better as regards both sense and meter. The fripada of the Anukr. is probably a misreading for dvipadâ ; the mss. agree with it in using no avasâna-sign in the verse, and ; SPP. very properly follows them ; the pada-mss. mark a cesura after râtik. The comm. makes cizrarâadhâs = bakuvidhan dhanan: yasya. d

3. May ye, issue (nâpar) of the height, sun-skinned Maruts, yield us breadthful protection.

The mss. all read at the end sagrâthâs, and SPP. retains it in his text; the comm. has ) saprathas, in accordance with our emendation. Cf. Lanman, Noun-Inflection, p. 560. ] The comm. further has yacchâta in c.

4. Do ye advance [us], be gracious ; be thou gracious to our selves (tanit), show kindness (mâyas) to our offspring (10kd).

Ppp. fills up the deficiency of a, reading su myâarâ susṅdarâa myâa no aghâbkyak ‘ stokâya tanve da (perhaps defective at the end). The mss., supported by the Anukr., make no division of the verse before âyas, and SPP. follows them ; the meter, how- : ever, is plainly gâyarri. The name given by the Anukr. is not used by it elsewhere; it doubtless signifies, as in the VS. Anukr., 7 + 7 + 7 = 21 syllables, the resolution -bhi-as being refused in b and c.

docs.title: 27. Against various evils
docs.text:
¹ [Atharoan (svastyayanakâmaṅ).— cândramasam ute ndrâṇidâivatan. ânugtubham: ¹ I. patkyâpaṅâti.]

Found in Pâipp. xix. For the use of the hymn with its predecessor by Kâug., see under 26; it is also reckoned to the svastyayana gaga (25.36, note) ; and vs. 4 appears by itself near the beginning of the svastyayana ceremonies, in the same rite as hymns 26 and 237. 4

Translated : Weber, iv. 421 ; Ludwig, p. 517; Griffith, i.32.— Griffith says the sloughs are to make the travellers invisible to highway robbers, and cites an old English analogue.

1. Yonder on the further shore are she-adders, thrice seven, out of d their sloughs (jarâynz) ; with the sloughs of them do we wrap up (427 uyâ) the (two) eyes of the malignant waylayer.

Jarâyn in the sense cast-off skin of a snake appears to be quotable only here; the comm. regards the word as so applied by a figure : jarâynwat carirasya vestakâas tvacak. Ppp. reads ims pare in a, and jarjarâyuwvak in b; the comm. has instead nirjarâ iva, explaining as jarârakhita deva iva.

2. Let the cutting one (77) go asunder, she who bears as it were a club (pânâka) ; asunder [go] the mind of her that returns to life (punarbk7 ) ; unsuccessful [are] the malignant ones.

Ppp. has no variants to cast light on this very obscure verse ; it adds at the end. ape ¹tas paripanthino "po 'ghâyur argatu. The comm. reads punarbhavâ in c; he : supplies « the army (senâ) of our enemies" as the missing noun in the verse, and explains the epithet as ⁴ reassembling after dispersal." He paraphrases krntart with . chindati. |SPP's pada-reading is punaṅebhṅvâk, against Index Verborum, p. 184 ¹ (corrected p. 383), and against Sṅz. Gr. § 352 a, which should be corrected by p. 4171 i of Lanman's Noun-Inflection.

3. The many have not been able together; the few have not ventured on [it]; like the sprouts (? ââga) of a bambob (veṇ7) round about, unsucbe cessful [are] the malignant ones. 4 The first half-verse in Ppp. is defaced, but apparently its text agreed with ours, except that at the end stands abhi Śhrsnuvan. As the second half is wanting, these two pâdas probably form one verse with the two reported above, under vs. 2. The 5 comm. reads Jââycus at end of b, and has uâgâ iva parâtas in c, explaining nâga ety- ; mologically as = ¢zk4â. The comment to Prat. iii. 13 quotes Jââṅ=ysus, and that to

ii. 38 gives aâgas among its examples ; neither aâga nor uâga appears to be quotable from elsewhere. el 4. Go forward, ye (two) feet; kick (spur) forward ; carry to the houses of the bestower (27); let Indrâṇt go first, unscathed, unrobbed, in front. ² Ppp. has gr kam and vakantu (yet pâadââr) in b, and, for 4, jhitvâ muktvâ patṅaâ. Ś i The comm. reads git in â; he ingeniously quotes from TS. (ii. 2. 87) Indragi is deity of the army" in explanation of her introduction here. Ct. Bergaigne, Reâgion 4 Vedigue, iii. 155 1.

docs.title: 28. Against sorcerers and witches
docs.text:
[Câtana. — svastyayanam. Śnugtutham : 3. virG(pathyâkyhati ; 4. pathyâpaṅKti.] 1 The hymn is not found in Pâipp. Though not mentioned as one of the câtanâni by the text of Kâug., it is added to them by the schol. (8. 25, note). It is once used by itself in a witchcraft ceremony (âbkicârika) for the relief of one frightened, accoma panying the tying on of an amulet (26. 26).

Translated : Weber, iv. 423 ; Griffith, i. 33.

I. Hither hath come forth god Agni, demon-slayer, disease-expeller, Ś burning away deceivers, sorcerers, kizidâns. : In our text, #94 is a misprint for #pa (an accent-sign slipped out of place to the ¹ left). The comment on Prat. iv. 3 quotes the first three words as exemplifying the dis- ¹ ( connection of prefixes from a verb.

2. Burn against the sorcerers, against the kimidâns, O god; burn up the sorceresses that meet thee, O black tracked one.

In c the comm., with two or three of SPP's authorities that follow him, reads ( : Śrsuavartmane (treating it as a vocative). ¹ 3. She that hath cursed with cursing, that hath taken malignity as ¹ her root (?mâ7a), that hath seized on [our] young to take its sap— let her eat [her own] offspring..

The verse is repeated below as iv. 17.3, and has there a parallel in Ppp. The comm. first takes mâram as for mâlam (as rendered above), but adds an alternative explanation as mârchâkaram, adjective to agham ; he has âdade in place of -de. i Jârâm is metrically an intrusion, but completes the sense. i

4. Let the sorceress eat [her own] son, sister, and daughter ? napt); then let the horrid-haired sorceresses mutually destroy (vi-han) one another ; let the hags (ary) be shattered asunder.

The comm. explains naptr as napiri or pautrasya (putrasya g) apatyar âpa sartari. He reads yaruâkânt (for -nzs) in a, and afṅa in c.

The 7 hymns of this anuvâka 1 5. ] have 28 verses, as determined by the quoted ¹ Anukr. : paṅcame stax. i

docs.title: 29. For a chief's success : with an amulet
docs.text:
[Vasistha.— sadycam. abkṅoartamaṇisṅṅtam. ânugiubham.] i

Found (except vs. 4) in Pâipp. i., and (with the same exception, in RV., chiefly x. 174 l : namely, AV. verses 1, 2, 3, 6 correspond respectively with RV. verses I, 2, 3, 5. See Oldenberg, Die Hymnen des RV., i. 243 J. Kâug. uses the hymn in the ceremony of restoration of a king, with preparing and binding on an amulet made of the rim of a chariot-wheel (16. 29 : the comm. says, vss. 1-4); the last two verses are specifically prescribed for the binding on. The comm. quotes the hymn as employed by the Nakṣatra Kalpa (19) in a mahâcânti called mâhendyt.

Translated : Weber, iv. 423 ; Griffith, i. 33.

I. With an over-rolling amulet (maṇâ), wherewith Indra increasedtherewith, O Brahmaṇaspati, make us increase unto royalty (:âs(râ).

Abki7, literally ' on to," so as to overwhelm. Our version spoils the consistency of the verse by reading -vâv7 dhe and varâkaya in b and dâ for RV. (x. 174.1) -vâor te and vartaya, which Ppp. also gives (Ppp. vartayak). Ppp. further has iam for asman in c. RV. reads kavâ5a for maṇânâ in a. The long 7 of abktvarta (p. abkicv-) is noted by Prat. iii. ra.

2. Rolling over our rivals, over them that are niggards to us, do thou trample on him who fights— on whoever abuses (durasy-) us.

RV. (x. 174. 2) has in d asyâti ; Ppp., by a not infrequent blunder, reads 2rasyatu. Pâda a lacks a syllable, unless we resolve Śarnân into three syllables.

3. Thee hath god Savitar, hath Soma made to increase, thee have all existences (bhṅrâ) [made to increase], that thou mayest be over-rolling.

The connection is again spoiled in our text by the substitution of awvyâhat in b for . avrvytar (which is read by RV. x. 174.3) ; with the former it is impossible to render the prefix abhi. This time Ppp. gives abkṅb ky (at instead, doubtless a mere cormption.

4. The over-rolling, overcoming, rival-destroying amulet be bound upon me unto royalty, unto the perishing (parâbhṅi) of rivals.

The verse is wanting in both RV. and Ppp. Its excision, with the following verse

¹ (which, however, Ppp. has), would leave the hymn of normal length, and composed of : : four out of the five verses of RV. x. 174], of the fourth of which the excision is called . for J. (i 5. Up hath gone yon sun, up this spell (vâzas) of mine, that I may be slayer of foes, without rivals, rival-slayer.

RV. x. I59. I a, b is to be compared (b reading ââ ayâm mamakâ bhâgak) ; Ppp.

appears to mix the versions of b, giving, ungrammatically, gyam with vacas. Ct. also

MP. i. x6. I.

6. A rival-destroying bull, conquering royalty, overpowering— that I : may bear rule over these heroes and the people (jâna). ‘ RV. (i. 174. 5) has instead of a our 5 d (found also as x. 6. 30 c, and xix. 46.7 b);

in c it reads bhutanam. Ct. MP. i.16. 5. ]

docs.title: 30. For protection: to all the gods
docs.text:
[Atharvan (TyuskEmak).— vâicvadevam. trâigubham : 3. ¢âkvaragarbhâ virâgjagatr.] 4 Found in Pâipp. i., but damaged and only in part legible. The hymn belongs, Hl according to the comm., to the âyzgya (' for length of life') gaza, although not found i among those mentioned (Kâug. 54. II, note) as composing that gaza; it is used in ceremonies for long life by 52.18 and 59. 1 ; also, with i.g and other hymns, in the G4 reception of a Vedic student (55.17), and in dismissal from Vedic study (139. I5). ¹ And vss. 3, 4 appear in Vaâit. (4. 4, r5) in connection with different parts of the garvan- ¹ y sacrifices. The comm. further quotes it from Naks. Kalpa 17 and 18 in two maṅâcânti 1 rites, styled zirâvarr and vââcvadevi, and from Paricista 5.4, in the puṣpavhiseka ceremony. ¹ Translated : Weber, iv. 424 ; Ludwig, p. 430 ; Griffith, i. 34. : I. O all ye gods, ye Vasus, protect this man; likewise ye Adityas, watch ye over him ; him let not one related (sânâbki) nor one unrelated

— him let not any deadly weapon of men (pââruseya) reach.

Ppp. has in b the false form jâgrata. The comm. paraphrases -aâ547 in c by garbhâgcaya. For the syntax, cf. Caland, KZ. xxxiv. 456.

2. Whoso of you, O gods, are fathers and who sons, do ye, accordant 4 (sâcetas), hear this utterance of mine ; to you all I commit this man; Ee happily unto old age shall ye carry him.

Ppp. has at the end nayâtha. The comm. reads in b #4âaz. : 3. Ye, O gods, that are in the heaven, that are on earth, that are in the atmosphere, in the herbs, in the cattle, within the waters — do ye make old age the length of life for this man; let him avoid the hundred other deaths.

The intrusion of pacâsu and apsâ in b spoils the meter or we may read y ntâriksa i âsadṅtso apsâ antâk ] , Ppp., omitting pacusu and antâr, makes it good. The Anukr. i ¹ requires us to scan the pada as of r4 syllables. Prat. ii. ror notes the lingualization in ¹ it forms of as after 7âvi, and the comment cites this passage (a) as example. The comm.

has in 6 v7nakta, and renders it as causative. [As to ror deaths, see Zimmer, p. 400.

4. Whose are the fore-offerings and whose the after-offerings ; the gods that share the oblation and that eat what is not made oblation of; you among whom the five directions are shared out — you do I make sitters at the session (sartrâ-) of this man. I

Ppp. reads in â 777 no 'smâi satrasadhak k-. The comm. explains akutâdas as balikaranâdidevâs ; in sattra he sees nothing more than simple sadzṅna. Both editions read satra-, in accordance with universal manuscript usage.

docs.title: 31. To the divine guardians of the quarters
docs.text:
[Brakman. — &;âpâliyam, vâstospatyam. &nugtubham : 3. virâttrigubh;

Ś. parânugtuptrigubh.]

Found in Pâipp. i. The hymn is called in Kâug. (38. 11) âgâpâlyarm, and is also reckoned by the schol. (8. 23, note) to the vâsiogpartyâni or vastu gana. It is used with xii. r in the ceremony (38. 16) for establishing a house, and again, except vs. 3, as dr kapnâni 'establishers' in a like rite (38. 11) ; it appears in one of the szwa-sacrifices. (64. r) with an offering of four dishes (catujgarâva), and in the portent ceremony (127. 6) against obscuration of the « Seven Sages" (the Dipper, or Charles's Wain) by a comet. Verse 2 (32. 27, note ; but the comm. says instead vs. r, quoting its pratika) is reckoned among the aṅkoliṅgâas, and applied in rites for healing, security, long life, etc.; and vs. 4 (50. rr) in one for good fortune in the night. In Vâit (36. 20) the hymn (as #âpaliya) accompanies in the agvamedka the turning loose of the sacrificial horse. And the comm. quotes it as used in Naks. Kalpa 14 in the aâŚhuta makâ;ânti.

Translated : Weber, iv. 425 ; Ludwig, p. 372; Griffith, i. 35. 4

I. To the four immortal region-guardians of the regions (ââ), to the overseers of existence (64714), would we now pay worship (v7) with oblation.

The verse occurs also, in TB. (ii. 5. 33) and ACS. (ii. ro. 18) : in the latter, without variants ; TB. inserts va after 4ânam in a. The comm. paraphrases aâs by prâzyadidigas, which is plainly its meaning here.

2. Ye, O gods, who are the four region-guardians of the regions — do ye release us from the fetters (pea) of perdition (z4-rti), from every distress (âṅkas).

The comm. reads szana for sthana in b. The Anukr. does not note b as metrically deficient, doubtless making the harsh resolution ca-tu--re.

3. Unlamed I sacrifice to thee with oblation ; unmaimed I make oblation to thee with ghee ; the god that is fourth region-guardian of the regions, he shall bring hither to us welfare (subkṅrâ).

At the beginning, 4râmas is read by half the mss. (including our E.I. 0. Op. K.Kp.) and by the comm. ; SPP. gives âsr- in his text, as we in ours. Aglnas in b in our edition is an erratum for âclopas. Ppp. has for a, b agronas te kavisâ vidhema macramas te ghrt-; the comm. also reads agronas. Ppp. gives turyas in e : the word perhaps means simply ' [any] one of the four.' The Anukr. appears not to sanction the resolutions to ru-2 which would fill out a and b. The pada-mss. mark the division between c and d after devas, as the sense, but not the meter, demands.

4. Well-being (svastt) be to our mother and father, well-being to kine, f to creatures (jâ4gat), to men (pâruga); all welfare [and] beneficence : ( suviddâtra) be ours ; long may we see the sun. 5 For jagare in b Ppp. has ara, with manifest advantage to both meter and sense;

and it reads pârusebhyas (with our H.s.m.), and in 4 ârceva. Many of the saṅkiramss. (including our H.K.) give zo after pit il a. The comm. gives three different interpretations (taking it always, however, from wid and not from JZ) for the ambigu-

; ous suvidâtra. The Anukr. appears to read ne 'stu in c, and jṅâg and sâri-am in d a, rather, jyâg and sâryarm, so as to make 11 +11: II + 8? ]. As to jagat, see Zimmer, p. ISO. ]

docs.title: 32. Cosmogonic
docs.text:
[Brakman.— dyâvâprthiviyam. ânugubham : z. kakummaṇr.]

Found in Paipp. i., next after our hymn 31. Used by Kâug. in a women's rite

(34. 1), against barrenness, and again (59. 3) in a ceremony for prosperity, to heaven ¹ and earth ; and the first verse (so the comm.) further (6. 17), as alternate to x. 5.23, f with conducting water into the joined hands of the sacrificer's wife, in the parvan- 3 sacrifices.

' Translated : Weber, iv. 426 ; Ludwig, p. 533 ; Griffith, i. 36. ¹ : I. Now, ye people, take knowledge; he will speak a great mystery ¹ ( brâkhman) ; that is not on earth nor in the sky whereby the plants breathe. ¹ : With a, b is to be compared the very similar line xx. 127. 1 a, b: i242 jana wpa i (ruta arâcaṅsâ stavigyare ; which makes it probable that the ungrammatical vidâtha means. vidarta or vedatha (accent is unmotived), and suggests also vaâigyate, passive;

the former seems confounded with the noun widârka, of which vidâthe, or, as Ppp. ¹ reads, vidârham, would make fairly good sense : will now be spoken at (or to) the i council' Ppp. reads yatas for yena in d. For prâṇânti, see Prat. iv. 57. ¹ 2. In the atmosphere is the station of them, as of those sitting 1 wearied ; the station of this that exists (54714) : that the pious know — or they do not.

cOf them ' (2sâm, fem.) in a the comm. explains to mean of the plants," and then, ¹ alternatively, of the waters"; doubtless the latter is correct, the waters being that fe “whereby the plants live" (1 4). Ppp. reads in a â4ntariksam, which means virtually i the same as our text: the reservoir of the waters is the atmosphere or is in it (not in ¹ heaven nor earth, I c). The analogy of vii. 95. 2 suggests gâvâm as wanting at the i Ś beginning of b: the waters are ordinarily as quiet as cows that lie resting : a comparison from the usual Vedic source. Weber suggested that sthâma be read twice ; and this R. favors. The Anukr. ignores the deficiency in the pada. For d, Ppp. has vidus ¹ kd bhesatodanak. Ś . 3. What the (two) quaking firmaments (6dasz)— and the earth— Ś fashioned out, that at present is always wet, like the streams of the ocean. Ś

In b the translation implies emendation to âzakṣatârn, as favored by the Ppp. reading nara-caksatam ; there remains the anomaly of letting the verb agree with rââasr (Ppp. has rodkhasr) ; perhaps we ought to read 347mes ‘out of the earth." The comm., with a disregard of the accent which is habitual with him, takes rââzsr and its epithet i as vocatives, and then supplies âyâus, vocative JAOS. xi. 66, in b to help make a dual subject for the verb! For d Ppp. has vidurassevavartasi. IForc, cf. CB. vi. 6.33. ] I

4. The one hath covered all ; this rests upon the other ; both to the heaven and to the all-possessing earth have I paid homage.

The first pada is translated according to the Ppp. version : wâvam anya "bhi vwavâra ; which is quite satisfactory ; Weber had suggested aâk) "vâ "ra. The gadareading is abhṅvâra, and the word is quoted under Prat. iii. 12 as an example of a compound showing protraction of the final vowel of the first member. TB. (iii. 7.103) and Ap. (ix. 4. 2) have the verse, and both have anyâ 'thṅvâvyâhâ. The comm. gives i abhtvâras, and explains it in three ways, as abkhito varapar châdananm, as abhivrtarn, d and as abhitah sambhajanayuktam. For b, Ppp. has vigvam anyasyâm adki gratarn. For vi vâvedase in c (Ppp. vigvavedhase; TB. Ap. vivâkarmaṇe) the comm. also gives two interpretations, from wid ' acquire ' and from vid 'know.'

docs.title: 33. To the waters : for blessings
docs.text:
[Cartâti.— cândramasam âpyam uta. trâi|ubhan.] ¹

Found in Pâipp. i, and also in TS. (v. 6.1), MS. (ii. 13.1), and the Mantrapâtha 11.2. 2—5 (Winternitz in Denksck. d. Wiener Akad. x1.44). [See also MGS. i. 2. II and p. 158.) Reckoned by Kâug. to the agârz szktâni ' hymns of the waters ' (1 21. I, and g 7. 14, note), also to both the cânti ganas (9. I, 4) ; appears further, with several other hymns, in a rite for good-fortune (41.14) ; and in the godâna ceremony to accompany bathing after the shaving (54.5), also in the feet-washing of a guest (90.9), against the portent of the appearance of water in a waterless place (121. 1), and against that of the causeless breaking of water-jars etc. (136. 8). And the comm. quotes it as employed by Paricista v. 2 in the puspathiscka rite..

Translated : Weber, iv. 428 ; Winternitz, Hochzeitsrituell, Wiener Denkschr. Śl. 44; Griffith, i. 37.

I. Of golden color, clean (gc cz), purifying, in whom [was] born Savitar, in whom Agni ; who, of beauteous color, assumed Agni as embryo — let those waters be weal, pleasant to us. In c, for dadkire, better, 'conceived'?] TS. and MS. read in b jâṅâṅ kacyâpo yâsv tndyah ; and Ppp. agrees with them ; MP. has agnt} instead of idrak. In c TS. MS. give vârṅpas for suvarpâs; and TS. omits y4s, and hence has dadhire (unaccented) ; MS. puts yâs after agnâm. MP. offers zz for nas in 4d. [As to svi = kacyapa, cf. Bloomfield, AIP. xvii. 403.

2. In the midst of whom goes king Varuṇa, looking down at the truth-and-falsehood of men ; who, of beauteous color, etc. etc.

The first half-verse is found also in RV. (vil. 49. 3 a, b), without difference of reading ; MP. agrees through the whole verse except ind, fe for nas J; TS. MS. have a wholly different c. The comment to Prat. ii. v1 gives awapagyaṅ janânṅm: as example of the general requirement that final # be assimilated to a following initial palatal, and ; half or more of our mss. so read ; but SPP., as elsewhere, gives -a7 j- lef. note to : g 3. They of whom the gods in heaven make [their] draught (54ak5â); ' they that come to be abundantly in the atmosphere ; who, of beauteous ¹ color, etc. etc.

Again TS. MS. have a different c (yâṅ prthivim pâyaso 'nâânti cukrâk). Our O.

has at end of c vâ7p%) (as TS. MS. in r c). MP. substitutes nfwistâs for bhavanti in b. The comm. renders Śhaksâm by upathogyam.

4. With propitious eye behold me, O waters; with propitious body touch my skin ; they that are ghee-dripping, clean, purifying — let those ⁴ waters be weal, pleasant to us.

The first half-verse appears again below as xvi. r. 12. It alone is found in TS. and : ¹ MS. ; but our c is RV. vii. 49. 3 c, and the two other texts have it after our 2 a, b gr all reading madhu- for ghyta- J. MP. reads civéna roâ câksusâ pagyantv âpaj, and in b sp7cantu and te. AB. (viii. 6. ro) quotes the whole verse in its TS. and MS. ver- ¹F sion. Our Bp. K. read (eyufas in c ; Ppp. has -(catas. The Anukr. ignores the redundancy of one syllable (or more) in b.

docs.title: 34. A love-spell : with a sweet herb
docs.text:
[Atharvan.— paṅcarcam. madughamaypisâktam. vânaspatyam. ânugubham.]

Verses I, 2, 5 are found in Paâipp. ii., vs. 3 in vi., and vs. 4 in part in viii. It is i used by Kâug. in a ceremeny for superiority in disputation (38. 17) : the ambitious disputant is to come into the assembly from the north-east chewing the sweet plant;

again, twice in the nuptial ceremonies, once with tying a madugha amulet on the finger

(76.8), and once (79. ro) on crushing the amulet at the consummation of the marriage. a The comm. further declares it used at the disputation in the agvamedha sacrifice ; but he quotes no authority for it. All these applications are evidently imposed upon the hymn, not contained in it.

Translated : Weber, iv. 429 ; Grill, 52, 78 ; Griffith, i. 38 ; Bloomfield, 99, 274. —

Ct. Hillebrandt, Veda-ckrestomarhie, p. 46. 2 I. This plant is honey-(mâdku-)born ; with honey we dig thee ; forth ee from honey art thou engendered ; [so] do thou make us possessed of honey. He The comm. calls the plant madṅuka, and uses that form of the name also in the Ś quotations from Kâug. (instead of madugha, madkhugka, etc. ; the mss. vary greatly in their readings).

2. At the tip of my tongue honey, at the root of my tongue honeyedness ; mayest thou be altogether in my power (krâtu), mayest thou come unto my intent (cittâ). 1 The second half-verse agrees nearly with that of iil. 25. 5 and vi. 9. 2, in both of el which the yâr4â2, here unexpressed, helps the construction (though the accent of sas does not absolutely need it, being capable of being viewed as antithetical). Ppp. has g for a jikvâya gre me madku, and for c, d yatha mar kâminy aso (our 5 e) yar: vâcâa ¹ mâm anvâyasi.. The comm. explains madkulakam by madkurarasabakulaṅ jalama- : ¹ âkulakavy ks apuspar: yarkṅ; he understands the plant to be addressed in c, d—which is plainly wrong.

3. Honeyed (mâdhumant) [is] my in-stepping, honeyed my forth-going; with my voice I speak what is honeyed ; may I be of honey-aspect.

Vadâni might be a better reading in c. The first half-verse resembles RV. x. 24.6 a,b (On. m. parâyapam mâdhumat pânar âyanam). Ppp. has for second half-verse vâca ¹ madkumad wbhyâama akso me madhusaṅdâycr. The comm. takes madhu and saṅdyâas in d as two independent words.

4. Than honey am I sweeter (mâdku), than the honey-plant more honeyed ; of me verily shalt thou be fond (? van), as of a honeyed branch.

The majority of our mss. (not Bp. I. E. D.) read here madhughât in b, as do also the Prat. mss. in both places (ii. 5 c ; iv. 16 c) where the verse is quoted ; but at vi.r02.3 all read -7u-; SPP. reads -â«- (as does our text), and makes no report of discordance among his authorities ; the comm. has -â-, and derives the word from madkudughṅa. All the mss., and both texts, give the unmotived accent vânâs in c; the comm. explains the word by sambhajes. He again regards the plant as addressed in the second half-verse. Ppp. (in viii.) has a and b, with [akan for asmi and ] madkhurmâṅ for madughat.

5. About thee with an encompassing (paritatni) sugar-cane have I gone, in order to absence of mutual hatred ; that thou mayest be one loving me, that thou mayest be one not going away from me.

The second half-verse is found repeatedly later, as ii. 30. I d, e and vi. 8.13 â, e. The pada-reading in d is âgacga, and the word is quoted under Prat. iii. 34 as one of the cases of irregular hiatus to which the rule refers. Disregarding this, SPP. alters the Ppada-text to dpacgâṅ, against all our pada-mss. and most of his, for no better reason than that the comm. seems to read so. Our Bp. (both copies) accents here apaxâ, as also at vi. 8. I, 3, but not at ii. 30. 1. The comm. allows this time that the address is to a woman. Ppp. has for bd yaksana kam avidvise yathâ na vidvavadvi na vithâva kadâ cana. As for the rite, cf. Pâraskara's Grhya-sitra, iii. 7¹, and Stenzler's note.

docs.title: 35. For long life etc. : with a gold amulet
docs.text:
[Atharvan.— kâiranyam ; Śindrâgnarm uta v3)vadzvam. Jâgatam : g. anugubgarbhâ

2:2. trigtubk.]

Not found in Pâipp. Of vss. I and 2, Schroeder gives the Katha version, with variants, Tâbinger Katha-kss., p. 36. ] Used by Kâug., with i.9 and v. 28, in two ceremonies for fortune and for power (11.19 ; 52.20); and the comm. considers it involved also at 57.31, in the upanayana. The comm. further quotes it from the ââ7tyâ makscant in Nakṣ. Kalpa 19 ; also from Paricista 4.1 and 13. 1.

Translated : Weber, iv. 430 ; Ludwig, p. 457; Griffith, i. 39.

I. What gold the descendants of Daksa, well-willing, bound on for Catânika, that I bind for thee, in order to life (âyus), splendor, strength, to length of life for a hundred autumns.

It would rectify the meter and improve the sense (considering that Jz kâyurvâ follows) to omit &ynge in c; the Anukr. notes the redundancy of the pada (14 syllables). VS. (xxxiv. 52) has the first half-verse, with a different second half ; and so has a RV. : . khila to RV. x. 128 (9, Aufrecht, p. 685). The Kaâug. speaks of yugmakyspala as the : amulet : probably a pair of beads of gold like Ś777ala berries. The comm. quotes

AB. viii. 21. 5 for Catânika. : 2. Not demons, not pâgâcâs overcome him, for this is the first-born force of the gods ; whoso bears the gold of the descendants of Daksṣa, : he makes for himself long life among the living.

VS. (xxxiv. 51) has the verse, reading ²âd for enam and taranti for sakante in a, accenting Ś5hârti in c, and giving devesn for jfvâsu in 4; and it repeats d with manugyu instead ; and the RV. khila (8, as above) follows it very nearly (but czranti in a, : and Jâksâyaṇâ hir- in c). The Anukr. ignores the metrical irregularities of a and b.

¹ 3. The waters' brilliancy, light, force, and strength, also the heroic : powers (o7zyâ) of the forest trees, do we maintain in him, as in Indra

Indra's powers (indriyâ) ; this gold shall he, being capable, bear.

The comm. explains dâksamaṇa in d by varâkhamâna. Omission of the superfluous indriyâṇâ in c would rectify the meter ; the pada-text marks the division wrongly before a : asmin instead of after it; the Anukr. likewise reckons asmân to d and describes the : fd pada as one of rq syllables. ¹ 4. With seasons of summers (? sâmâ), of months, we [fill] thee, with the milk of the year I fill [thee]; let Indra-and-Agni, let all the gods, approve thee, not bearing enmity.

Emendation to toâ kam at the end of a would rectify both meter and construction. rl Between c and d the pada-text wrongly resolves 2 zu into 2: ânu (as again at viii. 2. 21), and the pada-mss. put the sign of pada division before instead of after 72 apparently ¹ the Anukr. makes the true division after ze, accentless . The comm., too, understands ih v4. The combination -b4i5 fvâ is quoted as an example under Prat. ii. 84.

The concluding anuwâka 6. has again 7 hymns, with 31 verses ; and the quoted i Anukr. of the mss. says e(âdaga co "tare para syuj.

Some of the mss. sum the whole book up correctly as 35 hymns, 153 verses.

Here ends also the second grap âthaka.

Book II.

docs.title: 2.1 Book II
docs.text:
L THE second book is made up mostly of hymns of 5 verses each. It contains 22 such hymns, but also five hymns (namely, 3, 4, 14, 15, and 32) of 6 verses each, five hymns (namely, 5, 17, 27, 29, and 33) of 7 verses each, and four hymns (namely, ro, 12, 24, and 36) of 8 verses each. Compare page r. The possibilities of critical reduction to the norm are well illustrated by hymns ro, r2, 14, 27; see, for example, the critical notes to ii. ro. a.

The whole book has been translated by Weber in the Monatsberichte der Kân. Akad. der Wiss. su Berk, June, 1870, pages 462—524. This translation was reprinted, with only slight changes, in Jndische Studien, vol. xiii. (1873), pages 129-216. The following references to Weber have to do with the reprint.

docs.title: 1. Mystic
docs.text:
⁴ [Vena.— brakmâtmadâivatam. trâistublam : 3. jagati.] I

Found in Pâipp. ii., and parts of it in other texts, as pointed out under the several verses. [Von Schroeder gives what may be called a Katha-recension of nearly all of it in his TWâinger Katha-kss., pp. 88, 89.1 Used by Kâug. (37.3) in addressing various articles out of whose behavior afterward signs of success or the contrary, and the like oracular responses, are to be drawn (the comm. gives them in a more expanded detail). And V3âit. (29. 14) applies vs. 3 in the upavasatha rite of the agnicayana.

Translated : Weber, xiii. 129 ; Ludwig, p. 3935 Scherman, Pkilosophiscke Hymnen, p. 82 ; Deussen, Geschichte, ir 253 ; Griffith, i. 4I.

1. Vena (the longing one ?) saw that which is highest in secret, where everything becomes of one form ; this the spotted one (2777) milked [when] born; the heaven-(svâr)knowing troops (orâ) have shouted at it.

A bit of labored obscurity, like the verses that follow; books iv. and v. begin similarly ; no attempt will be made here to solve the riddles. The comm. explains at great length (nine gto pages), but evidently without any traditional or other understanding; he guesses and etymologizes this way and that, giving in part wholly discordant alternative interpretations. In this verse he first takes vâ7a as = Aditya ; and then, after a complete exposition on this basis, he says: yadwâ : venak parjanyârma maâhyamasthâno devak, and gives another ; p7cni to him is the common name of sky and sun."

The translation given implies emendation in c of jâyamânaâs to -aâ; but the epithet might belong to urâs (so Ludwig and the comm.), or be the second object of aduhat (so Weber). The variants of the parallel versions of other texts make the impression (as often in other cases) of rather aimless stumbling over matters not understood.

VS. (xxxii. 8) and TA. (x. 1.3) have the first half-verse : VS. reads in a pagyan nikitar: : : gukâ sââ, and TA. pâcyan vkvâ bhâvariant vidvân ; both have (kanidam at end of b. . The pratika is quoted in CCS. xv. 3. 8, with the addition i77 paṅca, apparently referring to this hymn. Ppp. has padam for gukâ in a, ekanagam in b, dhenur for pycnis in c

(with -nâs at the end), and, for d, svar vido '"bhyanuktir virâf. The phrase abhy ânasata vrâṅ occurs also in RV. iv. I. 16 4; Pischel (Ved. Stud. ii. 21 and 321 J) takes ¹ vrâs to mean women "; the comm. etymologizes it as avy tâtmânak. prajaṅ. I Cf. Śr RV. x. 123. 2. ]

2. May the Gandharva, knowing of the immortal, proclaim that highest abode that is in secret ; three quarters (padâ) of it [are] deposited in secret ; whoso knoweth them, he shall be the father's father. 4 Ppp. begins with g77kag (for pra tad), and for amytasya has -tarz na, probably g intending the amytan nâ of VS. (xxxii. 9) and TA. (x. I. 3-4: TA. reads also voce).

In b, TA. gives nâma (for dhâma); and for paramâm TA. has nthitam, and VS.

vâbky tam, while VS. ends with gâkâ sâr and TA. with g#kâsu. In c, Ppp. and TA. Ś 4 give padâ, and Ppp. #âkara ; and TA., this time with the concurrence of Ppp., ends the : ⁴ pâda again with gṅhasu. In â, TA. has râd for tâni, and savitâs for sâ pitis, while : Ppp. gives vas for yas at the beginning. Prat. ii. 73 prescribes the combination pitâs p- (in â), and both editions read it, though nearly all our sg74717-mss., and part : of SPP's, read 774] 2- instead. To make a good tristubk pada, we must resolve p7-4 i at the beginning. Hillebrandt, Ved. Myfrhol. i. 433, discusses the verse. ¹ 3. He, of us the father, the generator, and he the connection (bânâhu), : knoweth the abodes, the beings all; who of the gods is the sole nomen- ¹ clator, of him all beings come to inquire. . Here, as usual elsewhere cf. BR. iv. 1088, citations from TB. TS., AB. ), pracnaṇ gf is of infinitival value. Ppp. begins quite differently : sa no bandhur janitâ sa vidhartâ

]dhârmaṇi veda etc.; its c, d are our 5 c, 4, with variants for which see under vs. 5.

VS. (xxxii. 10) and TA. (x. 1.4) have a verse made up like that of Ppp., differing from the latter in the first half only by having idhatâ and dhâmâni. A corresponding verse in RV. (x. 82.3) reads in a yâs for sâ and again for sâ uzâ, accents of course veda in b, and has nzmadâṅâs in c and any? for sârva in 4; and with it agrees in all . points VS. xvii. 27; while TS. (iv. 6.2) and MS. (ii. ro. 3) also follow it closely in a, c, 4 (MS. widhartâ in a) but have a different b¹ y6 naj sats abky & sâj jajâna. Our el : O. has the RV, readings, vââa in b and nâmadhâs in c; and the latter is given by the i ¹ comm. and by nearly half of SPP's authorities ; the latter's text, however, agrees with d ours. The verse is no jagarr at all, but, if we make the frequent (RV.) combination

56°14 in a perfectly regular trâstubh. ²

4. About heaven-and-earth at once I went; I approached (upa-sthâ)

the first-born of righteousness (rtd), abiding in beings as speech in the speaker; eager (?) is he ; is he not Agni (fire) ?

Of this verse, only the first pada is found in VS. (xxxii. 12 a) and TA. (x. I. 4), VS.

reading itvâ for âyam, and TA. having at the end yanti sadyâk. Ppp. has for first i g half pari vigvâ bhuvanâny âyam. upâcaste prathamajâ rtasya, and for d âkâasraṅz nesana tveso agnik. The accus. vâcam in c suggests emendation to ss7ââm, in apposition with prathamajâm ; but then the comm. agrees with Ppp. in reading instead as, and emendation without any traceable sense to guide us is of no avail. The combination bhuvanesthâ (p. -neosthâ) is noted under Prat. ii. 94. In the pada-text of b is noted from our mss. no other reading than âpa: atisthe ; but SPP. gives 45a: atisthe, and reports no various readings ; as zezisthe (without any accent) is an impossible form L Skt. Gr. § 1083 a ] this is perhaps simply a blunder in his text; the comm., with a minority of SPP's mss., has -ti51het. i

5. Around all beings I went, the web (zânz7) of righteousness stretched out for beholding, where the gods, having attained immortality (amâta) bestirred themselves (? zaya-) upon the same place of union (yâui).

The proper rendering of d is especially doubtful, but 4747, by its independent accent (which is established by Prat. iv. 5), is clearly only a strengthener of the locative sense of y6nâu. In b, perhaps better ' to behold the web' etc. (the comm. absurdly explains d the particle kâ as sukhâtmakam brakma). The second half-verse is, as noted above, found in VS., TA., and Ppp., combined into one verse with our 3 a, b; Ppp. has in it ²nacana samâane dhâmann adâhi "rayanta ; VS. reads i ye dhâman for our samâne yonân ; TA., trttye dhâmany abhy atrayanta. Ppp. has as vs. 5 something quite different : for a, pari dyavâaprrhivr sadyâ "yam (exchanging 4a and 5a: see under 4); for b, our own b; for c, d devo devatvam abhiraksamâṇnas samânam bandhur vipa- — ricckad ekak. The first pada requires the harsh resolution wâ(2-7 to make it full 4vâni would be easier.

docs.title: 2. To Gandharvas and Apsarases
docs.text:
[Mâty nâ man. —gandharvâpsarodevatyam. trâigtubham : I. virâgjagarr ; 4. 3p. virâunâmagâyatri; 5. bhuriganugtubh.] I : Found in Pâipp. i. (only in the #âgarz copy). Called by Kâug. (8.24), with vi. rrr and viii. 6. (and the schol. add iv. 20: see ib., note), âty nârnâni 'mothernames' (perhaps from the alleged author) ; they are employed in a remedial rite (26. 29 : against seizure by Gandharvas, Apsarases, demons etc." comm.), and several times (94. 15; 95-45 96. 4; 101. 35 II4. 35 I36. 9) in charms against various portents (aâbkutâni). 1 And verse 1 is allowed by Vâit. (36. 28) to be used in the agwamedṅa sacrifice as alter native for one given in its text (27). Further, the comm. quotes the mâtynâmar hymns from the Canti Kalpa (16) as accompanying an offering in the sacrifice to the planets (grakayajṅa); and from the Naks. Kalpa (23) in the tantrabhutâ mahâcânti.

Translated : Weber, xii. 133 ; Griffith, i. 42; verses 3—5 also by Weber, 45k. Berliner Akad.1858, p. 350 (= Omina und Portenta).—CŚ. Hillebrandât, Ved. Mythol.i. 433.

I. The heavenly Gandharva, who is lord of being (Śkâvana), the only one to receive homage, to be praised (77) among the clans (vi) —thee being such I ban (yz) with incantation, O heavenly god ; homage be to thee; in the heaven is thy station.

Ppp. reads in c deva âyya. The comm. understands yâumi in c as " join (saṅyojayami) BR. vi. 138, (festhalten' : RV. i. 24. 11 a, 641 rvâ yami brâhmazâ, suggests emendation. The combination yâs p- in a is by Prat. ii. yo.

2. Touching the sky, worshipful, sun-skinned, deprecator of the seizure (kâras) of the gods—gracious shall be the Gandharva, who is lord of being, the only one to receive homage, very propitious. . ⁴ Ppp. begins with dâva sprsto, and inverts the order of c and d. The comm. explains . sṅryatvac by sâryasamânavarpa, and haras by krodka. The Anukr. does not heed that c is a jagarr pada. ; 3. He hath united himself (sam-gam) with those irreproachable ones (f.) ; in (4pi) among the Apsarases was the Gandharva ; in the ocean is, they tell me, their seat, whence at once they both come and go. : Ppp. combines jagmaâ "bkî] in a, and has in b apsarâbhis for -râsu ; its second half-t verse reads thus : samudrâ sau: sadanam âhus tatas saâyâ upâacaryanti. Weber takes sa7 jagme in a as 1st sing. The comm. gives two diverse explanations of the verse, the first taking the Gandharva as the sun and the Apsarases as his rays. ⁴ ² 4. O cloudy one, gleamer (âidyir), starry one—ye that accompany

(sac) the Gandharva Vigvâvasu, to you there, O divine ones, homage do : I pay. : : All those addressed are in the feminine gender, i.e. Apsarases. Ppp. has zamaâitu it for nama it in c.. The Anukr. if we assume that its name for the meter (as at i. 2.3; : ¹ iv. 16. 9) means rr + Ir + 11 passes without notice the deficiency of two syllables in a.

5. They that are noisy, dusky, dice-loving, mind-confusing —to those ¹ Apsarases, that have the Gandharvas for spouses, have I paid homage. Ś Ppp. reads in a tâmiys-, and two of our mss. (P.M.) give the same. Ppp. has also g4 aksikâmas in b. Our W.I. combine -Śkyo akaram in d. The verse is not bâurij (as 55 the Anukr. calls it), but a regular anustubh. On account of the epithet dice-loviag . in b, Weber calls the whole hymn « Wiirfelsegen " (' a blessing for dice").

docs.title: 3. For relief from flux: with a certain remedy
docs.text:
[Aṅgiras.— sadycam. bhâisajyâyurdhanvantaridâivatam. ânugutham: 6. 3-5. svarâgupariy- Ś rZnmakâby kat.) ¹ This hymn in Pâipp. also follows the one that precedes it here; but in Pâipp. vss. 3 el and 6 are wanting, and 4 and 5 are made to change places; and vs. I is defaced. Kau.

employs it only once (25.6), in a healing rite for various disorders and wounds (jvarar I ar Bt imutranâgrvr anesu, comm.), with i. z. Tr Translated : Weber, xiii. 138; Ludwig, p. 5075 Grill, 17,79; Griffith, i. 43; Bloomfield, 9, 277.

I. What runs down yonder, aiding (?), off the mountain, that do I make for thee a remedy, that thou mayest be a good remedy..

At the end, 4sqri would be a very acceptable emendation : (that there may be.'

Avatkâ (p. avatekâm : quoted in the comment to Prat. i. ro3; ii.38; iv. ²5) is obscure, but is here translated as from the present participle of root av (like gjazṅd, v.23.7 Ik abhimâdyatkâ, CB., viksinarkâ, VS. ]) ; this the comm. favors (vyâdhi- Ś parikârena raksakam) ; Ppp. has in another passage twice avatakarm (but evidently meant for avatkam : avatakark mama bhesajam avatakar parivâcanam). In a, our

P.M. read -7kâvasi.

2. Now then, forsooth ! how then, forsooth ? what hundred remedies are thine, of them art thou the chief (uttamâ), free from flux, free from disease (ârogaṇa).

In b, me are mine ' is an almost necessary emendation. Yet Ppp. also base : ad aṅgâg 1 catan: yad bhesajani te sahasraṅ: â ca yani te; and, in 9, arohagam ; cf. also vi. 44. 2. The obscure first pâda is here translated as if uttered exclamatorily, perhaps accompanying; some act or manipulation. Asrâva is rendered by the indefinite term 'flux,' its specific i meaning being uncertain ; it is associated with 79ga also in i. 2. 4; the comm. explains it as arisarâtimurranâgrvranâdi. Ct. Zimmer, p.392.]

3. The Asuras dig low down this great wound-healer; that is the g remedy of flux; that has made the disease (7âga) disappear.

The pada-text in b is aruhosrâpam, and the word is quoted under Prat. il. 4o as an d example of the assimilation of a final 2 to an initial sibilant; there can be no question, therefore, that the proper reading is arussrâṇa or aruṅsrâṇay yet the abbreviated equivalent (see my Skz. Gram. § 232 a) arusrâna is found in nearly all the mss. l both here and in vs. 5, and SPP. adopts it in his text. The comm. gives two discord- f ant explanations of the word: vranasya pâkasthanar: vrapamukkam 'place where it gets ripe or comes to a head '? J, and aru} syâyati pakvam bhavary anena. At the end, the comm. has agi amat (as our text in 4 â).

4. The ants (#pajikâ) bring up the remedy from out the ocean ; that is the remedy of flux; that has quieted (cam) the disease.

The comm. explains upajtkâs as valmtkanispadika vanmryak ; Ppp. has instead Ś upacikas,; elsewhere is found upad?kâ (see Bloomfield in AJP. vii. 482 ff., where the d word is ably discussed); ef. also Pali upacikâ]. The Ppp. form, upactkâ, indicates i a possible etymology, from wpa + câ ; Ppp. says in book vi.: yasya bhṅmyâ upacrkâ (ms. -kâd) grkarṅ kruvatrâ "tmane : tasyâs te vigvadkṅyaso viyadṅsanam a” bhare. The earth which ants make their high nests of, and which contains their moisture, has always been used as having remedial properties. The Ś ocean" here (cf. uâaka in vi. roo. 2), if not merely a big name for the reservoir of water beneath the surface, is a tank or pool. Ppp. has an independent second half-verse : ar aspâanam asy &tharvaṇo rogasthanam asy atharvanarn.

5. This is a great wound-healer, brought up from out the earth; that is the remedy of the flux; that has made the disease disappear.

Ppp. reads aruspânam (or -syâ-) in a, and in b g7thigya '54y.

6. Weal be to us the waters, propitious the herbs ; let Indra's thunderbolt smite away the demoniacs (rakgsâs) ; far away let the discharged arrows of the demoniacs fly.

In a all the mss. read gpâs, which SPP. rightly retains in his text; other examples : of the use of this accusative form as nominative occur in the text (see the Index Verâorum); the comm. has 7gas, as our edition by emendation. We may safely regard this unmetrical verse" as a later addition to the hymn ; so far as regards the number of syllables (12 : 12 + 14 = 38), it is correctly described by the Anukr., as the name makâ- Śrkati is elsewhere used in the latter, but apparently by no other similar treatise.

docs.title: 4. Against various evils : with a jaṅgiââ amulet
docs.text:
; [Atharvan.— sagycam. cândramasam uta Jjaṅgidadevatâkam. ânugtubkam : I. vir at prastârapankti.] ¹ Found also (except vs. 6 and parts of r and 2) in Pâipp. ii. Accompanies in Kâug. ¹ (42.23) the binding on of an amulet "as described in the text" (i mantroktam), against various evils (the comm. says, "for thwarting witchcraft, for protecting one's self, for putting down hindrances").

Translated : Weber, xiii. 140 ; Griffith, i. 45 ; Bloomfield, 37, 280 ; in part also by

Grohmann, Ind. Stud. ix. 417-418.— As to the ja7giâa, see Zimmer, p. 65 ; also Weber : and Grohmann, ll. cc. a I. In order to length of life, to great joy, we, taking no harm, all the 4 time capable (dakṣ), bear the jaṅgidâ, the viskanâha-spoiling amulet.

Ppp. has 1 a, b with 2 c, d as its first verse; very possibly the two half-verses between have fallen out in the ms. ; it has in b r5yambho rksamanaâ (for raks-) s-. The ² comm. has raksamanâs also; it is the better reading. The comm. gives no further ( identification of ja7ṅgââa than that it is a kind of tree " (adding vârâṇasyâam prasidâ- : âhak, ' familiarly known at Benares 'l) ; he defines viskandha in the same manner as 8 above, to i. 16. 3.

2. From jambhâ, from viarâ, from viskandha, from scorching (abki-

Ś6cana), let the jaṅgiââ, the amulet of thousand-fold valiance (-v7zyâ), protect us about on every side. ¹ Jambkâ is perhaps convulsion,' or lockjaw ; at Ppp. xi. 2. ro it is mentioned with t hanugraka ; below, at viii. 1. 16, it is called saṅzhannu ' jaw-closing '; the comm. gives t two discordant and worthlessly indefinite explanations. Pâarâ should signify something crushing or tearing to pieces ; Ppp. xi. 2. 3 names it with vârm-ha ; the comm. i says cariravigaranât. Ppp. has of this verse (see under vs. r) only the second half, g : and combines mapis sakasraviyas pari nas p-.

3. This one overpowers the vâskandṅa ; this drives off the devourers; ¹ let this jaṅgidââ, possessing all remedies, protect us from distress.

The first half-verse we had above as i. 16. 3 a, b, with idâm for ayâm. Ppp. begins he this time also with i227, has sate (mate ?) for sakate, and for b reads ayar rakso pa bâdkate ; it gives viskandkarm with our text.

4. With the amulet given by the gods, the kindly Jangidâ, we overpower in the struggle (wyâyâamaâ) the vâskandha [and] all demons. g Ppp. reads for 4 dâyâyase samakhe. The comm. explains uyâyâme fst by sarca- 0 raze, and then by sarcaranapradege.

5. Let both the hemp and the jaṅgiââ defend me from the vâskandha: â the one brought from the forest, the other from the juices (râsa) of ploughing. = That is, from cultivated ground. The “hemp " is doubtless, as the comm. defines

² it, that of the string by which the amulet is bound on. Ppp. has at the beginning Ś4anag ca rvâ ja-; and its second half-verse is corrupted into aranyad abky abkrtas krgya ¹ayo rasebhyak. Ś443 x

6. Witcheraft-spoiling is this amulet, likewise niggard-spoiling ; likewise shall the powerful jaṅgidâ prolong our life-times.

The absence of this verse in Ppp. indicates that the hymn originally consisted of five verses, in accordance with the norm of the book. The verse is very nearly xix. ¹ 34-4. Emendation to araridṅgapas (as in xix.) in b would rectify the meter; the. Anukr. takes no notice of its irregularity. At the end, two of our mss. (E.I.) and i three of SPP's read /ârsat. |For his sâhasvân, see note to i. 19. 4. ] j

docs.title: 5. Praise and prayer to Indra
docs.text:
[Bây gH Atharvana.— saptarcam. Findram. (trâigtubham : I, 2. uparigâad byhatr (r. nicyt; ¹

2. 9irâj) ; 3. virâtparkyâbyhati i 4. jagati purovirâj.] d

Verses 1, 3, and 4 are found in Paâipp. ii., and 5-7 elsewhere in its text (xiii). d Verses I—3 occur also in SV. (ii. 302—4) and CCS. (ix. 5. 2) 5 and the first four verses form part of a longer hymn in ACS. (vi. 3. 1). KB. (²vil. I) quotes by way of pratika vs. I a, b (in their SV. and CCS. form), and speaks of the peculiar structure of the i verses, as composed of twenty-five syllables, with nine syllables interpolated (three at the end of each of the first three five-syllabled pâdas) : cf. Roth, ZZŚ. d. AV", 1856, p. II ff., and Weber, notes to his translation. At TB. ii. 4. 3²e may be found RV. x. 96. 1 treated in a somewhat similar way (four syllables prefixed to each jagarz-pâda); d the first five verses of RV. x. 77 itSelf are another example ; [yet others are AV. vii. 14 (15). 1, 2; v.6.4 a, c; RV. i. yo. II as it appears-at ACS. vi. 3.1 ; cf. further RV. x. 21, 24,25 ]. LI suspect that these interpolations were used as antiphonal responses. ]

The hymn is used once in Kâug. (59. 5), among the ¥âmya rites, or those intended ³ to secure the attainment of various desires; it is addressed to Indra, by one desiring strength (balakâma). In Vaâit. (16. 11), it (not vs. I only, according to the comm.) accompanies an oblation to Soma in the agnisfoma sacrifice, and again (25. 14) a soga- ¢igraka. And the comm. quotes it from Nakṣ. Kalpa 17 and 18, in a maṅâcanri to Indra. None of these uses has about it anything special or characteristic. q

Translated : Weber, xiii. 143; Griffith, i. 46. — Verses 5-7 discussed, Lanman's Reader, p. 3601. d

I. O Indra, enjoy thou —drive on ;— come, O hero —with thy two bays ; — drink of the pressed [soma] — intoxicated here—loving the sweet [draught], fair one, unto intoxication.

Ppp. omits the three interpolations (as Weber reports certain Sttra-works to assert of the Atharvan texts in general), and reads indra jusasoa yâki cra piba sutag (a madhog cakâna cârwm maâarkak. The second interpolation in ACS. is kar7 â)a, d apparently to be read as kar "ka, for which then SV. and CCS. give the senseless kâriha. The third, in all the three other texts, is mattr nâ (like a wise one '?); the : translation above implies the heroic (or desperate) emendation of rater iṅâ to mattâ i 74â (to be read matte 'hâ); Weber conjectures mâder ka. AGS. and CCS. have the older madkvas for madhos. The comm. has no notion of the peculiar structure of d these verses : as, indeed, he has no phraseology in his vocabulary to suit such a case; he explains mates first as mananityasya, then as medhâvinas ; and cakânas as either tar payan or stṅyamaâanas. The Anukr. implies that the second half-verse scans as; 8:4 rr syllables, instead of 9+ Io. : : i 2. O Indra, [thy] belly —like one to be praised—fill thou with the T sweet [draught]—like the heavens— with this soma —like the sky

(seâr)—; unto thee have gone the well-voiced intoxications.

The omission of this verse in Ppp. is perhaps only an accidental one, due to the scribe. The first interpolation in the other texts is âuyan nâ; to get a sense, Weber boldly emends to nâuyan: na 'like [the hold] of a vessel'; the comm. explains by nâtanks (anenâa "darâticaya uktah !), taking no heed of the accent — which, however, requires to be changed to nâuyas, whichever sense be given it; perhaps nady) nâ like streams, would be most acceptable. In the third interpolation, SV. combines svâr ndâ and Acs. CCS. seâr nâ; and the mss. vary between the two; our edition reads the e : former, with the majority of our mss.; SPP. has the latter, with the majority of his ; one et or two of ours corrupt to swâr mâ 'pa. The three other texts have at the end asthus. g The comm. takes âi=nis as gen., supplying amrtena to govern it; and he takes soâr as of locative value. The Anukr. scans the verse as 8 + 8: 8 + ro = 34 syllables. ¹ 3. Indra, a swiftly-overcoming friend, who slew Vritra — like moving gf [streams] —, [who] split Vala — like Bhrgu —, who overpowered his foes ³ in the intoxication of soma.

The translation follows closely our text, though this, as the other versions show, is i badly corrupted in a, b, even to the partial effacement of the first interpolation. The ¹ others read accordantly : idras turâsân mitre nâ jaghâna or trâr yâtir nâ; our yattr i Ś may possibly be meant for yârrn 'as he did the Yatis.' The comm. explains yar?s first as asuryak prajaṅ, then as parivrâjakâk. Ppp. agrees with the other texts, only = omitting the interpolations : indras turâsad jaghâna wrtram ; it then omits the third if pâda, and goes on thus : szsâkâ (atrân mamug ca: vajrir made somasya. All the Ś AV. mss. read sasahe, unaccented, and SPP. admits this into his text; our edition ie â makes the necessary emendation to sasakâ in some copies (and so the Jndex Verbo- : rum); in others the accent-mark has slipped to the right J; the other texts rectify the meter 0: by reading sasâke (our O. agrees with them as regards the 7). Words of verses 2 and

3 are quoted in the Prat. comment, but not in a way to cast any light upon the ‘ readings. SPP., with most of his authorities and our Op., reads valârn. ] The metrical ¹ ; definition of the Anukr. is of course senseless ; it apparently implies the division . 9 + 7:8 + ro = 34 syllables. ee 4. Let the pressed [somas] enter thee, O Indra; fill thy (two) paunches; ¹ help, O mighty one l for our prayer (44) come to us ; hear [my] call, ² enjoy my songs; hither, O Indra, with self-harnessed [steeds]; revel

here unto great joy.

This verse is really, as ACS. plainly shows, made up of two like the preceding three, of five five-syllabled pâdas each, but without interpolations. The first half-verse is vs. 5 in ACS., where it reads thus : 7 fvâ vigantu kavir na sutâsa inâra toast na: â pr uasva kukst some nâ 'vighght (ira dhiyâ kiyânak. Of the two versions of the last pada, that of ACS. is doubtless the original, though ours (the pada has âkiyâ & ihi & naj) is ingenious enough to give a fair sense ; the reading âkâyeṅi is authenticated by the

Prât. comment, which quctes it more than once (to iii. 38 ; iv. II3-II5). The transl Ś4 lation implies the restoration of avigght, as the only true reading namely, an aorist ¹ : imperative from av — see Sz. Gram? § 908] ; the mss. all read 27âkght, which SPP's edition as well as ours properly emends to wigâkt. ] My copy of the printed text reads vidhdht ; but Whitney's Index Verborum and his Roots, Verb-for ms, etc. have vigâht, under vis. ] The comm. reads oy ââṅi, explaining it by vardhaya ? The second halfverse is rather more altered in its AV. version; in ACS. (as vs. 4), with the interpo- i lations, it runs thus : cruâht havark na indro na giro jusasva vajri na: indra sayugbhir didyun na marsoâ maâdâya make ranâya. Ppp. has only this half-verse (without the interpolations), reading thus : cruti kava me kiro jusasya indrasya gubhir matsa j madâya make rapâya. The Anukr. would doubtless have us divide ro + 13 Io + I3 = 46 syllables. As to uighgkt, see notes to Prat. i. 94. Accent of mâtsva, Gram.

We may conjecture that the hymn originally ended here, as one of five verses; the appended three verses that follow are of a wholly other character. ACS. adds one d more verse, which is RV. i. 7o. r1, with similar interpolations after each of its four five-syllabled pâdas.

5. Now will I proclaim the heroisms of Indra, which first he of the thunderbolt (ug7rin) did; he slew the dragon (447); he penetrated to the waters ; he split forth J the bellies (vaṅŚâṇâ) of the mountains.

Verses 5-7 are RV. i. 32. 1-3; and found also in TB. (ii. 5. 4"); vss. 5 and 6 further in MS. iv. 14.13, and vs. 5 in SV. (i. 613) : in these texts without any variant from the RV. reading ; they all have in 5 a p74, and put w7y2ṇâ before it. Ppp. also offers no variants from our text. SPP. reads prâ in a, with all the mss. exceptour O. J, i and our text should have done the same. The comm. renders âzu in c by tadanan- ¹aram, and fatarda by jikiṅsa? also vaksânâs in 4 by naâyas.

6. He slew the dragon that had resorted (cr) to the mountain ; Tvashtar fashioned for him the whizzing (?) thunderbolt ; like lowing kine, flowing (syand), at once the waters went down to the ocean.

The text is precisely the same as in the other passages. The comm. explains seazyâ as sustku preraṇiya (from sz + root 7), and fataksa as tikspar: cakâra?

7. Acting like a bull, he chose the soma ; he drank of the pressed [draught] in the tr/kadrukas; the bounteous one (maghâvar) took his missile thunderbolt ; he slew that first-born of dragons.

RV. (and TB.) combines in a -zo "vy uṅta, and some of the mss. (including our O.) i do the same. The comm. understands the f7ikadrukas as the three abhiplava days. I For d, rather, 'smote him, the first-born of dragons.' The difference is, to be sure, only a rhetorical one. ]

In the first annvâka, ending here, are included 5 hymns, of 29 verses; the old Anukr. says : paṅcareâdye (i.e. 'in the first division of the 5-verse book ') vâgateṅ sywr navo "râkhvarn.

docs.title: 6. Praise and prayer to Agni
docs.text:
ICâunaka (samparkâmaRk). — âgneyam. trâigubham :: 4. gp. ry pankti;

5- vir âtprastârapaṅkti.]

Found in Pâipp. iii.; also in VS. (xxvii. I, 2, 3, 5,6), TS. (iv. I. 7), and MS. (ii. r 2.5). oe Used by Kâug., with vii, 82, in a kZmya rite for success (sampad, 59. v5) and also, in the chapter of portents, alone, in one against bad years (sanâs).. Vait. has it in the ³ agnicayana ceremony (28. 4), at the beginning, and a little later (28. ro) vs. 3 alone, on . depositing the lump of earth on a lotus-leaf. The comm. quotes it from the Nakṣ. K.

(17 and 18), in a mahâcanti called Zgneyz; and, from Paricista 7.2, vs. 5 (with vii. 35),

. in a nightly rite. ] Observe (note to vs. 3) that Ppp. agrees with the Yajus-texts and

Kâug. in associating our vii. 82 with this hymn. J

Translated : Weber, xiii. 146; Griffith, i. 48. i I. Let the summers (sâmâ), O Agni, the seasons, increase thee, the years, the seers, what things are true; shine thou with the heavenly

¹ bright space (rocanâ); illuminate (2-547) all the four directions. : ¹ TS. reads at the end gr zhiuyâs (for cârasras). Ppp. has for b sa7zvarsara rsayo Ś ya nu sakkyâ, and in c gives dyumnena for divyéna. The comm. glosses samaâs by ut saṅvatsaras. If the translation implies that rocanâna is an instr. of accompaniment, ¹ it is less apposite than Mr. Whitney's earlier version, shine together with heavenly ¹ brightness '— which I take to be Agni's own (cf. RV. x. 4.2). His brightness is nil g by day-time. The «together " were better left out. Ś 2. Both do thou become kindled, Agni, and do thou increase this i man, and arise unto great good fortune ; let not thine attendants (zpa- ; sarâr) be harmed, O Agni; be thy worshipers ((rakmân) glorious, not " others. Ś el The other texts are in accordance in reading bodkaya (for varâkaya) in a, and Ppp.

nearly agrees with them, having prati bodkhaye ‘nam, for c the others give mâ ca risad . : upasatrtâ te agne.

3. Thee, O Agni, do these Brahmans choose ; be propitious to us, O

Agni, in the [sacrificial] enclosure (? sazzoâraṇa); rival-slayer, Agni, er conqueror of hostile plotters, be thou ; watch unremitting over thine own ie household.

MS. has the same text; the two others give a slightly different c: sapatnahâ no. 4 aṅhimârijic ca. Ppp. has for b civo gne prathrno nediki, and for d sve ksa âiâiky

aprayuchan,. it then inserts, before vs. 4, our vii. 82. 3 ; and it is very noteworthy that ¹ in the three Yajus-texts do the same. The comm. renders saṅvarane bhava by vidyama- ¹ nasya pi pramaâadasya samchâdane vartasva hide any oversight of ours' The ‘ Anukr. passes without notice the two jagarr-pâdas in the verse.

4. Take hold of thine own dominion ((5arrâ), Agni; with [thy] friend, ¹ Agni, strive (ya) in friendly wise; [as one] of midmost station among

[his] fellows (sgjarâ), [as one] to be severally invoked of kings, Agni, a : shine thou here. Ś VS. TS. read svâyus for svéna in a, and all the three parallel texts have mâtradhâye

(for -2ṅ7) in b, while Ppp. gives mitradheyam, and the comm. -2kâs. Inc, VS. TS.

g fill out the meter by adding eâ%z after 5744; MS. has instead kâyâya, Ppp. stheha i ga masyâ. Ppp. also has vacasoa at end of b. The three other texts accent vikagyâs in d. ¹ : The comm. joins 7â7ṅâm to what precedes, and sagely points out that Brahmans are Agni's fellows ' because, like him, born from the mouth of Brahman, and hence that sajâara here means Brâhmans. The metrical definition of the verse (11 + 11: 8 4 II = 41) is wholly artificial and bad.

5. Over enviers, over delinquents, over the thoughtless, over haters,— verily all difficult things, O Agni, do thou cross ; then mayest thou give. us wealth accompanied with heroes. g

The translation implies emendation of the impossible #ikâs to nidâs; the comm. shows his usual perverse ingenuity by giving two different etymologies of n7kas, from 77 + han and from zi + kâ ; neither of them is worse than the other. The three, parallel texts all have nâhas, Ppp. nukas. Both editions read sṅdhas, but it is only a g common error of the mss., putting 7 for 77; nearly half of SPP's mss. (though none of ours) have the true reading srââhas, which is that also of VS. and TS. (MS. sââhas). In c, all the pada-mss. present the absurd reading v4wâ) ; and nearly all the mss. leave fara unaccented, in spite of 47 and both printed texts leave it so, although three f of SPP's mss. have correctly âra, as also MS.; VS. and TS. give sâkasva for tara i tvam, and Ppp. has cara rvam. docs.text:
[Cukra.— krtyâpratikaraṇasâkiam ; ;rtyâdṅsapadevatyam. I. g2. virâdgâyarrt;

Reckoned as first of the kr2yâpratikaraṇa (' counteraction of witchcraft') gana (Kaâug. 39.7 and note) ; used in a charm for protection against witchcraft (39. 1), with binding-on of a sraktya amulet; and again later (39. 13; the comm. says, only vs r), in a similar rite. I. Spoiler's spoiler (dâgi) art thou; missile's missile (kert) art thou; weapon's weapon (ment) art thou : attain (2) the better one, step beyond the equal (samâ).

The body of the verse is addressed to the amulet; the refrain more probably to its wearer (so, too, Weber) ; but the comm. assigns the latter also to the amulet, and quotes to show it TS. ii. 4. 14, which rather supports the contrary opinion. He calls ment a vajranâman, deriving it from root 7 'damage.' See Geldner's discussion of ment ( hurt done to another in vengeful anger '), Festgruss an Bâhtzingk, p. 31, 32.

2. Sraktyâ art thou; re-entrant (pratisarâ) art thou; counter-conjuring art thou: attain the etc. etc.

The comm. says that srakti is the tilaka-tree, and svakiya means made from it; pratisara is something by which sorceries are turned back (upon their performer); it xr seems to mean virtually a circular amulet— such as a bracelet? For reentrant, Whitney has interlined revertent (sic), better, perhaps, reverting, trans. or intrans. J.

3: Conjure (abhi-car) against him who hates us, whom we hate : attain the etc. etc.

The comm., without explaining why, glosses sârt with abkijṅa knowing.'

5. Bright (ukrâ) art thou; shining (b4r7jâ) art thou; heaven (svâr) art thou; light art thou : attain the etc. etc.

The comm. thinks suâr to be jvarâdirogolpâdanena tâpakak, or else " the common name of sky and sun."

² 4. With thrice eighty sâman-singers, with the Adityas, the Vasus, the

Angirases — let what is sacrificed-and-bestowed of the Fathers aid us—

I take yon man with seizure (kâras) of the gods.

Ista artâm in e has probably already the later meaning of merit obtained by such sacred acts ; the comm. says (aâubhayajanitan: sukrtam. Haras he calls a krodha-

nâman. He understands the ' three eighties ' of a to be the triplets (ca) in gâyarri, usnik, and byhati, eighty of each, spoken of in AA. i. 4. 3—simply because they are the only such groups that he finds mentioned elsewhere ; the number is probably taken indefinitely, as an imposing one.

5. O heaven-and-earth, attend (â-âzdkz) ye after me; O all ye gods, take ye hold (â-rabk) after me ; O Angirases, Fathers, soma-feasting (somyâ), let the doer of abhorrence (apakâmâ) meet with (7-7) evil.

Ppp. reads in a diâhyatâm cf. Bloomfield, AJP. xvii. 417 ], and in d pâpasariccherv ap-. The comm. does not recognize â7âkr as different from diâ7, rendering âdzte bkavatam. l In a, the accent-mark under oz is missing. J

6. Whoso, O Maruts, thinks himself above us, or whoso shall revile our incantation (Śrâhman) that is being performed—for him let his wrongdoings be burnings (i4pus); the sky shall concentrate its heat (sam-1ap) upon the brâkhman-hater.

The verse is RV. vi. 52.2, with sundry variants. At the beginning, RV. has the better reading 447 va; in b, kriyâmânan: ninitsar ; for 6, brahmadvtsam abht tân: vocatu dyâiṅ. Ppp. follows RV. in d (but with coca for cocaru) ; in c it reads vr ajanâns. The comm. renders vzjinâni falsely by varjakâani badhakân.

7. Seven breaths, eight marrows : them I hew [off ] for thee with [my] incantation ; thou shalt go to Yama's seat, messengered by Agni, made satisfactory.

The last pada is xviii. 2. 1 (RV. x. 14. 13) 4d. All our mss. and about half of SPP's have in a majṅâs (for majjṅâs) ; yet SPP. adopts in his text the reading manyâs, because given by the comm., which explains it artificially as for dkamanyas, and signifying "a sort of vessels situated in the throat "; no such word appears to be known elsewhere in the language, and some of the mss. have in other passages of the text manyas for majṅâs. Our Bp. gives âyâ at beginning of c; the word is translated i above as 4yâs J, subjunctive of 7 with doubled subjunctive-sign (see my S&â. Graz. § 560 e), or of its secondary root-form ay ; the comm. takes it from yâ, which makes him no difficulty, since in his view imperfect and imperative are equivalent, and he declares it used for yâki. Ppp. reads for c yamasya gacha sâdanam. In many parts of India today 7 and ny are phonetically equivalent. Cf. SPP's mss. for ix. 5.23.

8. I set thy track in kindled Jâtavedas; let Agni dispose of (? v7) the body ; let speech go unto breath (? âsz).

The verse is in part obscure ; the comm. sets it in connection with one of the details of the Kâug. ceremony : "I set or throw in the fire the dust from thy track combined with chopped leaves: i.e. I roast it in the roaster ; let Agni, through this dust entering thy foot, pervade or burn thy whole body " ; he takes âsu as simply equivalent to grâṇa, and explains : sarvendriyauyavahâracânyo bkavatu, become incapable of acting for the senses : i.e. become mere undifferentiated breath — which is perhaps the true meaning. [Quite otherwise A. Kaegi—citation in Bloomfield, p. 294. ] The Anukr. apparently expects us to resolve at the beginning into a-4. Ppp. has in a 4 daâârmi, and for 4 inart gachatu te vasu.

The last two verses are so discordant in style and content, as well as in meter, with the rest of the hymn that we can hardly consider them as properly belonging to it.

. Their omission, with that of the borrowed RV. verse (our 6), would reduce the hymn to us78 : the norm of this book.

docs.title: 14. Against sadânvas
docs.text:
[Câtana.—sadrcam. (âlâgnidevatyam uta mantroktadevatikam. ânugubham : 2. bhuri;

4. uparigtâdoirâdbrkats.) g

All the verses are found in Pâipp., vs. 4 in v., the rest (in the verse-order r, 5, 6, 2, 3) i in ii. It is reckoned by Kâug. to the câtanâni (8. 25), and also among the hymns of 4 the brkackânti gana (9.1); it is used in the women's rites (str Zkar mâṇâ) to prevent abortion (34.3) ; also in the rite for expiation of barrenness in cattle (vacâcamana. 44.11); and in the establishment of the house fire (72.4), with sprinkling of the entrance, and finally in the funeral ceremonies (82. r4), with the same action. The comm. further refers to the use of the câtana and mâtynâman hymns in Naks. K. 23 and Cânti K. 15. All these uses imply simply the value of the hymn as exorcising evil influences or the beings that represent them, and do not help us to see against what it was originally directed : Weber suggests rats and worms and such like pests ; perhaps, rather, troublesome insects : as usual, the indications are so indefinite that wide room for conjecture is left open.

Translated : Weber, xiii. 175 ; Ludwig, p. 522; Grill, 1, 89; Griffith, i. 58 ; Bloomfeld, 66, 298. BCS See p. 1045.1

1. The expeller, the bold, the container, the one-toned, the voracious —all the daughters (napti) of the wrathful one, the saâdânvâs, we make to disappear.

By the connection, the obscure words in the first half-verse should be names of individual saâânvâs, but dhâsânam (the translation implies emendation to -zânz) is masculine (or neuter), and âṅr num (for which Ppp. reads âkisnyarz) not distinctively feminine. Missâlâ (SPP's text reads, with the sa7zhita-mss. generally, niâsâ-: p. niposâlâ) is taken by the letter of the text, as if from nâṅ-sâlay = ni}-sâray ; the comm. ² gives first this derivation, but spoils it by adding as alternative originating from the sâla, a kind of tree." R. suggests nââsâlamn " out of the house," adverb. The comm. shamelessly derives âkisapam from dkrṣ, and explains it as a seizer with evil, so named"; he also takes -wâdya as = vacana. All our pada-mss. commit the gross blunder of dividing jâghatosvârn, as if the word were a compound ; SPP. lets the division stand in his pada-text. Ppp. reads in c zapatiyas. Ś

2. Out of the cow-stall we drive you, out of the axle, out of the wagon-body (?); out of the houses we expel you, ye daughters (2ukhâtF) of magunds.

The comm. understands ugânasâr (for which two of our mss., P.M., read upamaânasâz) to mean «a granary "—or else a wagon full of grain"; and â45a = a gambling house.” He does not venture to etymologize magundt, but calls it simply the name of a certain pâcâci. The pada-mss. read magunâya, which SPP. properly emends to gy. Ppp. has for b the corrupt nir yoninnypânaca, in c magunâyâ, and at end of d cârayâmasi. The Anukr. takes notice of the metrical irregularity of c.

3. Yon house that is below — there let the hags be; there let debility (sed?) make its home (ni-uc), and all the sorceresses.

Ppp. has a different version of the first three padas : amugminn adkare grhe sarvâ svaṅnta râyah : ratra papma ui yacchatu. The comm. renders sedi by niry ti.

[Our accent-notation does not here distinguish a 57767a circumflex (ay-âcyantu) from an enclitic circumflex (sedâr nyâcyantu — as if it were the impossible nṅucyantu, accentless) ; nor do the mss. of SPP. but in his text, he here employs the stroke, like; long f" or the sign of integration, which does distinguish them.

4. Let the lord of beings drive out, also Indra, from here the saâân- — vas, sitting on the bottom of the house ; let Indra subdue them with the thunderbolt..

The omission of this verse, as being not found with the rest in Ppp. ii., would reduce the hymn to the norm of the second book. Ppp. (in v.) rectifies the meter of d by omitting indras. The metrical definition of the Anukr. is mechanically correct. The comm. understands bkââtaparâ to designate Rudra.

5. If ye are of the endemic (? kserriyâ) ones, or if sent by men; if ye are born from the barbarians (dâsyu)y— disappear from here, O sadânvâs.

All the mss., both here and in the next verse, accent at the end saâânwas, though the word is plainly a vocative, and is so understood by the comm. (who says nothing of the accent, and indeed in general pays no heed to it); SPP. retains the manuscript reading. Ppp. has for a yz devâ gha kserriyâd, and for c yad astu dacvibho jâ1a.

6. I have gone around the abodes (â7âman) of them as a swift [steed about] a race-course ; I have won (7) all your races (277) ; disappear from here, O sadânvas.

The translation implies the evidently necessary emendation aszrazz at end of b; Ppp. has it, and also the comm. ; both editions give asaran, with all the mss. But Ppp. agrees with the mss. in giving just before it the false reading gâszhârm for kâ- (our text emends, but, by an oversight, gives c7r instead of (7) before it); and SPP. retains gâ-. The comm. has instead glâsthâm, and explains it as " the further goal, where one stops (s747) wearied (glâna)."

docs.title: 15. Against fear
docs.text:
[Brakman.— saây cam. prânâpânâyurdevatyam. tripâdgâyatram.] ² Found also in Pâipp. vi., but in a much fuller form, with thirteen verses, of which our six are, in their order, vss. 1, 4,3, 7, I2, I3 ; the others deal with wind and atmos- ‘ phere, cow and ox, Mitra and Varuṇa, Indra and Indra's might (inâriya), hero and heroism, breath and expiration, and death and immortality (aṅz7tam) ; after bibher is added in vs. I evâ me "pana ma rigayâ, and, at the end of the hymn, the same, but with risa for rigsayâ. In Kâug. (54.11), the hymn is used, with vi. 41, at the end of the godâna ceremony, on giving food to the boy. It is also counted by the schol. (ib,, note) to the Zyusya gana. The comm. makes no reference to the goâârna rite, but declares the use to be simply by one desiring long life (7yuskâma).

Translated : Weber, xiii. 179; Griffith, i. 59.

I. As both the heaven and the earth do not fear, are not harmed, so, my breath, fear not.;

IMGS., at i. 2.13, has evam me prâna ma bibha evar me prâna ma risaj. J

2. As both the day and the night do not fear etc. etc.

The comm. here applies for the first time the term paryâya to these sentences, correspondent but with elements in part different.

3. As both the sun and the moon do not fear etc. etc.

4. As both sacrament (â7âhman) and dominion (ksarrâ) do not fear etc. etc.

That is, the Brahman and KŚatriya castes (br âkmaṇajati and ksatriyajari, comm.), as the words might properly enough be translated.

¹ 5. As both truth and untruth do not fear etc. etc. — 6. As both what is (Śhṅṅâ) and what is to be (Śkâuya) do not fear ee etc. etc.

¹ The comm. paraphrases bhutâm by sattam prâaptam vastujatam ; the past would 1 . seem to be a better example of fixity than the future ; but neither is “ untruth " (vs. 5) eee ug to be commended as an example. Weber would read ca yââm.

I Not metrical. This hymn (but not its four successors and counterparts) is found in Paipp. ii.; also in MS. (i.5. 2: in verse-order I 4, 3,2, 5) and Ap. (vi. 21.1 in 3 ¹ verse-order 3,4, I, 2, 5) ; further, in K. Its first pratika (but regarded by the schol. and by the comm. as including all the five hymns) is used by Kâug. (47.8) to accompany the purastâd komas in the witchcraft rites. The Anukr. has a common description of the five hymns, 19-23, as paṅca sâktani paṅcarcani paṅcapatyani (? or cazapâaty-)

tripâdâgâyatrâny ekavasânani. The mss. blunder; but paṅcâparyâni is probably fh: right ; see note to Kâug. 47. 8.

ee ¹ Translated : Weber, xiii. ISI ; Griffith, i. 62,

I. O Agnil with the heat that is thine, be hot against him who hates us, whom we hate.

MS. leaves (in all the verses) the a of asmâr unelided, and both MS. and Ap. insert ca before vayânm.

; z. O Agnil with the rage (4âras) that is thine, rage against him who

¹ ⁴ hates us, whom we hate.

re ¹ st Prâri kara has to be strained in rendering, to preserve the parallelism of the expres-

Ś sion. Or, ⁴with the seizing-force that is thine, force back him' etc. ?

3. O Agnil with the gleam (areâs) that is thine, gleam against him : Ś who hates us, whom we hate.

4: O Agnil with the burning (cocis) that is thine, burn against him ee who hates us, whom we hate.

5. O Agni! with the brilliancy (fas) that is thine, make him unbrilliant who hates us, whom we hate.;

Ppp. has jyotis for tzjas, and prati daha for atejasar kyu; for the latter, MS. and Ap. read prati titigâhi (also K., tityagdht).

The meter is alike in the four hymns r9—2z2 ; the Anukr. restores the a of asmân, and in vss. I-4 scans 6 + 7 + Io = 23, and, in vs. 5, 6 + 9 + ro = 25.

docs.title: 20. The same: to Vâyu (wind)
docs.text:
This and the three following hymns are mechanical variations of the one next preceding, differing from it only by the name of the deity addressed, and in hymn 23 by the pronouns and verbs being adapted to the plural deity. They are wanting in the other texts. The comm. does not deign to explain them in detail, but prefixes a few introductory words to the text of this one. For the Anukr. descriptions of the meter, and for the use by Kâug., see under hymn 19. It would be space wasted to write out the translation in full. They should all be regarded as non-metrical. ] They are briefly treated (not translated) by Weber, xiii. i182, and Griffith, i. 62.

I. O Vâyu! with the heat that is thine etc. etc.

2-5. O Vayu! with etc. etc.

docs.title: 21. The same : to Sûrya (sun)
docs.text:
I. O Sârya! with the heat that is thine etc. etc.

2-5. O Strya! with etc. etc.

docs.text:
I. O moon! with the heat that is thine etc. etc.

2—5. O moon ! with etc. etc.

docs.title: 23. The same: to water
docs.text:
I. O waters! with the heat that is yours etc. etc.

2—5. O waters! with etc. etc.

Here the meter, owing to the plural verbs, is different; the Anukr. calls that of ' vss. I—=4 (6 +8 + ro = 24) samavisamâ, a gâyarri 'of uneven members," and vs. 5 (6 + ro + 10 = 26) the same, with two syllables in excess searâg-wâsamâ.

docs.title: 24. Against kimidins, male and female
docs.text:
[Brakman. — agtarcam. &yugyam. pânktam J

I Not metrical. ] Part of the hymn is found in Pâipp. ii., but in a very corrupt con- Gon dition : see under the verses below. Kâug. makes no use of it that is characteristic, or that casts any light upon its difficulties, but prescribes it simply as to be employed in a certain ceremony (19. 9-13) for prosperity (according to the comm., for removal of a bad sign), called " of the sea" (samudra : the comm. says, offering in a câperastha; fire, in the midst of the sea); it is also reckoned (19. I, note) to the #antras called pustika ' for prosperity. The words that precede the refrain in each verse are apparently the names of kmiâins. The Anukr. says that Brahman in each verse praised with . verses the deity mentioned in it; and gives a long description of the meters that is ¹ ; too confused and corrupt to be worth quoting in full.

Translated : Weber, xiii. 182 ; Griffith, i. 6z.

r. O gerabhaka, cerabha I back again let your familiar demons go;

back again your missile, ye kimidins I whose ye are, him eat ye; who hath sent you forth, him eat ye; eat your own flesh. ¹ Ppp. reads : carabhaka seragabha punar bho yanti yadavas punar hatis kimtâinak yasya stha dam atta yo va prâkt tam urtan masaṅsâ manyatâ. The comm. in the last phrase gives sa instead of su, and has much trouble to fabricate an explanation ² for it (as = rasya, or else for sâ hetik). Cerabhaka he takes as either sukhasya prâpaka ² or carabhavat sarvesâan: kinsaka, but is confident that it designates a ' chief of yara-

Jhânas." Of the refrain, the first part seems metrical, and the second prose, in three phrases ; and it may be counted as 8 +8: 6 + 7 + 5 (or 7) =34 (or 36) : the prefixed names add 7 syllables (vss. I, 2), or 5 (vss. 3,4), or 3 (vss. 6-8), or 2 (vs. 5). [Bloomfield comments on 4â¢ and the like, ZDMG. xlviii. 577.

2. O gevydhaka, cévrdhal back again let your familiar etc. etc.
