3. O mrokâ, anumroka I back again let your familiar etc. etc. . 4. O sarpâ, anusarpa ! back again let your familiar etc. etc.

5. O jâryi I back again let your familiar demons go ; back again your missile, ye she-kâmidins ; whose ye are etc. etc. 4 ¹ 6. O upabdi I back again let your familiar etc. etc. ; 7. O ârjunt I back again let your familiar etc. etc.;

8. O Ś4arâyi I back again let your familiar etc. etc. y i To represent all these verses, we find in Ppp. cevy ka cevy dha sarpan sarpa mrokârn mre jyarnyatro jarjânvapaprado punar vo yanti yâdaval : punar juris kimi naṅ : : yasya stha dam atta yo na praki tam utvas sâ mâṅsâny arta. It has not seemed worth while to try to translate the names, though most of them contain intelligible elements see Weber, p. 184, 186 J, and the comm. forces through worthless explanations . for them all. In vs. 8 he reads bkarâci, and makes an absurd derivation from roots 347 i and ac (going to take away the body"). [In the first draft, W. notes that the four i feminine names of vss. 5-8 might be combined to one z77sfubk pâda, which with the ¹ common refrain would give us the normal five verses." g

docs.title: 25. Against kâṇvas : with a plant
docs.text:
[Câtana.— vânaspatyam. &nugtubham : 4. bhurâj.] a Found in Pâipp. iv. Both Weber and Grill regard the hymn as directed against : abortion ; but no sufficient indications of such value are found in its language, though ( some of the native authorities intimate their discovery of such. Kâug. (8. 25) reckons it : to the câtana hymns ; and it is employed, with ii. 7 and other hymns, in a remedial ceremony (26-33-36) against various evils, specially accompanying the smearing of the designated plant with sacrificial dregs (sampâta) upon the patient. ; Translated : Weber, xiii. 187; Grill, 20, 92 ; Griffith, i. 64 ; Bloomfield, 36, 302.

I. Weal for us, woe (âam) for Nirrti (perdition ') hath the divine spotted-leaf made; since it is a formidable grinder-up (âmbhana) of kâyuvas, it, the powerful, have I used (54a).

The comm. makes no attempt to identify the g7guiparṇz as any particular plant, but simply paraphrases it with citraparyy ojadhik. R. discusses the word as follows : the preniparpt is, I. according to the commentary to KCS. xxv. 7. 17, the same with zâsaparṇṅ, i.e. Glycine debilis ; 2. according to other schol., the same with Jaksinaṇâ, a plant having upon its leaves red spots, in which the form of a child is claimed to be seen. Bhâvapr., i. 208, calls it also putrajant, and Râjanigh., vii. 1 14, putrakandaâ, or purradt, or purrkandâ, indicating a bulbous plant; it is credited with the power to cure barrenness of women ; 3. according to Am. Kog. and the other Nighaṇtus, it is a leguminous plant, identified by Chund Dutt (Mat. medica) with Urarâa lagopodioides Dec., having hairy leaves without colored spots. The second of these identifications would suit the hymn. AŚâkaksi might mean ' I have partaken of or drunk '; but neither Kâug. nor the comm. know of such a use of the plant. The strange appearance in this hymn (only) of kâpva as name of evil beings is passed by the comm. without a word of notice; he simply paraphrases the word with 74a. But see Bergaigne, Rel. ved. ii. 465, and Hillebrandt, Ved. Mythol. i. 207.) Ppp. reads in b nirytaye karat, and in d twa karsam for abhakyi.

2. This spotted-leaf was first born overpowering; with it do I hew [off] the head of the ill-named ones, as of a bird (ca4ânz).

Cakaâ- is misprinted aZ7-. ] The reading w7gcâami, without accent (which is given in both editions, on the authority of all the mss.) implies that the fourth pâda begins with ¢âras, the preceding three words being (as is easy) resolved into eight syllables; and the pada-mss. also mark the pâda-division before ¢7ras. The Anukr., however, regards the verse as a simple anustubkh, which it plainly is, (fas belonging to c; the accent should therefore be emended to vygcâmi. Ppp. reads sadanvâghnt pr- for a, and, in c, 4, aya kanvasyar: crag chinadmi ¢ak-. The comm. explains the ill-named" as dadruvisarpakagvitrâdikustharogavigesas, or varieties of leprosy.

3. The blood-drinking wizard, and whoso wants to take away fatness, the embryo-eating Śâṇva do thou make disappear, O spotted-leaf, and overpower.

One or two of our mss. (W.I.), and several of SPP's, read in b jâhirâsati I. has -7775- ]. Ppp. has at the end sakasvatl.

4. Make them enter the mountain, the life-obstructing (:yopana) kâṇwas; do thou, O divine spotted-leaf, go burning after them like fre.

LAs to kapwâṇ, cf. i. 19. 4 n. As to yopana, see Bloomfield, AJP. xii. 423. ] This verse and the next are too much defaced in Ppp. to admit comparison in detail ; but its text differs somewhat from ours. The Anukr. refuses to sanction the common abbreviation to agnâr 'va in d.

5. Thrust them forth to a distance, the life-obstructing kâṇvas ; where the darknesses go, there have I made the flesh-eaters go.

docs.title: 26. For safety and increase of kine
docs.text:
[Savitar.— pacavyam. rrâistubham. 3. uparigâdvirâdbrhati 4 5. anugubh (4. bhuri).] : : Found in Pâipp. ii. Used by Kaâug. (19. 14), with iil. 14, iv. 21, and ix. 7 not vi. II.

3 —see comm. to ix. 7 = 12 , in a ceremony for the prosperity of cattle.

Translated : Weber, xiii. 188; Ludwig, p. 371; Griffith, i. 65 ; Bloomfield, r42, 303 ; i vss. I and 2, also by Grill, 64, 92. —Cf. Bergaigne-Henry, Manuel, p. 138.

I. Hither let the cattle come that went away, whose companionship

(sakacârâ) Vâyu (the wind) enjoyed, whose form-givings Tvashtar knows;

in this cow-stall let Savitar make them fast (ni-yam).

Or, 'whose forms,' râpadkeya being virtually equivalent to simple 7Zga. Ppp. reads in b sakatâram. The cow-stall" does not probably imply anything more than an enclosure. The Anukr. passes without notice the jzgat7 pada d. ¹ 2. To this cow-stall let cattle flow-together [stream together ] (sar- â srx) ; let Brihaspati, foreknowing, lead them hither; let Sinivâli lead ² hither the van (âgra) of them; make them fast when they have come,

O Anumati.

I In the prior draft of 3, Mr. Whitney has 'stream.'] Ppp. has at the end yacchâr, one of SPP's mss., yacchat. The comm. gives anugate (= he anugamanakâri z) in d. : The value of pra in the common epithet prgjâanânt (rendered foreknowing ') is obscure and probably minimal. As to the deities here named, see Zimmer, p. 352, and Hille- ⁴ brandt, Ved. Mythol. i. 422.

3. Together, together let cattle flow [stream J, together horses, and 4 together men, together the fatness that is of grain; I offer with an oblation of confluence.

For the oblation called of confluence, to effect the streaming together of good ¹ things, compare i. r 5 and xix. I. The change of meter in this hymn need not damage ‘ its unity, in view of its occurrence as one hymn in Ppp. Ppp. reads in b pâurusâs, and in c sphâaribhis (for ya spâ-). The metrical definition of the Anukr. seems to reject the ( obvious resolution -vâ-e-na in d.

4. I pour together the milk (Ś5774) of kine, together strength, sap, with sacrificial butter ; poured together are our heroes; fixed are the ' kine in me rather, with me [as] kine-lord.

Ppp. reads valanz in b, combines -k4â 'smâkam in c, and has for 4 mayi gâvag ca ⁴ ; goparâu, The redundant syllable in 4 (noticed by the Anukr.) would be got rid of by changing âyiâ to the old locative m4] ; but with better metrical result, by adopting

Ś the Ppp. reading J. With the second half-verse is to be compared ACS. ii. 11. 6: arisz eŚsnâkar: VEG MYL GhVR) SANtU KOparân. The comm. says that gavâm in a means

( grt nam ' of heifers (having their first calf). 55. I bring (7-kr) the milk of kine; I have brought the sap of grain; fs brought are our heroes, our wives, to this home (âstaka).

Ppp. has akargarm in b, in c Zharisam (for âkytâs) and virân, and in d 2 parninz e dam. Our Bp. gives akârisam (and H. akarâarisam) in b, and 4727s in.

The anuvâka 4. ] has this time 9 hymns, with 48 verses ; the old Anukr. says âzynan: [artârâdhant] turkyap.

docs.title: 27. For victory in disputation : with a plant
docs.text:
[Kapiṅjala.— saptarcam. vânaspatyam. ânugtubhant.] I

Found in Pâipp. ii. Kâug. uses the hymn in the rite or charm for overcoming an adversary in public dispute : one is to come to the assembly from the north-eastern direction (because of its name aparâjita 'unconquered'), chewing the root of the plant, ' and to have it in his mouth while speaking ; also to bind on an amulet of it, and to wear a wreath of seven of its leaves (38. 18-21). Verse 6, again, is reckoned (30. 13, note) to the râudra gana. The comm. further quotes from the Naks. error for Cânti] K. (17, 19) a prescription of the use of the hymn in a makhâ;ânti called aparâjâz.

Translated : Weber, xiii. igo ; Ludwig, p. 461 ; Grill, rst edition, 18, 51 ; Bloomfield, JAOS. xiii., p. xiii (PAOS. May, 1885), or AJP. vii. 479; Grill, 2d edition, 23,93 ; Griffith, i. 66; Bloomfield, SBE. ii. 137, 304. — Bloomfield was the first to point out (on the authority of Kâug.) the connection of p7â with root prack, and to give the true interpretation of the hymn. Grill follows him in the second edition.

I. May [my] foe by no means win (7) the dispute; overpowering, overcoming art thou; smite the dispute of [my] counter-disputant ; make them sapless, O herb.

« Dispute " (277) is literally 'questioning.' The comm. renders the word in a by prastar questioner, but in c gives us our choice between that and pragnc ' question, and in 7 a acknowledges only the latter meaning. Prâtiprâgas is translated here as genitive ; the comm. takes it secondly as such, but first as accus. pl.; the Ppp. reading favors the latter : sa man pratiprâco jaya rasa kr- With either understanding, the accent is anomalous ; we ought to have pratiprâas. Arasân also is in faver of th plural. If we could emend grâcam in c to pra (in the disputation, ft would make. things much easier. For a Ppp. has yag catrân saṅjâyât. Ned in â is simply the emphasized negative. CE

2. The eagle discovered (znu-vid) thee ; the swine dug thee with his snout : smite the dispute etc. etc. Se

Pâda b shows that the root is the part of the plant employed. If we struck off the impertinent refrain from vss. 2—5, and combined the lines into twe verses, the hymn would conform to the norm of the second book (as in more than one case above Lp 370

3. Indra put (7) thee on his arm, in order to lay low (sz7) the Asuras: oo smite the dispute etc. etc.

The comm., both here and in the next verse, understands -bk4ya(k) stârtave as -³ṅyas ¹4rF, though he then explains tzrṅtave by star tum. Pâda a is rendered in accordance with the comm. and with Weber ; Grill, (took thee into his arm.'

4. Indra consumed (vi-ag) the pâ1â, in order to lay low the Asuras:; smite the dispute etc. etc.

The comm. reads in a pâthân, and uses that form in all his explanations ; param seems to be given in all the mss., and in Ppp., and both editions adopt it; but the mss. are very little to be trusted for the distinction of 7 and 74. The plant is the Clypea hernandifolia, whose bitter root is much used. It grows all over India, and is said to be applied to ulcers in the Penjab and in Sindh (W. Dymock, Vegetable mat, med.y" (R.). In his note, Roth gives Śâ127 as Ppp. form; but in his collation, he gives as Ppp. reading in a, b pâyam indro uyâsnâan kantave as-. The Anukr. apparently expects us to resolve vi-â-gn-â¹ in a. 5. With it will I overpower the foes, as Indra did the sâlzvrkâs : smite the dispute etc. etc.

The translation implies emendation of the inadmissible saṅse to sâkgye, than which nothing is easier (considering the frequent loss of y after a lingual or palatal sibilant) or more satisfactory, for both sense and meter ; it is favored, too, by the Ppp. reading, saksiye. No other example of long & in a future form of this verb appear to be quot. able; but the exchange of a and a in its inflection and derivation is so common that this makes no appreciable difficulty. The comm. accepts sââṣe, rendering it by aŚ)â bhavâms. The Anukr. notes no metrical irregularity in the verse. In our text, accent sit vyhân (an accent-mark out of place). To Weber's note on sâlâvyṅâ, add Oertel, JAOS. xix.? 123 f. This allusion adds to the plausibility of W's suggestion about the Yatis, note to ii. 5.3..

6. O Rudra, thou of healing (?) remedies, of dark (n7lz) crests, deeddoer smite the dispute etc. etc.

Ppp. has for c,d pr31ar: durasyato jaki yo smâṅ abkhidâsari, which is plainly much better than the repetition of the refrain, and for which the latter has perhaps been substituted in our text. The comm. draws out to great length a series of derivations for rudra, and gives two for jalâya, and three different explanations of kzrmakrt. Bloomfield discusses jar etc. at length, AJP. x7. 425 ff. ]

7. Do thou smite the dispute of him, O Indra, who vexes us; bless us with abilities (;ââ7i) ; make me superior in the dispute.

Ppp. reads grsâam for prâcaṅ: tvam in a, and ends b with -ââ2sare. The comm. has prâgam instead of prâi in d and is supported in it by two of SPP's authorities. The prâcam in a he explains by vâZyarm, and that in his d by prastaranm.

docs.title: 28. For long life for a certain person (child ?)
docs.text:
[Cambhṅ.— jarimâyurdâivatam. trâigubham : I. jagati ; 5. bkuri.]

Found in Paâipp. (vss. i—4 in i; vs. 5 in xv.). Used by Kâuc. in the goââna ceremony (54. 13), as the parents pass the boy three times back and forth between them and make him eat balls of ghee; and the same is done in the cgâ or câula (hair-cutting) ceremony (53. 16, note); the schol. also reckon it to the Zyugya gana (54. 11, note).

Translated : Weber, xiii. 192 ; Grill, 48,94; Griffith, i. 67; Bloomfield, 5o, 306.

I. For just thee, O old age, let this one grow; let not the other deaths, that are a hundred, harm him; as a forethoughtful mother in her lap a son, let Mitra protect him from distress that comes from a friend (mâtrâya). a cpt

Ppp. has in b fvat for cararz ye, and combines in d mitre nam. The omission of either imâm or anye would rectify the meter of b. The comm. most foolishly takes jariman first from j7 'sing,' and explains it as ke stâyamâna agne then adding the true etymology and sense. The "jagarz" is quite irregular : 12 + 13: II + I2 = 48. [Bloomfield cites an admirable parallel from RV. iv. 55. 5; but in his version he has quite overlooked the verb-accent.

2. Let Mitra or helpful (? riâdâs) Varuṇa in concord make him one that dies of old age; so Agni the offerer (457ar), knowing the ways (vayâna), bespeaks all the births of the gods.

All our pada-mss. read in a 74âââ instead of -â2k ; SPP. properly emends to -22}. This wholly obscure word is found independently only here in AV.; its rendering above is intended only to avoid leaving a blank; the comm. gives the ordinary etymology, as kiṅsakanam atta; Grill, emending to arâaâdas, brings out an ingenious but unconvincing parallelism with Gr. éaiv4s; and, as noticed by him, Aufrecht also would understand arââdas very prominent.' Ppp. reads for a mitrag ca tuâ varupag ca rââdâân, and has at the end of d -mâni vakti. I

3. Thou art master (7) of earthly cattle, that are born, or also that are to be born; let not breath leave this one, nor expiration ; let not friends slay (vadk) this one, nor enemies.

All the mss., and the comm., read at end of b janttrâs, which SPP. accordingly retains, while our text makes the necessary emendation to jânitoâs, which Ppp. also has. Ppp. omits o in b; elides the initial a of apâno and amitrâj after mo ; and it puts the verse after our vs. 4. Pada b lacks a syllable, unnoticed by the Anukr. read jârâsas 2].

4. Let father heaven, let mother earth, in concord, make thee one that "dies of old age ; that thou mayest live in the lap of Aditi, guarded by breath and expiration, a hundred winters.

Ppp. reads ze for fvâ in a, and âzrgham âyuj for saṅrvidâne in b; also yzya for adites in c. The Anukr. takes no notice of the irregularity of the meter (9 + 11: Io +12 = 42: a poor zristubk'); the insertion of ca after pr2hivt in a, and emendation to JFtwâst in c, would be easy rectifications. [In order to bring the cesura of a in the right place, read âyâṅg and foâ each as one syllable and insert a ca also after pizâ. Thus all is orderly, II + II : II + I2. The accent-mark over p7- is gone.

5. This one, O Agni, do thou lead for life-time, for splendor, to dear seed, O Varuṇa, Mitra, king l like a mother, O Aditi, yield (yarn) him refuge; O all ye gods, that he be one reaching old age.

All the pada-mss. read at end of b mitracrâjan, as a compound ; and SPP. so gives it; the comm. understands 7âjan correctly as an independent word, but perhaps only as he in general is superior to the restraints of the paâa-readings. Ppp. (in xv.) has priyo for yam in b. The verse is found also in TS. (ii. 3. 103), TB. (ii. 7.75), TA. (il. 5.1), and MS. (ii. 3.4). All these give kr di for naya at end of a; TA. MS. have tigmâm Śjas instead of prâyârn: rétas in b; TS. TB. MS. read soma râjan at end of b, while TA. offers instead sâ giââadâht ; all accent jâradastis in 4d, and MS. leaves asar at the end unaccented.. In CGS. (i. 27), again, is a version of the verse, omitting zaya in a, reading (with MS.) tigmam ogjas and soma in b, and having aditik (arma yanṅusat in c. I Von Schroeder gives the Katha version, TâŚinger Kayha-kss., p. 72-3. 1

docs.title: 29. For some one's long life and other blessings
docs.text:
[Atharvan.— saptarcam. bakudevatyam. tr&[tubham I. anugubh ; 4. Pparâbykati nicytprastârapankti.]

Found in Pâipp.) but in two widely separated parts: vss. I-3 in xix., and vss. 4—7 7 in i. (next following our hymn 28). Used in Kâug. (27. 9 ff.) in a curious healing rite i for one afflicted with thirst: the patient and a well person are set back to back, wrapped in one garment together, and the latter is made to drink a certain potion apparently prepared for the other ; thus the disease will be transferred to the well person: a total perversion of the proper meaning of the hymn. Again, it is used (54. 18) in the goâdana and c#âa ceremonies, and, according to the schol. (58. 17, note), in that of name-giving; ¹ and the schol. (42. 15) further add it in the rite on the return home of a Vedic student. And vs. 3 accompanies in Vaâit. (22.16) the pouring of the âczr milk into the clarified soma in the pṅltabkrt at the agnisfoma sacrifice cf. comm. and Hillebrandt, Ritual-litteratur, p. 129.

Translated : Weber, xiii. 194 ; Ludwig, p. 493 ; Griffith, i. 63; Bloomfield, 47, 308.

I. In the sap of what is earthly, O gods, in the strength of Bhaga's self (fanṅ)— length of life to this man may Agni, Strya— splendor may Brihaspati impart.

Or it might be ⁴in the sap of earthly portion, in strength of body' (a, b); ' what is ¹ earthly ' would refer to some characteristic product of earth applied in the rite; the comm. understands the god Bhaga, but his opinion is of no authority. As Weber suggests, the exchange of zyagyâm here in c and Zyus in 2 a would rectify the meter of both verses : in neither case does the Anukr. note an irregularity. Ppp. has here zyur , asmâi, but follows it with some varca dhâtâ byk-. Some of our mss., with two or three of SPP's, accent Zyâgyan. The comm. takes dzvâs in a for a nominative.

2. Length of life to him assign thou, O Jâtavedas ; progeny, O Tvashtar, do thou bestow on him; abundance of wealth, O Savitar (impeller '), do thou impel to him ; may he live a hundred autumns of thee. d The construction of a dative with adhâ-ni-4hâ in b seems hardly admissible ; BR. lifi.or7 J, in quoting the passage, reads asmé, apparently by an intended emendation,; which, however, does not suit the connection ; asmtn is the only real help.

3. Our blessing [assign him] refreshment, possession of excellent progeny; do ye (two), accordant, assign [him] dexterity, property (â7âviga) ; [let] this man [be] conquering fields with power, O Indra, putting (k7) other rivals beneath him.

The verse is difficult, and, as the parallel texts show, badly corrupted. Śâr aas (for which Weber ingeniously suggested Zgirne) is supported by ââr nas in MS. (Gv. 12.3) and ââr me in TS. (iii. 2.85) and KCS. (x. 5.3) ; and all these versions give t : it.a verb in b, daâkâtu, instead of the impracticable dual Jkattarm, with which our sâce- c t2sâu is in the same combination. The alteration of this to the sâwarcasam of TS. . MS, or the suvarcasam of KCS. and Ppp., would indicate that of dkattam to -tâm (as middle), and allow sense to be made of the pada. All the other texts, including Ppp., Ś give in a suprajastvâm instead of the anomalous and bad sâupr-. TS. MS. KCS. ² have Śuam for dâksam in b. The translation implies emendation of jâyam in c to jâyan in accordance with the saṅzjâyan of the other texts; but Ppp. has saṅ jayat, which would be even more acceptable — only not with ak%âm, as all the four read for ayâom. TS. MS., finally, combine anyâṅ âdâṅ- in 4; KGS. elides zyârn. In KCS., as in Vâit., i the first word is to be understood as (tr; the comm. interprets both ways as from acâ blessing ' or from âcâ 'milk' ]. He regards the 2x of szupra- in a as simply "Vedic," and heaven and earth as addressed in b.

4. Given by Indra, instructed by Varuṇa, sent forth by the Maruts, hath the formidable one come to us; let this man, in your lap, O heaven-and-earth, not hunger, not thirst.

The thirst " of the patient in Kâug. has no more substantial foundation than the last two words of this verse. The text in Ppp. is defaced, but shows szṣ7as for câstas in a, and in c, d, after -thivi, pari dadâmi sa mâ. The Anukr. would have us scan II + 11 : 8 + 9 = 39, dividing before upâsthe ; but the pada-mss. mark the division correctly, after that word.

5. Assign refreshment to him, ye (two) that are rich in refreshment; assign milk to him, ye rich in milk; refreshment have heaven-and-earth assigned to him, [have] all the gods, the Maruts, refreshment [have] the waters.

Refreshment is the conventional rendering selected for the ambiguous word 77 and its varieties. Nearly all our mss. (all save P. M.), and all of SPP's, have the false accentuation devas in d; both editions emend to dzwâs, which the comm. also understands. So also with âyâvâprthâvâ in c, for which the mss. have either dy avagy thivz (so nearly all of ours and one of SPP's) or dyzvâgythivi (so, according to SPP., all his save one, with our O.D.); only our H. has the true reading, which is given by emendation in both editions. The verse (ro + 10: I2 + II =43) is far from being a good trâstubâ.

6. With propitious things (f.) I gratify thy heart; mayest thou enjoy thyself (mud) free from disease, very splendid ; let the two that dwell together (? savâsân) drink this stir-about (manthâ), putting on [as] magic the form of the (two) Agvins.

The second half-verse is said apparently of a married pair, who are by supernatural means to become as beautiful as the Agvins. Of course, the comm. follows Kâug. in understanding it of the sick and well man, and taking savâstn as '" dressed in one garment." The comm. supplies adbkts in a, which is plausible (so Weber). Ppp. reads in a rarpayantu, in b modamanag care 'ka, and in d agvinâu. Several of SPP's mss. give narhâm in c.

7. Indra in the beginning, being pierced, created this refreshment, [this] unaging svadkâ; it is thine here; by it live thou for autumns, very splendid ; be there no flux of thee ; the healers have made [it] for thee.

In d, susrot is here rendered as if it involved the idea of Zsâva 'flux'; the 7 seems to forbid its being taken to mean “let it not be spilled "; the comm., however, so understands it: pracyuto mâ hut. Some of our mss. (M.P.W.) read fvâyâ at beginning of c. The comm. has #7jam in b. Ppp. gives, in a, b, viâyo agram wraṅ svaâham ajarâan eram ea.

docs.title: 30. To secure a woman's love
docs.text:
[Prajâpati (kâminimane' bhimukhikaragakâmak).— âvinam. &nugtutham

I. pathyâpankti ; 3. bhurâg.]

Found in Pâipp. ii. (in the verse-order I, 5,2, 4,3). Used by Kâug. (35. 21 ff.), with vi.8 and other hymns, in a rite concerning women, to gain control over a certain person a mess of various substances is prepared, and her body smeared with it — which is much like the proverbial catching of a bird by putting salt on its tail.

Translated : Weber, v. 218 and xiii. 197 ; Ludwig, p. 5175 Grill, 52,975 Griffith, i. 70; Bloomfield, roo, 311. i I. As the wind here shakes the grass off the earth, so do I shake thy ¹ mind, that thou mayest be one loving me, that thou mayest be one not going away from me.

The last half-verse is the same with the concluding pâdas of i. 34. 5 and vi. 8. 1-3;

SPP. again alters the pada-text to âpacgâṅ (see under i. 34. 5) ; Ppp. has here for e evâ mama tvâyasi. Ppp. reads in a,b 6hâmyâ 'dki vatas (¹) fir-. We should expect ; in a rather ³hṅmyâm, and this the comm. reads, both in his exposition and in his quotation of the pratika from Kâug. ; but Bloomfield gives no such variant in his edition.

2. May ye, O Agvins, both lead together and bring [her] together d with him who loves her. The fortunes (Ś4â4ga) of you (two) have come together, together [your] intents, together [your] courses (vrazâ). ¹ Notwithstanding the accent of wâkgatrhas, it does not seem possible to understand ¹ cd in a as 'if' (Grill, however, so takes it; Weber as above), since the second half- : verse has no application to the Agvins (we should like to alter v2 in cto #2u). But see Bloomfield. ] The translators take (zm ânâ in a as for kâmânân the (two) lovers,'

which it might also well be ; the comm. says kâminâ maya. He also calls vrata simply ¹ a karmanâman, which is very near the truth, as the word certainly comes from root rt (see JAOS. xi., p. cexxix = PAOS. Oct. 1884). Ppp. reads nesitas in b for vaksa- ¹ thas; and, in c, 4, sarvâ 'ṅganâsy agmata saṅ caksunsi san: etc. Both here and in vs. 5 bkâga might possibly have its other sense of genitalia, or imply that by double meaning ; but the comm., who would be likely to spy out any such hidden sense, says

simply Śkâgyani. |In a, agvinâ is misprinted.—W's implications are that if vaksathas were toneless it might be taken as a case of antithetical construction and that there would be no need to join it with ce. . 3. What the eagles [are] wanting to say, the free from disease [are]

wanting to say —there let her come to my call, as the tip to the neck of the arrow (k4ṅnatla).

The first half-verse is very obscure, and very differently understood by the translaa tors ; the rendering above is strictly literal, avoiding the violences which they allow themselves ; the comm. gives no aid ; he supplies str 7oisayaṅz vâkyam to yar, and explains : anamtvas by arogino 'âptaR (? SPP, understands â7âtâṅ) kâmijanâk. Ppp. has an independent text : yas suparpâ raksâ a vâ na vaksana vâ (râtânpitan manak : calye el ¹va gulmalân: yarkâ —too corrupt to make much of. The Anukr. declines to sanction the contraction gaye (va ind..

4. What [was] within, [be] that without; what [was] without, [be]

that within ; of the maidens of many forms seize thou the mind, O herb.

In the obscure formalism of a, b the comm. thinks mind and speech to be intended. i

Why not 7âas and gâgas?] (Of all forms, i.e., as often elsewhere, ' of every sort and kind.' Ppp. reads aṅâkyar for bâkyar yad bâhyaṅr. ] i 5. Hither hath this woman come, desiring a husband ; desiring a wife have I come; like a loud-neighing (k7and) horse, together with fortune have I come.

That is, perhaps, ' I have enjoyed her favors.' None of the mss. fail to accent yâtṅa in c.

docs.title: 31. Against worms
docs.text:
i [Xâṇva.—maktdevatyam uta cândyam. ânugublam : 2. uparigâdvir ag kati; 3. ârg trigiubh ; 4. prâguktâ bykati; 5. prâguktṅ tri|tubk.]

Found also in Pâipp. ii. Used by Kâug. (27. 14 ff.) in an extended healing rite against worms ; the detail of the ceremonial has nothing to do with that of the hymn, and does not illustrate the latter. !

Translated : Kuhn, KZ. xiii, 135 ff. ; Weber, xiii. 199 ; Ludwig, p. 323 ; Grill, 6,98;

Griffith, i. 71 ; Bloomfield, 22, 313.— Cf. Zimmer, pp. 98, 393 ; Mannhardt, Der Baun- i kultus der Germanen, p. 12 ff.; K. Millenhoff, Denkmâler deutscher Poesic aus dem

8. bis r2. Jakrkundert 3, i. 17, 181; and especially the old Germanic analogues adduced by Kuhn, lL.c. Griffith cites Harper's Magazine, June, 1893, p. 1o6, for modern usages in vogue -near-Quebec. ³ I. The great millstone that is Indra's, bruiser (lârhaṇa) of every worm ¹ — with that I mash (2â5) together the worms, as #kdâlva-grains with a millstone. i Our mss. and those of SPP., as well as Ppp., vary, in this hymn and elsewhere, quite ¹ indiscriminately between krâmâ and kfmi, so that it is not at all worth while to report i the details; SPP. agrees with us in printing everywhere krânz. Two of our mss. i

(0. Op.), with one of SPP's, read kr âr in a. Ppp. gives at the end Śkalvâṅ iva. The comm. explains krimin by car irântargarân sarvân ksuârajantin.; ' 2. The seen, the unseen one have I bruised, also the kurâru have I bruised; all the algândus, the cakânas, the worms we grind up with our spell (vâcas).

The distinction of -Jga- and -13- in the manuscripts is very imperfect; I had noted only one of our mss. as apparently having agânâṅn, here and in the next verse ; but SPP.

gives this as found in all his authorities, including oral ones ; and the comm. presents it, and even also Ppp.; so that it is beyond all question the true reading. The comm., g explains it here as ezannâmunah krinmvigesân, but in vs. 3 as opitamansadṅsakaṅ jantin I — which last is plainly nothing more than a guess. Instead of Zurârusm in b, he reads : kurtram, with three of SPP's mss., and Ppp.; other mss. differ as to their distribution ; of and 7 in the syllables of the word, and two of ours (Op. Kp.) give Zyr “ram. Two.

of SPP's authorities give vârcasâ in d. Ppp. further has aârakarm for atyham both : times, and ¢al7lân in c. The omission of Zrânin in d would ease both sense and meter. g

LAs to sarvzs ck, ef. ii. 11. 5, iv. 8.3, and Prat. ii. 17, note. ] :;

3. I smite the alyâṇdus with a great deadly weapon ; burnt [or] unburnt, they have become sapless; those left [or] not left I draw down Ś by my spell (vâ), that no one of the worms be left.

It seems hardly possible to avoid amending at the end to uchigyâtai, passive. Ppp. reads in b dunââdunâ, and its last half-verse is defaced.

4. The one along the entrails, the one in the head, likewise the worm in the ribs, the avaskavâ, the vyadhvarâ — the worms we grind up with ¹ our spell (vâcas).

The comm., and two of SPP's mss., read in b pârsueyam (in the heel '; and SPP. admits into his text after it krâmin, against the great majority of his mss. and against the comm.; none of ours have it, but three (O. Op. Kp.) give krâm?m, which looks like an abortive attempt at it. For wyadhvaram in c, Ppp. has yarar ; all the mss. have wyaâhvarâm ; unless it is to be emended to uyaâvarâom (ct. vi. so. 3, note), it must probably be derived from Śyad) ' pierce '; but the paâa-reading wieadkhvarâm points rather to vi-adkvan ; the comm. takes it from the latter, and also, alternatively, from w7 and a-dkvara; avaskavâ is, according to him, avâggamanasvabhâva ; it seems rather to ; come from Vsâu 'tear.' The expression prâgukta as heretofore defined ' is not used elsewhere in the Anukr. ; it is used by abbreviation for ugaristadvirag (vs. 2); but why f the two verses were not defined together, to make repetition needless, does not appear. In d, again, krântn is a palpable intrusion.

5. The worms that are in the mountains, in the woods, in the herbs, in the cattle, within the waters, that have entered our selves (fanii) — that whole generation (jâniman) of worms I smite. 4

Two of SPP's mss. agree with the comm. in reading 72 for yâ at beginning of c; and the comm. has further lanvas for tanvam:. Ppp. inserts ye before vanegu, and ye (with an avasâna before it) also before osadṅṅyn ; for second half-verse it gives ye 'smâkarr tanno (i.e. lanvo) sthâma cakrir (i.e. cakrur or cakrire) indras tan hantu makatâ vaâk- Ś ena. Praguktâ in the Anukr. apparently repeats this time the superfluous ârṣ7 of vs. 3. 4 The anuvâka 5.4 has 5 hymns and 29 verses, and the extract from the old Anukr. says tate ‘parâtâi or parante.

docs.title: 32. Against worms
docs.text:
[Xâṇva.—sady cam. Śâityadevatyam. ânugtubham : r. 3-6. bhurig gâyatri; 6. 4:3. nicyd uspiṅ.]

This hymn occurs in Pâipp. ii. (with vs. 3 put last), next before the one that here precedes it. Kâug. applies it (27. 21 ff.) in a healing ceremony against worms in cattle.

1 The material appears in Ppp. in the order 1, 2 ab, 4 câab, 5 ab, 6, 3 abc 5 4d. The expression of Kâug. 27. 22, "with the words 72 .azâ] (vs. 5 4) at the end of the hymn," suggests the reduction of the hymn to the norm of the book, 5 vss. (see p. 37). This is berne out by Ppp., where the material amounts to 5 vss. and ends with our 5d. But what the intruded portions are it is not easy to say. The parts missing in Ppp. Ś are our 2 od, 3 4, 5c.

Translated : Kuhn, KZ. xiii. 138; Weber, xiii. zor; Ludwig, p. 500; Grill, 7, roo; Griffth, i. 72; Bloomfield, 23, 317. — Cf. Hillebrandt, Veâa-chrestomatkie, p. 47.

I. Let the sun (ââ4tyâ), rising, smite the worms; setting, let him smite [them] with his rays — the worms that are within the cow.

The change of âdityâs to sâryas in a would rectify the meter. But Ppp. has aââtyas; its b reads sâzyo nimrocan ragmibhir hantu; and for c it has ye ‘atlas krimayeo gavr nap.

2. The worm of all forms, the four-eyed, the variegated, the whitish — I crush (gr) the ribs of it; I hew at (api-orag) what is its head.

The mss., as usual, vary between p7stâs and prsthts in ec. Ppp. has a different version of the first half-verse : yo dviirsa caturaksas krimic cargo arjunak, with our 4 c,d as second half. The Anukr. expects us to make the unusual resolution a-sâ-a in c.

3. Like Atri I slay you, O worms, like Kaṇva, like Jamadagni ; with the incantation of Agastya I mash together the worms.

Ppp. rectifies the meter of a by reading ro krine ; it has agastyar in c, and, for d, our 54. The Anukr. ignores the redundant syllable in our a. Compare TA. iv. 36 (which the comm. quotes, though the editor does not tell from whence): ârina rua krime hanmi kânvena jamâdagninâ : vivâvasor brâhmaṇâ; also MB. ii.7. 1a, b: katas te arrinâ krimir hatas te jamadagnina. SPP. writes in a aztrivâd. Vss. 3-5 are repeated below as v. 23. ro—I2.

4. Slain is the king of the worms, also the chief (szâapâri) of them is slain ; slain is the worm, having its mother slain, its brother slain, its sister slain.

Ppp. has in b stâapacis, and in c, d (its 2 c, 4) -77213 for 72317, and -maṅatâ for bkrata. TA. (iv. 36) has again a parallel verse : Zarâ) krtmmar râja â4y esaz sthapârir hatâk : âthe matâ the pitâ ; cf. also MB. ii. 7. 3 a, b: hataṅ krimpâr: ksudrako; kal mara harah pia. The comm. explains stkapati by saciva.

5. Slain are its neighbors (? vgdâs), slain its further neighbors ? pârivegas), also those that are petty (Śsullakâ), as it were — all those worms are slain.

The translation of d implies the emendation of 7 to 4; all the mss. have the former, but SPP. receives the latter into his text on the authority of the comm., who so unâerstands the word. Ppp. reads in a, b ‘ya vesaso katâsas p- our cis wanting in its 5 text; our d it puts in place of our 3 d. Our k5uâlaka is a kind of Prâkritization of ksudyaka, quoted from MB. under vs. 45 TA. (ib) also has ârko sthurâ âthe ksudrâh. The comm. explains vegâsas as principal houses," and pârivecasas as “neighboring houses." We might suspect -weg-, from root z7g, and so attendants, servants. ‘

6. I crush up (pra-r) thy (two) horns, with which thou thrustest; I split thy receptacle (?), which is thy poison-holder.

The decided majority, both of our mss. and of SPP's, give in c kusâmbharn, which t is accordingly accepted in both editions ; other sporadic readings are kuzrsânbham, kusâbham, kacâbham, kusâtham, kusâmbham and two of SPP's mss. give sukumbhant, nearly agreeing with the sukambham of the comm. Our P.M.E. have wizudâin b. Ppp's version is as follows : pa te crnâami gr 7ge yâbhyâyattan vitaââyasi: atho Śkinadmi taṅ kumbhan: yasmin te nikatan visaṅz, which in c is better than our text, and is supported by the MB. (ii. 7. 3) form of c, 4: azkâi ¹sâanz bhinnakaṅ kumbkho ya esa: vigaâghânakak. The metrical definition of the verse (77: 746=27) given : by the Anukr. is only mechanically correct. (

docs.title: 33. For expulsion of yâksma from all parts of the body
docs.text:
[Brakman.— saptarcam. yaksmavibarhaṅam ; cindramasam ; Śyugyam. ânugtutham.

3. kakummatt; 4. 42. bhurig uspik ; 5. uparig(âdeirâdby hati ; 6. ugiggurtAc nicydanugtubh ; 7. patkyâpaṅkti.]

Found in Pâipp. iv. Corresponds, with important variations, to most of RV. x. 163

(found also in MP., the mantra-text to ApGS.: see Winternitz, Le., p. 99). [ Namely, . â our vss. I, 2, 4 ab with 3 cd, and 5 correspond to MP. i. 17. 1, 2, 3, and 4: the MP. version follows most nearly that of RV. ] The hymn is called by Kâug. (27.27) vṅarka

(from vs. 7 4), and is prescribed in a healing ceremony ; it is also reckoned (54. rr, note) ; to the Zyugya gana ; but the comm. makes up an aṅkolṅga gana of it and ifi. rr; iv. 13;

v.30; ix. 8, which is quite different from the one reported by Bloomfield from the gazamaâlâ in note to Kâug. 32.27 [ on page 89, but agrees with the one reported in B's supplement, page 334, except that for i. ro. 4 should be put iif, rr. 1 J. It (or vs. I) is also employed by Vaâit. (38. 1) in the purusamedâa. ² Translated : by the RV. translators; and Kuhn, KZ. xiii. 66 ff.; Weber, xiii. 205;

Griffith, i. 74; Bloomfield, 44, 321.— Oldenberg compares critically the RV. and AV.

versions, Jie Hymnen des RV., i. p. 243.

I. Forth from thy (two) eyes, (two) nostrils, (two) ears, chin, brain, tongue, I eject (vi-vyk) for thee the yâksma of the head. : ⁴ The verse is RV. x. 163. I, without variant. Two or three of SPP's mss., with the comm., read in b câbukṅât ; MP. has ci(ukâr in the Whish ms. ] ; Ppp. substitutes for it y nâsyâr (le. asyâr), has ata for 4dṅ7, and has for d lalârad vi vayemasi. ! 2. From thy neck (gr7vâs), nape (usṇthâs), vertebrae (kikasâ), back-bone, (two) shoulders, (two) fore-arms, I eject for thee the yâksma of the arms. : This, again, is precisely RV. x. 163.2. Ppp. reads in b anṅZyâs, and in â wrastas

(for bakubhyam) and vrhâmasi. The pl. grṅvâs for 'neck' designates, according to the comm., the r4 small bones found there ; and he quotes CB. xii. 2. 4. ro for authority.

The usnthâs he declares to be certain vessels (²âg7); the kiṅasâs, to be jatruvaksogatâsthini, which is quite indefinite.

3. Forth from thy heart, lung (klomân), hâliksṇa, (two) sides, (two)

mâtasnas, spleen, liver, we eject for thee the yâksma. : Weber conjectures « gall " for Zalzksna (Ppp. haltRsma), and “kidney " for matasna.

The comm. defines klomân as “a kind of flesh-mass in the neighborhood of the heart,"

haltksna as etatsarmyṅakar tatsambandkâan mâṅsapinâdavicesat, and matasnâbhyâm as whkayaparcvasambandhabhyârn: vy kyâbkyân tatsamipastkapitiadhârap arr 6 by an: va.

For a, Ppp. has Ślomnas te kydayâbkyo. Of this verse, only the latter half has a paral- : lel in RV, namely x. 163. 3 c,d, where d is vavied to yaknâṅ placâtkyo vt vrhâmi te. : The Anukr. foolishly rejects all resolution in b,

4. Forth from thine entrails, guts, rectum, belly, (two) paunches, put, navel, I eject for thee the yâkyma.

The comm. explains guââbkyas by Śntrasamypasthebkyo malamutrapravakaṇa- : margebkyak, and places by bakucchkidrân malapârrat; and he quotes CB. xii. 9. I. 3, He Ś where many of the names in the verse occur. RV. (also MP.) has the first half-verse, as 163. 3 a, b, reading k7dayat for udârâtl. Forb, c, 4, ] Ppp. substitutes our 6 b, c ] d, but with pâṇyor in c and vrââmasi at the end J. The Anukr. again rejects all resolutions, which would make the verse a fair anuṣtubk, and counts 748 : 7+ 7=29.

5. From thy (two) thighs, knees, heels, front feet, hips, fundament (? bhâṅsas), I eject for thee the yâksma of the rump.

In the translation here is omitted Ś4âsadam, the pure equivalent of bkasaâyâm, and hence as superfluous in sense as redundant in meter. Is not prâzâada ' toe '? The verse is nearly RV. x, 163. 4, which, however, omits bkasadyâm, and reads, after cronîbhyâam, bhâsadst, indicating the whole region of anus and pudenda. Ppp. ends the verse (like 2 and 4) with wyââmasi. Several of our mss., with two or three of; SPP's, carelessly begin with rṅ-. MP. has in b jaṅghâbhyâm for parsnibhyâm, and in d dkvaṅsasas. The verse seems to be scanned by the Anukr. as 8 + 7:8 + 1 I= 34.

6. From thy bones, marrows, sinews, vessels, (two) hands, fingers, nails, I eject for thee the yâksma.

Pâṇt is distinctively ' palm,' and might properly be so rendered here. Nearly all our sanhâtâ-mss., with most of SPP's, omit the visarga before snâvabhyo. Ppp. has a different a, c,d: Zastebhyas te mâṅnsebhyas . : yaksman: prŚri6ṅhyo magiabhyo nâdyâaṅ: virvahâmast. The Anukr. scans as 747: 9+38=31.

7. What [yâksma is] in thine every limb, every hair, every joint — the yâksma of thy skin do we, with Kagyapa's ejector (vztarkâ) eject away (vâsvatc).

The first half-verse corresponds to RV. x. 163. 6. a, b, which (as also MP.) reads thus : âṅgaâ-angal lémno-lomno jatâm pârvani-parvaṇi; and Ppp. agrees with it, except in having Śadâham for jâlam, Ppp. also omits d. In d our P. M., with some of SPP's mss., read viṅar-, as does also the comm. |vâ"arkanṇs J. In our edition, an accentmark has fallen out under -7caz7 in e.

docs.title: 34. Accompanying the sacrifice of an animal
docs.text:
[Atharvan.—pâcupatyam ; pagubhâgakaragam. trârstubkham.]

Found in Paâipp. iii.; and also in the Black-Yajus texts, TS. (iil. r. 43), and K. : (xxx. 8, in part). Used by Kaâug. (44. 7) in the vagâ;amana ceremony, accompanying the anointing of the vagâ ; in the same, vs. 5 accompanies (44- r5) the stoppage of the f victim's breath; and the same verse appears in the funeral rites (31.33), with verses from xviii. 2 and 3, in connection with the lighting of the pile. This hymn and the one f next following are further employed among the kâmyâni, with invocation of Indra and I Agni, by one who (desires the world" (59.21: “desires over-lordship of all the : world," comm.). In Vâit. (10.16), the hymn (so the comm.) is said on the release of : the victim from the sacrificial post in the paculandha.

Translated : Weber, xiii. zo7; Ludwig, P. 433 ; Griffith, i. 75. — See also Roth, Dzber qen AV. p. 14..

I. The lord of cattle, who rules over () the cattle, the four-footed, and who also over the two-footed —Ilet him, bought off, go to [his] sacrificial portion; let abundances of wealth attach themselves to (sac) the sacrificer. 1 In the TS. version, this verse comes second (the verse-order being 5, I, 3,4, 2). Both

TS. ard K. have at the beginning yârâm, which Ppp. supports by reading esârn, and â which rectifies the meter of a: this gives quite a different application to c, and a different cast to the meaning of the verse. TS. has also ca for yâs in b, ayâm ('yâm) for sâ in c, and it ends (better) with yâjamânasya santu. K. (Weber) has for b catuspada uta ye dvipâadaṇ, and for c niskrṅas te yajuiyam Śhâgar: yantu; and Ppp. differs from g it only slightly, adding v7 after uta in b, and ending c with yajṅiyâ yanti lokanm.

Apparently it is the lord of cattle who is to be bribed to content himself with his sacri:

ficial share, in lieu of taking the whole. The Anukr. does not heed the irregularities of meter in a, b. [The Ppp. form of b seems to be catuspadam uta vâ ye dvipadat ?

2. Do ye, releasing (pra-muc) the seed of being, assign progress

(garâ) to the sacrificer, O gods ; what hath stood brought hither (upâkrta), strenuous (cagamaândâ), let it go upon the dear path of the gods. 4 ² TS. (and K. ?) rectifies the meter of a (whose irregularity the Anukr. ignores) by reading pramuṅcâmaândâs ; it also has jṅvâm for priyâm in d. Ppp. gives gopa for retas in a, ¹ and in b makes âkatta and devâs change places; in â it reads ar7. Priyâm may qualify 1 the subject in d : let it, dear [to the gods], go ' etc. Upâṅrta and gacamândâ have their usual technical senses, ' brought to the sacrifice ' and ' efficient in the performance of ² religious duty '; the latter is explained by the comm. alternatively, as "being put to death " or leaping up " (root gag) ¹ Devas is, according to him, first « the breaths, sight ¹ etc.," then " the gods, Agni etc." E. Sieg discusses pârhas, Gurupâjakaumuds, p. 98.

3. They who, giving attention to (ann-âkr) the one being bound, looked after [him] with mind and with eye—let the divine Agni at first

(dgre) release them, he the all-working, in unison with (saz-7â) progeny. 1 TS. and MS. (i. 2. 15) have badhyâmanas for didkyanâs, and TS. follows it with abhyâtks-; and in c combines agnts tâṅ ; MS. also has (47. Both read in 4 prajâpatis for viguâkarmâ; and TS. ends with sa vidanâs. Ppp. has in c mumukta devas, and,;

for 6, prajâparis prajabhis sarvidanar ; it then adds another verse : yesân: prâapo na badknanti badâdkari gavṅn pacunâm uta paurusânam : indras tam (i.e. (3n agre ¹ pra etc.). The comm. reads in a vadkyamaâanawm, which is better ; he explains saz7rarânas by saha cabdâyamaânas, as if from the root 77 ' bark 'l Comparison with the 6 g next verse seems to show the other animals, comrades of the victim, to be aimed at in the verse. Cf. Weber's notes, p. 209, and esp. his reference to CB. iii. 7. 45.— MS.

has 747, p. tn : see above, page xe.

4. The cattle that are of the village, all-formed, being of various i forms, manifoldly of one form —let the divine Vâyu at first release them, Prajâpati, in unison with progeny. re TS. and K. have aranyâs ' of the forest ' in a, for grâmyâs, and TS. combines vâyâs

²7 inc, and ends again with -widanaṅ. TA. (iil. 11) has two versions (vss. 29, 32), of which the second precisely agrees with TS., while the first has grâamy7s, like our ⁴ text (and agnts (37 in c). Ppp. is quite different : ya ranyâs pacave vigvarâpâ uta ye kur vpaK:. mumukta devak prajâpatis prajabhis sam vidanar.

5. Foreknowing, let them first (pârva) receive the breath (27734)

coming to [them] forth from the limbs. Go to heaven; stand firm with thy bodies ; go to paradise (suargâ) by god-traveled roads.

Ppp. has devas for parve in a, tabkhyâam for divam in c, and at the end -Ś4âg civebhâṅ. TS. reads g7kuanti in a; and TS. K. MS. (ii. 5. ro c,d) invert the order of c and d, and give the better reading âsadkhṅsu for dfvan: gacha of. RV.x.16.3 J; MS. also has kutâs for svargam. The comm. makes p7rvz mean the gods previously stationed in the atmosphere "; perhaps it is ' before the demons get hold of it.

docs.title: 35. To expiate errors in the sacrifice : to Vigvakarman
docs.text:
[4 7giras.— vâicvakarmaṇam. trâigubkam : I. byhatigar 5Aâ ; 4, 5. bṅurâ.)

Found (except vs. 5, and in the verse-order 2, 3, I, 4) in Pâipp. i. The same four verses are found in TS. (iii. 2. 8v3 : in the order 2, 4, 3, I), and the first three in MS. (ii. 3. 8: in the order 1, 3, 2). The hymn is used by Kâug. (38. 22) in a rite intended, according to the comm., to prevent faults of vision (â7ṣtidosanivâranâya ; Kegava says " to prevent rain," vrstinivâranâya ; perhaps his text is corrupt), accompanying the eating of something in an assembly. Its employment (59.21) with the hymn next preceding was noticed under the latter. The comm. (differing in his reading and division of the rules from the edited text of Kâug.) declares it to be used in all the szva sacrifices, to accompany the purastâad homas (59. 23-4: uttarena savapurastââ”âhoman); and vs. 5 is used (3.16) with a purastad homa in the parvan sacrifices. In Vâit. the hymn appears (9.7) in the câturmâsya sacrifice, with two oblations to Mahendra and Vigvakarman respectively ; and again (29. 22) in the agnicayana. In all these applications there is nothing that suits the real character of the hymn.

Translated : Weber, xiii. 211 ; Ludwig, p. 302 (vss. 1-4); Griffith, i. 76.

I. They who, partaking [of soma] (Ś4aks), did not prosper (7âk) in good things, whom the fires of the sacrificial hearth were distressed about (anu-taya-) — what was the expiation (zvayâ) of their ill-sacrifice, may Vigvakarman (' the all-worker ') make that for us a good sacrifice.

The translation implies emendation of Jârâṣtis in c to -fes, and of r4n in â to 4m, tâm is read by the comm., as well as by TS. and MS., and SPP. even admits it into - his text, though nearly all his mss., as well as ours, read 747. Our P. and M. read avy dhis at end of a; TS. has any kis, MS. ânacâs. TS. elides the a of gnu in b; it begins c with iyâm for yâ, and ends it with â4ristyâi, thus supporting our emendation. Both TS. and MS. give Śrnorn in 4, and MS. puts it after viwâkarmâ. The pada- : mss. read in c avasyâ, but SPP. alters his pada-text to awa-yâj, on the authority of the comm. ; it is a matter of indifference, as the concluding element, in spite of the native grammarians, is doubtless the root yâ. Ppp. gives durâgyâ swigias in c, d. The various ; readings, here and in the following verses, are in good part of the kind which show ; that the text-makers were fumbling over matter which they did not understand. The : comm. is no better off. Here, in a, he is uncertain whether to take zdâ as tas if ' or ; ⁴not,' and to make vâsâni object of bhaksâyantas or of âanydhvs C= varâhitavantas, which is not bad). The fires, pada b, are personified in like fashion at AGS. iv. I. 253. The verse (12412: 9+ II=44) is much more irregular than the definition of the Anukr. admits.

z. The seers declare the master (2ât7) of the sacrifice by reason of sin disportioned, distressed about [his] offspring. What honeyed drops he offended in (? apa-râdk), with them let Vigvakarman unite (sam-sy7) us.

MS. has in a the equivalent yâjamânam; its b reads vihâya prajâm anutâṅyamânâh ; while TS. has prajâ(k) ntrbhaktâ(k) anutapyâmanâj, and Ppp. nirbkâgara bhâgâd anutagyamâanâ. TS. and MS. make the lost drops only two : madâka"yaṇ i stokâṅ . tâbhyâm, with 724 instead of yân, and hence rarâdâka. The translation ' implies correction to madhavwy-, as read by both the parallel texts and the comm.;

SPP's text agrees with ours in reading the mazkaguy- of all the mss. (except three of ¹ SPP's, which follow the comm.). All the sa7z4âtâ-mss. make the absurd combination ; nas rébhik in â, seeming to have in mind the participle zaszâ; SPP. retains nasrephis in his text, while ours emends to nas #bkis, as given in the comment to Prât. ii. 31.

Ppp. has our second half-verse as its 3 c, d; it reads madka"yâr stokân upa ya rarââha saṅ maâ tarâis syjad vigvakarmâ. The comm. takes anu and za5y- in b as two independent words ; he explains aga rarââṅa in c by antaritân krtavan, which is doubtless its virtual meaning. W's prior draft reads : "what honeyed drops he failed of "— that is, 'missed.'

3. Thinking the soma-drinkers to be unworthy of gifts ? adânyâ),

[though] knowing of the sacrifice, [he is] not wise (2ṅra) in the conjuncture (samayâ); in that, this man is bound having committed a sin, do thou, O Vigvakarman, release him for his well-being. Ś The offense here had in view is far from clear. Instead of adznyâ (which occurs only here), TS. has the apparently unintelligent ananyân ; MS. reads ayajṅîyâṅ yayatyân mâny- ' thinking the unfit for offering to be fit for offering ' (or vize versa); both have in b 4777 âsya for yajṅâsya, and samare for ye. Ppp. gives the second half-verse as 2 e, 4, and ends it with pra mumugdhy enar. TS.MS. have no yâr at beginning of ce; TS. gives énag cakyvân mâhi, and MS. eno makâc cakrvân b-, and TS. esâm for ed. : The comm. explains aâdânyan as ajṅarvâropena dânânarkân, takes na in b as particle of t comparison, and makes samaya equal sazgrâma : “as if one by confidence in the strength of his own arm should think the opposing soldiers despicable "! The verse 1 (11+ 11: Io+I2=44) has marked irregularities which the Anukr. ignores. ⁴ 4. Terrible [are] the seers ; homage be to them I what sight [is] theirs, and the actuality (sazyâ) of their mind. For Brihaspati, O bull (makisâ),

[be] bright (dyumdânt) homage ; O Vigvakarman, homage to thee l protect thou us. ¹ The translation follows our text, though this is plainly corrupted. TS. makes b less unintelligible by reading câksusas for câksur yâr, and sa#âkṅuâ for satyâm ; Ppp. has fF in the half-verse only minor variants : Śâzma for ghorâs, 'stu for astu, sanârk for satyam. Inc, TS. has makt sâr for the senseless makisa, and the comm. presents the same ; Ppp. reads brkaspate makisâya dive : name vigv-. TS, gives for 4 nâmo vigvâ- ; karmaṇe sâ u pare asmân. Ind all the pada-mss. have the strange blunder 474, for â pakt as required by the sense and by the sa7zkârâ-text; and SPP. adopts the blunder, a thus giving a pada-reading that is inconvertible into his own sa7z4itâ. The comm.

takes reayas in a as " the breaths, sight etc.," and satya in b as yazharthadargi and ; he founds on this interpretation the use in Kâug. 38. 22, "against faults of vision."

5. The sacrifice's eye, commencement, and face : with voice, hearing, mind I make oblation. To this sacrifice, extended by Vigvakarman, let the gods come, well-willing.

The verse is found in no other text, and is perhaps not a proper part of the hymn ; it is repeated below as xix. 58. 5. A few of the saṅṅitâ-mss. (including our O.) ignore the # at beginning of d. The comm. is not certain whether the three nominatives in a designate Agni or sacrificial butter ; but he has no scruple about making them objects to jukomi.

docs.title: 36. To get a husband for a woman
docs.text:
[Pativedana.— ag arcam. âgntsomiyam. trâ3igubkam I. bhurij ; 2, 5-7. anuṣtudṅ;

8. nicrtpuraugni-.]

Found (except vss. 6,8) in Pâipp. ii. (in the verse-order 1,3, 2, 4, 5, 7). Used by I Kâug. (34. 13 ff.) among the women's rites, in a ceremony for obtaining a husband; vss. 5 and 7 are specially referred to or quoted, with rites adapted to the text. Itis further regarded by the schol. and the comm. as signified by pattvedana (75. 7), at the g beginning of the chapters on nuptial rites, accompanying the sending out of a wooer or paranymph. i Translated : Weber, v. 219; xiii 214 ; Ludwig, p. 476; Grill, 55, roz ; Griffith, i. 78; I Bloomfield, 94, 322. — Ct. Zimmer, p. 306. I. Unto our favor, O Agni, may a wooer come, to this girl, along with our fortune (44443). Enjoyable (juṣtâ) [is she] to suitors (varâ), agreeable at festivals (sâmana) ; be there quickly good-fortune for her with a husband. The text is not improbably corrupt. Ppp. reads in a, b sumatiṅ skandaloke idan , ar kumaâryâmâno bhagena; but it combines c and d much better into one sentence by g reading for d osark patyṅ bhavati (-tn 7) subhage (yam. The comm. explains sambha- ¹ las as sambhâsakuk samâadâarâ vâ; er else, he says, it means kiṅsakak pârvam abkilzsavigharr kanyâm anicchan purusah. He quotes ApGS. i. 4 to show that varâ also means paranymph. Ju31â4 he quotes Paṇini to prove accented jâstâ. In d he reads ṅ3am, and declares it to signify sukhakaram. Bergaigne, Rel. ved. i. 159, takes sâmana as = 'marriage.' ] 2. Fortune enjoyed by Soma, enjoyed by Brahman, brought together by Aryaman; with the truth of divine Dhâtar, the husband-finder I perform (k7).

Ppp. has a mutilated first half-verse : somajasto aryampnâ sarbkṇto bhaga; and at the end patirvedanan. The comm. understands in a ;raṅma- to mean the Gandharya, who and Soma are the first husbands of a bride (xiv. 2.3, 4). He does not see in b4aga anything but kanyârâpam bhâagadkeyam ; but the meaning «favors " is not impossible.

I Both hagas ("fortune " or favors") and pativedanan: (the ceremony called a husband-finder") are objects of Z7nomâ; which, accordingly, needs to be rendered by 'make ' or ' procure ' for the one combination and by perform ' for the other. It : is hardly a case of zeugma.— Bloomfield notes that sâ7bk=rta contains a conscious ( allusion to sambkala, vs. I. ]

3. May this woman; O Agni, find a husband ; for king Soma maketh her of good-fortune ; giving birth to sons, she shall become chief consort (mâkisr) ; having gone to a husband, let her, having good-fortune, bear i rule (vi-7â7).

Three mss. (including our P.O.) read aârâ in a. |For videsza in a (Grammara

8 850 a), ] Ppp. has videstu; at end of b it reads a7 krportu; and it changes the second half-verse into an address by reading bk4avâsi, and subhage vi râ3jâ. The comm. explains sakhisi as makantyâ cresthâ bhâryâ. The fourth pada is best scanned a as jagatr, with resolution ga-tu-4 or insert sâ before subhâga.

4. As, O bounteous one (maghâuvan), this pleasant covert hath been dear to the well-settled (susâd ) wild beasts, so let this woman be enjoyed of Bhaga, mutually dear, not disagreeing with her husband.

The translation here involves emendation of the unmanageable susâdâa in b to suṣâ- ââm, as suggested by iii. 22. 6. SPP. has in his paâa-text suesâdâ) (as if nom. of ; susâdas), and makes no note upon the word — probably by an oversight, as of our gada-mss. only Op. has such a reading ; the comm. understands susâdzâs, and explains it by sukhena sthâtur yogyak ' comfortable to dwell in'; which is not unacceptable. The comm. also has in a maghauvân, and in d abkirâdhayantr (= abhivardhkayanti, or else pulrapacvââibhih samydâhâ bhavanir). Ppp. has at the beginning yarhz kharrar: : maghavaṅ carur eu, and, in c, 9, yan vaya justa bhagasyâ 'stu sanpr-. All our sam hitâ-mss. save one (H.), and half of SPP's, give esâṅ p7- in a-b; but the comment 4 to Prat. ii. 57 quotes this passage as illustration of the loss of its final visarga by egâs.

Kaâug. (34. 14) evidently intends an allusion to this verse in one of its directions : n7g3âkharad vedyâm mantroktâni 'the articles mentioned in the text on the sacrificial hearth from a wild beast's covert,' but the comm. does not explain the meaning. The

Anukr. ignores the redundancy of a syllable in c. Pronounce juṣtâ warm and reject nâri?— The use of sâmpriya in dual and plural is natural: its extension to the : singular is rather illogical (cf. TS. iv. 2, 4), unless we assign intensive value to san

(very dear). J : 5. Ascend thou the boat of Bhaga, full, unfailing ; with that cause to l cross over hither a suitor who is according to thy wish. I Or pratikâmyâ may perhaps mean (responsive to thy love.' Ppp. has in a 7 ruṅa, . f in b anuparas-, and for c, d frayo pâsa hitanṅ yas patis patikâmyak. The comm. ¹ understands #pa- in c as an independent word. With this verse, according to the . ² comm., the girl is made to ascend a properly prepared boat. fi 6. Shout to [him], O lord of riches; make a suitor hither-minded; ⁴ I turn the right side to every one who is a suitor according to thy wish.

g y g y

Circumambulation with the right side toward one is a sign of reverence. 4 krandaya in a is perhaps a real causative, ‘make him call out to us '; the comm. takes it so. His explanation [page 332] of the accompanying rite is : “offering rice in the night, one should make the girl step forward to the right.” 4 : 7. Here [is] gold, bdellium; here [is] âzk5â, likewise fortune; these have given thee unto husbands, in order to find one according to thy

Auksâ (ct. auksagandhi, iv. 37.3) seems to be some fragrant product of the ox; or

(it may perhaps come from uk5 ' sprinkle,' but not through uksan. The mss. vary here,

as everywhere else, in an indiscriminate manner between gâggulu and geâlguin ; here

the majority of ours have -k-, and the great majority of SPP's have Śg-; but gg- is accepted (as elsewhere) in our edition, and -k- in the other ; Ppp. reads -g-, the comm. gg Ppp. has further vayam ukso athe bhaga ; and, in cd, adkup patik-. The comm. defines guggulu as "a well-known kind of article for incense," and for 2u&ṣa he quotes from Kegava (k2ucikasâtrabhâagyakâraâs) the couplet given in Bloomfield's Kâugika on P-335 (but reading surabhin ganâhan ksiraṅz). The comm. p. 332, explains that with this verse is to be performed a binding on and fumigation and anointing of the girl with ornaments, bdellium, and zuksa respectively. I BR., iv. 947, suggest pratikâmyâya. 1

8. Hither let Savitar conduct for thee, conduct a husband that is according to thy wish ; do thou assign [him] to her, O herb.

The second nayatu is a detriment equally to sense and to meter ; the Anukr. counts it to a, and the pada-mss. mark the division accordingly. Emendation of toâm inc to ²âm is strongly suggested. The verse hardly belongs to the hymn as originally made up ; there has been no reference elsewhere to an herb"; nor does Kâug. introduce such an element.

In the concluding anuvâka I 6.] are 5 hymns, 31 verses: the Anukr. says accordingly triṅgadekadhiko 'ntyak.

This is the end also of the fourth pragaâthaka.

I One or two mss. sum up the book as 36 hymns and 207 verses.

Book III.

docs.title: 3.1 Book III
docs.text:
¹ L The third book is made up largely of hymns of 6 verses each.

It contains r3 such hymns, but also six hymns (namely 4, 7,

3, I6, 24, 30) of 7 verses each, six hymns (namely 5, 6, 11, IS, ² 19, 29) of 8 verses each, two hymns (namely 12, 17) of g verses each, two hymns (namely 20, 21) of ro verses each, one hymn

(namely 31) of 11 verses, and one hymn (namely ro) of 13 verses.

See Weber's introduction to his translation, p. 178. The possibility of critical reduction to the norm is well illustrated by hymn

31—compare pages r and 37. The whole book has been trans- â lated by Weber, fndische Studien, vol. xvii. (1885), pages 177-314.1

docs.title: 1. Against enemies
docs.text:
Lâtharvan.— senâmokanam. bakudevatyam. (trâigubham : 2. virâ3dgarbhâ bhurij;

3) 6. anustubh ; 5. vir âtpuraugpik.] 4, Found in Paipp. iii., next after the one which here follows it. In Kâug. (14.17), : this hymn and the next are called #okanâni 'confounders,' and are used in a rite

(14. 17-21) for confounding an enemy's army; its details have nothing to do with those ' of the hymns.

Translated : Ludwig, p. 518; Weber, xvii. 180; Griffith, i. 81 ; Bloomfield, rar, 325.

I. Let Agni, knowing, go against our foes, burning against the impre- ⁴ cator, the niggard ; let him confound (mokaya-) the army of our adversaries (pâra) ; and may Jâtavedas make them handless. fi Ppp. makes catrṅn and vidvân in a change places. SPP. reports that the text used by the comm. reads pal after agnir both here and in z. r a. The comm. signalizes the beginning of the book by giving absurd etymologies of agnâ at the length of nearly 1 a page. Pada c lacks a syllable, unless we allow ourselves to resolve sâna-ârm.

2. Ye, O Maruts, are formidable for such a plight; go forward upon

[them], kill, overcome l The Vasus have killed [them]; suppliant [are] : these; for let Agni, their messenger, go against [their foes], knowing. â The second half-verse is rendered literally as it stands, but is certainly badly corrupt. ¹ Ppp. has am ny dar vasavo nâthitebhyo agnir by egâr vidoan pratyetu catrân, which is much more acceptable : zârk- would be ‘for [us] who supplicate' D7âas seems to have blundered in here out of =. 1 a. Ludwig emends nâthîtâs to -t47, which would

Ś improve c, but leave it unconnected with 4. In our edition p7âty etu is an erratum for ¹ pratyetu, which all the mss. read. The comm., with his customary neglect of accent, af Sx eee takes ugrâs in a as vocative. He takes iâe as a locative (= apradkrṣye saṅgrâmalaksane karmaṇt), against the testimony of the other passages where the word occurs, and supplies matsakâyâs. In b, he reads (with a couple of SPP's mss. that follow him) mynâtas, and takes it (again against the accent) as accus. pl. Amir an inc herenders as an imperative. The meter of the verse (11 + II : 12 + I3=47) is capable of being fitted to the description of the Anukr. Ir +10: 124 12=45 ] by duly managing the resolutions. [Aufrecht, KZ. xxvii. 219 (1885), reconstructs the vs., putting my ââyata for mypâta in b and reading c, d thus: âmzmy dan vâsave nathitâso agnir kt catrṅn pratyeti vidhyan. Cf. Bloomfield, 326.— Roth gives (in his notes) m7 dara for mypṇata and (in his collation) yesâm for by esa, as Ppp. readings.

3. The army of enemies, O bounteous one, playing the foe against us — do ye (two), O Vrtra-slaying Indra, Agni also, burn against them.

The verse is found also as SV. ii. 1215, which reads ckatruyartm in b, and begins c with bhaâ tâm (44m is read by the comm., and is called for as an emendation in our verse); it also has the correct accent amâtrasenâm, which is found in only two of our mss. (O.0p.) and three of SPP's; both editions read -sézânz. In our text, âgnk in d is a misprint for agnâ. SPP. combines asmân ck-, badly: cf. i. 19. 4, note. J

4. Impelled, O Indra, forwards ? pravârâ) by thy (two) bays —let thy thunderbolt go forth, slaughtering (pra-m?) the foes ; smite the on-coming, the following, the fleeing (pârâṅc) ; scatter their actual intent.

The verse is RV. iii. 30. 6; which, however, reads at the beginning pr â si te (as does also the comm. ), accents in c praticâ anâcâṅ (and the comm. claims the same for our text), and has for 4 vk var satyâr: krnukhi vistâm astu, which is even more unintelligible than our text. Weber proposes visvaksatyâm as a compound, " turning itself in every direction"; this, however, makes nothing out of -s2zyaz. Ludwig translates e fulfil their design in all [both] directions," which is not very clear. Ppp. reads zâvaṅ: vistaP: kypuki satyam esâm ; also quite obscure. The comm. takes sazyan: as ² established, settled," and visvak krpukhi as scatter, unsettle, make uncertain. One would like to take vâsvak- as something like ' contrariwise,' with the general sense " turn their plans against themselves.” Ppp. has further aṅaj for anâcas in c.

5. O Indra, confound the army of our enemies; with the blast of fire;,— of wind, make them disappear, scattering.

The defective first half-verse is completed by Ppp. in this form: suanomohanar: krnva (i.e. ky navas 2) indrâ 'mitrebhyas tvan. The second half-verse is also 2.3 c, d. The comm. explains âkrâjyâ by dakanavisaye ya vegitâ garis ath vidhayâ vegagatya tayor eva va gatyâ.

6. Let Indra confound the army ; let the Maruts slay with force; let Agni take away its eyes ; let it go back conquered.

All the mss. read â1â7a, vocative, at the beginning of the verse ; but SPP's text, as well as ours, emends to dra s-; and this the comm. also has. The comm. further in c dhattam instead of dattâm.

docs.title: 2. Against enemies
docs.text:
[Atharvan.— senâmohanam. lakudevatyam. trâ(gubkam : 2-4. anugubk.] ¹ Found in Pâipp. iii., next before the hymn here preceding. Used in Kâug. only with the latter, as there explained.

Translated : Weber, xvii. 183 ; Griffith, i. 82 ; Bloomfield, 121, 327.—CfŚ. Bergaigne-

Henry, Manuel, p. 139.

I. Let Agni our messenger, knowing, go against [them], burning against the imprecator, the niggard ; let him confound the intents of our 4 adversaries ; and may Jatavedas make them handless.

All the mss. have in a the false accent prazy éru (seemingly imitated from 1. 2 d, where kâ requires it), and SPP. retains it; our edition makes the necessary emendation to prâty etu. Ppp. appears to have cazrân instead of vidvân at end of a.

2. Agni here hath confounded the intents that are in your heart; let him blow (dkam) you away from [our] home; let him blow you forth in every direction.

Ppp. has dkamâtu for -matn both times. The comm. renders amâmukat by moka- { yatu, in accordance with his doctrine that one verbal form is equivalent to another.

3. O Indral confounding [their] intents, move hitherward with [their]

design (âkṅri) ; with the blast of fire, of wind, make them disappear, : scattering. : The second half-verse is identical with I. 5 b, c. Pâda b apparently means (take ² i ¹: away their design, make them purposeless '; the comm., distorting the sense of arvâz, : makes it signify "go against [their army], with the design [of overwhelming it]." GH Ppp. reads zkâtyâ '7ki (i.e. -tyâs adki?). In our edition, restore the lost accent-mark over the -27a of (râra in a.

4. Go asunder, ye designs of them; also, ye intents, be confounded ; t= g also what is today in their heart, that smite thou out from them. ; All the mss. have in b câttâni, as if not vocative, and SPP. retains the accent, while i our text emends to ciâtâniy; the comm. understands a vocative. The comm. further : takes Śyâkâtayas as one word, explaining it as either virudâhâṅ sar:kalpâaṅ or else

(qualifying devs understood) as carrânân vividhakâtyutpâdakâk. For dâ, rather, I : (that of them smite thou out from [them]. ] . 5. Confounding the intents of those yonder, seizing their limbs, O

Apvâ, go away; go forth against [them] ; consume [them] in their hearts with pangs (gâka) ; pierce the enemies with seizure (grâkâ), the foes with darkness.

The verse is RV. x. 103.12, which reads in a cittâm pratilobkâyanii, and, for d, . : andkenâ 'mUrâs. timasâ sacantam; and SV. (ii. 1211) and VS. (xvii. 44) agree with an RV. Both pada-texts give in b gykâṇâ, as impv. ; but the word is translated above (in accordance with Grassmann's suggestion) as aor. pple. fem. gr427â, because this com- Cc bines so much better with the following gâre "ki. A number of the saṅṅilâ-mss. (including our P.s.m.E.s.m.I.H.p.m.) make the curious blunder of accenting agv2 in b: the comm. explains it as a pâpadevatâ, adding the precious etymology apavâyayati apagamayari sukham prânaṅe ca. Weber, ix. 482, thinks apo has reference to impurity (root 47) and to diarrhoea as caused by fear. To Weber's citation (xvii. 184) from the Puraṇa, add the line near the beginning of the Bhiyma book, MBh. ui. I. 18, crutvâ tu ninadar yodhâk cakyn-matram prasusruvuk. The Anukr. ignores the redundancy in a; emendation to cittâ would remove it.

6. Yonder army of our adversaries, O Maruts, that comes contending against us with force — pierce ye it with baffling darkness, that one of them may not know another.

The verse is an addition (as vs. 14) to RV. x. ro3 Aufrecht, 2d ed'n, vol. ii. p. 682 J, but forms a proper part of SV. (ii. 1210) and VS. (xvii. 47). RV.VS. read in ba?âyââi nas (for asmân âty abht) ; SV. has abṅyâti; all have in c gâhata for vidkyata; and with the latter Ppp. intends to agree, but has gukarta. For eâm in d, RV. gives amâsam, SV. etésam, and VS. amt and accordingly at the end jândân. It takes violence to compress our b into a zâ57ubk pâda.

docs.title: 3. For the restoration of a king
docs.text:
[Aâtharvan.—nânâdevatyam utâ" gneyam. trâigubham : 3. 42. bhurik paṅ2t ; 5, 6. anugubh.]

Found in Paâipp. ii. (our vs. 5 coming last). Used by Kâug. (16. 30), with the hymn next following, in a ceremony for the restoration of a king to his former kingdom. In Vâit. (9.2), vs. I accompanies a morning oblation to Agni anzkavant in the sâkamedha rite of the câturmâsya sacrifice; and again (30. 27), vs. 2 is used at the end of the Sâulrâmaṇt ceremony.

Translated : Ludwig, p. 441 ; Weber, xvii. 185 ; Griffith, i. 83 ; Bloomfield, rr2, 327. — Cf. Bergaigne-Henry, Manuel, p. 140.

I. He hath shouted ? krand) ; may he be protector of his own here; O Agni, bend apart the two widened firmaments (râ4asz) ; let the all. possessing Maruts harness (yz7) thee; lead thou hither with homage yon man of bestowed oblation.

This is a very literal translation of the obscure verse, which is plainly an adaptation or corruption, or both, of a RV. verse in a hymn to Agni (vi. II. 4: it is repeated, without variant, in MS. iv. 14. 15) : ddidyntat sv âpâko vibhâvâ 'gne yâjasva rédast urict: âyârnz nâ yâr nâmasâ râtâhavya aṅjânti suprayâsam pâṅca jânaṅ; and, what is very noteworthy, the latter half-verse of RV. is decidedly more closely reflected in the Ppp. version : amun naya namasâa ratakayyo yujanti suprajasain paṅca janak; Ppp. has also (kavat at end of a. It could not be expected to find concinnity and sense in a verse so originated ; the address seems to be changed from Agni to Indra, and some sort of comparison aimed at between the latter and the reinstated king. The paâa-text divides in a svaopâ}, and, as the word may be a part of the adaptation of the original to the purpose of this hymn J, the translation so treats it, instead of substituting, as Weber and Ludwig do, susapâk; the comm. explains it both ways: svakîyanâm prajanâm pâlakak sukarmâ v3. The comm. makes the king subject of âcikradâat in a, apparently takes vyâcasva in b as one word (= gyâapuuki), toc in c as designating Agni Cynṅjantu = prapnuvantu, tvatsakâyâa bhavantu), and amin in â as the king. The Anukr. ignores the jagarr pada (c) or lets it offset a counted as rol. The : usual compound is so-âpâs, but so-apâs, though not quotable, is quite possible. , 2. Indra, the inspired one, however far away, let the ruddy ones set in motion hither (â-cyâvaya-) in order to friendship, when the gods ven. ture (?) for him a gâyatrî, a bykati, a song (arkâ), with the sâutrâmaṇâ (ceremony).

This verse is nearly as obscure as the preceding, and probably as hopelessly corrupt. The Śruddy ones" in a are, according to the comm., priests (7zvij); Weber underd : stands « horses," Ludwig " somas." The comm. takes dââkysanta in â first from root â 7k (= adkârayan), then apparently from âkrs (purvarṅ: visrastavayavam inâram I punak sarvâvayavopelam akurvan, citing TS. v. 6.34); Ppp. has daây canta; perhaps dadyhanta might be made to yield the best sense ; restoration of the augment would fill out the deficient meter, which the Anukr. fails to remark. R. conjectures made firm for him the mighty gâyatr7 as bolt." About half the mss. (including our Bp.E.I.H.X.) accent in b saṅâyâya ; the same uncertainty as to this word appears elsewhere.

3. For the waters let king Varuṇa call thee ; let Soma call thee for the mountains ; let Indra call thee for these subjects (v7) ; becoming a falcon, fly unto these subjects.

Ś For" may of course be "from " in a and b, as preferred by the four ] translators â and comm. Ppp. reads, in a, b var uno jukâva somas (va yas kvayati; and again in , indras toa yan kvayati. With the proper resolutions, this verse is a decent (stub); the Anukr. scans it as II + 10: Io + IO = 41. The verses in our text are wrongly numbered from this one on.

4. Let the falcon lead hither from far (pâra) the one to be called, living exiled in others' territory (k5âtra); let the (two) Agvins make the road for thee easy to go; settle together about this man, ye his fellows. : The translation follows both previous translators, and the comm. (= kvârta"yanm), in implying kâyyao in a instead of kaṇyâm ' oblation'; yet Ppp. reads kawis, which supports kauyâm. The comm., with several of SPP's mss., has evar uddham in b; for the technical aparudâdṅag caran (and ava-garm, 6 4) compare especially PB. xii. 12. 6.

5. Let thine opponents call thee ; thy friends have chosen [thee] against [them] ( p7âri); Indra-and-Agni, all the gods, have maintained for thee security (Ś54ma) in the people (v4).

The comm., and a few of SPP's mss. that follow it, have at the beginning vâyantr (= saṅtatyena sevantâm). Several saṅhitâ-mss. (including our P.M.O.Op.) read pratijanâṅ ; Ppp. has the easier reading paṅca jana, with hkvayanti for -ntu, and, in b, varsata for avrsata; also it ends with adidharas. As in more than one other case, all the mss. accent # in the second half-verse, and the pada-text puts its double stroke of pada-division before the word; and both editions read 7, but it should plainly be 7, i as our translation renders, and as the comm. also explains it. The comm. combines in b gratimitras, making it mean " opposing friends"; the combination of 77 (choose ' Ś with p7ati is strange and obscure. te 6. Whatever fellow disputes thy call, and whatever outsider — making him go away (âpâ7c), O Indra, then do thou reinstate (ava gamaya) this man here.

The comm. explains szjârâ and nâstya as samabala and nikrstabala (¹) L as ati. 19.3 J, and ava gamaya as bodkaya. The Anukr. takes no notice of the metrical deficiency in a; emendation to -vâdati would fairly rectify it. |For ava-garm, see note to vs. 4.

docs.title: 4. To establish a king
docs.text:
[Atharvan.— saptakam. &indram. trâi|tubham: I. jagati ; 4, 5. bhurâj.]

Found in Paipp. iii. Used in Kâug. only with the next preceding hymn (as there explained), although the two are of essentially different application, this one referring to a king who has been called or chosen, and has to be inaugurated as such. In Vait. (13.2), in the agnistoma sacrifice, vs. 7 accompanies, with vii. 28, oblations to parkyâ svasti and other divinities.

Translated : Ludwig, p. 252 ; Zimmer, p. 164 ; Weber, xvii. go ; Griffith, i. 84; Bloomfield, 113, 330. — Cf. Bergaigne-Henry, Manuel, p. 141.

I. Unto thee hath come the kingdom ; with splendor rise forward ; [as] lord of the people (vas), sole king, bear thou rule (vi-777); let all the directions call thee, O king ; become thou here one for waiting on, for homage.

The translation implies in a agan, which is very probably the true reading, though the padz-mss. divide roâ: gan. The metrical redundancy in a, b is best removed by omutmg prâ7 (for which Ppp. and the comm. read 774), which seems (as meaning also in the east') to have been added in order to make yet more distinct the comparison with the sun implied in ââ iki; the pada-text reckons the word wrongly to b, and the comm. renders it pzrvan ' formerly ' ; he takes of râja as be resplendent," which is of course possible. The verse has but one real jagarr pada (a). [With â (= vi. 98. 1 9), of. nâmasopasâdâyas, used twice in RV. ]

sz. Thee let the people (vas) choose unto kingship (²âjâ), thee these five divine directions; rest (cr) at the summit of royalty, at the pinnacle (4akṅd) ; from thence, formidable, share out good things to us.

The verse is found also in TS. (iii. 3.92) and MS. (ii. 5. 10), with nearly accordant differences of reading: gâwo ‘er para râjyâya in a; toân havanta (MS. varâkanti) marâtaṅ svarkâ) for b; ksatrâsya kakubhi (MS. kakâbbhik) cicriyanâs in c. TB., moreover, has the second half-verse (in ii. 4. 77; the first half is our iv. 22.2 a,b), agreeing with AV. except by giving ksatrâsya kakṅbhis. Ppp. further varies the word by reading kakudhi; it also has in a oypurâam, and for d are vasṅni vi bhajâsy ugrak. A number of the mss. (including our O.0p.) read in a 7âjyâya, as, indeed, they generally disagree in threefold wise as to the accent of this word. P.M. W. have in a vorsatâm. The comm. renders vârsman by carire, grayasva by assva.

3. Unto thee let thy fellows come, calling [thee]; Agni shall go along as speedy messenger; let the wives, the sons, be well-willing ; thou, formidable, shalt see arrive (prati-pag) much tribute.

Ppp. has in a, byantu bhuvanasya jalâ 'gnir dṅte 'va jarase dadkâati, and combines in c jâyâs g-. The comm. finds in b an incomplete simile ; thy messenger, unassaili able like fire, shall " etc.

4. Let the (two) Agvins thee first, — let Mitra-and-Varuṇa both, let all the gods, the Maruts, call thee ; then put (47) thy mind unto the giving of good things ; from thence, formidable, share out good things to us.

With c compare RV. i. 54. 9 d, which rectifies the meter by reading k75va. The second half-verse is quite different in Ppp. : 5277180872 madhyamesthe 'hka masyâ (ct.

i. 6.4 c; iii. 8. 2 9) sve kretre savite vi râja. The third pada is made b4urij by the change of krsva to kr nuśva.
