5. Run forth hither from the furthest distance ; propitious to thee be ; heaven-and-earth both ; king Varuga here saith this thus; he here hath called thee; therefore (sâ)] do thou come to this place. ¹ Ppp. has babkutâm for ubhe stam at end of b, and akvat svenam eki at end of d.

SPP. reports all his pada-mss. as reading aka instead of âka in c; no such blunder has been noted in ours. His ms. of the comm. also appears to have z4wvat in d, but doubt- . less only by an oversight of the copyist (under the next verse it gives akvat in an ideng tical phrase of exposition). MS. (ii. 2. 11; p.24.3) gives a.pratika reading 4 prâhî paramâsyâh parâvâtak, while no corresponding verse is found in its text—or elsewhere, so far as is known, unless here.

6. Like a human Indra, go thou away; for thou hast concurred (sam- : 77) in concord with the castes (?) ; he here hath called thee in his own . station ; he shall sacrifice to the gods, and he shall arrange the people

(vas). ¹ The translation of this obscure and difficult verse implies much and venturesome emendation in the first half: namely, in a, (ndra iva manugyâk, and in b vârnaâis. ²

Weber also takes manugyâs as meant for a nom. sing., and renders it menschengestaltet "; the other translators understand manusy& vâas, as does the Pet. Lex. The

Ppp. version, inâre ⁴4are manugya pre ki, suggests -gyaṅ, and is decidedly better in preki (to be resolved into p7-e-47, whence perhaps the corruption to pareṅ7); the . repeated vocative Zndracindra (so the pada-text) is not to be tolerated. For b, Ppp.

has san ki yajṅiyâs toâ varunena sam vidânak, which is too corrupt to give us aid;

the emendation to vârnâis is a desperate and purely tentative one, as there is no evi- (ht dence that vârpa had assumed so early the sense of (caste.' Weber suggests that varuna here is equal to varaṇa elector '; Zimmer takes it as virtually for deoâis : both i entirely unsatisfactory. Ppp. ends the verse with so Zalpayâd âicak. To the comm.

there is no difficulty; the repeated vocative is out of reverence (âdarârtham) ; manu-

Śyas is a Vedic irregularity for yan, or else qualifies prajâs understood ; the plural varuṇâis is plur. majestaticus for varupena ; kalpayâr, finally, is svasvavyâparesu ² niyuṅktâm, The Anukr. passes without notice the jagarr pada d, it being easy to read a ṅ the verse into 44 syllables.

¹7. The wealthy roads, of manifoldly various form, all, assembling, ¹ have made wide room for thee; let them all in concord call thee; to the tenth [decade of life] abide here formidable, well-willing. : Parkyâ revarts, divinities of good roads and welfare, are explained by the comm. as patho nagera mârgakitakârigya etatsanjnâ devatâak, or else pathyâs is pathi saâkavak, and revatis is âpas, Both editions read in 4 vace 'k4, but the comm., with ¹ SPP's (rotriyas V. and K., read vase kâ, and the translation implies this. Ppp. offers no variants for the verse. Many of our sa7#hitâ-mss. (P.M. W.E.I.H.) retain the final visarga of saṅvidânâj before ko- in c; SPP. does not report any of his as guilty of such a blunder. ]V. and K. recognize vageââ as a variant.

Ppp. appends another verse : yadi jarena havisâ darvi gamayâmasi: air ta indras kevalir vito balikytas karat (cf. RV. x. 173. 6 c, 4).

docs.title: 5. For prosperity : with a parṇâ-amulet
docs.text:
[Atkarvan.— agtakam. sâumyam. ânugtubham : r. puro nugup trigubh ; 8. virâgurobyharr.}

Found (except vs. 8) in Pâipp. iii. Used by Kâug. (19. 22), with viii. 5 and x. 3, 6, to accompany the binding on of an amulet for general prosperity ((zj0âalâyur dkanâaṅpustaye, comm.). And the comm. quotes it from Naks. K. [ comm. should say Cânti K. — Bloomfield ] as employed in a makâcânti named âṅgirasi. In the prior draft, W. writes For success of a king : with" etc. as title of this hymn. Its place in the collection, next after iii. 3 and 4, and its second vs., seem to justify that title.

Translated : Weber, xvii. 194; Griffith, i. 86 ; Bloomfield, r14, 331.— Vss. 6 and 7, Zimmer, p. 184, with comment.

I. Hither hath come this pamâ-amulet, strong, by strength slaughtering our rivals; force of the gods, milk of the herbs, let it quicken me with splendor unremittingly.

Ppp. has for d mayâ râstraṅ: jinvatv aprayucchan. Aprayâvan in â, which is read by all the mss. (hence by both editions) and the comm., is unquestionably to be emended (as suggested by BR., v. ro15) to yâvasm Ski. Gram.² § 995 b, root yz; cf. yuck ; the word is quoted in the Prat. text (iv. 56), but not in a way to determine its form (ap7ayâvâdâr-). As the later verses show, garpa is to be understood here as the tree of that name (Butea frondosa : comm. palâcavy kya). The comm. raises no objection to âg7ay&van, and explains it as either man vihâyâ 'napagantâa san (with irregular exchange of case-forms), or else aprayatar, i.e. sarvadâa dhâryamâṇa.

2. In me [maintain] dominion, O parpâ-amulet, in me maintain wealth; may I in the sphere of royalty be familiar (? 7âjâ), supreme.

Compare the nearly corresponding vi. 54. 2, which suggests emendation of nzjâs to yujâs 'may I be supreme above [any] ally or fellow-king ' (yujâs as abl). Ppp. has râstram for ksatram in a, and its d reads yajz bhṅyâsam uttarâ, supporting the emendation. Our Bp. reads in c -vargr, as some of the mss. do in the other occurrences of this obscure word : the comm. explains it by Gvazjane svâdhinrkaraṇe ' appropriation, and nija by ananyasahâya. BR. give ' bestândig' for aâja. J

3. The dear amulet which the gods deposited hidden in the foresttree —that let the gods give to us to wear, together with length of life (4yas).

Ppp. has for b vâjint devâak priya: nidhim, and its second half-verse is izṅ ma indras sahâ "yusa manir dadâtu bhartave.

4. The parṇâ, Soma's formidable power, hath come, given by Indra, governed (câs) by Varuṇa ; may I, shining greatly, wear it in order to length of life for a hundred autumns.

The translation implies emendation in c of the unmanageable p7âyâsanz to Śhriyâsam, : an obvious improvement, adopted also by Weber, and supported by the reading of Ppp.,.

tam akan: bibhar mi, the comm., too, though reading p7ây-, glosses it with Śkriyâsar 4 dhârayeyam. In b, Ppp. has sakkyas for cisfas. The comm. finds in sâmasya parpâs in a allusion to the origin of the parṇa-tree from a leaf (Śarṇa) of soma, and quotes for it TS. iii. 5. 7¹. Râcamânas in c he uses as -nar, qualifying 4m. The metrical definition of the verse is wanting in the Anukr. mss. ; we may call it a nicrr 4 tristubh. See Weber's note on parpdâ.

5. The parpâ-amulet hath ascended me, in order to great unharmedness, so that I may be superior to patron (azyamân) and to ally (saṅoâd).

San vid is here taken as corresponding noun to the common adjective sai vidandâ

(the Pet. Lex., possession "; Weber, favor ") ; the comm. makes it szmânajnâanar . or samabalât; and aryaman, according to him, comes from arin yamayati, and means 4 aâkikabalak purupradatâ ca. Ppp. combines makyâ 'rist- in b, and has for d manugya aâdhi sangatak (or sammatak). All the mss., and SPP's text, read uṅtarâs in c;;

our ââtaras is a necessary emendation. As to azyamân, cf. Weber's note. . 6. They that are clever chariot-makers, that are skilful smiths—subjects to me do thou, O parṇâ, make all people (jâna) round about.

Ppp. begins yat taksâno rark-, and its second half-verse is sarvâṅs tvâ 'ny pa randhayo

¹pastim krnu medinam. The comm. renders âkzvâanas by dhtvarâ mârsikâṅ ' fisher- : men,' and gives the technical definition of the caste of rathakâras. Weber (p. 196 ff.)

treats with much fulness of these and other caste matters. Upastin the comm. explains, nearly enough correctly, by sevârthan samipe vidyamânâan upasinâan va.

7. They that are kings, king-makers, that are charioteers and troopleaders — subjects to me do thou, O pamâ, make. all people round about. ¹ a Our Bp. reads in b grâmaonyâṅ, emended to enyâṅ ; Kp. has grâmanyâṅ ; Op. and ga D. (and, so far as appears, all SPP's pada-mss.) gramanyâk ; the word is divided by the RV. pada-text (grâmacnîk), as in all reason it should be; and its division seems; : favored, if not required, by our Prat. iii. 76. Ppp. has a quite different text: zpastir g y ast vaya uta (udra utâ "ryaj for a, b, with c, d as in its version of vs. 6 (but with ¹ ¹ t3n rpa intending (ân parpa? ] instead of rez '#ypa). Weber, on authority of

CB. iii. 4. I. 7, proposes to emend a to yâ 7âjâno ; the comm. explains the râjanas Hd by anyadecadhipak ; and râjakttas by râjye '6hisiṅcantt ti sacivâṅ. In SPP's Cor rections (to p. 364), his J.P. are reported as dividing grâmaonyâṅ.

8. Parpâ art thou, body-protecting ; a hero, from the same womb

(760i) with me a hero; with the year's brilliancy — therewith I bind;

thee on, O amulet.

⁴ Wanting in Ppp. The second pâda is damaged, in meter and in sense, by the apparently intruded v7 âs.

The aznvzka x. ends here, having 5 hymns and 33 verses; the old Anukr. says:. : tr iṅcannimitâṇ sagycesu (mss. -garc-) kâryas tisraṅ.

docs.title: 6. Against enemies : with agvatthâ
docs.text:
= [Jagadbjampur usa. —aṣtarcam. vânaspatyâ vatthadevatyam. ânuṣubham.] la Found (except vs. 6) in Pâipp. iii. Used by Kâug. (48. 3.) in a rite of sorcery i against enemies; vss. 7,8 are specially quoted (48.6, 5), with actions adapted to the; text. The comm. also describes it as employed by the Naky. [comm. again errs; should be Cânti— Bloomfield ] K. (17, 19) in a makâcanti called âṅgirast.

Translated : A. Kuhn, Herabkunft des Feners etc., 1859, p. 224, or 2d ed, p. 198; Weber, xvii. 204; Grill, 21, 104; Griffith, i. 87; Bloomfield, 91, 334.

I. The male (pâmaââs) [is] born out of the male —the acvarzhdâ forth from the kkadirâ; let it smite my foes, whom I hate and who [hate] me.

A very acceptable emendation would be p47 jatâs, since pâri is plainly accessory to the ablative puṅsâs, as âdki to khadirâr in b (cf. dsatas pâri jayṅire, x. J. 25). Ppp. retains the initial a of acvarthas, and begins 4 with yâṅg ca 'kari. The agvatrtha begins as a parasite, usually on the cam? (fem.), this time from the hard 2%adira (masc.).

2. Crush them out, O agvatrthâ, our violent foes, O expelling one, allied with Vrtra-slaying Indra, with Mitra, and with Varuṇa.

The translation implies the reading of vâibâdka in b as an independent word; itis so regarded by BR., Weber, the later translators, and the comm. ; all the pada-mss. make it into a compound with ââââatas, and both editions so write it. Ppp. reads instead, for b, carr an mayi bâdha todkata. Some of our mss. (P.M.W.E.) read in a nt cr-; one of SPP's has s7z74i. The comm. explains dâdhatas as bhycar: kampayizrn ] but see Ved. Stud. ii. ro.

Ppp. adds a verse of its own: yathâ 'cvattha nispâmi pUroṅṅ jalan uti "parârn (ct. x. 3. Y3-15) : evâ pydanyatas tvam abhi tistha sakasvata.

3. As thou, O agvarthâ, didst break out [the kkadirâ] within the great sea, so do thou break out all these, whom I hate and who [hate] me.

“ The sea," doubtless the atmosphere, as explained by the comm. (and Weber). The comm. reads âbkinas in a, and two or three of SPP's mss. so far agree with him as to give the (blundering) #irâbhinnas; this reading exhibits a much less startling and anomalous crowding-out of the root-final by the personal ending than does -aâkanas (see my Sk. Gr. §555), and so is more acceptable. Some of SPP's mss. similarly mix up bhinâki and bkaṅdṅi in c; the comm., of course, has the former. A part of the mss. (including our Bp.P.M.E.H.) leave makati in b unaccented (as again at xi. 8. 2,6). Ppp. yarhâ 'coattha vibkinacchari takaty aryave: ev me carro cittâni vigvag bhiâki sakasvarâ (cf. our vs. 6 c, 4).

4. Thou that goest about overpowering, like a bull that has overpowered — with thee here, O aguatthâ, may we overpower our rivals.

Ppp. reads in a carati, as does also the comm., followed by two or three of SPP's mss. Ppp. further combines in b sâsaṅânâi "va rs and ends d with saz vis toaki. |The saṅkitâ-mss. all combine 7va 75 in b; see note to Prat. Śi. 46.

5. Let perdition bind them, with unreleasable fetters of death—my foes, O agvattkâ, whom I hate and who [hate] me.

Ppp. has avimokyâis in b, and (as in vs. r) begins 4 with yzâg ca 'kam. Several of our mss. (P.M. W.E.) have at the beginning the senseless reading sim atu.

6. As, O agvatrhâ, ascending them of the forest-trees, thou dost put them beneath thee (â2kara), so the head of my foe do thou split apart and overcome.

Ppp. (as we saw above) has the second half of this verse, with variants, as its 3 c, d.

What the vânaspatyâ is, as distinguished from vânaspâti, is as obscure as the similar relation of 744 and ârtawâ [ iii. ro. note ]; possibly ' they of that sort, they and their ' kind '; our translation marks, rather mechanically, the distinction. The comm. says that here vanaspati means " the place where trees grow," and vânaspatya the trees themselves— which is an explanation quite after his kind.

27. Let them float forth downward, like a boat severed from its mooring (bândhana) ; of them, thrust forth by the expelling one, there is no returning again. ¹ Ppp. reads in c nurbâadha ; our Op. has vâibâdkâ : pracnuttâanâam. Asru in d, for asti, would be an improvement. The comm. gives a double explanation of bandhana, as . either place or instrument of fastening. [ The vs. recurs at ix. 2. 12, with sâyaka- for vâibâdṅâ-.— W's collation of Op. gives prac, not prâe! J f 8. I thrust them forth with mind, forth with intent and incantation;

forth with branch of tree, of agvarthâ, we thrust them.

Ppp. has in a prai 'nân nuâdâmi (which makes the meter easier), and at the end cor- . respondingly the active zudâamasi, for b it gives pra crtyena brâhmanâ. The lingualization of the first z of eân is noted in Prat. iii. 8o, and the comment on that rule quotes the instance in c, but not that in a. According to Kâug. the thing “mentioned in the text ¹ (perhaps an effigy of the person aimed at, in the “vitals " of which something has been ( buried by the preceding rule) having been put upon a boat ] is with this verse and ix. 2. 4 pushed forth with a branch, and with vs. 7 made to float away.

docs.title: 7. Against the disease kṣetriyâ
docs.text:
[BhygUangiras.—saptarcam. yaksmanâanadâivatam uta bakudevatyam. ânugiubham

6. bhury.]

Found in Pâipp. iii., with few variants, but with vs. 5 at the end. Used by Kâug. i (27. 29) in a healing ceremony (its text does not specify the disease) ; and reckoned

(26. I, note) to the takmanâgana gana. And the comm. quotes it as employed by the

Naks. Cânti? ] K. (17, 19) in the makhâcânti called kâumart. ee Translated : Weber, xvii. 208 ; Grill, 8, roy; Griffith, i. 89 ; Bloomfield, rs, 336.

I. On the head of the swift-running gazelle (kariṇâ) is a remedy; he by his horn hath made the Z5erriyâ4 disappear, dispersing.

Vâsâpa is divided (viesânz) in the pada-text, as if from v7 + sz 'unfasten '— which is, indeed, in all probability its true derivation, as designating primarily a deciduous horn, one that is dropped off or shed; and in this peculiarity, as distinguished from the 4 permanent horns of the domestic animals, perhaps lies the reason of its application to a magical remedial uses. The verse occurs also in ApCS. xiii. 7: 16 where most mss. a have raghugyato J. For the ksefriya, see above, ii. S. BGS See p. 1045.

2. After thee hath the bull-gazelle stridden with his four feet ; O horn, ee do thou unfasten (vi-sz) the ksetriyâ that is compacted (?) in his heart. Fe Ppp. has a different d: yadi kimi ksetriyaṅ: kyâi. The word-play in c, between te 75373 and vi-s7, is obvious; that any was intended with vâsâcina in 1 d is very ques- : ⁴ tionable. This verse, again, is found in APCS. ib., but with considerable variants : azn toa haripo mygak pagbhi; caturbhir akramiât : visage vi Śyâî "tas granthin: yad asya gulphitan: hr di here it is a “knot " that is to be untied by means of the horn. One of our mss. (O.) has in c pagbhâts, ike ApCS. The comm., followed by a couple of i SPP's mss., further agrees with ApCS. by reading gulphitarm in c, and exphins it as gulpkavad grathitam. The occurrence of the rare and obscure gugpâta misprinted gustitam J in CB. iii. 2. 2. zo is also in connection with the use of a deer's horn.

3. What shines down yonder, like a four-sided roof (ckadâs), therewith we make all the kyerriyâ disappear from thy limbs.

In our edition, Z4na in c should be z47â, as read by nearly all the sa#k71â-mss. (all save our P.M.), and by SPP. The sense of a, b is obscure to the comm. as to us; he guesses first that it is the deer-shaped thing extended in the moon's disk," or else wa deer's skin stretched on the ground"; c4adts is the mat of grass with which a house is covered." Weber takes it as a constellation ; Grill (mistranslating paksa by «post "), as the gazelle himself set up on his four legs, with his horns for roof If a constellation, it might be the Arab ⁴manzil " v, 7, 7 Aquarii, which its shape and name connect with a tent: see Sâzya-Sidâdhânta, note to viii. 9 (under 25th asterism); this is not very far from the stars mentioned in the next verse A and v Scorpionis J.

4. The two blessed stars named Unfasteners (vicṅt), that are yonder in the sky —let them unfasten of the Eṣerriyâ the lowest, the highest fetter.

The verse is nearly identical with ii. 8. r above, which see b recurs at vi. 121. 3 b; v. Schroeder gives the Katha version of a, b, Zweâ kss., p. 15, and Tâbinger Katha-kss., p. 75]. Ppp. makes it in part yet more nearly so, by beginning with ud agatâm bkagavat, but reads in c-vâ ksetriyar: toa 'bky ânage cf. our 6 b J; and its end and part of vs. 6 (which next follows) are defaced.

5. The waters verily [are] remedial, the waters disease-expelling, the waters remedial of everything; let them release thee from kṣerriyd.

The first three pâadas are RV. x.137.6 8, b, c, save that RV. has sârvasya in c; but vi. 9I. 3 below represents the same verse yet more closely.

6. If from the drink (? Zsutz) that was being made the ksetriyâ hath come upon (vi-ag) thee, I know the remedy of it; I make the Ś5erriyâ disappear from thee.

The word asuṅz is of doubtful and disputed sense; Weber says " infusio seminis " [as immediate cause of the ⁴ Erb-Śbel," which is Weber's version of Egerrâyâ J; Grill, «gekochter Zaubertrank "; the comm., dravṅbhâtam anna 'liquidized food."

7. In the fading-out of the asterisms, in the fading-out of the dawns also, from us [fade] out all that is of evil nature, fade out (gga-vas) the ksetriyâ.

Ppp. has rate 'sasâm at end of b, and in c Zmayat for durbhutam. Emendation of asmâr in c to asmâr (as suggested by Weber) would notably improve the sense. The second pada has a syllable too many, unless we make the double combination vse ³sâsanm.

docs.title: 8. For authority
docs.text:
. [Atharvan.— mâitram uta vâivadevam. trâtubham : 2, 6. jagati; 4. 42. vir3dbr hatigarbkâ;

5. anuṣgubh.]

Verses 1-4 found in Paâipp. i., but defaced. The hymn is used by Kâug. (55. 17-18;

also 55. I, note), with i. 9, 30, etc., in the ceremony of reception of a Vedic student, and, according to the schol. (10. 19, note), in that for the generation of wisdom (the comm.

says, as belonging to the Zyugya gana). Verses 5 and 6 are the same with vi. 94.1, 2, and it is vi. 94, rather than these verses here, that is used in Kâug. r2. 5 (the comm. ² blunderingly prescribes the use under both passages). Verse 4 has the same pratika as xiv. I. 32 and one or the other of the two verses is taught in Vâit. (22. I) as used

« by Kâugika " in the agnigioma ; but our Kâug. has no such use, and it is doubtless 1 xiv. I. 32, 33 that he prescribes (79.17 ff.) in the nuptial ceremonies ; but the comm. ¹ reports the use here, as if it referred to vss. 4 and 5. The comm. further regards the hymn as employed by the Naks. K. (18), in the âââvatr rite, and by Paricista 5.3;

in both cases as an Zyzgya hymn.

Translated : Weber, xvii. 212 ; Griffith, i. go.

1. Let Mitra come, arranging with the seasons, uniting (? sam-vegaya-)

the earth with the ruddy ones (usriyâ); then to us let Varuṇa, Vâyu,

Agni, assign great royalty of union (? saṅvegyâ). ¹ The verse is very obscure, and probably corrupt, though found almost without variant (only tar for azka in c) in Ppp. also. The epithet saṅzvecyâ (found only here)

seems fashioned to correspond to the participle sa7vegâyan in b; but Weber renders the ppl. by “umlagernd " and the epithet by ruhsam "; the comm., by pervading"

(uyâpnuvan) and "suitable for abiding in" (sa7vecâarham avasthanayogyam). The : : comm. takes srâyâs as gavas, i.e. kiranâs 'rays.' R. ventures heroic emendations:

«Let Mitra come after ordering of the time, enlivening (sa7hâpayan or something i equivalent, since (putting to rest' is no result of the action of Mitra's rays) the earth g : with his rays; but let Varuna make wind and fire (vâyâm agnim), make our great ¹ realm go to rest. The first pâda is redundant, unless we make the double combination i mitrâ reṅbhik. I BR. take Zalp- as 'sich richtend nach.' J

2. Let Dhâtar, Râti, Savitar enjoy here (iââm) ; let Indra, Tvashtar, welcome my words (vâcas); I call the divine Aditi, mother of heroes ¹ (câra-), that I may be midmost man of my fellows.

The first pada is also vii. 17.4 a, and VS. viii. 17 a. The plural verb in b seems to imply that all the deities mentioned in the line are to be regarded as its subjects. 8 Maâhyamesthâ (like maâdhyamagi, iv. 9. 4), probably the one whom the others gather about as chief; the comm. has nothing valuable (sazyddhakâmah san svasamânâik ¹v ‘ segyak). The comm. takes 7âtâ in a as = Aryaman. Ppp. has grknantu for haryantu ¹hâ in b. The meter of 4 would be rectified by reading syâm (or âsam, as is perhaps assumable in this stage of the language) for âszzi. The verse as it stands (11 + 12:

11 + 12 =46) is ill described as a jagatr.

3. I call, with acts of homage, Soma, Savitar, all the Adityas, in the.

contest for pregminence ; may this fire shine for very long, kindled by

[my] fellows who gainsay not. Ś 5 Ś

The translation implies in b emendation cf. iii. 18. 4 ] to akamuttaratoâ (against all the mss. and both editions), as proposed by BR., i. 891 ; the comm. also takes it as two words, and renders witaratve by yajamânasya crâisthye. Ppp. reads devâr for adityan in b. The comm. has didayat in sam hitâ ; our pada-text has it, and Prat. iii. 22 and iv. 89 deal with its conversion to â7ââyat in saṅhitz.

4. May ye be just here; may ye not go away (parâs) ; may an active herdsman (gopâ), lord of prosperity, drive you hither ; do ye, with [your] desires, [attend] upon (?) his desire ; let all the gods conduct you together hither.

The translation implies emendation in d of wantu to -nayantz, as called for by both meter and sense, and also the addition of a verb, szz or ita, at end of c, for a like reason. If, as seems very probable, the verse is originally addressed to kine, kânstuzs in c is quite natural ; if not, we may regard wâas as understood : the sense is ⁴ be your desires sub. ject to his.' Ppp. has a different reading: asmaâi vas kama upa kâmintr vigve devâ upasatyâm (ka. The comm. regards kâminis as addressed throughout, and explains it finally as meaning sâriyak gâvaj (perhaps the text is defective or incorrect ; the general explanation of the verse implies stziyaṅ). The comm. reads guras for paras in a, and in b divides #yas, deriving it from root 77, and rendering it margaprerakas V pada has #yas]. The Anukr. calls for 11 + II : 9+ II = 42 syllables, and strictly requires at the end -âantu ; but no inference as to a difference of reading is to be drawn from this. Ppp. combines in b vâjat.— Weber says: asnâi diesem, dem Hausherrn, kâmâya zu Liebe ; oder gehŚrt asmaâi zu kâmâya selbst?" ]

5. We bend together your minds, together your courses (vralâ), together your designs ; ye yonder who are of discordant courses, we make you bend [them] together here.

This and the following verse, not found with the others in Ppp., occur again below as vi. 94. I, 2 cf. also ii. 30. 2, and vs. r occurs in Ppp. xix., with the other material of our sixth book ; they are so far discordant in subject with the preceding verses that we may fairly call them out of place here. This one exists in MS. (ii. 2.6), with anazsata for namâmasi, and sthâ for sthkâna. A RV. Fkila to x. 191 has 7ânatâ in a for sa vratâ, akntis in b, and, for c, 4, asâu yo vimana janas tan samaâavartayâmasi. The first half-verse, further, nearly accords with VS. xii. 58 a, b, TS. iv. 2. 5' a, b, MS. ii.. II a, b (they have vâm for vas, and, for b, sânm a ci âny â ¹kar am). Nearly all our sam kitâ-mss. read 27) before sthâna, nor is there anything in the Prat. to prescribe the omission of the visarga in such a situation, while the comment to ii. 40 expressly quotes the passage as an example of the assimilation of it to a following initial sibilant. The comm. reads sana instead of stkana. Three of our mss. (P.M.E.) read at the end -nayâmast.

6. I seize [your] minds with [my] mind; come ye after my intent with [your] intents ; I put your hearts in my control; come with [your] tracks following my motion (yâtâ).

The comm, reads gr kami in a, and three or four of SPP's mss. follow him; he also makes in b a compound of anucittebhis. Quite a number of mss. (including our P.M. W.H.s.m.I.) very strangely combine at the end -ânar é1a. MB. has a somewhat similar verse at i. 2. 21. How heedless the Anukr. is of metrical irregularity is well illustrated by c, where the desirable alteration of vâcesu to vâce, and the abbreviation of kFdayâni to the equivalent (yz (both suggested by Weber) would leave a good tristubh pada ; there is no jagatr character to any part of the verse. The combination

-maânarera looks as if it had blundered in from the end of b. J

docs.title: 9. Against vigkandha and other evils
docs.text:
; [Vâmadeva.— dyâvâgythiviyam uta vâirvadtvam. ânugubham : 4. 42. nicyd brhati; : Found in Pâipp. iii. (with vs. 6 at the beginning). Used by Kâug. (43. I) in a charm against demons and the hindrances caused by them. : ¹ Translated : Weber, xvii. 215 ; Griffith, i. or ; Bloomfield, 67, 339.

I. Of the kargâpha, of the vigaphd, heaven [is] father, earth mother:

as, O gods, ye have inflicted (abki-kP), so do ye remove (2pa-47) again.

The whole hymn contains much that is obscure and difficult, and the comm. gives no real help anywhere, being as much reduced to guessing as we are. Ppp. begins with Zaryabhasya visabkyasya, which rather favors Weber's opinion, that the aga of the two names is a suffix, related with ab4a ; probably two varieties of viskandha are intended, though none such are mentioned in the later medicine. The comm. finds j capha hoof in both: one = krcacaphasya (uyâghrâdek), the other either vigata- : caphasya or vispastacaphasya. SPP. reads in b âyâr ṅ p-, which is doubtless preferable to our 4y7âs p-; it is read by the majority of his mss. and by part of ours (H.IK.);

Ppp. also has it. Ppp. further omits a5 in c, and reads ag7 for apa in d.

2. Without claspers they held fast (J4âraya); that was so done by

Manu; I make the oâkandka impotent, like a castrater of bulls. : : Ppp. begins with aclesamâṇo 'âk- ; some of the mss. (including our 0.) also give aglesmâṇas, and it is the reading of the comm. ; he gives two different and equally artificial explanations ; and, what is surprising even in him, three diverse ones of vââṅ7î, without the least regard to the connection ; one of the three is the right one. Ppp. adds ca after vadkri in c. Weber plausibly conjectures a method of tight tying to be the subject of the verse ; castration is sometimes effected in that way. f : 3. On a reddish string a Z4ṅgala—that the pious (vedkâs) bind on;

let the binders (?) make impotent the flowing (?), puffing (?) kâ5avd.

All obscure and questionable. Ppp's version is : for a, sâtre picunkhe khugilar: ; in b, yad for iad, for c, gravasyar: cusma kâababam (the nâgari copyist writes kzvardham). ( The comm. also has in c (ravasyam, and three or four of SPP's mss. follow him; the Ś8 translation assumes it to be for szao-. The comm. explains kk galam by tanutrânanm ¹ . ⁴armor,' quoting RV. ii. 39.4 as authority ; cravasyam by bâlarâpam annam arkati

(since gravas is an annanâman'); câsmam by cosakam see Bloomfield, ZDMG. he xviii 574 1; k25ava as a hindrance related with a kaṅz, which is a speckled (karbura- 4 varṇa) cruel animal; and bandhiras is either the amulet bound upon us, or it is for ras, "the amulet, staff, etc., held by us." Śe 4. Wherewith, O flowing ones, ye go about (car), like gods with

Asura-magic (-nâyâ), like the ape, spoiler of dogs, and with the binder (?)

of the kabavdâ.

Or gravasyṅ is quick, lively' (Pet. Lexx.) ; the comm., "seeking either food or glory." Ppp. reads in c, 4 dâsanar: vandharâ kâbhavasyaṅ ca. The comm. explains Śanâhurâ by sambaddhâ âhrtâ khaâgadirupa hetik. The verse is scanned by the Anukr. as 9+ 9: 9 +8 = 35; the usual abbreviation of za to 'va would make b and c good anustubh padas. [Read cravasyâ, voc., in a?

5. Since I shall bind thee [on] for spoiling, I shall spoil the ²75avâ; ye shall go up with curses, like swift chariots.

The translation implies emendation of 4kartsyâmi (our edition) or bhazsyâmi (SPP's and the comm.) to bhantsyâmi, from root bandh, which seems plainly indicated as called for ; the comm. explains Śkats- first as badknâmi, and then as dṅayâami; the great majority of mss. give Ś4arts-. Ppp. is quite corrupt here : justi toâ kaṅrecha bhi josayitvâ bhawvaiz. The comm. has at the end carâgyatha (two or three of SPP's mss. agreeing with him), and he combines in c uââcavas into one word, "harnessed with speedy horses that have their mouths raised for going."

6. A hundred and one vâskandkas [are] distributed over the earth; thee have they first taken up, of them the vâskandṅa-spoiling amulet.

That is, 'an amulet that spoils those vâskandkas' (Weber otherwise). Inc, for the ² Jjaharus of all the mss. and of both editions, we ought of course to have jaârus; this the comm. reads : such expansions of r with preceding or following consonant to a syllable are not rare in the manuscripts. Ppp. has a different second half-verse : t2sân: ca sarvesâan idam asti viskandâhadṅsanam. The second pâda is found, in a different connection, as MB. ii. 8.4 b. The comment on Prat. ii. ro4, in quoting this verse, appears to derive viskandha from root skznâ. The verse is made b4urif only by the false form jakarus. For ⁴o1," see note to iii. 11. 5. ]

docs.title: 10. To the ekâaṣtakâ (day of moon's last quarter)
docs.text:
Lârkarvan.— trayodacarcam. âstakyam. ânugtubkham : 4, 5, 6, 12. trigtubk ; 7. 3-av. 62. , vir âdgarbhâtijagati.)

Found, except. vss. 9 and r3, in Pâipp. i, but witha. very different order of verses (1-4, 6, 11, 10, 8, 5, I2, 7). Used by Kâug. in connection with the zṣ722â ceremony, or celebration of the festival of the moon's last quarter (19. 28, and again, with more fulness, r38. r—16), or of a particular last quarter, regarded as. of special importance. The details of the Kâug. are expanded and explained by the comm. ; they are not of a nature to cast light upon the interpretation of the verses. Weber (pp. 219 ff.) discusses at considerable length the questions connected with the festival. Vaâit., which does not concern itself with the aszakâ, yet employs vs. 6 (13.6) at the agnâtoma sacrifice, in connection with the somakrayaṇz cow; and also vs. 7 cf (9. 4) in the sâkamedka rite of the caturmasya sacrifice. The comm. quotes vss. 2, 3, 7 as employed by Paricista 6. I.

Translated : Ludwig, p. 189 ; Weber, xvii. 218 ; Griffith, i. 93.

I. She first shone out; she became a milch-cow at Yama's; let her, rich in milk, yield (âuk) to us each further summer (? sâmâ).

The verse occurs also in several other texts: in TS. (iv. 3. 115), MS. (ii. 13. 10), K. (xxxix. 10), PGS. (iii. 3. 5), and MB. (il. 2. 1 ; 8. I); and its second half is RV. iv. 57.7, d, and MB. i.8.8 c, 4; ii. 2.17 c, 4, and also found below as 17.4 c, d. The version of K. agrees (Weber) throughout with ours; TS, has, for a, yâ prathamâ uyâṅchat, with dhuksoa at end of c, and PGS. agrees with it; MS. has âuke at end of c; MB. (in all four occurrences) has Juhâ utt-, and in 8. 1 also arkapâ putra vâsa for a. The comm. takes sâmâm in d as an adverbial accus. (= sarvesu vatsaresu), as ' does Weber. Ct. Hillebrandt, Ved. Mythol. i. soo.

2. The night which the gods rejoice to meet, [as] a milch-cow coming unto [them], which is the spouse (pâzni) of the year —let her be very auspicious to us.

The verse is found also in PGS. (iii. 2. 2), HGS. (il. 17.2) [ MP. (ii. 20.27) and : MGS. (ii. 8. 4c) J, and its second half in MB. (ii. 2. 16 c, 4) ; the first four have the better readings janas in a and io "yatim in b and MGS. has ratrtm J. Ppp. has in ' ¹ b âhenu râtrim up-, and at the end gal3. For saṅvatsarâsya pâtnz (cf. vs. 8 a, b)

the comm. quotes TS. vii. 4. 8. ( 3. Thou, O night, whom we worship (upa-âs) as model (pratimâ) of the year —do thou unite our long-lived progeny with abundance of ¹ wealth.

Or, perhaps better (so the comm. and Weber), do thou [give] us long-lived progeny ; unite [us] with abundance of wealth.' Ppp. has for b ye tvâ râtrim upâsate, and in c tegâm for sâ nas. I MGS. has the vs. at ii. 8. 44 (cf. p. 156), agreeing nearly i with Ppp. ] The first half-verse is read also in TS. (v. 7. 27), K. (x1. 2), PGS. (iii. 2. 2), and MB. (ii. 2. 18) : TS. gives at end of b upâsate, MB. yajâmake ; PGS. has pratimâ ya taṅ rârrim upâasmake. In our edition, restore a lost accent-mark over the sz of s7ja in d.

4. This same is she that first shone out; among these other ones (f.) v she goes about (car), having entered ; great greatnesses [are] within her;

the bride (vadkâṅ), the new-going generatrix, hath conquered.

This verse is repeated below as viii. 9. rr. It occurs, with considerable variants, in a whole series of other texts: TS. (iv. 3.117), MS. (ii.13. 10), K. (3xX]X. IO),

CGS. (iii. 12.3), and MB. (ii. 2. 15). For âso âŚarâsa, TS. and CGS. have antâr a asyâm; MS., also Ppp., 4 ¹psv ântâs; MB., se yam apsv antas. All of them, with

Ppp., invert the order of c and â; and they have a different version of our c: frâya i (but Ppp. trita) enam makimânah sacante (CGS. -ntâm), but MB. vive by asyâm 7 makimâno antak; while, for jigâya in d, TS. and CGS. give jajâna, and MS. and

Ppp. mimâya, CGS. following it with navakry; and MB. reads prathama for our navagât. CGS., moreover, has in a gyuckar. These variants speak ill for the tradi- : tion. The comm. gives four diverse explanations of wavagâr: going in company with ¹ each new or daily rising sun ; pervading the new originating kind of living creatures; ae going to a daily originating new form; or, finally, going to the nine-fold divisions of Sh. the day; and the comment to TS. [reported by Weber ] adds a fifth, “newly married";

if the last is the meaning, jajâna is better with it than jigâya: “as soon as wedded to 4 the new year, she bears the days that follow.” The meter is really redundant by a syllable in a [âyâtwâ? ]. Further, MB. has in a e377 "va sa ya parva vy-; and Ppp. (5. ends 4 with janitrim.—BR., v. 1538, give 'erstgebârend ' for navagâr. ll 5. The forest-tree pressing-stones have made their sound, making the ¹ oblation of the complete year (parivatsartga); O sole âstakâ, may we, having good progeny and good heroes, be lords of wealths.

«Stones " : i.e. probably, blocks of wood used instead of stones [see Hillebrandt, Ved. Mythol. i. 162, 161 ]; or the wooden mortar and pestle (so the comm.). Ppp. reads for c ekâstakayr (= -k2yâi ) kavisâ vidhema. Some of the mss. combine kavâk kr- in b; the comment to Prat. ii. 63 requires kawâ k-, which both editions accept. Some of our mss. (P.M.W.Op.) give in c suprajâasas. HGS. (ii. 14.4) and MB. (ii. 2.13) have a corresponding verse : HGS. begins with #27kkalâs, combines kavij k- and reads -riRâm in b, and has supraja viravantas in c; MB. gives for a zwlâkkalâk samprawadanti grâvanas, ends b with 27âm, and has for d jyog jrvema balikrto vayar: te. It recurs also at MP. ii. 20. 34 and MGS. ii. 8.45. ] The first pâda is jagar, unmoted in the Anukr. As to agtak3, cf. Zimmer, p. 365.

5. The track (padâ) of Ida [is] full of ghee, greatly trickling ; O Jaâta- i vedas, accept thou the oblations. The cattle of the village that are of all forms —of those seven let the willing stay (47727) be with me.

Versions are found in ACS. (ii. 2.17), APCS. (vi. 5.7), HGS. (ii. v7.2), and MB. (ii. 2. 14), and of the latter half in TA. (iii. iI. 12, VS. 3I a, C). MB. agrees with our text throughout ; the three others have carâcaram at end of a, and all three kavâr dar: jusasva (for prati etc.) i b; HGS. begins with igâyai syptam, and ApCS, combines idâyah p-; then, in 49, ApCS., HGS., and TA. read 7kâ instead of 7âyi and ACS. pustis for ramtis; HGS. ends with ran tir astu pustik. The comm. reads zyâs in a; he renders sarisypam by atyarthar: sarpat, raṅris by pritis, and specifies the seven village (i.e. domestic) animals as cow, horse, goat, sheep, man, ass, camel ; but the number seven is doubtless used only as an indefinite sacred one. Pada a is again Jagati, as in vs. 5. |Pâda c is our ii. 34.4 a; between vi warâ#pâs and lesan APCS. inserts virâpaâs (a fragment of our ii. 34.4 bl). — Prat. ii. 72 requires gâyas p--

7. [Set] thou me in both prosperity and abundance; O night, may we be in the favor of the gods.

O spoon, fly away full; fly back hither well-filled ; jointly enjoying all sacrifices, bring to us food (7), refreshment (â7)).

The first two pâdas, which seem to have nothing to do with the rest of the verse, are 1 wanting in Ppp. What follows them is a complete anustubṅ, and quoted by its pratika in Vaâit. (see above) ; its first half is found in several other texts: VS. (iii. 49), TS. Ś((.8. 45), MS. (i. ro. 2), K. (ix. 5), ACS. (il. 18. 13) ; of these, VS. TS. ACS. read âzr vi for darve, as does also the comm., with a few of SPP's mss. Ppp. has sap carr isam in the last half-verse. The comm. understands 7 sthâpaya in a, as in the translation ; 54aja would answer an equally good purpose. He explains that the spoon is to go forth with oblation and to return with the answering blessings. SasmbhuRjatr he renders by kavisâ samyak pâlayantr prinayanti. Finally, he points out that, as c is quoted as a pratika, a and b have a right to the character of a separate verse ; but that in the paṅcapatalikâ the whole is made a verse, with three avasâuas ; the statement, but not the title, appears to fit our Anukr. ; this scans as 8 + ro: 848: 8 + 8 = 50, needlessly counting only ro syllables in b. In our ed, read ma for me. Ct. iv. 15. 12

8. Hither hath come the year, thy spouse, O sole âs7akâ; do thou unite our long-lived progeny with abundance of wealth.

Instead of repeating the second half-verse of vs. 3, Ppp. gives for c, 4 tâas31 Juhomi : kavisâ ghrtena (au nag arma yacckatu. Against his usual habit, the comm. explains c, d anew, but quite in accordance with his former explanation,

9. I sacrifice to the seasons, the lords of the seasons, them of the seasons (ârtavâ), and the winters (kâyanâ), to the summers (sâmâ), the years, the months ; for the lord of existence I sacrifice. : The change of case, from accusative to dative, in 4, doubtless intends no change of 4 construction. The verse, as noted above, is wanting in Ppp. ; it is in part repeated below, as xi. 6. 17. According to the comm., the “lords of the seasons " are the gods,

Agni etc. ; the ârzavas l cf. iii. 6. 6 note are parts of seasons ; other unspecified divi-

sions of time, sixteenths, kâ5zhas, etc." ; and although sama, sarvatsara, and kâyana are synonymous, yet kâyana here signifies “ days and nights," and sama " half-months."

10. To thee for the seasons, them of the seasons, the months, the years, the Creator (âkârâr), the Disposer (vidkâtâr), the Prosperer : (? samydF), the lord of existence, do I sacrifice.

All the sa7thitâ-mss. combine in a -Ś4yas rvâ, and SPP. accepts the reading in his ¹ text ; ours emends to -Ś4yas tvâ ; such treatment of final as is common in Ppp., and sporadic examples of it are found among the AV. mss., but it is hardly to be tolerated in a text like ours; and the comment to Prat. iv. ro7 quotes the passage as -54yas tv. y The comm. at xix. 37. 4 ] deems this verse and not v. 28. 13 J to be the one repeated as xix. 37. 4 ; see under that verse. Ppp. has, for a, b, yajur rtvighhya ârtavebhyo mâbhyas ¹ sanvatsarâya ca, which at any rate rids the text of the embarrassing foâ. Here the comm. declares the ârzavas to be “days and nights, etc." ; samydk he explains as samarâhayitre etannamne devâya.

11. We, making oblation with 22— I sacrifice to the gods with what is rich in ghee; unto houses not disorderly ()âubkhyant), rich in kine, may we enter together.

Or, it might be, 'may we lie down, go to rest'; the translation would imply more naturally sam âpa viema the Index Verborum takes #pa as an independent « casegoverning" preposition ] ; the comm. says wpe "kya san vigema sukhena ni vasema) he ¹ comfortably removes the anacoluthon in a, b by declaring yaje = yajamake, and takes alubkyatas as either nom. (gârâhyam akurvanâs) or accus. (gardkyarakitan). Ppp.

reads for 4 ârsadesvpagomata.

12. The sole âstakâ, paining herself (f24yâ-) with penance, generated an embryo, a greatness, Indra; by him the gods overcame their foes; : slayer of the barbarians became the lord of might (câcz).

The verse is found also in TS. (iv. 3.113), K. (xxxiX, IO), PGS. (iii. 3. 5), and i MB. (ii. 3.21) ; and a is identical with HGS. ii. 15.94 land MP. Hi. 20.35 a]: TS. rt accents iâgya- in a (the comm. does the same), and its c,d read: Śna dâsyṅn vy Ś âsakanta devâ kantâ 'surânâm abhavac châcwhik, and K. PGS. have the same ver- ¹ ‘ sion ; Ppp. agrees with them in reading asurânâm for dâsyṅnâm, and MB. has their d, but our c, except aszhanta for vy asak-. The gs of 7y â5- is distinctly required by

f Prat. ii. 92 ; but SPP, gives in his text gy âs-, against a majority of the mss. reported by him. Our P.M.W. are corrupt at the end, but P.M. show distinctly -z547%, indicating the reading of TS. etc. The comm. gives three different explanations of gârââham in b, Śâ adding garantyanm or stutyam (from gr 'sing'), and then garbhasthavad adyyan : Ś45 kg (from gr 'swallow'), to the true meaning. The eṅâstakâ he defines to be « eighth day : of the dark half of Mâgha." The concluding pâda is jagatI.

13. Thou whose son is Indra, whose son is Soma, daughter art thou of Prajâpati ; fulfil thou our desires; accept our oblation.

Wanting in Ppp., as above noted.

The second anwuvâka contains 5 hymns, 4o verses; and the quotation from the old Anukr. is simply daca.

docs.title: 11. For relief from disease, and for long life
docs.text:
[Brahman and Bhygoaṅgiras.— agtarcam. &indrâgnâyugyam, yaksmanâanadevalyar.

trâigtubham : 4. gakvarigarbhâ jagatr; 5, 6. anugubh ; 7. ugpigbrhatgarthâ pathyâpaṅkti ; 8. g-av. 6-3. byhatigarbhâ jagatr.) I

The first four verses are found in Pâipp. i., with the bulk of the 4-verse hymns ; they are also RV. x. 161. I-4 (RV. adds a fifth verse, which occurs below as viii. I. 20). The hymn is used by Kâug. (27. 32, 33) in a general healing ceremony (without specif cation of person or occasion ; the schol. and comm. assume to add such), and, in company with many others (iv. 13. I etc. etc.), in a rite for length of life (58. 11) ; and it is reckoned to the fakmanâgana gana (26. I, note) and to the Zyugya gana (54. 1, note; but the comm., ignoring these, counts it as one of the aṅkoliṅga gana). In Vat. (36. 19), vs. 8 accompanies the setting free of the horse at the agvamedha sacrifice; and the hymn (the edition says, i. ro. 4; the pratikas are the same) is employed, with ii. 33 etc., in the purusamedâṅa (38. 1).—| See also W's introduction to i. 33.

Translated : Weber, xvii. 231 ; Griffith, i. 95 ; Bloomfield, 49, 341.—In part also by Roth, Zur Literatur und Geschichte des eda, p. 42.

I. I release thee by oblation, in order to living, from unknown yâksma ; and from royal yâkgma ; if now seizure (grâṅ7) hath seized him, from it, O Indra-and-Agni, do ye release him.

RV. inserts va after yââi in c. Ppp. has, in the second half-verse, grâṅya grkito yady esa yatas lata inâ-. The comm. explains râjayaksma as either "king of yakgmas" or else «the y. that seized king Soma first," quoting for the latter TS. ii. 5. 65 see references in Bloomfeld's comment. The first pâda is jagat. 5

2. If of exhausted life-time, or if deceased, if gone down even to the presence (antikâ) of death, him I take from the lap of perdition; I have won (sp7) him for [life] of a hundred autumns.

The translation implies in d âspârsam, which is the reading of our edition, supported by RV., and also by the comm. (=prabalan karomi?), and two of SPP's mss. that follow the latter ; the âspârgam of nearly all the mss. (hence read by SPP.), and of Ppp., can be nothing but a long-established blunder. Ppp. has at the beginning yad ukkarayur y-. lAtii. 14.3 SPP. used the = long f" to denote the ksââpra circumflex; with equal reason he might use it here for the praglista of n}ta = ntita.

3. With an oblation having a thousand eyes, a hundred heroisms, a hundred life-times, have I taken him, in order that Indra may lead him unto autumns, across to the further shore of all difficulty (2urizâ).

RV. has in a qatâcaradena for catâviryena, and makes much better sense of c, 4 by reading gatâr for âidras, and (ndâras for 41 (it also has imâm for ena).

4. Live thou increasing a hundred autumns, a hundred winters, and a hundred springs; a hundred to thee [may] Indra, Agni, Savitar, Brihaspati [give] ; with an oblation of a hundred life-times have I taken him.

Our text, in the second half-verse, ingeniously defaces the better meter and sense given by RV., which reads inârâgnâ for ta tndro agnt) in c, and ends with kavâge

¹mâm pânar duk. The verse is fairly correctly defined by the Anukr., its c having r4 ¹ syllables (;akvarz), and making the whole number 47 syllables (agar less 1).

5. Enter in, O breath-and-expiration, as two draft-oxen a pen (zrâjâ); rr let the other deaths go away (v7), which they call the remaining hundred. : In this verse, as in the preceding and in vs. 7 and elsewhere, SPP. makes the inde- ¹ fensible combination 7 ck, instead of 7 ck, as the result of mutual assimilation of 7 and g

Left. note to i. 19.4.

[As to the one hundred and one deaths," cf. viii.2.27; x1.6.165 i. 30.3;

⁴kagata in Index ; and the numbers in the notable passage; xix. 47. 3 ff. ; Kuhn's most interesting Germanic parallels, KZ. xiii. 284. ; Wouttke, Deutscher Volksaberglaube,

301, 335 ; Hopkins, Oriental Studies . . papers read before the Oriental Club of

Philadelphia, 1888-1894, p. I52 ; Zimmer, p. 400. Cf. also the words of. the statute,

I8 Edward I., §4, concerning the Fine of Lands," “unless they put in their claim within a year and a day." ]

6. Be ye just here, O breath-and-expiration ; go ye not away from here; carry his body, his limbs, unto old age again. : At the end of b, the comm. reads javam (=¢âghram, akâle) instead of yuvâm, and ‘ two or three of SPP's mss., as often, follow him. i 7. Unto old age do I commit thee; unto old age do I shake thee down ²

(ni-dkṅ) ; may old age, excellent, conduct thee; let the other deaths go away, which they call the remaining hundred. Ś The Anukr. scans the verse as 9 +8 : 7 + 8 +8 = 40, not admitting any resolution in c.

8. Old age hath curbed (2647-443) thee, as it were a cow, an ox, with : a rope ; the death that curbed thee, when born, with easy fetter —that

Brihaspati released for thee, with the (two) hands of truth. Ś The verb-forms represent the noun abhidhânt halter, or bridle, or rope for confining : and guiding. ] A case of “reflected meaning": discussed, Lanman, 7ransactions of the Am, Philol, Association, vol. xxvi, p. xiii (1894). Cf. note to iv. 18. I. ] Aṅ'in many other cases, the comm, renders the aorist akira (for adkita) as an imperative, 5addhari ¹ karotu. On account of jâyamânarm in â (virtually ' at thy birth) Weber entitles the i = hymn ⁴ on occasion of difficult parturition," which is plainly wrong. Perhaps it is for : the same reason that the comm. regards it as relating to a child, or to a person diseased

. from improper copulation. In our text, at the beginning, read 347 (an accent-sign lost under a-). There is no Ś kart element in the verse.

docs.title: 12. Accompanying the building of a house
docs.text:
[Brakman. —navarcam. câlâsṅktam. vâstogpatiâlâdâivatan.. trâiubham: =. vir âgjagarr ¹ : 3. brkarz; 6. gakvarigarbhâ jagatr ; 7. Gr5y anugtubh ; g. bkuri ; 9. anugtubâ.] ( Ce The first eight verses are found in Paipp., but only 5, 7 together, in fii. vs. 6 being ¹ gre in xx. and vs. 8 in xvii. [More or less correspondent vss. recur at-MP. ii. r5. 3 ff. and. at MGS. ii. 11. 12 ff. (cf. D. 148 i%47vâ). ] The hymn is reckoned by Kâug. (3. 23) to the vâstogpariya hymns, and is used with them in. a house-building ceremony (43. 4 ff.; the two dkruvas," mentioned in 43. 11 are doubtless the same as the " two âhruvas" mentioned in 136. 7; land the latter ] are, according to the comm. to vi. 87, not vss. I and 2, but hymns vi. 87 and 88) ; vss. 6 and 8 are specially quoted (43.9, 10). Vait. (16. 1, in the -agnistoma sacrifice) gives a pratika which is nearly that of vs. 8, but with adkvaryo for nari. IVs. 9, q.v., occurs in Ppp. with others of our ix. 3. d

Translated : Ludwig, p. 463 ; Zimmer, p. Ifo; Weber, xvii. 234; Grill, 59, 108; Griffith, i. 97 ; Bloomfield, 140, 343. — Cf. Hillebrandt, Veda-chrestomathie, p. 44; and Bloomfield's references ; also M. Winternitz, Mittheilungen der Anthropologischen Gesellschayt in Wien, vol. xvii, p. [38].

I. Just here I fix (ni-mi) [my] dwelling (cââ) firm ; may it stand in security, sprinkling ghee ; unto thee here, O dwelling, may we resort (sam-car) with all our heroes, with good heroes, with unharmed heroes.

Ppp. reads aki instead of upa in d. Pâdas a, b are found in PGS. iii. 4. 4, with I ¹5thatu for -3t44; and b in CGS. iii. 3, with Ś574a for the same; HGS. (i.27. 2) has the whole verse, with zâ57kari in a, anu (for apa) in â, and suvirâs before sarvav- in c.

2. Just here stand thou firm, O dwelling, rich in horses, in kine, in pleasantness, in refreshment, in ghee, in milk; erect thyself (uz-gr) in order to great good-fortune.

Ppp. leaves the a of agvâvarr in b unelided. PGS. (ibid.) has pâdas b and â, making one verse of them with 3 c, 4; pâdas a, b are also found in CGS. (ibid.), with considerable variants : stââṇe for dhruvâ, dkruvâ for câlk, and silamavatrt for sâzy- ; and HGS. (ibid.) has again the whole verse, with #rjasvari payasa pinvamâana for c. I The comm., with the usual queer perversion of the sense of sâzy13, renders szṅrtâvarr by bakubhik priyasarvavâgbhir bâladinarm van bhir yuktâ. Pâdas b and c are jaguar.

3. A garner (? dkaruṇṅ) art thou, O dwelling, of great roof, of cleansed grain; to thee may the calf come, may the boy, may the kine, streaming in at evening.

This translation of the difficult and doubtless corrupt first half-verse implies emendation of -chandas to -chadis, and of pâri- to parâ-—whichlatter is, in fact, the Ppp. reading. In â, SPP. adopts the bad reading âspândamanâs, claiming to find it in the i majority of his mss. ; but the scribes are so wholly untrustworthy in their distinction of d sy and sp that the requirement of the sense is sufficient to show that they intend sy here ; the comm. reads -syanâ-, and so does CGS. (iii. 2) in the parallel passage : enâz cul krandaty 3 kumâra â syanâantân: dhenavo nityavatsâh ; PGS. (ibid) has z rvâ cicur a krandatv â gave dhenavo vâgyamanâak. MGS. i. 11.12) refects our vs. 7.1 The comm. lets us understand by âharuṇt either bhogajâtasya hE rayâtrr or pragcastâai stambhâir uperâ ; and by brhackandas either prabhâtâachâdana or makadbhic chandobhir vedair uperâa ; putiâhânya is ⁴having corn malodorous from age" —a sign of stores unexhausted. The Anukr. apparently scans as 7 +8 Io + II=36: a very poor sort of Ś74ari. Note that of SPP's authorities for Zsyand-, K and V were d men, not mss. ; none of his living authorities gave Zspanâ-. The blunder is easy for the eye, not for the ear.;

4. This dwelling let Savitar, Vâyu, Indra, Brihaspati fix, foreknowing;

let the Maruts sprinkle it with water, with ghee; let king Bhaga deepen

(ni-tan) our ploughing.

Ppp. reads in a, b vâyur agnis tvagta hota ni, and has somas (which suits 77a better) for b/agas in d. In c it begins with the true reading wksantu; this is so naturally suggested as emendation of the uckântu of the mss. that all the translators assume it (Weber, strangely mistaking the plain statement of the Index Verbor um, accuses us of having wrongly altered wksântn in our edition to uckântul) ; wksântu is also read by the comm., and by two or three of SPP's mss. that follow him; and SPP. very i properly admits it into his text. SPP. also reads after it nânâ, with the comm., but against all his mss. except the grotriya K J; there is no instance where uânâ and udnâs ‘ are correctly read in any of them (here, our Bp.O.Op. have uznâ, P.M. urvâ, the rest * unnâ : our edition gives unnâ, and Weber has failed to see that it was corrected

¹ in the Index Verborum under uâân J). The comm. makes d refer to the ploughing of the site of the house : câlabhâmel karsaṇarn: nitarân karotu. [*E.H.D.K.Kp. and

Ppp. have unnâ; I. has art ; W. has -z ¹v2. I For uckantu, see x. 9. 23 n. J

5. O mistress of the building (? mâna), as sheltering, pleasant, hast thou, a goddess, been fixed by the gods in the beginning; clothing thy- I self in grass, mayest thou be well-willing ; then mayest thou give us wealth together with heroes..

Ppp. has, for c, 4, #nnaṅ: vasanâ sumanâ yacas team rayin. no hi subhage suviran'.

Ś Grass" in c refers probably to a thatched roof. 3âna the comm. gives two explanations for : either “of the reverend (mânaniya) lord of the site (vâstupati)," or else

«of the spoiling (? miyamâna) grain etc." (patnâ in this case signifying pâalayitri). In 4 b the comm. reads nirmârâ. HGS. (i. 27.8) has a, b, c (with a wholly different d) in a corrupt form : ma nak saparnak caragal syonâ devo devebhir vimitâa 'sy agre: (ypaṅ:

vasanâah sumanaâ asi tvam ; but our d (with -wzrâṅ: r-) occurred just before (i. 27. 7).

6. With due order, O beam (vaṅgâ), ascend the post; formidable, bearing rule, force away (2pa-u77) the foes; let not the attendants (upasattâr) of thy houses be harmed, O dwelling ; may we live a hundred autumns with all our heroes.

Ppp. reads sthupa 'âki in a, and in c, d has -7â7ro 'tra virâjan jroâIr caradag

(arâni. Both meter and sense indicate that grââṇâm is an intrusion in c; and suwâras i at the end would rectify the meter of d. The first pâda is the beginning of a verse in

AGS. ii.9; and HGS. (i. 27.7) has the first half-verse, with szkṅ7uâu in a, and #râdkvas Ś and apa sedka in b cf. MP. ii. 15.6; MGS. Hi. 1. I4 is corrupt The comm. reads argan for risan in c; he explains rténa by abaâkhyena rṅpena saka, and upasattâaras by : upasadanakartâras. The verse (1I + II : 14 + I2 =483) is defined by the Anukr. with 9 mechanical correctness. a 27: To it the tender boy, to it the calf, with moving creatures (jâgat), de to it the jar of parisrâr, with mugs of curd, have come. : Ppp. has 72 for imâm in a and c, and in c parkrtag ; and it ends 4d with kalagag ca

J. The mss. vary between parisrâras and (râr- (our Bp. H.O.0p Kp. have g) ; the comm, has s, and renders the word by parisravanacuâsya maâhunak ' foaming over Ś sweet The word is quoted in the comment to Prât, ii. 106 as an example of s after 7 (a protected from lingualization by a following 7. The comm. reads in c kumbhâs, and in d kalagts ; half the mss. (including our Bp.E.I.H KX.) accent alacââs. The comm. explains jâgatâ as gamanagilena gavâdinâ, which is doubtless its true sense. The verse is found also in AGS. (ii: 8. 16), PGS. (iil. 4. 4), CGS. (iii. 2.9), and HGS. (i. 27. 3) the first two and the last have (like Ppp.) rvâ, and CGS. reads enam (for ¢ 'mâm); for jâgatâ, PGS. has jagadâis and AGS. jâyatam; CGS. gives bknvanas, with garâ for sakâ all differ again as to the last word, presenting za (PGS.), ayan (AGS. ), ayann d iva (HGS.) or gaman (CGS.); and CGS. has further kumbâyas in c, while for parsrâtas AGS. has pariritas and HGS. kiraumayas see also MP. ii. 15. 4 and MGS. i ii. r1. 125]. The epithet âry7, added by the Anukr. to the metrical definition of the i verse, is without meaning as aistinguishing it from vs. g I ef. iii. 14. 6, note ].

8. Bring forward, O woman, this full jar, a stream of ghee combined (sam-bky) with ambrosia (amjta) ; anoint these drinkers (?) with ambrosia; let what is offered-and-bestowed defend it (f. : the dwelling?).

The well-nigh universal reading of the mss. in c is ânâ7 paryn, which SPP. accord- d ingly presents in his text, in spite of its grammatical impossibility (of our mss., E. gives f pâtren, tren being a misreading of -7n found also more than once elsewhere ; P. has I padân, and W. pâtran); we emended imâm to imân ; but perhaps imâm pârrin this drinking-vessel,' which the comm. has, would be preferable, as better suited to sân i aṅdhi; and enâm at the end would then refer to it. The comm. has sam indkhi instead i of sâm aṅdhi ; he makes enân: imply câlâm. The corresponding verse in Ppp. (xvii) is quite different, and corrupt; pârnân: nâbhiri pra harâ '5hi kumbham apa ramaṅt osadhinân ghytasya : imam paâtrer amytâir i sam agdht sthirâ virâs sumanaso bhavantu : this suggests imâm pâtrâir amytasya in c ' anoint this [dwelling] with ves sels of ambrosia '; but also its separation from the preceding verses makes uncertain its belonging to the same ceremony with them. In the ceremonial use, it accompanies the entrance into the new dwelling, the wife first, carrying a water-jar.

9. These waters I bring forward, free from yâksma, yâksma-effacing; I set forth ? pra-sad) unto (âpa) the houses, along with immortal (am â+ta) fire.

The verse, as already noted, is wanting in this connection ] in Ppp., and neither Kâug. nor the comm. specify anything as to its use. Itappears again below as ix. 3. 23 ¹ with Ppp. version . The comm. gives no explanation nor paraphrase of p7â sg. Prepositions" discussed, Prat. iv. 3, note.

docs.title: 13. To the waters
docs.text:
IB ky gu. — saptarcam. vârupam uta sindkudâivatam. ânugtubham : r. nicrt;

5. virâgjagarr ; 6. nicrt trigtubh.]

The first six verses occur in Paâipp. iii., and also in TS. (v. 6. 1), MS. (ii. 13.1), and K. (xxxix. 2). The hymn is used by Kâug. in a ceremony for directing water into a certain course (40. 1 ff); the pâdas of vs. 7 are severally employed in it (see under that verse); it also appears, with other hymns (i. 4-6, 33, etc. etc.), in a rite for good-fortune (41.14). And the comm. describes it as used by one who desires rain. Verse 7 is d further employed, with a number of other verses, by Vaâit. (29.13), in the agnicayana, y accompanying the conducting of water, reeds, and a frog over the altar-site.— Berlin g ms. of Anukr. reads sindhvabââivaram.

Translated : Weber, xvii. 240 ; Griffith, i. 99 ; Bloomfield, r46, 348.—Cf. Bergaigne- Henry, Manuel, p. 143 ¹ I. Since formerly (? adâs), going forth together, ye resounded (zac)

when the dragon was slain, thenceforth ye are streams (zadi ) by name: ¹ these are your names, O rivers. ¹ The pada-mss. all commit the very gratuitous blunder of writing (4 instead of 7 at the beginning of d, as if it belonged to siadṅavas instead of to nâmâri; SPP. emends Ś to 7%, and the comm. so understands the word. The comm. takes ads as Vedic subs titute for amusmin, qualifying 4kâu. None of the other texts gives any various reading ¹ for this verse. Pâda d sets forth, as it were, the office of the first four verses, in finding i punning etymologies for sundry of the names of water. ¹ 2. When, sent forth by Varuṇa, ye thereupon (4) quickly skipped 4 (valg) together, then Indra obtained (42) you as ye went; therefore are i ye waters (42) afterward. ( TS. and MS. have in â pas (nomin.), and this is obviously the true reading, and assumed in the translation ; both editions follow the mss. (except our Op.) in giving 5 Fpas. MS. begins the verse with samprâcyutâs ; for &t in b MS. has yâz and TS. ts. (88 In d, Ppp. elides the a of anu; TS. leaves stṅana unlingualized. The comm. reads co instead szana.

3. As ye were flowing perversely (zpakâmâm), since Indra verily hin- 4 dered (var) you by his powers, you, ye divine ones, therefore the name water (vâr) is assigned you. : Ppp. has for c iâro vas saktabhir âevâis. TS. combines in 4 wâr pâra. The ge ṅr comm. apparently takes kâkam as a single word (the TS. pada-text so regards it), quot â ing as his authority Nâighapntuka iii. 12 ; and again in â, if the manuscript does not do : z him injustice, he reads kâkam for hâṅan:. ge e 4. The one god stood up to you, flowing at [your] will; the great Śr ones have breathed up (u4â-an)," said he; therefore water (udakâ) is [so] Ś â called. d The name here really had in mind must be, it would seem, zzâa rz, but dakâm has to ¹ be substituted for it in the nominative; none of the other texts offer a different form. et TS. improves the meter of a by omitting vas, and TS. and MS. leave the a of ²77 ² fi unelided. Ppp. differs more seriously : eko na deva upâarithat syandamana npetyerk: ¹ rl Yathâvagam in b might be (at his will,' opposed to apaṅâmâr in vs. 3. The sense of ¹ : c is rather obscure ; the comm. understands: saying 'by this respect on the part of

Indra we have become great,' they breathed freely (or heaved a sigh of relief : zckhea-

¹ sâtavatyas) " —which is senseless. R. suggests Indra put himself in their way with the polite address and inquiry: (their worships have given themselves an airing '; and conducted them on their way again"; Weber understands them to sigh under the burden of the god standing “upon " (427) them. The comm. declares a57 to have the ¹ sense of adkht.

5. The waters [are] excellent ; the waters verily were ghee; these —— waters verily bear Agni-and-Soma ; may the strong (7orâ) satisfying savor (râsa) of the honey-mixed (pc) come to me along with breath, with splendor. ;

TS. reads asus for âsan at end of a, and both TS. and MS., as also the comm., have gan at the end (MS p. agaz). MS. combines differently the material of our vss. 5 and 6: first our 6 a, b with 5 c, â, then our 5 a, b with 6 c, 4; and for our 5 a it reads âpo devtr ghrtaminvâ u 4pas. This last seems also to be intended by Ppp., with its apo devir gh tam itâpâkus ; and it has âyâ instead of iz (7s at end of b, and combines gama mâ in c-4. The comm. renders maâkuprcâm by madhunâa rasena sampyŚtâ- l nam ; the description in pada c almost makes us fancy some kind of mineral water to ( be had in view.

6. Then indeed I see, or also hear; unto me comes the noise, to me the voice of them; I think myself then to have partaken ambrosia f (am71a) when, ye gold-colored ones, I have enjoyed (72) you. i

TS. has the inferior readings nas for mâ at end of b and yâd for yadâ in d. MS.is corrupt in b; its pada-text reads vâk: nu: âsâm, but the editor gives in sa7hâtâ-text fl vâr no asâm. The comm. combines vâg ma. Ppp. has at the beginning yâd for âd. i The comm. takes the opportunity of the occurrence of âiraṇya- in â to bring forward an etymology of it which he here and there repeats ; it is kita-ramaṇzya? The verse is t improperly reckoned as niczt. [In the edition amâtastha is a misprint for -sya. l

7. This, O waters, [is] your heart, this your young (vatsâ), ye righteous ones ; come thus hither, ye mighty ones, where I now make you enter. {

The preceding verses have been simple laudation of the waters; this appended one ¹ (which is found neither in Ppp. nor in the other texts) adds a practical application, and is the sole foundation of the employment of the hymn by Kâug. With the first pada a piece of gold is buried in the desired channel; with b a prepared frog is fastened there; with c the frog is covered with a water-plant; with d water is conducted in.

docs.title: 14. A blessing on the kine
docs.text:
[Brahman —nânâdevatyam uta gosthadevarâ kam. ânustubham : 6. ârgr trigtubk.]

The hymn (except vs. 5) is found in Paâipp. ii. (in the verse-order 2, 4, 6, I, 3). It is used by Kâug., with other hymns (ii. 26 etc.), in a ceremony for the prosperity of cattle (19.14). In Vâit. (21.26), vs. 2 accompanies the driving of kine in the agnsstoma. The Vaâit. use does not appear to be mentioned by the comm., and his report of the Kâug. use is mostly lost from the manuscript (but filled in by the editor).

Translated : Ludwig, p. 469 ; Weber, xvii.244; Grill, 64, i I2; Griffith, i. ror ; Bloomfield, 143, 351.

I. With a comfortable (susâd) stall, with wealth, with well-being, with that which is the name of the day-born one, do we unite you.

Ppp. reads in b sepustya for subkṅtyâ. The obscure third pâda is found again below as v.28. rz c; it is altogether diversely rendered (conjecturally) by the translators (Weber, “with the blessing of favorable birth"; Ludwig, with [all] that which one calls day-born "; Grill, ⁴ with whatever a day of luck brings forth "); R. suggests with all (of good things) that the day brings, or that is under the heaven": none of these suits the other occurrence.

2. Let Aryaman unite you, let Pâshan, let Brihaspati, let Indra, who is conqueror of riches ; in my possession gain ye what is good.

In my possession,' lit. ' with me' (bei mir, chez moi). The comm. takes pugyata . as = poyayata ; and so do the translators, unnecessarily and therefore inadmissibly; GE or, we may emend to pugyarn, with vâsu as subject. Unite " calls for the expression

; of with what; this is not given, but the verse may be regarded as (except â) a continuation of vs. i. The three pâdas a—c are found as a gâyatri-verse in MS. (iv. 2. ro : with . po3â for pṅsâ in b). Ppp. has (ka pugyatâ at beginning of d. . 3. Having come together, unaffrighted, rich in manure, in this stall, bearing the sweet of soma, come ye hither, free from disease. i Three of the pâdas (a, b, d) again form, with considerable variants, a gâyarri in MS. sh (ibid.) immediately following the one noted above : MS. has âuikrutâs for âbibkyuyrs, 8 4 purisânis for kar-, and, in place of our d, suvaverâ na i gata. Ppp. gives, as not sel- 4 dom, in part the MS. readings, corrupted : it begins saṅrjanâanân: vikytâm, has hkawis ² for madhu in c, and, for d, svâveâsa efana. The combination of p. upacâtana into s. : upcrana is one of those aimed at by Prat. iii. 52, according to the comment on that rule; ² : but it would equally well fall under the general rule (iii. 38) as to the order of combina- (of tion when z comes between two vowels (zpa-â-itana like indra-a-iki etc.). [Ct also I Lanman, JAOS. x. 425.

4. Come ye just here, O kine, and flourish here like ¢â(â ; also mul- 4 tiply (Praja) just here ; let your complaisance be toward me. c Câke 'va (p. gâkâoiva) in b is very obscure : Weber renders "like dung" (as if Śt câ)a=câkyz); Ludwig, ⁴ with the dung" (as if ¢âkâ = cakṅnâ); Grill, “like plants" ul (implying (âkam iva or (âkâ iva); the comm. says multiply innumerably, like flies" i ¹ (aka = makŚikâ); this last is, so far as can be seen, the purest guesswork, nor is any- ¹ : thing brought up in its support; and the "dung " comparisons are as unsuitable as they Ś i are unsavory. The explanation of the comm. accords with one among those offered by ' the commentators on VS. xxiv. 32 (= MS. iii. 14.13) and TS. v. 5. 185, where (âkâ also ¹ 4 occurs. Ppp. reads sakâ iva. SPP. reports his pada-mss. as accenting gâvaj in a, but ¹ emends in his pada-text to gâval ; the latter is read by all ours, so far as noted. I ¹ 5. Let your stall be propitious ; flourish ye like (ârigâkâ; also multiply just here ; with me we unite you. i There is no Ppp. text of this verse to help cast light on the obscure and difficult ¹ ¹ (âricaka (p. carkâkâcioa). The comm. (implying -kâs) explains the word as meaning

“kinds of creatures that increase by thousands in a moment," but offers no etymology or

; other support; the translators supply a variety of ingenious and unsatisfactory conjec-

¹ tures (Weber, like ¢cârâ-dung," câri perhaps a kind of bird; Grill [fatten yourselves]

¹ like the cârikâ" or hooded crow; Ludwig simply puts a question-mark in place of a translation). R. offers the conjecture (ârâ (= calik) aka iva (like rice in manure.

Our P:-M.E I. accent (âricâ ke "via.

I Bloomfield emends to câri-gukeva (= -kâs (ua), ' thrive ye like starlings and par- ¹ : rots.' True, these birds are habitual companions in literature as in life (see my trans-

; lation of Karp âra-maṅjan, p. 229, note), loquacity being their salient characteristic;

but what is the tersium comparationis between the thriving of cows and of starlings? 6. Attach yourselves, O kine, to me as lord of kine; this your stall

¹ here [be] flourishing; to you, becoming numerous with abundance of wealth, to you living, may we living be near (zpa-sad).

Bhâvantas in c would be a desirable emendation. Zṅa-sad may be rather wait upon ' (so Grill), only then we should expect rather sadâma (comm., upagacckema). 1 W's implied difference between saâema and sadâma is not clear to me. ] Ppp. reads in a gopatyâ, and its b is mayi vo gostha (ka posayâri. The epithet ârsi seems to be i as meaningless here as at iii. 12. 7—see note, end. ]

docs.title: 15. For success in trade
docs.text:
[Atharvan (panyakâmak).— agtarcam. vâivadevam utâ: "ndrâgram. trâigtublam:

I. bhurii ; 4. 3-av. 6-9. byhatigarbhâ virâdatyaṇti ; 5. virâdjagali ; (

7. anustubk ; 8. nicrt.]

Four of the verses are found in Pâipp. xix. (I, 4, 6, 2, in this order). The hymn is used by Kâug. in a rite for good-fortune in trading (so. 12), and again (59.6) for a simi- f lar purpose ; also (or vs. r) in the indramaṅotsava ceremony (140.16); also vss. 7 and; 8 in the appeasing of the flesh-eating fire (70. 13, 14). In Vâit. (6. 9), vs. 7 is employed in the ceremony of establishing the sacrificial fire. The usual statement of these various uses appears to be lacking in the manuscript of the comm., and is supplied, only in part, i by its editor.

Translated : Ludwig, p. 215; Zimmer, p. 258 (except vss. 7, 8); Weber, xvii. 247; Grill (vss. 1-6), 69, 113; Griffith, i. ro2 ; Bloomfield, 148, 352.—Cf. Hillebrandt, Veda-ckrestomathte, p. 38. !

I. I stir up (cud) the trader Indra; let him come to us, be our forerunner; thrusting [away] the niggard, the waylaying wild animal, let him, having the power (7), be giver of riches to me.

Or paripanthtnam and mygâm in c may be independent of one another (so comm., and translators except Weber and Zimmer). Ppp. has, for a, b, indrarz vayarz vaṇijan: havâmakhe sa nas trâra pura etn prajanan. The Anukr. notices c as jagazz pada. ( 1 Indra, the trader ": cf. Bergaigne, Rel. wâd., ii. 480.— Many Jâtaka tales (e.g. no's I, 2) give vivid pictures of the life of the trading caravans. I

2. The many roads, travelled by the gods, that go about (saṅz-car) between heaven-and-earth —let them enjoy me with milk, with ghee, : that dealing (k77) I may get (â-47) riches.

Ppp's version is very different: kai 'vas panthâ bakavo âewayânânt anu âyzvâ- 2rthivE supranttil : tesâam aknân varcasy a dadhâani yarhâ kltva diana: âvakan. The comm. allows us alternatively to understand âeva. in a as "by traders "; he renders Jjusantâm in c by sevantâm, as if it were causative. His text has at the beginning ye te panth- The emendation, suggested by Weber, of 2 in c to 7ze would help the sense. The first half-verse is found again below as vi. 55. r a, b. To make a regular tristubk, we must contract to p77hot in b, and expand to krṅtu-Ś in 4; the Anukr. perhaps regards the two irregularities as balancing one another.

3. With fuel, O Agni, with ghee, I, desiring, offer the oblation, in order to energy (z4ras), to strength ;— revering with worship (Śrâkmaz), so far as I am able —this divine prayer (47), in order to hundred-fold winning.

The verse is RV. iii. 18. 3, without variant — save that RV. accents of course juhâziâ, as does our edition by necessary emendation, while SPP. follows all the mss. in giving juhomiâ (the pada-text puts a sign of pâda-division after the word, but also before it).; The verse is not at all likely to have been an original part of our hymn; the word ataseyâya in d has caused its addition. The comm. renders târase by vegâya cighragamanâya, and applies yâvad Śe in two ways, to the winning or to the worshipping.

4. This offense (? qarâyi) of ours mayest thou, O Agni, bear with (75), what distant road we have gone. Successful (cunâ) for us be bar- ( gain and sale; let return-dealing make me fruitful ; do ye two enjoy this oblation in concord; successful for us be our going about and rising.

The first two padas are wanting in the Pâipp. version of the hymn (though they occur, in another connection, in Ppp. i.), and they are plainly an intrusion here, due to the mention of distant travel in b; they form the first half of RV. i. 31. 16 (but RV. reads for b imâm âdhvânaṅ yâm âgâama ânrât; LCS., in its repetition of the RV. verse at iii. z. 7, agrees with AV. in preferring âṅram). The insertion dislocates the comm's division of the hymn ; he reckons only the frst 4 pâdas as vs. 4, then the last two with the first two of our 5 as vs. 5, and the latter half of our 5 with the former half of our 6 as vs. 6, making a vs. 7 of only the two concluding pâdas of our 6, and number ing the two remaining verses as 8 and 9. Some of our mss. (P.M. W.E.I.) divide and number in the same way to the middle of our vs. 6, then making vs. 7 consist of 6 pâdas and end where our vs. 7 ends. Ppp. has for its verse a different version of our cf: paṇo for cunam at the beginning (with "ste after no), godhani nas for phalinam ma, and, for our e, se7rarânâ kavir idan: jusantân.. The Anukr. seems to scan the verse as II +9: I2 + II: II + 12=66, though c and f are properly to be made regularly trâstubh by elision to 'szu. The comm. renders carânâ in a by “injury " (kâṅsâ), and explains it as either that arising (to Agni) from the intermission of sacred rites in consequence of the householder's absence from home, or else that to the absentee from his long journey as expressed in b—mzmy sas being in the first case = kyamasva, and in the second = marsaya or Śtiksaya ' cause us to endure ' : perhaps the second is, after all, the better. |For d, rather, ' may barter make me abounding in fruit,' i.e. ‘may barter bring me its reward.

5. With what riches I practise (ca?) bargaining, seeking riches with riches, ye gods—Ilet that become more for me, not less; O Agni, put down (ni-sidk) with the oblation the gain-slaying gods.

Or, possibly, ' the gods of the gain-slayer ' (sâtaghnâs as gen. sing. ; the comm. takes it as accus. pl, and Zimmer and Ludwig so translate). The omission of âevân would rectify the meter and better the sense, and Weber and Grill and Hillebrandt ] leave it out. The Anukr. gives a mechanically correct definition of the verse as it stands. (

6. With what riches I practise bargaining, seeking riches with riches, ye gods—therein let Indra assign me pleasure (? râci), let Prajâpati, Savitar, Soma, Agni.

Ppp. has a better version of a: yat papena pratipanan: carâmi, and it arranges c; differently : indro me tasmin ream &; and reads Śrhaspatis for prajâp- in d. HGS. (i. 15. I) has a kindred verse, with second pada nearly identical with ours, and rucam in ec. [See also MP. ii. 22. 4.) R7ci, lit. brightness, is variously understood by the i translators : Zimmer, "attractive power"; Ludwig, " pleasure ; Weber, “understanding"; Grill, "consideration "; the comm, explains it by sarvajanapritin dhanapraâanena "danecckâm,. Ppp. seems to omit dkanena in b.

7. Unto thee with homage do we, O priest Vâigvânara (' for all men '), give praise ; do thou watch over our progeny, our selves, our kine, our breaths.

Two of our pada-mss. (Bp.Kp. ; also D.p.m.?) divide vââvânara} : turnak in b; P.M.W. give sâm for sâ at beginning of c. This verse and the next seem to be additions to the original hymn. Under siz, BR. and Index. VerŚorwm join pa with stu;. correct Jadex under #pa accordingly. ] i

8. Every day may we bring constantly for thee as for a standing horse, O Jâtavedas ; rejoicing together with abundance of wealth, with food, may we thy neighbors, O Agni, take no harm.

The verse nearly accords with xix. 55. I, below; the second half is the same as there ; the first half here is more unlike the parallel verse in other texts (VS. xi. 755 ¹ CB. vi.6. 4.1; TS. iv. I. or; K. xvi. 75 MS. ii. 7. 7) than is xix. 55. I ab— see under xix. 55. I; in the second half they vary only by putting âgne at the beginning of â; they make a more manageable sentence by furnishing an object, ghâsâr: ' fodder,' for bharema. The comm. renders ris hate by svagrhe vartamânâya. 4

Here, at the end of the third anavâka, of 5 hymns and 38 verses, the old Anukr. i says simply asian (but O.R. give aszatriâgat).

The fifth prapâthaka also ends with this hymn.

docs.title: 16. Morning invocation to various gods, especially Bhaga
docs.text:
[Atharvan.— saptarcam. prâtaṅsakiam. bârkaspatyam uta bakudevatyam. trâigtubkham

I. 3rŚi jagati ; 4. bhurikpaikti.] ¹

Found in Pâipp. iv., with very few variants. It is a RV. hymn (vii. 41), repeated ¹ also in VS. (xxxiv. 34—40) and TB. (ii. 8. 979) and MP. i. 4. 1-7, in the same order as here]. It is used by Kâug. with hymns vi. 69 and ix. 1 J, in the rite for generation of wisdom (ro. 24), to accompany washing the face on arising from sleep ; also in certain ceremonies for splendor " (varcas : 12.15; I3.6), with hymns vi. 69 and ix. I ; and it is reckoned to the varcasya ganas (xz. ro, note ; 13. I, note). In Vait. (5.17), vs. 6 i accompanies, in the agnyâadkeya, the horse's setting his foot on the boundary; and its; latter half, an oblation in the cârurmaâsya sacrifice [ Vâit. 8.14].

Translated : as RV. hymn, by Grassmann, i. 3536, and by Ludwig, no. 92; as AV. ¹ hymn, by Weber, xvii. 251 ; Griffith, i. ro4.— Cf. Winternitz, Hockzeirsrituell, p. 97, and notes. i

I. Early (prâtâr) do we call Agni, early Indra, early Mitra-and-Varuṇa, early the (two) Agvins, early Bhaga, Pâshan, Brahmaṇaspati, early Soma and Rudra do we call.

The other texts, and Ppp. with them, read at the end of 4 kxvema.

2. The early-conquering formidable Bhaga do we call, the son of Aditi who is disposer (vidhartâr), to whom every one that thinks himself weak [or] strong, to whom even the king] says: “apportion [me] a portion."

Bkakst in 4d might also be rst sing. mid. of the s-aorist, ' may I obtain (so Weber, ( etc.) ; the comm. explains it both ways. Again all the other texts, including Ppp, ( have kuvema for kavâmake in a; the Anukr. ignores the metrical irregularity caused by our reading. [Note the play on the god's name : portion ' is Śkâga. J i Sr 3. O Bhaga, conductor, Bhaga, thou of true bestowal, Bhaga, help upward this prayer (77), giving to us; O Bhaga, cause us to muitiply with kine, with horses, O Bhaga, with men, — rich in men may we be. ¹ In this verse AV. and RV. agree throughout ; TB. reads gva with unlengthened final in b, and VS. zo with unlingualized nasal in c.

4.
