Both now may we be fortunate (b4âgavant), and in the advance 4 (? prapituâ) and in the middle of the days ; and, O bounteous one, at the 1 up-going of the sun, may we be in the favor of the gods. ¹ As to the difficult word grapitvâ, see Bloomfield, JAOS. xvi. 24 ff. ; “ up-going" is ŚŚCŚ probably here ⁴ out-going, disappearance '; the comm. renders prapitvâ by sâyâkṅne, Ś his understanding of ṅââ¹âu is lost out of the manuscript. The other texts read #â71a.

I For this vs., see especially p. 35 end, 36 top, of BI's paper. : 5. Let the god Bhaga himself be fortunate ; through him may we be Vt fortunate ; on thee here, Bhaga, do I call entire ; do thou, O Bhaga, be fil g ga, (a our forerunner here. ed RV. (with VS. and TB.) leaves the final of 7a unlengthened at beginning of b; ed and RV. and VS. make the sense of c better by reading jokawṅti) all the three have { at the end of a the voc. dzvzs. Comm. to TB. makes johavimi=âkhvayati oe 6. docs.title: 17. For successful agriculture
docs.text:
. ¹ : [Vigvâmâtra.— navarcam. sââdevatyam. Śnugubham : I. Brgi gâyatrz; 2, 5, 9. (rigtubk;

i z Four verses of this hymn are found together in Pâipp. ii., in the order 2, 1, 5,4 5 vs. 3

occurs in Pâipp. xix., and there are verses in Paipp. xii. and xix. resembling our vs. 6. Ś Much of its material appears also in RV. x. lor, iv. 57, and parts in VS. TS., TA., and Ś ¹ P

MS.: see under the several verses. The hymn is used by Kâug. (zo. 1 (.) in an extended eo ceremony for success in plowing, the details of which, however, do not help the inter- " — ; pretation of the verses; vs. 8 (ib. ro) is specially quoted as accompanying an oblation . ¹ to Indra at the further end of a furrow, or of each one of three furrows ; the comm. also jue regards it as intended by cunâsirâni at 166. 8, in the book of portents, in a charm against the portent of mixed-up plows (whatever that may be ) ; vs. 4, again, accompanies the marking out of the sacrificial hearth at 137. 19. In Vâit. (28. 30-32), vss. I, 3, and 2 b appear in the agnicayana, in the ceremony of plowing the sacrificial hearth, and vs. 7 (9.27) at the end of the cârurmâsya sacrifice, with an oblation to the cunaâsira. *1 Wenn zwei Pfliige sich verstricken beim Ackern," says Weber, Omina, p. 368. ]

Translated : Weber, xvii. 255; Griffith, i. 106.— Vs. 3 is elaborately discussed by d Roth, Fesigruss an B6htlingk, p. 95 ff. See also Weber, Omina und Portenta, p. 371. ¹

I. The poets (kav) harness the plows (sâ7a), they extend severally the yokes —they the wise ones (â%7ra), with desire of favor (?) toward the gods.

The verse seems to imply a hidden comparison of the poet's work with the plowman's. The other texts (RV. x. roI. 4; VS. xii.67; TS. iv. 2.55; MS. ii. 7.12 ( K. xvi. 11 ; Kap. xxv. 3) read sumnayâ (but K. has yu} : Kap. not noted), which the i translation adopts, yâ7 seeming an unintelligent corruption of it; but the comm. gives I a double explanation of yâz, one as "desiring a happy-making sacrifice" and qualify- i ing yajamane understood, the other as from sumna-ya (ya for root yz) and qualifying balrvardân understood! He makes sia equivalent with lz7gala, and takes vi tanvate i as = «put on the oxen's shoulders "; vâ-Yan as here applied seems imitated from its use of stringing a bow; in TB. ii. 5. 8:2 we have even vf tanoti stran. ¹

2. Harness ye the plows, extend the yokes; scatter (oa) the seed here in the prepared womb ; may the bunch (?) of v774 be burdened for us ; may the sickles draw in (2-yu) the ripe [grain] yet closer.

In the first half-verse, RV. (ib. 3) and VS. (ib. 68) have tan udkvarr for tanota, the; rest (ibid.) agreeing with our text (but K. has kro yonir) ; Ppp. reads ksetre instead of yonâu; yânau, of course, involves a hidden comparison of sowing with impregnation. In the difficult and obscure second half, the other texts (not Ppp.) give girâ ca for the unintelligible virâjas, and âsaz (with accent apparently meant as antithetic) for asaz, which is read in all the mss., but in our edition (not in SPP's) emended to âsaz, the d same texts accent grustâs (and our edition was emended to agree with them; SPP. accents the first syllable, with all the mss.).. SPP. reads cnâsṇis, with the majority of his authorities (including oral reciters), and with the comm. ; among his mss. are found also crâ31âs, gli-, srâ-, suṅ-, and gnugyrs. Part of our mss. also (E.I.H.Op.) are noted ¹ as seeming to intend g7â-, and, as Ppp. supports it by reading sunzstis sabk, the reading cnâstik is adopted in the translation as also at viii. 2. r J. The manuscripts are i not at all to be relied on for distinguishing cuz and cra cf. iii. 30. 7 and note The comm. explains it by Zguprâpakaṅ stambah, and sâbkarâs as phalabhârasakitas ' heavy with fruit'; of vâ7âj he makes easy work by identifying it with anna, on the authority of TB. iii. 8. 104: 4nnanm vât virât? In â, fually, the chief discordance of the versions is at the end, where, for Z yavan (Ppp. Gywvart), RV.VS.Kap. read ¢ ¹yaz, and TS. MS.K. 7 "yar. But TS. has s7ayâ (instead of as), apd some of our mss. (P.M. W.), with the majority of SPP's, combine Zârnyâs or âxkrnyâs, implying crayâs. The Anukr. does not heed that pada d is, as it stands, jagazi. [W., in his own copy and i in Index, Seems to approve the accentless asaz.— Comm. has â yawanm in â.

3. Let the plow (Jâṅgala), lance-pointed, welllying, with well-smoothed handle, turn up (uâ-vap) cow, sheep, an on-going chariot- ( frame, and a plump wench.

That is, apparently, let all these good things come as the reward of successful agri- ⁴ culture. The verse, not found in RV., but occurring in VS. (ib. 71 ; and thence quoted 0 in the Vasitha Dharmasâtra ii. 34 and explained in Ś. 35), as well as in TS.MS.K. (as : Śc above), has many difficult and questionable points. For pavirâvat (Ppp. puts it before g: âṅgalam) VS. accents pâviravar, and TS. MS K. substitute pâviravam ; for sugiman ¹ all have sugevam very propitious '; the Pet. Lex. suggests sustznam having a good et parting i.e. of furrows, or 'even-furrowed'; and R. refers to MB. i. 5. 2, sznânaṇṅ:

nayâmi. Ppp. reads suvegam, which probably means suceoam. The impracticable

; somasar-saru (so in pada-text) is somaptt-saru in VS., MS. K., and Vasistha, and somath pitsalam: in Ppp. ; Vas. renders it " provided with a handle for the drinker of soma," â implying the division somapi-tsaru Weber conjectures a noun wan 'strap,' and 9% emends to soma (= sa-uma) satsaru, " with strap and handle." But TS. reads sumatt- ŚŚ ofsaru, and this is adopted in the translation, mari being taken not as from man but Ś ¹ as the word found in marrky and its derivatives, and related with matya etc. (Weber also refers to this meaning and connection.) The comm. explains sucimarm by karsa- Śâ kasya sukhakaram, without telling how he arrives at such a sense ; and somasatsara â : (disregarding the pada-division) as from zsaru, either a concealed going in the ground" fey (root sar, explained by ckadmagatâu), or else "a kind of part to be held by the plow- 4 ! : man's hand "; in either case a producer of the soma-sacrifice" (i.e. soma-sa). For . ¹ ratha-vâhana the frame that carries a chariot when not in use,' and prasthâvat, et here virtually ' with the chariot on it,' see R. in the Festgruss an Bohtlngk, p. 95 ff;

the comm. interprets as agvabalivardadikan rathavâhanasamartham. VS. reads at ² ² the beginning of c r4â âd vapati, and TS. 4d 7 krŚati; Ppp. has dadata kryṣata; : ; VS. TS. MS. PPD. gVe fOr e grapharyyân: (Ppp. yânz) ca prvarim and VS. TS. invert . the order of â and e J; the comm. also has pzvar zm (= sthâlâm); prapharor he explains as prathamavayâk kanya. The first pada is defective unless we resolve -âṅ-.

I Zimmer, p. 236, refers to Sir H. M. Elliot's Memoirs, ii. 341, for a description of the I Penjab plow. ]

4. Let Indra hold down the furrow; let Pâshan defend it; let it, rich ¹ : in milk, yield to us each further summer. : it This verse is found only in RV. (iv. 57. 7), which reads ânn yachatu for abhz raksatn ¹ i Ppp. has makyan: instead of abki. We had the second half-verse above, as iii. ro. r c, d. of 5. Successfully (;unâm) let the good plowshares thrust apart the earth ; successfully let the plowmen follow the beasts of draft; O Cuna-

; sirâa, do ye, (two), dripping (?) with oblation, make the herbs rich in 4 el berries for this man. I Ś VS. (x5. 69) and MS. (ii. 7. 12) have the whole of this verse; RV. (iv. 57.8) and ¹ Ś TS. (iv. 2. 56), only the first two pâadas. For supâalâs in a, VS. (also our I.) has sz ¹ phṅlas, and RV. TS. nak pṅ”lâs, both preferable readings; RV. VS. have krsantu for ¹ ¹ fudantnu. In b, TS. gives abkt for ânu (our P.M. have â5htnu); MS. has kmâco ¹ Ś 2abhy Mu vâkâtṅ ; RV.VS., (a abkt yantu vâhâtk. In c, the comm. gives rosamâṇa, z ee explaining it by tugyantân. In d, the mss. vary (as everywhere where the word occurs) ²Ś ll between pâpalâs and pigâalâs ; about half are for each; VS.MS. end the pada with

¹ kartanâ ‘sme. Ppp. has a peculiar version: cunaṅ: kenâco anv etu vâkan cunan:

phâlo vinadann ayatu bhumin : unâswâa havisâ yo yajatrai supippala osadhayas

santu tasmâi. The comm. [quoting Vâska declares Cânâstr an to be Vayu and Aditya 1 Ś (wind and sun); or else, he says, Cana is god of happiness and Sz a of the plow.

6. Successfully let the draft-animals, successfully the men, success. fully let the plow (lâṅgala) plow; successfully let the straps be bound; d successfully do thou brandish the goad.

This is RV. iv. 57.4, without variation; it is also found, with the two following verses, in TA. (vi. 6. 2, vss. 6-8), which reads narâs instead of nâras atend of a. Part f of our mss. (P.M. W.E.) have â577âm in d. The comm. declares Cuna to be addressed in the last pada. Ppp. has in xl. cunaṅ: vrtrâam âyaccha (unan: astrâm ud ingay ah cunaṅ: tu tapyatârn: phâla cunar: vahatu lâṅgalam; and in xix. the same a,b ending a J, but, for c, 4, cunark vahasya cuklasyâ 'strayâ jaki daksinanm.

7. O Cunâsirâ, do ye (two) enjoy me here; what milk ye have made in heaven, therewith pour ye upon this [furrow]. fl

⁴ Milk,' i.e. nourishing fluid. Weber implies at the end earth" (instead of furrow"), which is perhaps to be preferred. RV. (iv. 57. 5) reads for a cânâszrâv imâr vâcar: ju-; TA. (as above) the same, except that it strangely omits the verb, and thus i reduces the Śistubkh pada to a gâyatri; both texts mark the principal pada-division after b. The comm. changes all the three verbs to 3d dual. The Anukr. forbids in a ' the resolution -s7râ ikâ. In our edition the verse is numbered 6, instead of 7.

8. O furrow, we reverence thee; be [turned] hitherward, O fortunate one, that thou mayest be well-willing to us, that thou mayest become of good fruit for us.

RV. (iv. 57.6) inverts the order of a and b, and both it and TA. (as above) end c and â respectively with subhâgâ 'sasi and suphâlâ 'sasi. All the pada-mss. have the blundering reading susphalâk in d. The Anukr. perversely refuses to make the resolution 72-7 in a.

9. With ghee, with honey (mâdkhu) [is] the furrow all anointed, approved (gnu-man) by all the gods, by the Maruts ; do thou, O furrow, turn hither unto us with milk, rich in refreshment, swelling with fulness of ghee.

The verse is found also in VS. (xii. Jo), TS. (iv. 2. 56), and MS. (ii. 7. 12). VS. MS. read -gjyatâm for -aktâ in a; all make c and â exchange places, and at the beginning of c read asmân for sâ nas; and VS. TS. put pâyasâ in place of gkrtâvat in d, while i MS. gives 7rjâ bhâgâm mâdâkumar pinv-. i

docs.title: 18. Against a rival wife : with a plant
docs.text:
[Arharvan.— vânaspatyam. ânugubkam : 4. 6. anugubgarthâ uspik;

6. uspiggarbhâ patkyâpankti.] This peculiarly Atharvan hymn has found its way also into the tenth book of the Rig-Veda (as x. 145, with exchange of place between vss. 3 and 4; it is repeated in RV. order at MP. i. 15. 1-6). Only three verses (our 4, 2, I, in this order) are found in. Paipp. (vii.). Kâug. uses it, among the women's rites, in a charm (36. r9—2r) for getting the better of a rival; vs. 6 a and b accompany the putting of leaves under, and upon the (rival's) bed. And the comm. (doubtless wrongly) regards vss. 5: and. 6 to; be intended by the pratika quoted in 38. 30, instead of xii. I. 54, which has the same i beginning. Gg Ta U3 ( os Translated : as RV. hymn, Ludwig, ii. 554, no. 932; Grassmann, ii.415; as AV.

hymn, Weber, v. 222; Zimmer, p. 307 ; Weber, xvii. 264 ; Griffith, i. 108 ; Bloomfield,

107, 354; further, by Winternitz, Hockzeitsrituell, p. 98. (¹ I. I dig this herb, of plants the strongest, with which one drives off

(6ââk) her rival ; with which one wins completely (sam-vid ) her husband. I RV. reads in b the accus. viṅâdkam. For â, Ppp. gives krnute kevalam patim. a The comm. (with our Op.) has osadktm in a; he understands throughout the herb in question to be the pâzṅz (ct. ii. 27. 4), though Kâug. and the Anukr. speak only of (â22- 49 parṇt ' arrow leaf ' (not identified). Ś 2. O thou of outstretched leaves, fortunate, god-quickened, powerful, elt do thou thrust away my rival, make my husband wholly mine. it : ¹ Outstretched,' lit. supine ; horizontal, with the face of the leaf upward. RV. has SH âdhama for nuda in c, and the modern Zurn for kydki at the end. Ppp. offers only the

( first half-verse, in this form : uttânaparnâr subhagar sakamânar: sakasvatmn ; MP. cu also has sakamane instead of devayute.

3. Since he has not named (grak) thy name, thou also stayest (ram)

not with him as husband ; unto distant distance make we my rival go.

This translation of the first half-verse follows closely our text. RV. has a very difet ferent version : nahy âsya nâma grbhuâmi ne asmin ramate jâne since I name not Śoe her (its ?) name, she (it?) also does not stay with (find pleasure in) this person (people ?).' i Winternitz applauds and accepts his commentator's explanation of b: nor finds she Gut pleasure in me" (taking gyasṅz janas in the much later sense of ⁴ I"), but it seems el wholly unsatisfactory. The meter calls for emendation in a to jagrâha ' I have named,' ¹ equivalent to the RV. reading; and R. makes the emendation, and retains the jâne of ¹ RV., rendering (as addressed by the woman using the charm to the plant) I have not named [to her] thy name; and thou stayest (stayedst) not with the person (bei der i Person). The comm. regards the rival as addressed, and conveniently makes ramase et =ramasva : "stay thou not with this my husband.” Weber renders ramase by ² «kosest," thou dalliest not. No satisfactory solution of the difficulty is yet found. ¹ ¹ 4. Superior [am] I, O superior one; superior, indeed, to them (f.) that ¹ are superior ; below [is] she that is my rival; lower [is] she than they (f.) = that are lower.

g RV. has the better reading 4247 for aâkhâs in c, allowing c and d to be combined into one sentence; and the comm. gives correspondingly aâka. Ppp. is more discordant and corrupt : uttarâ ham uttarabkyo uttaro ed âdharabhyah : adhah saparnt samarthy ¹ ¹ adâkared adharabhyaṅ. R. conjectures in a urtarâhâhamuttare, for âttarâa 'kâm akham-

¹ uttare cf. iii. 8. 3]. The verse, even if scanned as 7-7: 8+7=29, ought to be called ¹ (or 5. I am overpowering ; likewise art thou very powerful ; we both, ¹ ⁴ becoming full of power, will overpower my rival. ¹ i The verse xix. 32. 5 is a variation on this. RV. reads â74a for âthe in b, and the older ³âarvt for Jhurvâ in c.

[ : : 6. I have put on (ab47) for thee the overpowering one (f.); I have put to (âpa) for thee the very powerful one; after me let thy mind run forth as a cow after her calf, run as water on its track.

RV. reads âpa for abkt in a, and has for b abht tvâ 'dhâr: sâkiyasâ. The application of a and b as made by Kâug. (see above) would suit the prepositions as found in RV. decidedly better than as in our text; but much more appropriate is the use made d by MP., elements of the root being secretly bound on the arms of the wife, with which she embraces the husband below and above so that one arm is under him and the ⁴ other over him]; then in aby adkâm is further implied (as elsewhere e.g. iii. rr. 8 J) 4 the value of aâhidhâant, the halter or bridle with which a horse is controlled. The Anukr. does not sanction the resolution za-âm in c.

docs.title: 19. To help friends against enemies
docs.text:
[Vasistha.— agtar cam. vâicvadevam uta cândramasan ut3i "ndram. ânugtubkam :

I. patkyâbyhatr ; 3. bhurigby hati ; 6. 3-av. 6-2. trigtupkakummatigarbâc I

The verses are found in Paâipp. iii. (in the verse-order 1, 2, 4, 3, 5, 7, 6, 8). The; hymn is applied by Kâug. (14. 22—24) in a rite for gaining victory over a hostile army,. and reckoned (14. 7, note) to the aparâjita gana. The Vâit. uses vs. I. in the agnâ- g cayana (28. 15) in connection with lifting the zkṅya fire, and vss. 6-8 in a sattra sacrifice (34. 16, 17), with mounting a chariot and discharging an arrow.

Translated : John Muir, Original Sanskrit Texts, i.² 283 ; Ludwig, p. 234 ; Weber, i xvii: 269 ; Griffith, i. rog.

I. Sharpened up is this incantation (? brâkman) of mine ; sharpened up [my] heroism, strength; sharpened up, victorious, be the unwasting authority (45atrâ) [of them] of whom I am the household priest (pu7âkita).

Or brâhman and kgatrâm may signify respectively the Brahman and Kṣatriya quality or dignity of the purâhita and his constituency. The verse is found also in VS. (xi. 81), TS. (iv. I. 103), TA. (il. 5. 2, vs. 15), MS. (ii. 7. 7), and K. (xvi. 7, Weber). The first two of these agree in all their readings, omitting idâm in a and gjâram astu in c, and reading in c, 4 ji nṅ yâsyâ 'hâm âsmi; and TA.MS. differ from them only by adding; me before jispâ Ppp. has ks arrani me jisyu, but agrees with our text in d. The comm. moreover has jisu, and the translation implies it; jpâs can only be regarded as a blunder. Ppp. further gives mayt 'dam for ma idam in a, and mama for balan in b. Our original c has apparently got itself mixed up with vs. 5 c.

2. Up I sharpen the royalty of them, up their force, heroism, strength; I hew [off ] the arms of the foes with this oblation.

The translation implies emendation of the syâmi of all the mss. and of both editions to cyami, it is obviously called for (suggested first by the Pet. Lex.), and the comm. reads gyami,; Ppp. probably intends it by pagyâmi. The latter halfverse is found i , again below as vi. 65. 2 c, 4; its text is confused here in Ppp. (v7camâ catrâpân: bâkâ sam agvâm agvân akam). The Anukr. ignores the redundant syllable in a. i

3. Downward let them fall, let them become inferior, who shall fight against (priany-) our bounteous patron (sṅrâ); I destroy the enemies by Ś : my incantation ; I lead up our own men.

Ppp. reads adkas pad- at the beginning, and indram for sârimn in b. The second half-verse is found in VS. (xi. 82 c,d), TS. (iv. I. IO3), and MS. (ii. 7.7), with the various readings &sânâmiâ and suâṅ ; the comm. also gives ksiomi. The comm. renders ¹Ś sârim by kâryâkâryavibhâgajṅan. The Anukr. should call the verse virârt prastârate pa7kti, since it properly scans as rr +11 :8+8=38. ⁴ 4. Sharper than an ax, also sharper than fire, sharper than Indra's thunderbolt — [they] of whom I am the household priest. ¹Ś Emendation to inâravajrâr would rectify the meter of c; but the Anukr. apparently "au accepts the redundancy there as balancing the deficiency in a. ² 5. The weapons of them I sharpen up; their royalty having good 4s : heroes, I increase ; be their authority unwasting, victorious ; their intent ce let all the gods aid.

The translation again (as in vs. 2) implies emendation of syâmi in a to cyâmi, which is read by Ppp. and by the comm. Most of our mss. (all save O.0p.), as of SPP's, (ee accent in b sâviram, and both editions have adopted the reading ; but it ought, of a course, to be suvtranm, as always elsewhere (and as the comm. here describes the Ś word). Ppp. has vardhayasva at end of b, and its d is gram esâr citar: bakuâha Ś vivarṅpa. The definition of the verse as Ś7âstubk is wanting in the Anukr. London ms. J, doubtless by an error of the manuscripts, which are confused at this point.

I The Berlin ms. does give it.

6. Let their energies (vâina) be excited, O bounteous one (naghâvan);

let the noise of the conquering heroes arise; let the noises, the clear el (kctumânt) halloos, go up severally ; let the divine Maruts, with Indra as a their chief, go with the army. ¹ With the first two pâadas compare RV. x. 103. 108, 4: Śd dharsaya maghavann i Ś Śyudhani. âd râthanar: jâyatanm yantu ghts ak. Some of our mss.(P.M.W.0.0p.Kp.), = as of SPP's, read in ec uṅlâyas, but both editions give Zu; the comm. has wllulayas, ) ¹ and declares it an imitative word. The omission either of zZulâyas or of ketumântas ⁴ a would make a jagatr pâda of c, and that of âroâs would do the same for â; as the Ś ¹ verse stands, the Anukr. scans it i +11:848 :6-48=52. Part of our mss. (I.0.Op.) ¹ agree with the comm. in ending this verse with ââ trarâm, and throwing the two i ¹5 remaining pâadas into vs. 7, to the great detriment of the sense, as well as against the Ś 4 ¹ probable earlier form of the verse. Ppp. reads : udâharsantân vâjinârn: vâjinâbhy ad ¹ ³ ¹ vâiranan jayarâm etx ghosan: prthag ghosâa ulalayas ketumantn udiratâm; with

(iv. 6.44) has the same two pâdas together, but reads #a pre

¹a jâyata nara sthirâ val etc. Ppp. has the first half-verse (with pra yata and vas), ¹ fe adding as second half indro vag carma yacchaty anââkrŚyâ yarkâ 'sati. The verse ¹ eh is not wârâj 748 :r1 + 12, if the obviously proper resolutions are made. I Ś : 8. Being let loose, fly thou away, O volley, thou that art sharpened up by incantation ; conquer the enemies; go forth; slay of them each best one; let no one soever of them yonder be released.

Pâdas ac and e are RV. vi. 75. 16, a verse found also in a number of other texts SV. ii. 1213 5; VS. xVil. 45; TS. iv. 6. 44; TB. iii. 7. 623 ; APCS. iii. 14. 3. RV.ŚV.VS. g agree throughout, having gâcka for jâya at beginning of c, and, for 6, mâ 'mâsâr: kâr cand 'c chisaṅ; the others have this d, except that they put eg in place of am?5âm; they also give via for padyasva at end of c, and TS. has the nom. docs.title: 20. To Agni and other gods: for various blessings
docs.text:
[Vasistha.— dagarcam. âgneyam uta mantroktadevatyan. ânuggubham : 6. patkyâpaṅṅti;

8. virâgjagati.)

Excepting the last verse, the hymn is found in Pâipp. iii. (in the verse-order I-3, 7 41 6, 5, 8, 9). It includes (vss. 2—7) a whole RV. hymn (x. 141), with a single RV. verse (iii. 29. 10) prefixed, and only the last two verses occur nowhere else. It ¹ is used in Kaâug. (18.13) in the nirytikarman, with an offering of rice mixed with pebbles ; again (40. 1), in the rite of the removal of the sacrificial fire, with transfer of it to the fire-sticks or to one's self; again (41. 8), with v.7 and vii. I, in a rite for sucy. cess in winning wealth; and the comm. directs vs. 4 to be used in the save sacrifices (ity anayâ bhrgoaṅgirovidag catura ârseyân akvayer). In Vâit., vs. r appears in the agnistoma sacrifice (24. 14), and again in the sarwamedka (38. 14) with the same use i as in Kâug. 4o. 11; and also in the agnicayana (28. 25), with the laying of the gâra-; patya bricks ; further, verses 2—4 and 7 and 8 in the agnicayana (29. 19) ; vs. 4 a,b in the agnâstoma (15.16), as the adkvaryu follows the fre and soma; vs, 5 in the same (23. 20), with certain offerings; and vs. 6 in the same (19.2), with a graka to Indra and Vayu. .

Translated : Weber, xvii. 2725 Griffith, i. rrr. — See Weber, Berliner Ś5., 1892, i p. 797.

I. This is thy seasonable womb (yâ7i), whence born thou didst shine; knowing it, O Agni, ascend thou ; then increase our wealth.

The verse is found in numerous other texts: besides RV. (iii. 29.10), in VS.. (iii.14 et al.), TS. (i. 5. 52 etal), TB. (i. 2. 16 et al.), MS. (i. 5.1 etal.), K. (vi. 9 et al), Kap. (i. 16 et al), JB. (i. 61) : in nearly all occurring repeatedly. VS. TS. TB.]B. differ from our version only by reading ârkâ for âdkâ at beginning of 4; Ppp. and the comm. have athar MS.K. substitute ras; but RV. gives further szâa for roha in c, and i gras for raytm in . The comm. in accordance with the ritual uses of the verse, ² declares ayâm at the beginning to signify either the fire-stick or the sacrificer himself.

2. O Agni, speak unto us here; be turned toward us with good-will ; â bestow upon us, O lord of the people (v7) ; giver of riches art thou toe us.

RV. x. 141 begins with this verse, and it is found also in VS. (ix. 28), TS. (â. 7, 102),. : MS. (i. II. 4), and K. (xiv.2). RV.VS.MS.K. have 2râ no y- in c, and, for vkâm (4 pate, RV.MS.K. read vias pate, TS. bhuvas g-, and VS. sakasrajit; VS. goes on with fwâr ht dhanadâ âsi for 4; VS. TS. further have pr âti for pratyâṅ in b. Ppp. g combines in d dkanada 'si. ² 3. Let Aryaman bestow upon us, let Bhaga, let Brihaspati, let the god- ¹ desses ; let the divine Sânrtâ also assign wealth to me.

Found also in the other texts (RV. x. 141. 2; VS. ix. 29; the rest as above; and Ś Kap. 29. 2). All of these, excepting TS., leave zo in a again unlingualized ; VS.K. sub- ¹ stitute p757 for bhâgas in b, and omit c; the others have âzvâs instead of devâs, for d, i RV. gives 77ys devi dadâtu nak, while the others vary from this only by 274 vâk for ¹â râyâs. By Sânrta (lit. 'pleasantness, jollity ') the comm. understands Sarasvati to be gr intended.

4. King Soma [and] Agni we call to aid with [our] songs (g7) ; [also] ¹ Aditya, Vishyu, Sârya, and the priest (5raṅmân) Brihaspati. ¹i Found in RV. (x. 141. 3), SV. (i. 91), VS. (ix. 26), and TS.MS.K. (as above). The 7 only variant in RV. is the preferable âââtyân in c; it is read also by the other texts : except SV.K. ; but SV.TS.MS.K. give vârupam for âuvase in a; and they and VS. ¹ â have anv & rabhâmahe for girbhtr havamahe in b. The comm. takes brakmâṇam in d as « Prajapati, creator of the gods."

5. Do thou, O Agni, with the fires (agnt), increase our worship (5râṅrma7) and sacrifice ; do thou, O god, stir us up to give, unto giving wealth.

The second half-verse is of doubtful meaning— perhaps (impel to us wealth for givfr ing' etc.—being evidently corrupted from the better text of RV. (x. 141.6; also SV. ¹ ii. 855), which reads in c âewâtâtaye for deva dâtave, and in d râyâs for raytm; even el 57 zy, ZY ae Ppp. has Jevatâraye. The comm. has dânave (rendering it " to the sacrificer who has given oblations ") for dâtave, also nodaya for codaya. â ¹ 6. Indra-and-Vâyu, both of them here, we call here with good call, that ¹ to us even every man may be well-willing in intercourse, and may become gr desirous of giving to us. Ś Found also (except the last pada, which even Ppp. repudiates) in RV. (x. 141. 4), ¹ i VS. (xxxiii. 86), and MS K. (as above). For wṅhâw iṅâ in a, RV. reads bf haspâtim,

and the other texts susarzâycâ. For â, VS. has anamroâ) saṅmgâme for sârmgatyâam, 1 and MS. the same without anamrvâs; TS. has (in iv. 5.12) a nearly corresponding ¹ ¹ ¹ half-verse : yârhâ nak sârvam t jâgad ayaksmân sumânâ âsat. Ppp. omits a, per- I ¹ haps by an oversight. The comm. takes sukâuâ in b as for suhâvâu, which is perhaps 4 i ¹ better. In our edition, the word is misprinted susâe-.

¹ 7. Do thou stir up Aryaman, Brihaspati, Indra, unto giving; [also] ¹ hi Vâta (wind), Vishyu, Sarasvati, and the vigorous (vâj47) Savitar.

Found also in RV. (x. 141. 5), VS. (ix. 27), and TS.MS.K. (as above). All save ll RV. read wâcam instead of vâtanm in c, and so does the comm. ; K. puts vâcam after ¹ eT visu Land for a it has our vs: 4 a. . ve 8. In the impulse (7asavâ) of vigor (? v4ja) now have we come into being, and all these beings within. Both let him, foreknowing, cause him to give who is unwilling to give, and do thou confirm to us wealth having all heroes.

The verse seems to have no real connection with what precedes and follows, nor do its two halves belong together. They are in other texts, VS. (ix. 25 and 24) and TS. (in i. 7. 107), parts of two different verses, in a group of three, all beginning with vâjasya followed by prasavâ, and all alike of obscure and questionable interpretation, and belonging to the so-called wâjaprasavâyâani, which form a principal element in the d vâjapeya sacrifice (see Weber's note on this verse also his essay Uzber den Vâjapeya, Berliner Sb., 1892, p. 797). Instead of 77 in a, TS. and MS.K. (as above), as also Ppp., have the nearly equivalent izâm ; and all (save Ppp.) read 4 Śabhâva instead of i sânz babhṅvima at end of a, and sarvâtas instead of zntâr at end of b, omitting the meter-disturbing z74 at beginning of c; VS.K. read in ec dâpayati for -tx ; and all save K. give the preferable yackatu at the end (the comm. has yacckât); then VS. gives sâ no d rayâm in â, and K. has a peculiar a : some rayir sahkaviran ni yamsat. Ppp. is defective in parts of this verse and the next; it reads at the end of c gra7anaz. Pâda a is the only one that has a jagarr character. ITS. has sârvaviram.

9. Let the five directions yield (47k) to me, let the wide ones yield according to their strength ; may I obtain all my designs, with mind and heart. All the pada-mss. divide and accent p74 : 4peyam, but SPP. emends to grâ: âpeyan' see Sansk. Gram. §850 ; the comm. reads âpeyan:z. The comm. declares urvis to designate heaven and earth, day and night, and waters and herbs.

ro. A kine-winning voice may I speak ; with splendor do thou arise upon me; let Vâyu (wind) enclose (3-rudk) on all sides ; let Tvashtar assign to me abundance.

Several of our mss. (P.M. W.O.Kp.) read ruâhâm in c. The comm. explains z rundham by prânatmanâ "vy pnoru.

This fourth anuvâka contains 5 hymns, with 4o verses, and the quotation from the old Anukr. is simply daca.

docs.title: 21. With oblation to the various forms of fire or Agni
docs.text:
[ Vasigtha.—dacarcam. âgneyam. (râigtubham : I. puro 'nugtubk ; 2,3, 8. bhuri ; 5. jagatr;

6. uparigtadvir âgbr hatr; 7. virâggarbhâ ; 9, ro. anugtubk (9. nicy?).] 1

The whole of the hymn is found in Pâipp., vss. r= in iii., vs. ro in vii. The materialis i used by Kâug. in a number of rites: it is reckoned (9. 1; the comm. says, only vss. 1-7) to the br kackânti gana ; it appears in the charm against the evil influence of the flesh-eating fire (43. 16-21 ; according to the comm., vss. I-7 are quoted in 16, and the whole hymn in 20); again, in the establishment of the house-fire (72.13 ; vss. I-7, comm.); again, in the funeral rites (82. 25), on the third day after cremation, with obla- ¹ : tion to the relics; once more, in the expiatory ceremony (123. 1), when birds or other ) creatures have meddled with sacrificial objects. Moreover, vs. 8 (the comm. says. vss. 8-10), with other passages from xii. 2, in a rite of appeasement in the house-fire ceremony (71. 8). In Vâit., vss. i—7 are used in the agniszoma (16.16) on occasion of the soma becoming spilt; and vs, 7 in the sâkamedha part of the câturmasya sacrifice 9.17].

Translated : Weber, xvii. 277 ; Griffith, i. rr3; vss. r-7 also by Ludwig, p. 325.

I. The fires that are within the waters, that are in Vrtra, that are in ² man, that are in stones, the one that hath entered the herbs, the forest. ¹ trees—to those fires be this oblation made. rr Verses 1—4 are found also in MS. (ii. 13.13) and in K. (x1. 3) ; both texts read yâs ¹ for ye through the first half-verse, and âcmani for ârmasu; MS. begins yâ apse ântâr agnir, and K. y6 apso â;gnir antâr; K. further has bhuvanâani viva for âsadkrr yo ¹ vânaspâtins. Ppp. reads yo apsv antar yo vytre antar yak puruse yo ‘(mani : yo vivega oga-, and combines in d tebhyo 'gni-. Part of the mss. (including our P.M.W.I.) te combine vives Ś5adk- in c, and both editions have adopted that reading— doubtless ⁴ wrongly, since the Prat. prescribes no such irregularity, nor is it elsewhere found to occur with ogyadki. The comm. explains what different fires" are intended : the 6 wâgdava etc. in the waters; that in the cloud (by Nir. ii. 16) or else in the body of the

¹ Asura Vrtra ; in man, those of digestion ; in stones, those in the sâzyakânta etc.

(sparkling jewels) ; those that make herbs etc. ripen their fruits. Weber regards the i : stones that strike fire as intended, which seems more probable. The division of the Śa verse by the Anukr., 8+ II II II, is not to be approved. [Pâdas a and b rather as ⁴ rr+8; pâdas c and d are in order, r2+1.— In c, correct to Zviveâṅsadkir, as MS.

reads. J

2. [The fire] that is within soma, that is within the kine, that is entered into the birds, into the wild beasts (m7gâ), that entered into ee bipeds, into quadrupeds— to those fires be this oblation made. : 4 : MS. and K. begin b with vâyâṅsi yâ âuivera; Ppp. with yo visto vayasi. The ¹ ¹ comm. takes the kine in a as representing the domestic animals in general, the fire ⁴ ( being that which makes their milk cooked instead of raw, as often alluded to. SPP. ¹ follows the mss. in reading in b vâyajsz; our alteration to the equivalent vâyassa

= was needless. The verse (1011134 I1=45) is Śkurij, but also irregular enough. i Pâdas b and d are in order, each a zrigtubk; and c, if we throw out the second yâs, ¹ ¹ : is a good jagatz; a is bad. ] ¹ 3. He who, a god, goes in the same chariot with Indra, he that u belongs to all men (vâ7vânarâ) and to all gods (?), whom, very powerful ¹ in fights, I call loudly on —to those fires be this oblation made.

MS. and K. have for a yénâ 'ndârasya râthan sambabhuvâr, and Ppp. partly agrees oh with them, reading ye 'udrena sarathaṅ sambabhṅva. In b, the translation ventures ¹ i to follow Ppp's reading wkvaâz"yas instead of -2âyyâs, because of its so obvious Ś preferability in the connection ; -ââ=yas is quite in place in vs. 9, and may perhaps

¹ have blundered from there into this verse ; but MS. and K. have -âââyâs. they further

‘ exchange the places of our 3 c and 4 c. Pâda b is a very poor Śrâstubk, though capable

¹ of being read into 11 syllables read u24 va? ].
  1. He who is the all-eating god, and whom they call Desire (kâma), ee whom they call giver, receiving one, who is wise, mighty, encompassing, ne unharmable —to those fires be this oblation made. 5 gee ṅ MS. begins the verse with vṅvââam agntm ; K., with hutâdam agnim ; of b, both ¹ spoil the meter by reading gratigrakttâram ; MS. begins c with âktro yâk K's cis a corrupt. Ppp. reads ka for kus in a (not in b also). The comm. simply paraphrases

¹ pra gr knântanm by pratigrakuâran 5 the reference is probably to the offerings which Agni receives in order to give them to the various gods. In our edition, an accentmark belonging under â of âZâs in a has slipped aside to the left. !

5. Thou on whom as priest (kâtar) agreed with their mind the thirteen kinds of beings (64âuvanâ), the five races of men (mânavâ): to the splendor-bestowing, glorious one, rich in pleasantness—to those fires be this oblation made.

The unusual and obscure number « thirteen " here seduces the comm. into declaring first that bhâuvanâ signifies month," coming from bhnvana year"; and then the mânavâs are the seasons But he further makes the latter to be the four castes, with the nisâadas as fifth, and the former the thirteen sons, Vigvakarman etc., of a great sage named Śkuwana (because of viwakarman bhâuvana in AB. vill. 21. 8-11). Pp). reads bhuvanâ for bhâuwanâs. The Anukr. does not heed that the last pada is zrâszubâ.

6. To him whose food is oxen, whose food is cows, to the soma-backed, the pious : to those of whom the one for all men (eââcoânarâ-) is chief — to those fires be this oblation made.

The first half-verse is RV. viii. 43. II a, b (also found, without variant, in TS. i. 3. 147). MS. (ii. 13.13) has the whole verse as pâdas a, b, â, e, interposing as c the pâda (st6mair vidhema 'gnâye) which ends the gâyarri in RV. TS. The meter (8+8 :8-+11) is, as brkatr, rather nicyt than vir7)..

7. They who move on along the sky, the earth, the atmosphere, along the lightning; who are within the quarters, who within the wind—to those fires be this oblation made.

Our P.M. W. read in b vidyâtan, and P.M.W.I. end the pâda with carari. SPP. regards the exposition of the comm. as implying that the latter takes anu in b as an independent word : ânu sanzc-. In the definition of the Anukr., wirâj appears to be used as meaning a pada of ro syllables (11 +10: 10+ II=42). Read ye ca vâre?

The three remaining verses of the hymn are plainly independent of what precedes, concerning themselves directly with the appeasement of an ill-omened fire ; but the combination of the two parts is an old one, being found also in Ppp. The ejection of the evidently patched-together vs. 6 would reduce the first part [ vss. i-7 to the norm of this book.

8. Gold-handed Savitar, Indra, Brihaspati, Varuna, Mitra, Agni, all the 4 gods, the Angirases, do we call; let them appease (ganz) this flesh-eating fire.

Ppp. inverts the order of a and b. [ MGS. has the vs. at ii, 1.6. ] The comm. gives 4 a double explanation of «gold-handed " : either ⁴ having gold in his hand to give to his praisers," or having a hand of gold"; he also allows us to take â7girasas either as 4 accusative or as nominative, " we the Angirases." The Anukr. notes that c is jegatz.

9. Appeased is the flesh-eating, appeased the men-injuring fire ; so also ¹ the one that is of all conflagrations, him, the flesh-eating, have I appeased. Ś

Ppp. has azko purusaresinal for b, and this time vâvadaṇyas in c. The anntubk i is rather oirâj than nicyt.

ro. The mountains that are soma-backed, the waters that lie supine, ¹ the wind, Parjanya, then also Agni—these have appeased the flesh-eating one. Ś All our mss. save one (O.), and all SPP's save two or three that follow the comm., ( read agama (apparently by infection from the end of vs. 9) at the end ; both editions ¹ emend to -man, which is the reading of the comm. Ppp. has the vs. in vii. (as noted Ś above), and combines 757kâ "pa in a-b and pârjanyâ "d in c.— For “soma-backed," ŚŚ4 1 see Hillebrandt, Ved. Mythol. i. 6o t.

docs.title: 22. To the gods : for splendor (vârcas)
docs.text:
¹ I Vasigha. —varcasyam. bârkaspatyam uta vâigvadevan:. ânugtubham : I. Vir ât trigtubk; â 3- 52. par nustub virâdatijagati ; 4.3-av. 6:2. jagats.]

Found also (except vs. 6) in Paipp. iii. Is reckoned to the varcasya gana

(Kâug. ra. ro, note), and used in a charm for splendor (13.1), with binding on an amulet of ivory. The comm. quotes the hymn also as employed by the Naks. KX. in a on makâcânti called brâkmâ, for attainment of brakman-splendor ; and by Parig. iv. I, in i the daily morning consecration of an elephant for a king.

Translated : Ludwig, p. 461 ; Weber, xvii. 282 ; Griffith, i. irs. â4 I. Let elephant-splendor, great glory, spread itself, which came into : A being from Aditi's body; that same have all together given to me —all the gods, Aditi, in unison. [Ct vil. 17. 3 n. ¹ A number of the mss. (including our Bp.Op.) read &ââtyâs [accent] in b, and several of ours follow it with yâm instead of yâr. Ppp. rectifies the meter of d by reading devâasas. Emendation in a to Ś7hâdyagas would be acceptable. CB. (iii. 1.3.45 ee ¹ : perhaps on the basis of b?) has a legend of the production of the elephant from something born of Aditi (see R. in Jnd. Stud. xiv.392). The comm. explains prathatân: in Śn a by asmaâsu prathitam prakhyâtam bhavatn be proclaimed as belonging to us. In . our edition, an accent-mark has dropped out from under the ba of -³abhâva. An irregular gr verse, scanned by the Anukr. as 12410 : 10 + IO=432, but convertible into 45 syllables by resolving ranâ-as, sâru-e, viu-e (of which only the first is unobjectionable). If we

¹ read devâsas in d, the vs. is in order (12411: 2411), except in c (247 # sârve ?). hl 2. Let both Mitra and Varuṇa, Indra and Rudra, [each] take notice;

¹ the all-nourishing gods —let them anoint me with splendor. ¹ All the mss. read cetatus at-end of b, and so does Ppp., and our edition has it; but ( He SPP. follows the comm. and substitutes cetatu,; SV. i. 154 has s6maj pusâ ca cetatuk;

the translation implies cezaru, the other being probably a false form, generated under ¹ â stress of the difficult construction of a singular verb with the preceding subjects.

¹ Weber takes it as ceratns, 3d dual perf. of root car " frighten into submission." The

Anukr. takes no notice of the deficiency of a syllable in a. So W's two drafts ; but his He collations note P.M. W. as reading cezutaṅ (1) and Op. as reading cetatâ. Ś 3. With what splendor the elephant came into being, with what the ¹ king among men (maṅnugyâ), among waters, with what the gods in the beginning went to godhood — with that splendor do thou, O Agni, now —_ make me splendid.

Śpsâ, in b, is an impertinent intrusion as regards both sense and meter; it is wanting - in Ppp. In call the mss. give Zyam (sak. âyart); our edition makes the necessary emendation to yan, and so does SPP. in his pada-text; but in szṅkîtâ (perhaps by an I oversight) he reads âyan, unaccented ; the comm. has âyan (accent doubtful): f. ( iv. 14. I c, where the mss. again read aya for âyan in the same phrase. Ppp. has a very different second half-verse : yena dev jyotisa dyam uââyan tena ma 'gne varcasâ sar syje ha. The comm. makes zpsu in b mean either [creatures] in the waters," or else [Yakshas, Gandharvas, etc.] in the atmosphere." The metrical definition of the Anukr. is mechanically correct 52—2=50 ] if we count 13 syllables in band combine varcasâgne]) l

4. What great splendor becomes thine, O Jâtavedas, from the offering; how great splendor there is of the sun, and of the âsura-like elephant — so great splendor let the (two) Agvins, lotus-wreathed, assign unto me.

All the mss. read in b bkavati, and SPP. accordingly adopts it in his edition; ours makes the necessary correction to Śkâwazi. The comm. reads âhute, vocative, at end of b; Ppp. has instead âkutam ; and then adds to it, as second half-verse, our 3 â, e (with abhya for adyâ, and kr di for krpu), putting also the whole [ i.e. our 4 a, b+ 3d, e] before our vs. 3; and then it gives the remainder (cf) of our vs. 4 here, with Zr utân: for dhattâm, and in c yavad varcal sâr-.

5. As far as the four directions, as far as the eye reaches (sam-ag), let so great force (indriyâ) come together, that elephant-splendor, in me.

The comm. reads saz efu in c.

6. Since the elephant has become the superior (artist hâvant) of the comfortable (? sugâd) wild beasts, with his fortune [and] splendor do I pour (sic) upon myself.

That is, 'I shed it upon me, cover myself with it' The comm. understands the somewhat questionable sugââ nearly as here translated, "living at their pleasure in the forest"; and aṅâsthâvant as possessing superiority either of strength or of position.

Weber entitles the hymn, without good reason, Ś taming of a wild elephant."

docs.title: 23. For fecundity
docs.text:
IBrahman. — cândramasam uta yoniâzoatyam. &nugtubham : 5. upariŚâdblurighy katt;

6. skandkogrroibr hati.].

Found in Pâipp. iii. Used by Kâug. in the chapters of women's rites, in a charm (35. 3) to procure the conception of male offspring, with breaking an arrow over the mother's head etc.

Translated : Weber, v. 223; Ludwig, p. 477; Zimmer, p. 319 ; Weber, xvii. 285 ; 4 Griffith, i. 116 ; Bloomfield, 97, 356.

I. By what thou hast become barren (veââz), that we make disappear from thee ; that now we set down elsewhere, far away from (âpa) thee.

Vekât is perhaps more strictly ‘liable to abort'; the comm. gives the word here either sense. Ppp. is defective, giving only the initial words of vss. I and 2.

2. Unto thy womb let a foetus come, a male one, as an arrow to a quiver ; let a hero be born unto thee here, a ten.months' son. ¹

This verse and the two following occur in CGS. (i. 19.6), and this one without variant. Also this one in MP. li. rz. 9 ] (Winternitz, p. 94), and in an appendix to AGS. i i.13.6 (Stenaler, p. 48), with yonim after garbkas in a (and AGS. reads âifu), and omitting ara in c; and further in HGS. (i. 25. 1), like MP. in a, but retaining a?a. ¹ 4 3. Give birth to a male, a son; after him let a male be born ; mayest Ś thou be mother of sons, of those born and whom thou shalt bear. ⁴ All the mss. save one or two (including our E.) read at the end yâ.; both editions gt 6 make the necessary emendation to yân, which the comm. also gives. At beginning of Śe b, Ppp. reads rua, as do also the comm. and a couple of SPP's mss.; and Ppp. ends 35 with janayâmi ca. MB. (i. 4.9 c, d) has the first half-verse, reading vindasva for ¹ janaya ; and MP. (as above) i. 13. 2 ] also, with pâmâṅs te purrâ aâri for a. And gY CGS. (as above) has our a, b, with, for c, 9, z2sâm mârâ bkavigyasi jârânâr: janayâṅns: el ca the end corrupt, as in Ppp..

¹ 4. And what excellent seeds the bulls generate, with them do thou Śâ acquire (vid) a son ; become thou a productive milch-cow. 4 : CGS. (as above) has for b purusâa janayanti nak; it rectifies the meter of c by read- HH ing rebhis t- for 134s r (and it has janaya for vindasva); in â, it gives suprasâs; which Ss is better than our sâ pr-. MP. (as above) li. 13.3 ] repeats our verse very closely, only Śr with nas for ca in b, and purrân in c; and it has, just before, the line r7ni bhadrâni ot b1jâny rsabhâ janayantu nau. docs.text:

I. Rich in milk [are] the herbs, rich in milk my utterance (vâcas); accordingly, of them that are rich in milk I bring by thousands.

The first half-verse occurs again, a little changed, as xviii. 3. 56 a,b; it is also RV. x.17. 14 a, b, etc. : see under xviii. 3. 56. The comm. reads in â bkargyam for bhare ham, he understands " be " instead of “are " in a, b. For second half-verse Ppp. has atho payasvarân paya a harami sahasragat.

2. I know him that is rich in milk; he hath made the grain much; the : god that is collector" by name, him do we call, whichever is in the house of one who sacrifices not.

That is, away from the service of the impious to that of us, the pious. A god collector " (sambhytvan) is not known elsewhere. Or nadâs might be nom. sing.; the comm. of course takes it as plural ; gpa he understands as a kind of animals" (grânijâaram). Our O.Op. have at the end -vakârn. Ppp. reads for b manavârk paṅca grstayak (cf. grsti for krŚt in 9.13.3); and, for c, 4, sarvâg car bhâr mayobhuvo vrse (apart nadir iva.

The metrical deficiency in a calls for a change of reading, and the usual correlation i of evâ in c suggests yârhâa, and, as Ppp. reads yarkâ, the translation ventures to adopt it, as Śz instead is hardly better than unmanageable. Weber supplies aca; Ludwig, ⁴ «I open, as it were"; the comm. says that uz means wdbkawati, and does not trouble i himself about its construction with an accusative ; we may take the verse as a virtual te continuation of vs. 3, and the nouns as governed by samâvaṅkân. O hundred-handed one, bring together; O thousand-handed one, pile together ; of what is made and of what is to be made do thou convey ¹ i together the fatness here.

Ppp. has for b szâasyâi 'va samgirak, for c yathe ya spṅâtir âyasi, and for â our c. : ¹ : The comm. reads samâvakham at the end, rendering it samgrâpto ‘smi, to the adjec- : tives in c he supplies dkaradkânyâdeh. |Sâṅ kira, ' overwhelm, i.e. ' bestow abun.

dantly.'] i i 6. docs.text:

(except vs. 2, perhaps accidentally omitted, and vs. 6). A similar invocation occurs further in TS. v. 5. 103-5, not so closely related that the readings need to be compared in detail. Hymns 26 and 27 are called in Kâug. Jgyâktz connected with the quarters, and are used (14.25), with vi.13, in a battlexite, for victory over a hostile army ; and also (50.13), with vi. 1 etc., in a' ceremony for good-fortune (and the comm. regards them as signified by yuktayos in 5o. v7 in aicharm against serpents, scorpions, etc. ; but this is probably a mistake |? [); yet. again, the comm. adds them in a ceremony (51. 3-5) of tribute to the quarters. ¹LâSerpentincantation " (Schlangenzauber) is the title given to this hyms and the next by Weber. Roth (in his notes) rejects Weber's view ; but Griffith accepts it. T think the two hymns are snake charms for the following reasons. They are employed by Kâug. (so. 17) in connection with vi. 56. and xii. 1. 46, which latter are clearly directed, against snakes etc. See also Kegava on Kâug. 50.17, 18, 19, Bloomfield, p, 354. Kegava shows, I think, that the comm. is not mistaken. about yuktayos. "Weber, in his 4 valuable notes, observes, p. 292, that the schol. to TS. v. 5. ro reckons that passage as g belonging to a sâṅpakuti. Anukr.. Weber's. pote,. p: 2975 that these hymns are not used by Kâug., should be deleted. Whitney in bis i note to vi. 56 duly reports the connection of iii. 26 and 27 with that snake charm, That, Ś he does not do so here and at xii. 1. 46 is, I think, an oversight. 1....

us ; to you there be homage, to you there hail

docs.title: 27. The same : with imprecation on enemies
docs.text:
[Atharvan.— râudram ; agnyâdibakudevatyam. âgtikam : r-6. 54. kakummatgar ht 'Śi;

2. atyagti ; 5. bhuri.)

I A prose hymn. ] Found (except vs. 3, apparently omitted by accident) in Paipp. iii, after h. 26, but at some distance from it. Compare xii. 3. 55-60, where the quarters are rehearsed with the same adjuncts. Compare further TS. v. 5. 1o².2 (a passage immediately preceding that parallel with our h. 26; a bit of brâ@hmaṇa between the two I explains that these divinities are to protect the fire-altar when constructed) ; and MS. Śi. 13. 21 : both these omit all mention of arrows. A yet fainter parallelism is to be noted with TB. iii. iI. 5. For the concluding imprecation, compare also VS. xv. 13. For the use in Kâuc. with h. 26, see under that hymn. For the general significance of the hymn, see my addition to the introduction to h. 26. ] i

Translated : Weber, xvii. 295 ; Griffith, i. rar.;

I. Eastern quarter; Agni overlord; black serpent defender ; the Adityas arrows : homage to those overlords ; homage to the defenders; homage to the arrows; homage be to them; who hates us, whom we hate, him we put in your jaws (jâmbha).

Ppp. has rsiṅkyas instead of isubkyas, and vas instead of ebkyas ; and it adds further to the imprecation fan u prâpno jakâru, which our text has in a similar connection at vii. 31. I ; X. 5. 25-35 ; Xvi. 7.13. The “defender " is in each case a kind of serpent; and this, which is but an insignificant item in our two hymns, has a more important bearing on the application of the corresponding TS. and MS. passages. The TS. passage runs thus : thou art the eastern quarter, convergent by name ; of thee there Agni is overlord, the black serpent defender ; both he who is overlord and he who is guardian, to them (two) be homage ; let them be gracious to us; whom we hate and who hates us, him I put in the jaws of you (two) "; and the MS. version differs only in one or two slight points. The comm. supplies each time to the name of the quarter asmadanugrakârthan vartatam or something equivalent. There seems to be no natural way of dividing these verses into 5 pâdas; the refrain is probably counted by the Anukr. as 42 syllables, and the addition of the other part brings the number in each verse up to from 62 to 66 syllables (2577 is properly 64).

2. Southern quarter ; Indra. overlord; cross-lined [serpent] defender; the Fathers arrows : homage to those etc. etc.

Ppp. makes the Vasus arrows. MS. calls the serpent tragtnarâj ; TS. makes the adder (Ś7dâaku) defender here.

3. Western quarter ; Varuṇa overlord ; the adder (pṅdâku) defender;; food the arrows : homage to those etc. etc.;

The comm. explains prââkus as kursitagabdakârr : an absurd fancy. TS. and MS.; give here Soma as overlord, and the constrictor as defender. i

4. Northern quarter ; Soma overlord ; the constrictor (seâjâ) defender; 4 the thunderbolt (agâni) arrows : homage to those etc. etc.

The comm. gives for svajâ a double explanation, either ⁴self-born " (svaja) or else “inclined to embrace " (root soâ7). Both the other texts assign Varuṇa as overlord; ¹ 6 for defender, TS. designates, the crosslined serpent, MS. the g7ââku (in the corrupt ' . form sâdâkn or -3gu: the editor adopts the latter). Ppp. makes wind (vâra) the Śk arrows. t 5. Fixed quarter; Vishpu overlord; the serpent with black-spotted : (kalmâsa-) neck defender; the plants arrows : homage to those etc. etc.

Ppp. reads knlmâṣa- ; the comm. explains the word by k7snavarpa. TS. calls the Ch quarter iyâm this; in MS. it is 4vâci' downward ' ; TS. treats of it after the upward one, and makes Yama the overlord. In our edition, an accent-mark under the -5i- of i raksitâ has slipped to the right, under za. ⁴ 6. Upward quarter; Brihaspati overlord ; the white (gvitrâ) [serpent]

defender ; rain the arrows : homage to those etc. etc.

Ppp. has here the thunderbolt (agant) for arrows. Part of the mss. (including our

E. OK Kp.) give citrâ instead of gvârâ as name of the serpent; TS. reads guâzrâ, but (i MS. (probably by a misreading) citrâ. TS. calls the quarter kr kati 'great.' TS. (after ( the manner of the AV. mss.) leaves out the repeated part of the imprecation in the ⁴d intermediate verses (2-5); MS. gives it in full every time. ] Reference to this vs, as i Śl made by Bergaigne, Rel. ud. iii. 12 (cf. Baunack, KZ. xxxv. 527), is hardly apt.]

docs.title: 28. To avert the ill omen of a twinning animal
docs.text:
. ¹ [Brahman ( pacupotanâya).—yâminyam. Śnugubkam : r- atiakvarigarbhâ 40. atijagati; Śet 4. yavamadkyâ virâtkaRubh ; 5. trigtubh i 6. virâggarbhâ prastârapankti.] ¹ Not found in Pâipp. Used by Kâug., in the chapter of portents, in the ceremonies of expiation for the birth of twins from kine, mares or asses, and human beings (109.5; ¹ me.4; 1r.8).

The comm. reads vyadkvart, but he defines it first as coming from adkvan, and meaning ' possessed of bad roads, that cause unhappiness," or, second, as from aâkvara; and signifying “having magical sacrifices, that give obstructed fruit"! ] See note to vi. 5o. 3, where W. corrects the text to zyadvarâ : accent of masc. and fem., Gram. § 1171 a, b. ]

3. Be thou propitious to men (gâruga), propitious to kine, to horses, propitious to all this field (k5ârra) ; be propitious to us here.

Field seems taken here in a general sense, and might be rendered (farm. The ! Anukr. takes no notice of the irregularities in c and d, probably because they balance each other.

4. Here prosperity, here sap—here be thou best winner of a thousand; make the cattle prosper, O twinning one.

The comm. supplies bkavatn to the first pada: All the mss. agree in giving the false accent sakâsrasâtamâ in b; it should be sahasrasâtamâ—or, to rectify the meter, simply -sâ. Its pada-division, sakâsracsâtama is prescribed by the text of Prat. iv. 45. The first half-verse is also that of vi. r 20. 3 (which occurs further in TA.). Some of SPP's miss. write in b Zanv2s, protracting the kampa-syllable. 6. The omission of the superfluous yârra in b would rectify the meter. The Anukr. should say âstârapankti instead of prastâra-; its virâj means here a pada of ro syllables.

docs.title: 2. To the unknown god
docs.text:
[ Vena. — agtarcam. âtmadâivatam. trâ>i|tubham : 6. puro 'nugtubh ; 8. uparigâ;)yotis.]

Found in Pâipp. iv. (in the verse-order 1, 2, 4,3, 5,6, 8, 7). The hymn is mostly a ‘ version, with considerable variants, of the noted RV. x. 121, found also in other texts, as TS. (iv. 1. 8), MS. (ii. 13.23), and VS. (in sundry places), and K. xl. r. It is used by Kâug. in the vagâcamana ceremony (44.1 ff.), at the beginning, with the preparation : of consecrated water for it, and (45. r) with the sacrifice of the foetus of the zagâ-cow, ; if she be found to be pregnant. In Vaâit. (8.22), vs. I (or the hymn?) accompanies an offering to Prajapati in the cârurmasya sacrifice ; vs. 7 (28.34), the setting of a gold : man on the plate of gold deposited with accompaniment of vs. 1 of the preceding hymn ¹ (in the agnicayana) ; and the whole hymn goes with the evaââna offerings in the same ceremony (=8. 5).

Translated : as a RV. hymn, by Max Miiller, Ancient Sanskrât Literature (1859), P- 569 (cf. p. 433); Muir, OST. iv.³ 16; Ludwig, no. 948; Grassmann, ii. 398 ; Max ¹ Miller, Hibbert Lectures (1882), p. 301; Henry W. Wallis, Cosmology of the RV.; p. 50; Peter Peterson, Hymns from the RV, no. 32, p. 291, notes, p. 244 ; Max Miller,; Vedic Hymns, SBE. xxxii. r, with elaborate notes ; Deussen, Gesckichkte, i. I. I32; as ( an AV. hymn, by Griffith, i. 131 ; Weber, xviii. 8.— See Deussen's elaborate discussion, le. p. 128 ff. ; von Schroeder, Der Rigveda bei den Kathas, WZKM. xii. 285; Oldenberg, Die Hymnen des RV. i. 314 f.; Lanman, Sanskrit Reader, p. 391-3 ; and Bloomfeld, JAOS. xv. 184.

I. He who is soul-giving, strength-giving ; of whom all, of whom [even] the gods, wait upon the instruction ; who is lord (7) of these bipeds, who 2 of quadrupeds — to what god may we pay worship (vââ)) with oblation? ¹ In the parallel texts, our vs. 7 stands at the beginning of the hymn. They also com- 4 bine differently the material of our vss. r and 2, making one verse of our I a, b and ¹ ¹ 2 c, d, and another of our 2 a, b and 1 c, 4; and in this Ppp. agrees with them. RV. â and VS. (xxiii. 3) read in c 4e asyâ. The comm. renders âtmadâs “who gives their soul (or self) to all animals"; of course, with the native authorities everywhere, he ¹ explains kâsmâi in d as "to Prajapati." The Anukr. ignores the jagarFeharacter of c. 4 IRV. TS. MS. VS. omit the second yâs of our c. MS. has ke y6 asyâ; TS. has yâ #e Śeâ asya at iv. I. 8, but asyâ at vii. 5. 16. Pâdas a— recur at xiii. 3. 24.— In view of the i history of this hymn in Hindu ritual and speculation (cf. SBE. xxxii. 12 ; AB. iii. 21), (6 it might be better to phrase the refrain thus: Who is the god that we are to worship. ge with oblation?' ¹ ¹ ld 4) 2. He who by his greatness became sole king of the breathing, wink- ¹ : ing animal creation (jâgat) ; of whom immortality (am7tam), of whom i death [is] the shadow —to what god may we pay worship with oblation? Śi RV. VS. (xxiii. 3) TS. rectify the meter of b by adding 47 after (kas; VS. has the i bad reading aimesatâs. MS. gives a different version: aimisatâ; ca râjâ pârir vâi vasya jâgaro 6-; and Ppp. agrees with it, except as substituting wiâhartâ for ca râja. ( ⁴ His shadow" (in c), the comm. says, as being dependent upon him, or under his Śe control. The Anukr. passes without notice the deficiency in b. ² g ¹Ś 3. He whom the (two) spheres (krândasz) favor when fixed; whom the terrified firmaments (âdasr) called upon; whose is yon road, traverser ¹ 4 of the welkin (râjas)— to what god may we pay worship with oblation? ¹ fe The translation implies in b ââvayerâm, as read by the comm., and by one of SPP's d er mss. that follows him; all the other mss., and both editions, have -ezṅâm. The first halfverse is a damaged reflex of RV. 6 a, b, with which VS. (xxii. 7 a, b) and TS. agree: if yâr: krândas âvasâ tastabhant ablyâtksetâim mânasâ rgamâne ; MS. and Ppp. have ¹ yet another version: yâ imâ âyâvapythiot tastabhane (Ppp. -nâ) â7harayaâ (Ppp.

dkâred) rdasi (Ppp. avasâ) réjamâanc. For c, Ppp. gives yasminn adki vitata eri ar sârap, and MS. the same (save sra Ś7); our c agrees most nearly with RV. 5 c (TS.

and VS. xxxii. 6 the same) : yâ antârikse râjaso vimânak. The comm. âpparently hh takes 4vatas as ava-tâs = avanât ' by his assistance fixed "; he offers no conjecture as to â what ⁴ road" may be meant in c, but calls it simply dyulokasthak. ¹ 4. [By the greatness] of whom the wide heaven and the great earth,

[by the greatness] of whom yon wide atmosphere, by the greatness of ¹ whom yon sun [is] extended — to what god may we pay worship with ŚŚ ¹Ś The translation follows the construction as understood by the comm. ; it. might be Ś ee also whose [is] the wide heaven etc. etc., extended by his greatness." Extended". ¹ : applies better to earth etc. (a and b) than to sun; comm. says vistrṇâ jârâa etc. The

¹ verse-resembles only distantly RV. 5, with which, on the other hand, Ppp. nearly agrees, g reading yena dyaur ugrâa prthivr ca dra (RV.VS. MS. dr âhâ, TS. dydhe) yena soa stabkitar yena nzkar: (the rest -kak) : yo antariksar vimame vargyak (so MS. ; the

¹ gh offers as reported above, under vs. 3). Our third pada most resembles' RV. 6c: yâtrâ i ¹âki sâra Śdito wibhâti (so also VS. xxxii. 75 TS. 4ditân wyeti) Ct. MGS. 4.11. 14" a. 4 and p. I 54, yena gyâur. ugra. The Anukr, ignores the marked irregularity of b. 5. Whose [are] all the snowy mountains by [his] greatness ; whose, verily, they call Rasâ in the ocean; and of whom these directions are the (two) arms —to what god may we pay worship with oblation? The comm. extends his construction of vs. 4 through a, b here, and is perhaps right in so doing; the translation assimilates them to c. The verse corresponds to RV. Ś (with which VS. xxv. r2 precisely agrees) ; in a, RV.VS.TS. have 7m for vâ ve, and MS. ime vâgve girâyo m-; for b, all of them read yâsya samudrâr rasâyâ sahkâ "kâs (save that MS. puts yâsya after samudrâr ; and Ppp. has the same b as MS.) inc, RV.VS.TS. begin yâsye 'mâh pr-, while MS., with Ppp, reads â4o yâsya praââak (Ppp. -4a5) pâṅca devik. The ocean" is of course the atmospheric one ; and Rasa, the heavenly river, can hardly help having been originally the Milky Way; but the comm. takes it here as simply a river, representative of rivers in general. Pââas b and c are irregular, being defective unless we make harsh and difficult resolutions.

6. The waters in the beginning favored (a7) the all, assuming an embryo, they the immortal, order-knowing ones, over whom, divine ones, the god was —to what god may we pay worship with oblation?

Here a, b correspond to RV. 7 a, b, and c to RV. 8 c, all with important variants, which are in part unintelligent corruptions: RV. reads ââ0 ka yâd Śrhatir vans âyan g- a- janâyantir agntm ; and y6 devés âdhi devâ (ka Śsit; VS. (xxvii. 25 a, b, 26C) agrees throughout; TS. has makattr in a, and dâksam (for gârbham) in b; MS. also has makattr, and it lacks c. Ppp. has a text all its own: âpo ka yasya vivam Zy«r dadhâna garbhar janayanta maâtarâ: tatra âevanâm adhi deva astha ekastkhune vimate dy dhe ugre. And TA. (i. 23. 8), with an entirely different second half, nearly agrees in a, b with RV., but has gârŚharm for vâvam, and svayambhân: for agntn. All the mss. (except, doubtless by accident, our I.) give in c as7, which SPP. accordingly adopts in his text; ours makes the necessary emendation to âsâ. The comm. reads in c dzvesu, as a Vedic irregularity for -o75u; he renders zvan in a by araksan or wpacitam akurvan; perhaps we should emend to & vran (covered ²] Further, TA. has dâksam for gârbham of RV.

7. The golden embryo was evolved (sam-v7z) in the beginning; it was, when born, the sole lord of existence (kṅtâ); it maintained earth and heaven —to what god may we pay worship with oblation? As noted above, this is the first verse in the other continuous versions of the hymn (it is VS. xiii. 4). The others agree in reading at the end of c grthivirm âyâm ute I ¹mâm ; and, in addition, PB. (ix. 9. 12) gives thṅtânam in b; some of the texts contain the verse more than once. But Ppp. is more original, reading kâragya ulvâ "si yo "gre varso ajâyata: tvar yo âyororbhra (?) vanttyospa vy apasyad agur maktṇ.. The comm. understands kiranyagarbha as "the embryo of the golden egg." MGS. i. 10. Io, cites the hymn as one of 8 vss. and as beginning with kiraṇyagarbha ; see a Pp. 158, s.v.—Kirste, WZKM. ix, 164, reviewing Deussen, suggests that the golden g embryo is the yolk of the mundane egg.] The Anukr. makes no account of the deficiency of a syllable in c.

8. The waters, generating a young (vatsâ), set in motion (sam-ṅray) in the beginning an embryo; and of that, when born, the fostal envelop (4152) was of gold—to what god may we pay worship with oblation?. Ś gu Ppp. makes varsam and garbham change places, and reads gyan it also omits the refrain, as it has done in vss. 6 and 7. GB. (i. I. 39) appears to quote the pratika bE with gar bkam, or in its Ppp. form [ as conjectured by Bloomfield, JAOS. xix.e rr J. The f comm. paraphrases garbharz sam âirgyan by Kvarena visystam viryan: garbhâcayan: : 2Śrâpayan. The verse (8-48: 8484 r1=43) is ill defined by the Anukr. i

docs.text:

  1. kakummatigarbho parigâdbykati.] ¹ : Found in Paâipp. ii. (except vs. 5, and in the verse-order 1-3, 7, 6, 4). Used by Kâug.

li 3. Both thy (two) eyes and thy mouth, O tiger, we grind up; then : ( all thy twenty claws (rakkâ).

Ś The majority of mss. (including our Bp.I.0.Op.K.D.) read at the beginning aṅ5âṇ, i as do also Ppp. and the comm., but only (as the accent alone suffices to show) by the eH ordinary omission of y after g or 5; both editions give aZ5yâṅ. ¹ our text emends to gyâgâra, but should have given instead 9yâgṅra (that is, vâ-aghra â see Whitney's Skt. Gr. §314 b). Ppp. reads kana instead of mukham in a. Anukr., ¹ a London mis., has akgyâu. ]

Ś 4. The tiger first of [creatures] with teeth do we grind up, upon that ¹ ¹ also the thief, then the snake, the sorcerer, then the wolf.

be The conversion of szenâm to gte- after u is an isolated case. The verse in Ppp. is f le defaced, but apparently has no variants.

â 5. What thief shall come today, he shall go away smashed; let him go by the falling-off (apadkvaṅsâ) of roads ; let Indra smite him with the thunderbolt.

The first half-verse is identical with xix. 49.9 a, ro d. The comm. separates aga from dkvaṅsena, and construes it with eru ; dkvaṅsa he renders “Śad road " (Fastena margena).

6. Ruined (mârṇâ) [are] the teeth of the beast (m7g4â) ; crushed in also [are its] ribs; disappearing be for thee the goâkâ; downward go (grat) the lurking (? gagayṅ) beast.

The comm. takes mâṅrnâs from mârck, and renders it maghâs; in b he reads api cirspâs, the latter being horns and the like, that grow on the head." The second half-verse is extremely obscure and doubtful : Ludwig translates "into the depth shall the crocodile, the game go springing deep down"; Grill, with lame sinew go to ruin the hare-hunting animal." docs.title: 4. For recovery of virility: with a plant
docs.text:
[4tharvan.—agtarcam. vânaspatyam. ânugtubkam : g. puraugṇih ; 6,7. bkuri.]

Found in Pâipp. iv. (except vs. 7, and in the verse-order r-3, 5, 8, 4, 6). Used by Kâug. (40. 14) in a rite for sexual vigor.;

Translated : Griffith, i. 134 and 473 ; Bloomfield, 31, 369 ; Weber, xviii. 16.

I. Thee that the Gandharva dug for Varuṇa whose virility (?-Śhrâ)). was dead, thee here do we dig, a penis-erecting herb. 4

The meaning of Ś4râj cf. vii. 9o.2 J has to be inferred from the connection; the i comm. paraphrases by zastâvirya. The plant intended he declares to be that called 4 kapitthaka " (Feronia elephantum). The pada-reading of the last word is gepajohdrsanân, and Prat. ii. 56 prescribes the loss of the visarga of epak in saṅhîtâ ; the com- 4 ment to Prât. iv. 75 gives the reading thus : czpokargan im iti cepakoharsanin ; and one of our pada-mss. presents it in the same form, adding kramakâle ¹ this is the krama- e reading'; and the comm. has gepoka- ; but Ppp., cepakarsinṅ. As câpa is as genuine g and old a form as gepas, there seems to be no good reason for the peculiar treatment of the compound. hn ¹ 2. Up, the dawn; up, too, the sun; up,'these words (vâcas) of mine; Ś up be Prajapati stirring, the bull, with vigorous (vâ)ân) energy (câsma). 4 i Ppp. has a different b, uc chusma osadktnâm (compare our vs. 4 a); and it has at ¹ the end of d vâjinâm, it also inserts between our 1 and 2 this verse : vy pas re khana- : : 1âro v733 tvâ pagy osadkhe vrsâ 'si vrsuyâvarr vysane tvâ khanâmasi; and this is a Ś verse given in full by Kâug. (40. 14) after the pratika of vs. r of our hymn (with the ²4 4 corrections oy saṇas and khani- in a and vrsâa tua asy in b, and the vocative -var7 in c). oo The editor of Kâug. fails to understand and divide rightly the material, and so does not (4 4 recognize the quotation of this hymn. The first two pâdas of the added verse are as Ś it were the reverse of our iv. 6. 8 a, b, which see. ¹ 46 3. As forsooth of thee growing up (? vi-ruk) it breathes as if heated Gh (? abhi-tap)— more full of energy than that let this herb make for thee. (4 Altogether obscure, and probably corrupt. It is wanting (as noted above) in Ppp. All our pada-mss. make in c the absurd division Śrâma : seârgajeroa, instead of krâmasva : Feyaheiva ; but SPP. strangely reports no such blunder from his mss.
