Lex. takes sââz at the end as instr. of sââ position in coitxs," and the connection strongly favors this; but the accent and the gender oppose it so decidedly that the translation does not venture to adopt it. The comm. takes sâââ as always," and reads before it znz valgṅyalâ (for 4navaglâyarâ), supplying manasa for it to agree with. The verse is Śṅu7 7 only if we refuse to make the common contraction -7gye 'va in c.

8. Of the horse, of the mule, of the he-goat and of the ram, also of the bull what vigors there are— them do thou put in him, O self-controller.

The omission of 47 would rectify the meter of d, and also make more suitable the accentuation asmin. The great majority of mss. favor in c the reading tha 73-, which SPP. has accordingly adopted (our edition has ârka rs-). The comm. again (as in 4) has at the end tanṅvagam, understanding it adverbially (car rasya waco yathâ bhavati tathâ).

docs.title: 5. An incantation to put to sleep
docs.text:
[Brahman.—svâpanam, vârsabham. ânugtubham : a. bhurâ; 7. purastâjyotis triggubh.]

Found in Pâipp. iv., next after our hymn 4. Part of the verses are RV. vil. 55. 5-8. Used by Kâug. among the women's rites, in a rite (36. 1 ff.) for putting to sleep a woman and her attendants, in order to approach her safely.

Translated : Aufrecht, Ind. Stud. iv. 340; Grill, 51, II9; Griffith, i.135; Bloomfield, 105, 371 ; Weber, xviii. 20. — Discussed by Pischel, Ved. Sud. ii. 55 Ś. ; see also Lanman, Reader, p. 370, and references ; further, the RV. translators ; and Zimmer, p. 308.

I. The thousand-horned bull that came up from the ocean — with him, the powerful one, do we put the people to sleep.

The verse is RV. vii. 55. 7, without variant. Ppp. reads at the beginning kârazya-, ¢crṅgas. The comm. takes the «bull " to be the sun with his thousand rays —but that is nothing to make people sleep ; the moon is more likely, but even that only as typifying I the night.

2. The wind bloweth not over the earth ; no one soever seeth over [it] ; both all the women and the dogs do thou make to sleep, going g with Indra as companion..

Ppp. has in b the preferable reading sâzyas for kâc canâ. Part of our mss. ; (P.M. W.E I.H.K.), with apparently all of SPP's, read sv2pâyas * at end of e, but both editions accept suâpâya, which the comm. also has. The comm. understands the wind Ś to be meant as Indra's companion in 4. The verse is not Śhurij, if we read vâ26 ti : in a. ]And so Op.]

3. The women that are lying on a bench, lying on a couch, lying ina i litter ; the women that are of pure odor —all of them we make to sleep. ²

For falpesayâs in a, Ppp. has pusti-, and RV. (vii. 55.8) vaṅyes-; both give t225a- 9 ‘(tvarṅs (Ppp. 77) at end of b. RV. further mars the meter of c by giving gandṅas.

4. Whatever stirs have I seized ; eye, breath have I seized; all the et limbs have I seized, in the depth (azâarvarâ) of the nights. : ¹ Ppp. reads in 4 4a carvare; the comm. explains aṅâc- by tamobhtyisthe madkya- Ś râtrakâle. of 5. Whoso sits, whoso goes about, and whoso standing looks out — of 4 them we put together the eyes, just like this habitation (karmyâ). ¹eṅ RV. (vii. 55. 6) rectifies the meter of a by adding ca before cârazi (the Anukr. takes

¹ no notice of the deficiency of a syllable in our version) ; its b is yâc ca pâcyari no Sa jânah ; and in c it has kanmas for dadkmas, and (as also Ppp.) aksâpi. The comm. i gives no explanation of the obscure comparison in d, nor of the word karmyâ, but ⁴ simply says as this karmya that we see is deprived of the faculty of sight." Is not (he the zertium compargtionis simply the closing? We close their eyes as we close this Śâ house. The comm. renders sâr dadhmas by nimilitâni kurmas.— For the loss of ca eg before cârati, cf. iv. 18.6 a= v. 31. II a (sâ before jagâka ?), and vi. 91. 2 a ("va before vari 2). Other cases (vii. 81. 1 c, etc.) cited by Bloomfield, AJP. xvii. 418. ] a 6. Let the mother sleep, the father sleep, the dog sleep, the housemaster (vigpâri) sleep; let the relatives (j7ârâ) of her sleep; let this folk round about sleep. ¹ : For soâptu (5 times) and svâpantu, RV. (vii. 55. 5) gives sâstu and sasântu ; also, a in , sâroe ' all for asyai ‘of her '—which latter is to us a welcome indication of the 4 ¹ reason for allthis putting to sleep, and marks the Atharvan application of the hymn, whether that were or were not its original intent. In b, all the mss. have su instead of l ¢vâ ; both editions-emend to the latter, which is read also by the comm. [ For asyar, (he 7. O sleep, with the imposition (abkikarazṇa) of sleep do thou put to ¹ sleep all the folk ; till sun-up make the others sleep, till dawning let me ht be awake, like Indra, uninjured, unexhausted. ht Several of SPP's mss. have at the beginning svâpnas. Ppp. reads svapnââhik-, ¹ â and so does the comm. (explaining adkik- as adkisthânarṅ: cayyadr) ; the latter has in ¹ ¹ ; â âZyyṅsam ; and Ppp. gives caratâr for jagyar. A khila to RV. vii. 55 has a corre- 1 sponding verse, reading for a svapnâṅ svapnââhikâraṇe (thus rectifying the meter), in c â saryâm, and for d doyṅgârnt jagriyad akâm. The Anukr. uses the name jyotis so loosely that it is difficult to say precisely how it would have the verse scanned; itis really

“ea a bkuriy paṅkti. HH The 5 hymns of the first anuvâka contain 37 verses ; and the old Anukr., taking 30 ¹ I as norm, says simply sapta. ²

docs.title: 6. Against the poison of a poisoned arrow
docs.text:
¹ IGarutman. —astarcam. taṅmkadevalyam. ânugubham.]

Ś Found (except vs. I) in Paipp. v. Used by Kâug. (with, as the schol. and the y comm. say, the next following hymn alse) in a rite (28. 1 ff.) of healing for poison, with

¹ homage to Takṣaka, chief of the serpent gods; and the schol. (but not the comm.

¹ â 3 ? g declare it to be employed elsewhere (29. 1; 32. 20) in similar rites involving Takgaka. There is no specific reference in the hymn to serpent poison, but distinctly to vegetable poison ; and the comm. regards kanda or kandamâla (' tuber ' and ( tuber-root ¹) as the plant intended.

Translated : Ludwig, p. 512; Griffith, i. 136 ; Bloomfield, 25, 373 ; Weber, xviii. 23. — Cf. Bergaigne-Henry, Manuel, p. 145. I. The Brahman was born first, with ten heads, with ten mouths; he first drank the soma; he made the poison sapless.

The absence of this verse in Ppp., and the normal length of the hymn without it, together with its own senselessness, suggest strongly the suspicion of its unoriginality. To put meaning into it, the comm. maintains that the serpents have castes, as men have; : and that their primal Brahman was Takṣaka.

2. As great as [are] heaven-and-earth by their width, as much as the seven rivers spread out (vi-sthâ), [so far] have I spoken out from here these words (vâr), spoilers of poison.

T&vattm in â for tâm itâs would be a welcome emendation. The first halfverse occurs in VS. (xxxviii. 26 a, b: not quoted in CB.) and TS. (in iii. 2.67) : VS. omits varimuâ, TS. has instead makâtoâ ; both rectify the meter of b by adding ca after y&vat (Ppp. adds instead vz) ; and for our rather fantastic vitasthire (p. victasthire) VS. has -zasthire and TS. -fastkâs. The comm. also reads -stkire; the lingualization is one of the cases falling under Prat. ii. 93. The comm. glosses in b sindhawas by samudrâs, and vitasthire by vyâvartante. This irregular grastârapaṅkti is overlooked by the Anukr. in its treatment of the meter.

3. The winged (garârmant) eagle consumed (av) thee first, O poison; thou hast not intoxicated (mad), thou hast not racked (rz) [him] ; and thou becamest drink for him.

At beginning of b, va is read only by Ppp. and ] by the comm, and by one of SPP's mss. that follows him; all the rest have the gross blunder v427 (both editions emend to uâa). Ppp. gives âdayat in b, and its second half-verse reads zz 'ropayo nâ ¹mâdayo tâsmâ bhavan piruR, thus removing the objectionable confusion of tenses made by our text. Our arârupas is quoted as counter-example by the comment to : Prat. iv. 86. The first pada might be rendered also ⁴ the wellwinged Garutmant,' ¹ and the comm. so understands it, adding the epithet vâinareya to show that garutmant =Garuda. He also takes the two aorists and the imperfect in c—d alike as impera-; tives (nâ 'rurupas = vimugham ma kârgik). The Anukr. does not note a as irregular.

4. He of five fingers that hurled at thee from some crooked bow — ) from the tip (calyâ) of the apaskambṅâ have I exorcised (777-vac) the poison. I Apaskambhâ is very obscure ; the Pet. Lex. suggests perhaps the fastening of the ¹ arrow-head to the shaft"; Ludwig guesses barb," but that we have in vs. 5—as we also have calya, which seems therefore premature here; and, in fact, Ppp. reads instead i : of it 37kwos; and, as it has elsewhere apaskantasya bâkwvos, we might conjecture apa ⁴ skanâkhasya eftc., ' from shoulder and arms': ie. from wounds in them. Or, for gṅa-. : skam?bha as a part of the body might be compared Sucruta i. 349. 20 —unless apastambe

(which at least one good manuscript reads) is the true text there Calcutta ed. reads apastambkâu ]. The comm. has no idea what apaskambka means, but makes a couple Sh of wild guesses: it is the betelnut (,ramuka)-tree, or it is an arrow (both based 6n ¹ v senseless etymologies). In a, Ppp. reads ulis. : Ś 5. From the tip have I exorcised the poison, from the anointing and Ht from the feather-socket ; from the barb (2735744), the horn, the neck Gl have I exorcised the poison. 1 Ppp. reads vocam instead of avocam in a and d, and its b is 27janat parpadher uta. 6 Prat. ii. 95 regards apâstha as from apa-sthâ, doubtless correctly ; between the "barb" Gra and the “horn " there is probably no important difference. To the comm., the apâṣtṅa Ś â Ś is a poison-receptacle (apaṅrstâvasthad etatsaṅnynad visopadanât). i 6. Sapless, O arrow, is thy tip; likewise thy poison is sapless; also ¹ thy bow, of a sapless tree, O sapless one, is sapless. i The comm. strangely takes arasârasam at the end (p. arasa: arasâr) as a redupliary. cated word, " excessively sapless." â4 7. They who mashed, who smeared, who hurled, who let loose—they 4 [are] all made impotent ; impotent is made the poison-mountain. ¹ That is, as the comm. is wise enough to see, the mountain from which the poisonous ; plant is brought. Let loose" (ava-szj) probably applies to arrows as distinguished from spears; though hurl" might be used equally of both. Ppp. has in ec saṅin i i instead of Zr2â2s. According to SPP., the text used by the comm. combines ye â5an; She aptsan is an anomalous form for ggiṅgan, with which the comm. glosses it.

8. Impotent [are] thy diggers; impotent art thou, O herb; impotent

(3 [is] that rugged (pârvara) mountain whence was born this poison.

As was pointed out above (under iv. 4. 2), the first half-verse is a sort of opposite dt of one found in Ppp., and quoted by Kâug. (at 40. 14). With pârvata girt of. mygâ8e

docs.title: 7. Against poison
docs.text:
ar [Garutman. — vânaspatyanm. Enugubham : 4. svarâj.] Found in Pâipp., but not all together ; vs. I occurs in v., vss. 2-6 in ii., and vs. 7 in ¹ vi. Not used by Kâug. unless it is properly regarded by the schol. and the comm. (see ¹ : under h. 6) as included with h. 6 by the citation (28. r) of the latter's pratika (the comm, puts it on the ground of the parâbkâsa rule grakanam â grakayât, Kâug. 8. 21).

Ś Translated : Ludwig, p. 2015 Grill, 28, r2r; Griffith, i. 38 ; Bloomfield, 26, 376;

k: Weber, xviii. 26. ¹ tI. This water (oâr) shall ward off (vâray-) upon the Varaṇâvati; an

(3 on-pouring of ambrosia (a#ta) is there; with it I ward off thy poison. The significance of the verse lies in its punning upon vr and var; the name vara- 73â7atr is not found elsewhere, but has sufficient analogies elsewhere; it is formed, as i ee the comm. points out, from the tree-name wargya (Cratacva Roxburghir). Ppp. has in i Ś b a âifferent pun: varuṇâd abhy tam ; and for â it reads fac cakârâ 'rasar: vigam.

a The first pada lacks a syllable, unless we resolve 72-47. [Ct. x. 3: I n.] 2. Sapless is the poison of the east, sapless what is of the north ; also this that is of the south is exchangeable with gruel (kzrambiâd). That is, is no stronger or more harmful than gruel. Except our Bp., which has adharâcyâm, all the mss. accent -7âcyam, and SPP. follows them; our edition emends to -râcyânz, to accord with the two adjectives of like formation in a, b. Ppp. puts arasam after vigam in a.

3. Having made gruel of sesame (?), teeming with fat, steaming (?), thou dost not rack, O ill-bodied one, him that has eaten thee merely from hunger.

The verse is full of difficulties and doubtful points. The translation implies in â emendation of jaksivânt sâ to jakstvârsanm, as suggested by BR., s.v. 725 (Grill rejects it, but unwisely) ; Ppp. reads jakṣivipyasya. The construction of the augmentless aorist-form rârupas with nâ instead of m7 is against all rule and usage ; the easiest emendation would be to nâ 'rârupas ; Ppp. gives nu rârâpak. SPP. unaccountably reads rârupal in pada-text, both here and in 5 d and 6 â, against all but one of his pada-mss. in this verse, and also against Prat. iv. 86, which distinctly requires rurupaj and (in all the three cases alike) the pada-mss. add after the word the sign which they are accustomed to use when a pada-reading is to be changed to something else in 4 san kitâa. In c, the pada-reading is dustano ti dujstana ; the case is noted under Prat. ii. 85. 7Vryâm in a is rendered as if t7lyâm, from tila (so the Pet. Lex); the comm. derives it from Ś7ras, and renders it tirobhavam vanishing," which is as senseless as it is etymologically absurd ; Ppp. reads instead fzriyam. According to Râjan. xvi. 23, a sort of rice (as ripening in three months) is called tirâya (tirima ?), but the word appears to be only a modern one, and is hardly to be looked for here. [I cannot find it in the Poona ed.®] Grill makes the very unsatisfactory conjecture aziriyanm « running over.” In b, all our mss. (as also the comment on Prât. ii. 62) read p7asphakâm (p. préakephâkân, which the comment just quoted ratifies), as our edition reads ; SPP., on the other hand, prints pṅhaspâkârn (comm. pivaspâkant, explained as «fat-cooking ") and declares this to be the unanimous reading of his authorities : this discordance of testimony is quite unexplainable. The translation implies emendation of the pada-reading to pṅbajespkâkân.. Ppp. reads adakytam for the problematic udârathim ; but the latter is supported by RV. i. 187. ro (of whose first two pâdas, indeed, our a, b seem to be a reminiscence) : karambhâ osadhe bhava ptvo vr kkâ nâarathtf.- The comm. explains the word as udriktârtijanakar (Sâyaṇa to RV. entirely differently). In a supplementary note, Roth reports : Ppp. has pâwâassakan; R. has, pm, piâlaspâ-, corrected to praspâa-; T. has proaspa-. ] Correct the verse-number : for 6 read 3. J ¥ Or is nirapa, at p. 2204, a variant of triya? The two are casily confused in; nagart. J

4. Away we make thine intoxication fly, like an arrow (arâ), O intoxicating one (f.) ; we make thee with our spell (vâcas) to stand forth, ] Ś like a boiling pot.

The comm. (with a pair of SPP's mss.) reads garâm in b*; it also (alone) has â Jjesantam (= prayatamânanr) in c; one of our mss. (Op.), with two or three of SPP's, g give instead pesantam. Ppp. has a peculiar c: parâ tvâ varmi vegantam. The verse ² is regular if we make the ordinary abbreviation of a to 'va in b and c. *] The ¹ reciters K and V gave carâm: comm, renders as if ¢4ruṅz (arrow. BR. render the er verb in 4 by 'wegstellen' When you set the pot aside (take it off the fire), it stops boiling ; and so the poison is to stop working. But see also Weber's note. Ś8 5. With a spell we cause to stand about [thee] as it were a collected e : troop (grâma) ; stand thou, like a tree in [its] station ; spade-dug one (f.), â ; thou rackest not.

(i The comm., here and in 6 â, reads abṅrisâare (-sate=-labdhe), which looks like a fa result of the common confusion of 44 and 5. SPP. reads in pada-text rârupaṅ, and

this time without any report as to the readings of his paâa-mss.— doubtless by an over- (4 sight, as all but one of them give rr in both 3 d and 6 d. The true scanning of c is

¹â probably v7 kse ‘va sthâ-mn-i. EŚŚ ; i a 6. For covers (? pavâsta) they bought thee, also for garments (? dzrgâ), ¹ for goat-skins ; purchasable (? prakrt) art thou, O herb; spade-dug one, ² thou rackest not. Shar The comm. knows nothing of what gavasta and âârga mean, but etymologizes the er : former out of pavana and asta (pavanâyâ stâik sammaârjanttynâik), and the other Ge out of Jus and yeya (âustarcyasambandkâbhik)¹ Prakris he renders by prakarsena rele 7. Who of you did what first unattained deeds —let them not harm G1 our heroes here ; for that purpose I put you forward. i ¹ This verse occurs again later, as v. 6. 2, and in Ppp. makes a part of that hymn alone.

Its sense is very questionable, and its connection casts no light upon it, either here or et Ś there ; and Grill is justified in omitting it as having apparently nothing to do with the i 6 rest of this hymn. All the pada-mss. save one of SPP's read ânaprâ (not 27k) ; and Gr all save our Bp. read prathamârṅ (Bp. -mâ) ; SPP. gives in his pada-text-1â} and -mâṇ;

i the translation here given implies -4z and -mâ, without intending to imply that the other rr readings may not be equally good ; the comm. takes ânâpiâh (= ananukâlak ¹ El unkindly' [) as qualifying arr avas understood, and pratkamâ as qualifying kârmaṇi.

docs.title: 8. Accompanying the consecration of a king
docs.text:
⁴ it [Atharvâṅgiras.— râ(yâbhisckyam, câindramasam, 3pyam. ânustubham Ś I, 7. bhuriktrigtubk ; 3. trigtubh ; 5. Vir tprastârapankti.]

â Found in Pâipp. iv. (in the verse-order r-3, 7, 4-6). For occurrences in other texts, see under the verses. Used by Kaâug. (17. 1 ff.), and also in Vait. (36. 7) in connection

4 : with the râjabhiseka or râjasâya ceremony ; and Vâit. (29. 12) further employs vs. 5 in

1 the agnicayana, with pouring of water around the erected altar. ot i Translated : Ludwig, p. 458 ; Zimmer, p. 213 ; Weber, Ueber den Râjasâya, Berliner

⁴ Abk., 1893, p- I39 (with full discussion) ; Griffith, i. 139; Bloomfield, rri, 378 ; Weber,

I. The being (bkṅtâ) sets milk in beings ; he has become the overlord of beings ; Death attends (car) the royal consecration (râ7asâya) of him ; let him, as king, approve this royalty.

¹ er The meaning is obscure. Very possibly Ś47t4 is taken here in more than one of its

¹ senses, by a kind of play upon the word. Weber renders it the first time by powerful"

(ârâytig), nearly as the comm., whose gloss is samrââhak ; the latter gives it the same sense the second time, but the third time simply p7âninâm. The introduction of « death" in the second half-verse suggests the interpretation (R.) that the deceased predecessor of the prince now to be consecrated is besought to give his sanction to the ceremony from the world of the departed (547424). The comm. regards death as brought in in the character of âharmarâja, as he who requites good and evil deeds. TB. (in ii. 7. 15) is the only other text that has this verse, reading in a car ati prâviytaj (for pâya & dadhâti)and in c mr tyââ : the variants are of a character to make us distrust the value of the matter as admitting any consistent interpretation. Ppp. reads in c sa te for zâsya. 2. Go fb6rward unto [it]; do not long (? ven) away, a stern (zgrâ) corrector (cettâr), rival-slayer ; approach (â-stkâ), O increaser of friends; may the gods bless (adki-brṅ) thee.

Found, with vs. 3, in TB. (in ii. 7. 8r), and also, with the remainder of the hymn, in K. (xxxvii. 9). It seems to be a reminiscence of the Inâra-verse, RV. v. 31. 2, applied, like vs. 3 of this hymn, to the king. ] TB. reads in a (for mâ pa venas) virâyasva, and Ppp. has vigayasva ; TB. gives, as also the comm., the nom. mârravârâkanas (a later repetition of the verse, in ii. 7. 16, presents vr trakântamas instead) ; and it ends with bravan,* which is better, and might have been read in our text, as near half the mss. give it; but SPP. also accepts (ruvan, with the comm. The comm. takes the throne" as object of the first verb, and renders mâ 'pa venas by apakâmam anicchâm mz kârsik of. vi-ven in BR. J. (Weber renders ven by "see.") But the Poona ed. p. 716, has (ruvan. J

3. Him approaching all waited upon (pari-bkṅg) ; clothing himself in fortune, he goes about (car), having own brightness; great is that name of the virile (vâsan) Asura; having all forms, he approached immortal things.

This is a RV. verse (iii. 38. 4 : repeated without variant as VS. xxxiii. 22), transferred from Indra to the king; RV. reads, as does Ppp., crâyas in b. TB. (as above) has svârocâs at end of b, and asyâ for vfsnas in c. At the beginning of c, the comm. has maṅas (but explains it as = mahat) tad visṇo, and a couple of SPP's mss. support him. He renders pâri abkugsan either ala kurvantu or sevantâm : that the form is imperative is the point he is sure of; and as alternative value of asurasya he gives catrâRâr: nivasituf I lls not 4surasya nâma a simple periphrasis of asuzyâsr, the divinity that " doth hedge a king," in which gods are said to clothe themselves at RV. iii. 38. 7? Nâma might then be construed with vâsânas, or else as above. J

4. A tiger, upon the tiger's [skin], do thou stride out unto the great quarters; let all the people (vas) want thee, the waters of heaven, rich in milk. g

That is, let the rains not desert thee Tso the comm. also). This verse and the two. following are found, in the same order, in TB. ii. 7. 153-4; it puts 4dk7 after vâyyâghTE Ś (sic) in a, reads crayaswa in b, and has for â mâ toâd râgtrân âdhi bhragcat (found below as vi. 87.1 d, and in other texts: see under that verse). Ppp. gives yazti or anti? instead of vaRchantu in c. ¹

5. The waters of heaven that revel with milk, in the atmosphere or also on the earth — with the splendor of all those waters do I pour upon. (abki-sic) thee. â ¹¹ The version of the first half-verse given by TB. is quite different: yâ âiuyâ âpak pâyasâ sambabhuvij : yâ antârikse utâ pârthivir yâh ; and Ppp. so far agrees as to ² have uta pârthivâ yak ; TB. also reads rucâ for apâm in c. The comm. renders ¹ madanti as if causative : prâninas tarpayanti. The abhiseka process, instead of an

; anointing with oil, is a pouring of water upon the person to be consecrated. The : ‘ verse (11 +10 : 8+8=37) lacks three syllables of being complete, rather than two. Put ⁴ another yâs at the beginning of b and the verse is orderly, rr +11: 848. Sl Ś Perhaps mad here approaches its physical meaning, boil (cf. CB. iii. 4. 3 end, and (ff my Reader, p. 211), bubble over, overflow '; used of the rains that 'drip abundantly 8. with pâyas or life-giving moisture. W's prior draft rendered mad by "intoxicate"; x6 over this he interlined ⁴revel."— This, says Weber, is the verse of the act of conseor â¢ cration proper. The celebrant transfers to the king the wârcas or glory-giving vigor (4 ⁴ : of the waters of all three worlds. Ś 6. The heavenly waters, rich in milk, have poured upon thee with

(Hf splendor ; that thou be an increaser of friends, so shall Savitar make thee. ( 5 Instead of our asâṅcan, SPP. gives, as the reading of all his authorities, asican, ey ; which is decidedly preferable, and implied in the wanslation (our Bp. is doubtful ; other el mss. possibly overlooked at this point) ; TB. has instead asicam ; Ppp. and. the comm., Ś aszjan. Then, for b, TB. and Ppp. give diuyena pâyasa (Ppp. pây-) sakâ; and in c Gh TB. has râstravârdk-, which is better, and before it yârhâsa (regarded by its com- 4 mentary as yâzha : &sa).

7. Thus, embracing the tiger, they incite (47) the lion unto great good-fortune ; as the well-being ones (subk7) the ocean that stands, do ¹ they rub thoroughly down the leopard amid the waters. ¹ Found also in TB. (ii. 7.164) and MS. (ii. . 9 : besides K.). In b, MS. has myjanti be for kinvanti, and dhânâya (which rectifies the meter) for sâ7âbhagâya. For c, MS. has i : a much less unmanageable version, makâsânm nah subkoânt, and Ppp. supports it by Ś giving makisans nas subkavas: thus, in each pâda the king is compared to a different â ( powerful animal —which is the leading motive of the verse. But TB. differs from our text only by giving sukhâwam? for subhtvas. Subhoâm, with a further slight emendation : of samudrâm to-ârâ, would give a greatly improved sense : him who stands comfortable : : in the ocean, as it were," or bears himself well under the water poured upon him. The I Ś phrase samndrân: nâ subkoâj occurs also at RV. i. 52. 4 b (and its occurrence here in ¹ such form may be a reminiscence of that); Sâyana there understands subâuâs of the

“streams " that fill the ocean ; and our comm. gives a corresponding interpretation here ¹ (nadir nga apak) ; samudrân he allows us alternatively to take as = varupam. He 4 also, most ungrammatically, takes en at the beginning as enâs = those [waters]. Ppp.

further has pari myjyante for marm- in 4. ¥| Poona ed., p. 750, reads sukâvam. J

docs.title: 9. For protection etc. : with a certain ointment
docs.text:
4 : LB ky gi. — dagar cam. trâikaRudânjanaââivatam. ânustubham : 2. ka kummati;

Ś 3. pathyâpaṅkti.];

5 Feund mostly in Pâipp. viii. (in the verse-order 9, 3,2, 5,6, 8, 10, 4, 7). Used by Kâug.

(58. 8) with the binding on of an ointment-amulet, in a ceremony for long life of the oo Vedic pupil after his initiation. And the comm. quotes it from the Naks. K. (19) error ¹ Ś for Cânti, says Bl. as employed in the makhâganti called 2irâvatt.

Translated : Ludwig, p. 5075 Grill, 35, 123; Griffith, i. 141; Bloomfield, 61, 3813; Weber, xviii. 32.— As for ointment and ointment-legends, see Bloomfield, AJP. xvii. 404 ff. 4

I. Come thou, rescuing the living one; of the mountain art thou for the eyes (?), given by all the gods, an enclosure (garâdk?) in order to living. Jruâm in a might also be cotrdinate with rrâyamanan ; the comm. understands it as translated. The meter indicates that the true reading at the end of bis âk"yarz, and this is read by SPP., with the alleged support of all his authorities save one, which follows the comm. in giving âksam ; our Bp. has â&yar, and our edition accepted that (our Op. has akgyâm, our I. âkgyâm); but akgya is unknown elsewhere, and its meaning in this connection is quite obscure ; perhaps allusion is intended to a legend reported in MS. iii. 6. 3 (p. 62.8; cf. also TS. vi. I. 15 and CB. iii. I. 3. 12): "Indra verily slew Vrtra; his eye-ball flew away; it went to Trikakubh; that ointment of Trikakubh he spreads on." The ointment of this mountain is most efficacious for the eyes, and hence also for the other purposes here had in view. The comm. gives caṅsus as the value of his aksam. Grill suggests emendation to aksayyam or aksaranz. We have to make the harsh resolution v4cu-e- in c or leave the pâda defective.

2. Protection (paripâṇa) of men (pârusa), protection of kine art thou; in order to the protection of coursing (4rvant) horses hast thou stood.

The comm. says in c “of horses and of mares (vagavânâanz). The resolution âr-va-ta-am fills up c quite unsatisfactorily ; the Anukr. refuses all resolution, and counts the pada as of 6 syllables.

3. Both art thou a protection, grinder-up of familiar demons (yâtâ), O ointment, and of what is immortal thou knowest; likewise art thou gratification (-Ś44jana) of the living, likewise remedy of jaundice (kârila-).

Contrary to rule, the a of asi in â has to be elided after 70 in 4; probably emendation to 4244 'si is called for; one of our mss. (O.) reads âtko si. Ppp. rectifies the meter of a by giving ute "uâ si ; for e, 4 it has utâ 'mytatvesye "gig utâ 'sas pet bho-; jananm. The comm. takes amṇtasya as the drink of immortality, and -Śkojana as either anigtanivartanena pâlaka or bhogasâdkana. The last pada hardly belongs with the rest.

4. Of whomsoever, O ointment, thou creepest over limb after limb, joint after joint, from thence thou drivest away the yâkgma, like a formidable mid-lier (madhyamagt).

Found also as RV. x. 97. 12 (repeated, without variant, as VS. xii. 86), which version, however, begins with yâsyâan 'sadht] prasârpatha, and has in c correspondingly Ś2â7ka- & dkve. The comm. has in c bââhare, but regards it as for â2âkhase. Ppp. reads rasrât for tatas. Madkyamagt is of obscure meaning; "arbiter," as conjectured by BR. ¹ seems very implausible BR. express their conjectural meaning by the Latin word ¹ intercessor ; by which, I suspect, they intend, not mediator,' but rather adversary" or ¹ ⁴ preventer ' of the disease, which would be plausible enough J; more probably Śmid- ¹ most man," like madhyamesthâ or chief (see under iii. 8. 2), and maâkyamagr used . especially of the leader about whom his men encamp, for his greater safety, in the night. IB. has madkyamagtvan at ii. 408, but the passage is too corrupt to cast valu-

; able light upon the word. To the comm., it is either Vâyu, the wind in mid-air, or else

the king, viewed as surrounded first by foes, and further by their foes, his friends (on ¹Ś the principle of arir mâtram arer ; mitram) mitra-mâtram aah param etc. I find el the verse at Kâmandakiya Nitisâra, viii. 16. To judge from the Later Syriac Version cl (Kalilah and Dimnah, Keith-Falconer, p. 114), one would expect to find it in Paficaee tantra ii., colloquy of mouse and crow, in Kosegarten's ed., p. rio or thereabouts. Cf. a Manu vii. 158 and the comm. : ⁴ 5. Curse attains him not, nor witchcraft, nor scorching ; vâkandṅa

¹¹ reaches him not who beareth thee, O ointment. 44 : Ppp. reads tam for enam in a, and niâskandham in c. lIt inserts just before our gr vs. 7 the vs. given under vi. 76. 4 and ending with yas tvân bibharty aṅjana. ² ¹ 6. From wrong spell, from evil dreaming, from evil deed, from pollu- Ga tion also, from the terrible eye. of an enemy — therefrom protect us, a O ointment. : : Ppp. has, for b, kserriyac chapathâd nia. The Pet. Lexx. understand asanmantrâ Ś : as simply c untrue speech" (so Grill, ⁴ Ligenrede ") ; the comm. reads instead -nzzyat, as Ś adjective qualifying dusvapnyat, and signifying produced by base bewitching spells.”

Durkârdas in c might well be adj., ‘hostile (so comm.).
  1. Knowing this, O ointment, I shall speak truth, not falsehood ; may ¹ Ś I win (saz) a horse, a cow, thy soul, O man (pṅrusa). : The latter half-verse is RV. x. 97. 4 c, d (which is also, without variant, VS. xii. 78 c, 9), where we read vâsas instead of zhâm ; Ppp. too, gives vasas. All the mss. and the ¹ lt comm. have at the end the absurd form purusas (nom., but without accent) ; the comm. el (whose text, as SPP. points out in more than one place, is unaccentuated) understands pre «I, thy man (retainer). Both editions make the necessary emendation to purusa ¹ gd ¹ ls. parusa Ppp. gives paurusa. SPP. makes a note that sanâyarm is so accented by — ' all his authorities —as if anything else were possible does he have in mind sâneyam gr Ve see Whitney, Roots, p. 183 ]. The first pâda is defective unless we resolve vi-du-ân or Sh ¹ 7-aṅyana .—] R's supplementary report of Ppp. readings ends a with zṅjaṅas and has . i for d jana tar va paurusak. As noted above, this vs. stands at the end in Ppp. and et before it is inserted the vs. given under vi. 76. 4.

¹ 8. Three are the slaves (ââsâ) of the ointment —fever (takmân), balâsa, es then snake : the highest of mountains, three-peaked (zrikakâd) by name,

¹k [is] thy father.

El ¹ For the obscure Śalâsa, the comm. gives the worthless etymology balam asyatâ, and 1 Ś ¹ adds saṅniparadiṅ ' collision [of humors] or the like; ⁴ snake" he explains as for Ś Ś snake-poisoning ; perhaps, if the reading is genuine, it is rather the name of some

(constricting?) disease.

â 9- The ointment that is of the three-peaked [mountain], born from

the snowy one (kâmâvanty— may it grind up all the familiar demons and ¹ ² all the sorceresses.

Pâda b is repeated below as v. 4.2 b. The first half-verse is, without variant, TA. vi. 10. 2, VS. 9 a, b; and it occurs also in HGS. (i. iI. 5), which reads ugar7 at the end for pari and so at MP. ii. 8. rr a, b]. The second half is VS. xvi. 5 c, 4, and also found in TS. iv. 5.12 and MS. ii. 9. 2; all these have âṅ7z instead of yâtân, and read jambhââyan (pres. pple.) ; and our jambhâyar may, of course, be pres. pple. neut. ; some of the mss. (including our Bp.M.I.) indeed read yan here, though no masc. subject is implied; the comm. paraphrases with nâcayad vartate. SPP., with his customary defiance of grammar upon this point, reads sârvân instead of -2i or -47 l cf. i.19. 4, note].

ro. If thou art of the three-peaked [mountain], or if thou art called of the Yamuna — both thy names are excellent; by them protect us, O ointment.

Te in c might perhaps be emended with advantage to 7. The Yamunâ is not elsewhere mentioned in AV. Nâmmi is to be read, of course, as of three syllables, and there is no reason why the text should not give us nâmant.

docs.title: 10. Against evils : with a pearl-shell amulet
docs.text:
LAtharvan.— caṅkhamaṇisâkâtam. taddâivatam. Enugubham: 6. pathyâpaskii;

7- 5-2. parânugtup cakvarr.]

Found (except vs. 5) in Pâipp. iv. Used by Kaâug. (58. 9) in the same ceremony with the preceding hymn, but with an amulet of mother-of-pearl ; the schol. (not the comm.) also add it in an earlier part of the ceremony (56. 17). The comm. quotes it further from Naks. K. (19), as employed in a makâgânti named vârupi.

Translated : Ludwig, p. 462 ; Grill, 36, 124; Griffith, i.142; Bloomfield, 62, 383; Weber, xviii. 36.— Bloomfield cites an article in ZDMG. (xxxvi. 135) by Pischel, who, in turn, cites a lot of interesting literature about pearl.

Although rain-drops are not expressly mentioned in this hymn nor in xix. 30.5 (which see), I think it safe to say that the bit of Hindu folklore about the origin of pearls by transformation of rain-drops falling into the sea (Jnâisckhe Sprâche, 344) is as old as this Vedic text and the one in xix. The references here to sky and sea and lightning, and in xix. to Parjanya and thunder and sea, all harmonize perfectly with that belief, which is at least ten centuries old (it oocurs in Râjagekhara, goo A.D.) and has lasted till today (Manwaring's Marârht Proverbs, no. 1291). See my translation of Karpâra-maṅjart, p. 264 f., and note 5. Pischel, Le., reports as follows : “ According to Aelian (wepl (ov, x. 13), a pearl forms when the lightning flashes into an open seashell; according to an Arabic writer, when rain-drops fall into it, or, according to Pliny (ix. 107), dew." — The persistency of popular beliefs in India is well illustrated by the curious one concerning female snakes : see my note to Xarpâra-maṅyarr, p. 231. J e

I. Born from the wind out of the atmosphere, out from the light of lightning, let this gold-born shell, of pearl, protect us from distress.

Of course, all the four nouns in the first half-verse may be coŚrdâmate ablatives. The beauty and sheen of the material connect it traceably with gold and lightning, but ¹ how even a Hindu 737 can bring it into relation with wind from (or and) the atmosphere ⁴ is not easy to see. Xygana ought to mean the pearl itself, and is perhaps used in the Ś hymn appositively = ⁴ which is itself virtually pearl"; the comm. explains i in this. verse as kargayita catrunâr tanâkarta. Ppp. has in c kâragyadâs.

2. Thou that wast born from the top of the shining spaces (rocandg), out of the ocean — by the shell having slain the demons, we overpower the devourers. Ppp. combines in a yo 'graro r-. Grill takes agratas as " first"; and the comm. as = agre, and not qualifying jajṅâse : “at the top or front of shining things, such as stars."

3. By the shell [we overpower] disease, misery; by the shell also the sadânvâs; let the all-healing shell, of pearl, protect us from distress.

Ppp. has in a avaâyam instead of âmatini. The comm. takes âatim from root man see BR's note, s.v. 3 dmati J: "ignorance, the root of all mishap (anartha)"; and, forgetting his explanation of only two verses ago, he this time declares kana a Śname of gold."

4. Born in the sky, ocean-born, brought hither out of the river, this gold-born shell [is] for us a life-prolonging amulet.

Ppp. has sam uâratas at end of a, and in c again (as in 1 c) kiranyadâs. Nearly all our mss. (except O.K.), and some of SPP's, with the comm. read in d Zyuṅpr- cf. Prat. ii. 62 n. J; but the point is one in regard to which each ms. is wont to follow its own course, regardless of rule, and both editions very properly give Zyugpr-, as required by the Prat.

5. The amulet born from the ocean, born from Vrtra, making day — let it protect us on all sides from the missile of gods and Asuras.

The comm. makes Vrtra here signify either the demon Vrtra or the cloud ; doubtless the latter is intended ; then he explains doâkara as the sun, and jâra as "released," and renders «as brilliant as the sun freed from the clouds," which is extremely artificial; âvâkara need mean no more than (flashing with light.' The comm. also foolishly understands in d ketyâ instead of -s (p. ketyâk). Dev-, ablative by attraction, from gen.—ct. Skt. Gram. §982 a.] The first pada is deficient by a syllable, unless we resolve szmudrât into four syllables.

6. One of the golds art thou; out of soma wast thou born; thou art conspicuous on the chariot, lustrous (rocanâ) on the quiver thou. May it prolong our lives

The last pada, which occurs in four other places (ii. 4. 6 etc.), looks like a late addition here ; as elsewhere, some of the mss. (five of SPP's) read rârsar. Except our Op., all the padâa-mss. blunderingly resolve sâmâtvâm (as it would be permissibly and customarily read by abbreviation: see Whitney, Sz. Gr. Ś232) into s6mâ : toâm instead of sâmâr : toâm.; the comm. understands sâmâz, and both editions give the full reading. Here one is strongly tempted to translate sora by “ moon," and the comm. takes it so (amy tamayar somamaṇgalar) ; but Ppp. discourages it by reading sa kosâd (for -mâd 2) adki. The comm. glosses rocana by rocamâna dz yamâna. For c, Ppp. has rathesu dargatar.

7. The gods' bone became pearl; that goes about within the waters, possessing soul; that do I bind on thee in order Yo life-time, splendor, strength, to length of life for a hundred autumns : let [the amulet] of pearl defend thee. ŚKaṅanâs in e, though read by all our mss. and nearly all of SPP's, is hardly to be tolerated; we should have either kṅcanas, as above, or kârganas, which the comm. offers, with two or three mss. that follow him, and which SPP. accordingly adopts kâr¢ands J; our edition gives karg-; Ppp. has kâarginas. Ppp. also has simply ca for our whole â (after bal7yay. The comm. reads aszi instead of aszṅi in a. The verse (I +11: 14+ 11 +8=55) lacks a syllable of being a full aZwari. Reject either Guype or varcase and the meter is good.—In c, 72 'for thee' (comm., as gen.), is, I suppose, virtually = on thee.'

The second anuvâka, ending with this hymn, contains 5 hymns and 39 verses ; the Anukr. quotation is nava ca.

docs.title: 11. In praise of the draft-ox
docs.text:
[BhygUaṅgiras.— dvâdararcam. ânaguham. itrâigubham : I, 4. jagati; 2. bkur(j ; 7. 3-av.

6-4. anugubgarbho ¹parigâyâgatâ nicycchakvarr; 8-ra. arugtubh.]

Found in Pâipp. iii. (in the verse-order 1, 4, 2, 5, 3, 6, IT, I2, 9, 8, IO, 7). Used by Kâug. (66. 12) in a sava sacrifice, with the draft-ox as sava. The hymn offers an example of that characteristic Hindu extollation, without any measure or limit, of the immediate object of reverence, which, when applied to a divinity, has led to the setting up of the baseless doctrine of henotheism."

Translated : Muir, OST. v. 399, 361 (about half); Ludwig, pp. 534 and r9o ; Deussen, Geschichte, i. I. 232 ; Griffith, i. 144; Weber, xviii.39.—Cf. Deussen, lc., p. 230 f. Weber entitles the hymn ⁴ Verschenkung eines Pfugstieres zur Feier der Zwâlften (i.e. nights of the winter solstice—see vs. rr)."

I. The draft-ox sustains earth and sky; the draft-ox sustains the wide atmosphere ; the draft-ox sustains the six wide directions; the draft-ox hath entered into all existence.

That is, the ox in his capacity of draft-animal : the comm. says, cakatavâhanasamartho vrsabkah ; later in the hymn he is treated as female, without change of the name to a feminine form (the fem. -gukr or -goâht does not occur before the Brâhmaṇaperiod of the language). But the comm. also allows us the alternative of regarding âJharma, in ox-form, as subject of the hymn. The "directions" (pr adâ) are, according to him, “east etc," ; and the "six wide " are " heaven, earth, day, night, waters, and plants," for which ACS. i. 2. 1 is quoted as authority. With the verse compare x. 7. 35, where nearly the same things are said of skambka. Ppp. reads in a -vṅṅ âyâm ulz mum. In the second half-verse, two accent-marks have slipped out of place in our edition: in c, that under gz should stand under gu; and, in â, that under s27 should stand under za. The verse is jagati by count, but not by rhythm. lI, with Weber, we pronounce naguâr, it becomes a regular frâs7ubk.

2. The draft-ox [is] Indra; he looks out from (for?) the cattle; triple ways the mighty one (cakrâ) measures out (traverses?) ; yielding (a7) the past (?bkṅtâ), the future, existing things (Śhṅvana), he goes upon (car) all the courses (vratâ) of the gods.

Ppp. reads in a indrasya for indraj sa, and in ec it adds sanz before bkâtarz, and has (kuvanant instead of -nâ. The comm. has in b the curious reading styân for trayân, and hence we lose his guess as to what may be meant by the “triple ways." He takes pagubhyas in a first as dative, and then as ablative. He understands bkâvant as virtually present " ; more probably it has its usual sense of 'existences,' and the two preceding adjectives qualify it distributively, or are in apposition with it: wall existing

things, both what is and what is to be." ] If we pronounce again nagvân, the vs. loses (es its 6hurij quality. The cadence of b is bad.

4. 3. Born an Indra among human beings (manugyâ), he goes about (car) Gd shining brightly, a heated hot-drink (gharmâ); he, being one of good : offspring, shall not go in mist (?udârâ) who, understanding [it], shall

( not partake of (ag) the draft-ox. 2 The verse is obscure, and the translation in various points very doubtful. The 444 second pada is apparently a beginning of the identification of the ox with the ghar ma, i 4 a sacrificial draught of heated milk, which we find further in vss. 5, 6; he is, since his ¹ kind yield warm milk, as it were an incorporation of that sacrifice. And the second ¹ Ś half-verse is then a promise to whoever shall abstain from using the ox as food. Ppp.

reads gga instead of jâtas in a, and saṅgâânas at end of b. In c, 4 the comm. reads

sar for san, ud âre as two words, and zo '(niyâr, and of course makes very bad work et of its explanation, finding metempsychosis in sam . . sarsat (na saṅ:sarati punal ¹ saṅsaradhar man na prâpnoti). Gharma he takes first as "blazing sun," and then, cl alternatively, in its true sense. There is no other occurrence of an s-aorist from s7; 4 and it is altogether against rule and usage to employ a subjunctive and an optative Ch (agniyar) in two cobrdinate clauses this seems to me to be a slip —see Skz. Gram. a Ś575 b; and the clauses are hardly coârdinate J; so that the reading is very suspicious. dp ur A few of our mss. (P.M. W.E.) read a4 after ndâre. Ludwig conjectures suprayâs gc for 7s. ¹ 4. The draft-ox yields milk (274) in the world of the well-done; the purifying one fills him up from in front; Parjanya [is] his streams, the ¹ Maruts his udder, the sacrifice his milk, the sacrificial gift the milking es fl of him. ¹ ¹ Ppp. appears to have read in b gyâyer, which would rectify the meter; in c it com- . bines maruto "âdko. Pâvamaâna in b might signify the wind (then purâstâr ' from the ¹ east '?) or soma; the comm. takes it as the latter (pavitrena codhkyamaârno "my tamayat lt somak) ; and ⁴ the sacrifice" in d as “ the sawa sacrifice now performed." The verse Ś gr is rhythmically a trigfubk with redundant syllables (rr +13: 124 11=47). On dakŚina, ¹il see Bloomfield, AJP. xvii. 408 f.

5. Of whom the lord of the sacrifice is not master (7), nor the sacrifice; not the giver is master of him, nor the acceptor; who is all-conquering, all-bearing, all-working — tell ye us the hot-drink which [is]

four-footed.

Which " in d is yatamâ, lit. ' which among the many.' The intended answer, of ¹ course, is that this wondrous sacrificial drink is the ox. Ppp. begins e with yo vâvadyg ¹ vigvakrd v-. The comm. declares the first half-verse to convey the universal masterg hood and not-to-be-mastered-hood of the ox; in d gharma is, according to him, " the ¹ ⁴ ² Ś blazing sun, which the four-footed one tells us" (4r7ra is read, but declared equivalent to braze).

6. By whom the gods ascended to heaven (suâr), quitting the body, to the navel of the immortal, by him may we go to the world of the well-done, desiring glory, by the vow (vraṅâ) of the hot-drink, by penance.

Ppp. appears to have read in a suvâ ruhanta; in b it has dhâma instead of nâbhin, and it ends 4 with yacasa tapasayâ. The comm. has jesma (= jayema) in c instead of gesma (Skt. Gram. § 894 c) I; gharma is to him once more ' the blazing sun." [As to the stock-phrase in c, cf. Bloomfield, AJP. xvii. 419.] The verse (ro+ II: 1o0+13=44) is a very poor fri rubh.

7. Indra by form, Agni by carrying (vâka), Prajâpati, Parameshthin, Virâj; in Vigvânara he strode, in Vâigvânara he strode, in the draft-ox he strode ; he made firm, he sustained.

This is the obscurest verse of this obscure hymn, and no attempt will be made to solve its riddles. Ppp. has a quite different text: inâgro balenc 'sya paramesyht oralenai ‘na gus tena vâKvadevak : yo 'sman doesti yar ca wayaṅ dvismas tasya praâpân asavakhes tasya pranan vi varkak. The two concluding clauses of our text most obviously belong with vs. 7 rather than vs. 8, and both editions so class them; but SPP. states that all his authorities reckon them to vs. 8, ending vs. 7 with the third akramata (which some of the mss., including our P.M.W.E.O.Op., mutilate to akramatr). He adds that the Anukr. does the same; but this is evidently an oversight, our mss. of the Anukr. calling vs. 8 a simple anustubh (madkvam ctad anaguha iti paṅca 'nusiubhak) and giving of vs. 7 a lengthy definition (see above), implying the division 9+ 10: 84-848 : 12=55 (restoring both times the elided initial a in f) ; perhaps, then, SPP. is also mistaken in regard to the unanimity of his mss. and Vâidikas "; at any rate, part of our mss. (Bp.I.H.Op.K.) divide with the editions. The comm., however, does not; as, indeed, he is repeatedly at discordance with the Anukr. on such points. He explains vâka in a as the part that carries (vakati) the yoke; the shoulder," and has nothing of any value to say as to the general sense of the verse. The identification of the draft-ox with Agni seems to rest on Agni's chief function of — “ carrying"; cf. RV. x.51. 5 4; 52.1 6, 3 4, 4 a.

8. That is the middle of the draft-ox, where this carrying (vâ)a) is set; so much of him is in front (prâcâna) as he is put all together on the opposite side.

The virtual meaning of the second half-verse appears plainly to ve that the two parts of the ox, before and behind the point where the pull comes (i.e. where the yoke rests) are equal ; but it is strangely expressed, and the reason why the point is insisted on does not appear. The comm. so understands it: czam prâṅpratyagblâgâar ubhâc i api samânâu,; he renders vaha this time by Śhâra; Ludwig takes it as « the hump." In 74is verse, b can hardly mean where the pull comes," but rather where the burden is put,' i.e. the back; cf. Deussen, lc., p. 231. Nevertheless, see BR. under waa, 2 a and 2 b.

9. Whoso knows the milkings of the draft-ox, seven, unfailing, both progeny and world he obtains : so the seven seers know. â

Ppp. reads anapadasyatas both here (b) and at 12 â; it also combines septars- in 6, ¹ as does the comm., and a couple of SPP's authorities. For consistency, our text ought Ś to combine in a-b Jâkânt s-; SPP. also leaves out here the connecting 7. The comm. ge explains the seven milkings or yields of milk alternatively as the seven cultivated plants, ³ rice etc." or the seven worlds and oceans "—not happening, apparently, to think of any other heptad at the moment. He quotes the names of the seven seers from Agva- Ś layana. ] The number of this vs, is misprinted.

ro. With his feet treading down debility (sed?), with his thighs;

(jâ7ghâ) extracting (ut-khid) refreshing drink — with weariness go the 5 draft-ox and the plowman unto sweet drink (2742).

docs.text:

(28. 5) in a healing rite : Kegava and the comm. agree in saying, for the prevention of flow of ¹ blood caused by a blow from a sword or the like ; boiled JzEsâ-water is to be poured on the wound etc. The schol. to Kâug. 28. 14 also regard the hymn as included among t the lâk5âliṅgas prescribed to be used in that rule.

Translated : Kuhn, KZ. xiii. 58, with Germanic parallels ; Ludwig, p. 508; Grill, 18,

1255 Griffith, i. 146; Bloomfield, rg, 384; Weber, xviii. 46.— Cf. Hillebrandt, Vzâaa ŚŚ ckrestomathie, . 48.

² I. Grower art thou, grower ; grower of severed bone ; make this grow, r ¹ O arundhati. : i ¹ ee Śrundhati, lt. 'non-obstructing,' appears to be the name of a climbing plant having

— : healing properties ; it is mentioned more than once elsewhere, and in v. 5 (vss. 5 and 9)

Hh along with l2k5Z (VS. 7) ⁴lac'; and the comm. to the present hymn repeatedly declares lzksa to be the healing substance referred to in it; probably it is a product of the arundhati. Ppp. has every time rokini instead of rohan, and so the comm. also reads; the manuscripts of Kâug., too, give rok7nr in the pratika, as does the schol. under 28. 14. There is evident punning upon the name and the causative rokaya- 'make grow '; perhaps the true reading of a is râhany asi rohini ' thou art a grower, O red one,' bringing in the color of the lac as part of the word-play ; the comm. assumes rokiṇ, voc., at end of a (ke lohitavarpe lâkse). Ppp. further reads ciruasya instead of ckinnâsya ; and has, in place of our c, rokiuyâm arha ata 'si rohinyâ 'sy osadhe, making the verse an anustubkh. The comm. gives asnas for asthnas in b.

2. What of thee is torn (77), what of thee is inflamed (? âyut), is crushed (? péstra) in thyself —may Dhâtar excellently put that together again, joint with joint.

Ppp. reads in a cirpar: for rigtam; it reads (7 "tmana} in b; and in c, â it has far sarvan kalpayât san: dadat. The comm. (with one of SPP's mss.) reads presthan (= priyaramam) for the obscure pestram in b (found elsewhere only in vi. 37. 3 below, where the comm. has pestam) ; the conjecture "bone" of the Pet. Lex. seems altogether unsatisfactory; it is rendered above as if from pâ. The comm. paraphrases dyuttâm by dyotitam, vedanaya prajvalitam iva, which seems acceptable.

3. Let thy marrow come together with marrow, and thy joint together with joint ; together let what of thy flesh has fallen apart, together let thy bone grow over.

Ppp. rectifies the meter of a by omitting re, and has for d |? b? szrṅstrâvam asx parva re. A few of the mss. (including our H.O. Op.) give vârastanz in c. The comm. — reads cam instead of sam in every pada. A couple of SPP's mss., by a substitution found also elsewhere [see ii. r2. 7, note J, have manyâ for majjṅâ in a. The Anukr. ignores the redundant syllable in the first pada.

4. Let marrow be put together with marrow ; let skin (cârman) grow (24) with skin; let thy blood, bone grow; let flesh grow with flesh.

The third pada is translated as it stands cf. vs. 5 c, but we can hardly avoid emending âszk to asthnâ, or else âszṅi to asnâ, to agree with the others ; the comm. las an alternative J fills it out to two parallel expressions, for both blood and bone. Ppp. has, for bd: astknâa 'sthi vi rokatu snâva te sam dadkmas suâvnâ carmaṇa carma rokatu..

5. Fit thou together hair with hair ; fit together skin (fvâc) with skin; let thy blood, bone grow; put together what is severed, O herb.

The prolongation of the final vowel of a pâda is so anomalous that we can hardly help regarding Zalpayâ in a as wrong, perhaps imitated from b; Ppp. avoids the diff- ¹ culty by reading in a san: dkiyatâm. For c, compare vs. 4.] Ppp. also has for â i our 4 d.

6. Do thou here stand up, go forth, run forth, a chariot well-wheeled,. well-tired, well-naved ; stand firm upright.

Ppp. is very different : ut tistha pre "hi samudhâ ki te par uj: sari te dkârṅ dadharr Ś tan no virisiaṅ rathasya cakra Śy upavaryathâir yathâi ti sukkasya nabhis prati Ś Yistha evarz. The Anukr. scans the Verse as 9+ I 1 ¹5=25 syllables. ft 7. If, falling into a pit, he hath been crushed (saṅ-r), or if a stone hurled (pra-kr) hath smitten [him] —as a Rbhu the parts of a chariot, ele may it put together joint with joint.

Ś A number of the mss. (including our P.M.O0.0p.) read kârtum for kartâm in a; ¹ the comm. explains kartam as meaning kartakan: chedakam âyudharm, and makes it subject of sargagre = samhinasti; he takes rbkus as one of the three Rbhus (quoting - CH RV. i. 11I. I), NOt giving the word any general sense. Ppp. again has an independent eo text: yadi vajro visysta sthâraku jâru patitrâ yadi va ca ristam : vykâad vâ yadi vâ g wibhyasi cirsa rbhâr iti sa evar saṅ dhâmi te paruj. docs.text:
Ś 5 [Cartâti.— cândramasam uta vâigvadevam. ânugtubham.] Śât Found in Pâipp. v. (in the verse-order 1, 5, 2-4, 6, 7). Vss. 1-5, 7 are in RV. x. 137, g GH and vs. 6 occurs elsewhere in RV.x. Only vss. 1-3 have representatives in Yajur- ( ee Veda texts. The hymn is called a7 tâtiya in Kâug. It is . used (58. 3, II) in the ceremonies for long life that follow the initiation of a Vedic oh i student. In Vait. (38. r) it appears, with ii. 33 and iii. ir etc., in a healing ceremony ¹ ¹ for a sacrificer see comm. ] who falls ill. i : Translated : by the RV. translators ; and Aufrecht, ZDMG. xxiv. 203 ; Griffith, v.

I. Both, O ye gods, him that is put down, O ye gods, ye lead up y again, and him that hath done evil (gas), O ye gods, O ye gods, ye make to live again.

2. These two winds blow from the river as far as the distance; let the one blow hither dexterity for thee; let the other blow away what complaint (âpas) [thou hast]. g . Besides RV. (vs. 2), TB. (ii. 4.17) and TA. (iv. 42. I, vs. 6) have this verse. Both ¹ accent in c zvârṇ, as does SPP's text, and as ours ought to do, since all the mss. so 4

Ś read, and the accent is fully justified as an antithetical one ; our text was altered to agree with the 4 vatu of RV., which is less observant of the antithetical accent than AV., as both alike are far less observant of it than the Brahmaṇas. All the three other texts have pâra for uf at beginning of 4; and TB. TA. give me instead of ze in c. The second pada is translated in attempted adaptation to the third and fourth ; of course, the two ablatives with a might properly be rendered cobrdinately, and either hither from ' or ‘hence as far as'; the comm. takes both in the latter sense.

3. Hither, O wind, blow healing ; away, O wind, blow what complaint [there is]; for thou, all-healing one, goest [as] messenger of the gods.

TB. TA. (as above) put this verse before the one that precedes it here and in RV. All the three read in c vk uâbhesajas, and Ppp. intends to agree with them (-Ś4¢jajo ae). The comm. offers an alternative explanation of âevâaârm in which it is understood as = indriyanâm ' the senses' Von Schroeder gives a, b, Tâbinger Katka-kss., p. 115.

4. Let the gods rescue this man, let the troops of Maruts rescue, let all beings rescue, that this man may be free from complaints.

In RV., this verse and the following one change places. In a, RV. reads 7kâ for imâm, and in b the sing. 7r&yatâm . . gapâk. Ppp. ends b with maruto ganâiṅ, and ] with agado 'sati. The first pâda is defective unless we make a harsh resolution of a long 2. We had d above as i. 22. 2.

5. I have come unto thee with wealfulnesses, likewise with uninjurednesses; I have brought for thee formidable dexterity ; I drive (sz) away for thee the yâkgma.

The RV. text has in c re bhadrâm & 'Śhargam; both editions give the false form â ¹bhârisam, because this time all the mss. (except our E.p.m.) chance to read it; in such cases they are usually divided between the two forms, and we need not have scrupled to emend here; the comm. has rsa. Ppp. reads in c te bhadram risa, and, for 4, parâ suvâmy ânuyat.

6. This is my fortunate hand, this my more fortunate one, this my all-healing one; this is of propitious touch.

This is, without variant, RV. x. 6o. 12 ; it takes in our hymn the place of RV. x. 13.7.6.

7. With (two) ten-branched hands — the tongue [is] forerunner of voice — with (two) disease-removing hands : with them do we touch thee.

RV. (vs. 7) has for c, d anâmayitn tb byâm: toa tâbhyan tos pa spr(âmasi. The Anukr. takes no notice of the redundancy in our c.

docs.text:

Verses 1-6 are found also in Pâipp. iii. (in the verse-order 1, 2, 5, 4, 6, 3), and in various Yajur-Veda texts (vss. r and 6 not in company with the rest); vss. 7-9, in Pâipp. xvi. The hymn is used in Kâug. (64. 23 ff.) in the sava sacrifices, with goat or goatrice-mess (ajândana) as sava: vss. 2-4, at 68. 24—7 (and also, the comm. says, in recitation in all szva sacrifices) ; vs. 5, at 63. 9 (the comm. says, with oblation ¹ in all); vs. 6, at 64.17; vs. 7 (vss. 7 and 8, according to the comm.), at 64. 18—0. (with setting up the goat); vs. 9, at 64. 22 (with offering the skin having head and feet left attached to it). In Vâit, vs. I is used (29. 3) in the agnicayana, with building in a goat's head ; vss. 2-5 (29. 17), in the same ceremony as the priests mount the altar; e ¹ vs. 5 (8.17), in the parvarn sacrifices, with transfer of the fires, and again, in the q : agnistoma (15. 9), when the fire is brought to the uṅtaravedi; and the comm. regards vs. 3 as quoted at 27. 6, in the vâjapeya rite. ¹ Translated : Griffith, i. 149; Weber, xviii. 51 (elaborate comment). er I. 3. From the back of earth I have ascended to the atmosphere ; from a the atmosphere I have ascended to the sky; from the back of the sky, ¹01 of the firmament (nâka), I have gone to heaven (svâ7), to light.

The other three texts (VS. xvii.67; TS. and MS. as above) agree in omitting

5. O Agni, go forth first of the divinities, eye of gods and of human beings (mânusa)— pressing on (? iyaksa-) in unison with the Bhrgus, let the sacrificers go to heaven (swâr), to well-being.

The other texts (VS. xvii. 69 ; TS. and MS. as above) all read mârtyânârm at end of b; and for devâtanâm in a VS. I. Let the directions, full of mist (nâbhasvant), fly up together; i ² let clouds, wind-hurried, come together ; let the lowing [cows] of the ¹ Ś resounding misty great bull, the waters, gratify the earth. 6 Ppp. combines in 4 vârâ "pak ; the comm., in c, makars- as the meter requires I;

2. Let the mighty ((avisâ), liberal (sudânu) ones cause to behold together; let the juices (râsa) of the waters attach themselves (sac) to the herbs; let gushes (sârga) of rain gladden (makay-) the earth; let i herbs of all forms be born here and there (p7hak). ge ¹ The mighty ones" in a are doubtless the Maruts ; 75ay- is perhaps an error which

Ppp. has for a samâksad vicvag vâto napansy ; at end of b, patantu for vijantam in d, osadkayas (as in 2 â ] of the editions ]).
