4. Let the troops of Maruts sing unto thee, O Parjanya, noisy here and there ; let gushes of raining rain rain along the earth.

Ptthak, lit. ' severally, separately, is used in these verses rather in the sense of all about, everywhere." Ppp. has in d s7jantu for varsantu. The Anukr. makes the pâda-division after mârutâs, and the pada-mss. mark it accordingly, thus leaving parjanya without excuse for its accentlessness ; but all the mss. read so, and both editions follow them. Doubtless either mârutâs or parjanya is an intrusion ; so the meter indicates. The comm. gives in c varṣantas.

5. Send up, O Maruts, from the ocean ; brilliant [is] the song; ye make the mist fly up; let the lowing [cows] of the resounding misty great bull, the waters, gratify the earth.

We had the second half-verse as r c, 4; but Ppp. gives an original half-verse instead pra varsayanti tamisa sudanavo "pan rasir osadhr sacantân. The first half is translated literally as it stands; but it is pretty certainly corrupt. Ppp. reads 7ayanta, tees ¹rkâ, parayantn² ; and the true reading is perhaps toesâ arkâ nâbha ir pâtayartu let our brilliant songs make ' etc. The comm. finds no difficulty, since his ideas of grammar allow him to make roesâs and arkâs qualify nâbkas (rveso âtptimad arke 'reanasâdhanam udakaṅ taâyuktar: nabhak). TS. (in ii. 4. 82) and MS. (in ii.4. 7) have a first pâda nearly agreeing with our a (TS. zayathâ, MS. yatâ), the rest of the verse being wholly different. A couple of our mss. (0.0p.), with two or three of SPP's, read samudrajâs at end of a. ]Roth, in his collation, gives pârayanta; in his notes, -u. J

6. Roar on, thunder, excite (ard) the water-holder ; anoint the earth, O Parjanya, with milk ; by thee poured out, let abundant rain come; let him of lean kine, seeking refuge, go home.

That is, let the herdsman whose animals have been thinned by the drought, now be even driven to shelter by the abundance of rain. Ppp. makes sz stars and warsant change places, and is defaced at the end. The first three words are those of RV. v.83.7. ( The comm. (with two or three of SPP's mss. that follow him) reads in d ZsârâZâ, and renders it «seeking concursence of streams "; our 0.0p. have -7ââf. The comm.. makes Śr¢agus signify « the sun, with his rays made slender"! and, of course, he is to set" (astam 7), or be made invisible by the clouds. The Anukr. makes no account of the fact that a is jagari. For &âra, see Lanman, Trans. American Philological Association, xv. (1884), p. vil. J ²

7. Let the liberal ones favor (sam-au) you, also the fountains, great serpents (azjagarâ); let the clouds, started forward by the Maruts, rain along the earth.

Ppp. omits vas in a, and combines sudâanavo 'tsâ "jagarâ; and its second half-verse d is vârâ vargasya varsatus gravakantn py thivim anu. The comm. renders avantu by

¹ tarpayantn ; ajagarâs here by ajagaratmanâ vitarkyamanâk, and under vs. 9 by : ajagarasamânâkarap : i.e. that look like great serpents as they wind sinuously ed along" ; he takes sudânavas in a alternatively as vocative, notwithstanding its accent.

8. Let it lighten to every region (47) ; let the winds blow to (from?) g every quarter; let the clouds, started forward by the Maruts, come ge together along the earth. Gy Ppp. has in d varsantu, as our text in the preceding verse. The comm. also points g:. out the possibility of taking â7âs as either accus. pl. or abl. sing. The Anukr. someg64 how omits to define the metrical character of this verse and of vs. 14. a 9. Waters, lightning, cloud, rain—let the liberal ones favor you, also

the fountains, great serpents; let the clouds, started forward by the

Maruts, show favor (pra-av) along the earth. Ś Ppp. begins with vâzas instead of âpas, and omits (as in 7 a) vas in b; and, for the 7 last two pâdas, it reads 27â pyâyasva pra pity sva saṅ: bhumin payasâ srja. The Ee comm. again takes suâânavas as vocative, and makes the elements mentioned in a eo subjects of sam avantn; in â he reads plâvantn but regards it as for prâ 'vantu St I parallel with palâyate etc. (W's Gram. § 1087 c), for which he cites Pâṇini viii. 2. rg J. a 10. Agni, who, in unison with the waters' selves (zanṅ), hath become Ś overlord of the herbs —let him, Jâtavedas, win (van) for us rain, breath for [our] progeny, am7ta out of the sky. i ¹ The comm. paraphrases anytan with amy tatvaprâpakam. The Anukr. duly notes the redundant syllable in d. I 11. May Prajâpati from the sea, the ocean, sending waters, excite the go water-holder ; let the seed of the stallion (vâ5an âua) be filled up ; come ¹ hitherward with that thunder, — a To this verse really belongs the first pada of our vs. 12, as the sense plainly shows, ll as well as its association in RV. (v.83. 6 b, c, d) with the two closing padas here. CŚ. ¹ Lanman, Reader, p. 370 ; misdivision as between hymns. ] But the mss., the Anukr., ¹ the comm., and both editions, end vs. rr with 6 "44. RV. reads in our c ginvata for ntl . : ³ :.

2yâyatâm, and dhârâs for râtas. Ppp. combines in b 32' z7ayann, and begins c with of p73 py-. The comm. gives wiguos instead of v7sṇas in c, and explains both it and

{ salad in a by gyâpanagtla, which is one of his standing glosses for obscure words;

A arâayari he paraphrases with racmibhir âdanena pṅâayarn, and udaâhim simply by

jaladhinm. This verse is as much bkâurâj as vs. ro, unless we combine &pe "râyan in b. For -aṅnâhi, see Prât. iii. 38, note.

  1. Pouring down waters, our Asura father.

a Let the gurgles of the waters puff, O Varuṇa ; let down the descending waters; let the speckled-armed frogs croak (vad) along the water-courses

68 What is left of the verse after transferring its first 4457ubh pâda to vs. 11, where it belongs, is (but for the intruded word war uṇa, which is wanting in Ppp.) a regular g

Ś44 : anustubh, having its avasâna division after szja ; and this is the division actually made in all the mss., and in SPP's text. Ppp. combines gazgarâ pam. The comm. declares gargara an imitative word (777 gâhvaniyuktah pravâkâr), and the translation so renders it; as second pâda of the anustubh he reads avanicir (avanim aṅcanti, i.e. bhṅrrin gacchantil) apa syja ; his first account of asura is as from as throw' (eghânân ksepra). Discussed and translated, apropos of âiṇa, by Pischel, Led. Stud. ii. 223.

13. Having lain for a year, [like] Brahmans performing a vow, the frogs have spoken forth a voice quickened by Parjanya.

The mss. (except one of SPP's, which follows the comm.) absurdly read vâtan at beginning of c; both editions emend to wâcam, which the comm. gives, and which is also read in the corresponding RV. verse, vii. 103. I. Ppp. has sâṇâṅkâ in 4. In our edition, correct two printer's errors, reading saṅvatsarâṇ: and br hmanâ. l Bloomfield discusses this vs. and the following, JAOS. xvii. 174, 179.

I4. Speak forth unto [it], O she-frog; speak to the rain, O zâ7uri; swim in the midst of the pool, spreading thy four feet.

Many of our mss. (P.M.E.I.H.K.) accent pa cf. Prat. iv. 3 ] at the beginning. Ppp. reads manânkâ in a, and (â#dkurâ in b. The comm. defines (7dur as she-offspring of the fadura," but gives no explanation of taâura. The verse is also found in a Śkila to RV. vii. 103, reading in a upaplâvada, and in c playâsva. I For 14, 15, see Weber, Berliner S)., 1896, p. 257. As to metrical definition of 14, see vs. 8 n.

15. O Fhapvakhâ! O khkâimakhâar in the middle, O ladurz! win ye rain, O Fathers; seek the favor (mânas) of the Maruts.

The verse (as already noted) is unfortunately wanting in Ppp. The first pada is misprinted as regards accentuation in our edition, being marked as if the final syllables were kampa, instead of mere protractions. That is, the horizontal under the first syllable k4a- should be deleted ; and the signs above and below the two 3's should also be deleted. They are printed aright, khâuvakâṣi khatmakhâ3i, in nâgari, by Whitney, Prât. p. 392, footnote, and on p. 400, and by SPP.] Prât. i. ro5 quotes the words (with the two that follow) in its list of words showing protraction; and i.96 points out that the final 7 in each is grave. The comm. says that the three vocatives (he quotes the stems as kkanvakhâ sâimakhâa tadurr) are special names for kinds of she-frogswhich seems likely enough ; the two former appear to involve imitations of croaking (but in LCS. iv. 3.18 the householder's female slaves are to call out kâimaṅâg, as they circumambulate the maârjâliya, filling new water-holders). SPP. (p. 598, note) asks why, if the words are vocatives, they are not accented simply Śhânvakkâ3t Ehât makkâ3i—being apparently ignorant of the fact that a protracted final syllable is regu- Ś larly and usually accented, without regard to any other accent the word may have (see Whitney, Sṅz. Gr. § 78 a). Several of our mss. (E.I.H.O.Op.), and a couple of SPP's, leave the first syllable of each word unaccented. It would much help both meter and sense to supply kradâsya (or else plavasva) after mâdkye in b; the comm. either supplies Zradasya or reads it in his text. All our mss., and our printed text, have at the end ickatak ; SPP. follows the comm. and about a third of his manuscript authorities in reading ickata, which is doubtless the true text, and implied as such in the translation above. The comm. explains piraras as pâlayitâro mapâgâkak ! SPP. regards him as ¹ reading mârutam in â, but this appears doubtful. The Anukr. scans +5: 8-8. ] ¹

16. The great vessel (6a) do thou draw up (ud-ac); pour on; let there be lightnings; let the wind blow ; let them extend the sacrifice, : ( being manifoldly let loose; let the herbs become full of delight.

eâ : Ppp. reads mahantan at beginning of a, and wisyytam at end of c. The first pada

; is nearly RV. v.83. 8 a, which, however, reads 7d acâ nt Śifca. Our P.M.W. read fanvântam in c. The comm., doubtless correctly, understands the waters as the

³ them " of c; #d aca he explains as samuârad udakapârpam uddṅara ; he supplies

SF antariksain to savidyutam ; the expression is better understood as an impersonal one.

With b, d, cf. RV. v.83. 4 a, b..

46.66: Here ends the third anuvâka, having 5 hymns and 51 verses ; the quoted Anukr. Hl says ekavingaliṇ.

docs.title: 16. The power of the gods
docs.text:
1 [Brakman. — navarcam. satyânytânvikganasiktam. vârupam. trâigubham : I. anugubh;

1 5. bhurij ; 7. jagati ; 8. 3.p. makâbyhatr ; 9. virâunâmatripâdgâyatri.]

Five verses of this hymn (in the verse-order 3, 2, 5, 8, 7) are found together in

Pâipp. v., and parts of vss. 4 and 6 elsewhere in the same book. It is used by

Kâug. (48.7) in a rite of sorcery against an enemy who comes cursing"; and vs. 3 eT also in the portent-ceremony of the seven seers (127. 3), with praise to Varuṇa. Ś ; By reason of the exceptional character of this hymn as expression of the unrestricted ³ d ; presence and influence of superhuman powers, it has been a favorite subject of trans- I i ; lation and discussion. Translated: Roth, Ueber den AV., p. 29; Max Miiller, Chips ¹ From a German Workshop, i. 41 (1867) ; Muir, OST. v. 63 ; Ludwig, p. 388 ; Muir, Ś 4 ¹ Metrical Translations, p. 163 ; Kaegi, Der Rigveda, p 89 f. (or p. 65 f. of R. Arrowfr smith's translation of Kaegi), with abundant parallels from the Old Testament; — Grill, 32, 126; Griffith, i. 153; Bloomfield, 88, 389 ; Weber, xviii. 66. Some of the above do not cover the entire hymn. — See also Hillebrandt, Veda-chrestomathie, â i p- 38 5 Bergaigne-Henry, Manuel, p. 146; further, Grohmann, Jad. Stud. ix. 406; ¹ed Hermann Brunnhofer, ran und Turan (1889), p. 188-196 ; Weber, Berliner Sb., 1894, uy p. 782 f. ¹ I Weber entitles the hymn Ś Betheuerung der Unschuld, Eidesleistung"; see his

¹ instructive note, Jud. Stud. xviii. 66, note =. Comes cursing" hardly takes account g of the voice of cagyamânam as used by Kâug. 48. 7. ]

I. The great superintendent of them sees, as it were, from close by;

whoever thinks to be going on in secret, all this the gods know.

¹: The verse is altogether wanting in Ppp. All the mss. read in ab 24 ant- (p. 44:

i ant), with irregular absence of combination across the cesura ; the case might be one

¹ of those contemplated by Prat. iii. 34, although not quoted in the comment on that rule;

g SPP, reads with the mss., and our edition might perhaps better have done the same

(it is emended to 74 'nt-). But SPP. also reads in c yâs ¹3yâr, instead of yâ (i.e. yâṅ) ¹ stâyârŚ, while nearly all his pada-mss. (with all of ours) require the latter ; his wholly

insufficient reason seems to be that the comm. adopts zâyat; the comm. also has, as part of the same version, carat, and views the two words as contrasted, stable . ou (sani fatyena vartamânan: sthiravastu) and Ś transient" (caranagilar: nagvaran ca I ee ¹. vastu), which is absurd : he is great, because he knows (manyare=jâanâati?) all varieties of being The comm. understands g;âm as meaning "of our evil-minded enemies,"

Br ft tt and keeps up the implication throughout, showing no manner of comprehension of the ² ee meaning of the hymn. ] See Prât. Hl. 40, note, p. 426 near end. ]

2. Whoso stands, goes about, and whoso goes crookedly (vaṅc), whoso goes about hiddenly, who defiantly (?pratânkam)— what two, sitting down together, talk, king Varuṇa, as third, knows that.

Ppp. reads in a manasa instead of carati, and in b pralâyam instead of grataṅkanm, and for c it has dvâan yad avadatas sannisadya. The pada-mss. give in b nolâyan, as if the assimilated final nasal before c were 7 instead of 7 ; and SPP. unvwisely leaves this uncorrected in his pada-text, although the comm. correctly understands yam. The comm. regards a and b as specifying the «enemies " of vs. 1 a; vaṅcati ' he paraphrases by kâutilyena pratarayati, and prataṅkan by prakarsena krecârajrvanam prâṅyas; nileyam he derives either from nisi or from ni+ i. The true sense of prataṅkarm is very obscure ; the translation seeks in it a contrast to nilâyam,; the translators mostly prefer a parallel «gliding, creeping," or the like. The Anukr. apparently balances the redundant a with the deficient c. Note that W's version connects it with nâ-lna of vs. 3; cf. Gram. § 995 a, and my Reader, p. 394.

3. Both this earth is king Varuṇa's, and yonder great sky with distant margins (-ânta); also the two oceans are Varuṇa's paunches ; also in this petty water is he hidden.

Ppp. has, for a, b, ute (yam asya prthivr samict dyṅur Śrhatir antarikṣar:; and, at end of d, udakena maktâk. The comm. declares that the epithets in b beléng to «earth " as well as to sky"; kuksr he paraphrases by daksipottaraparcvabhedena ¹vasthite dve udare.

4. Also whoso should creep far off beyond the sky, he should not be released from king Varuṇa ; from the sky his spies go forth hither; thousand-eyed, they look over the earth.

Only the second and third pâdas are found in Ppp. (and, as noted above, not in company with the main part of the hymn), which gives 74a for divas and ime "sya for idam asya (both in ). The saṅzkitâ-mss., as usual, vary between gid] and dud before sp-. The comm. has purastâr in a.

5. All this king Varuṇa beholds (vi-cak5) — what is between the two firmaments (râdasr), what beyond; numbered of him are the winkings of people ; as a gambler the dice, [so] does he fix (?ṅ7-m i) these things.

Ppp. reads for d aksân na cvaghnt bhuvanâ mamite, which gives a rather more manageable sense ; our text is probably corrupt (of cinori ?) ; the comm, explains uz minoti by ni ksipati; and to the obscure (77 (not relating to anything specified in the verse) he supplies pâginâan: ciksâkarmaṇi. He has again (as in 4 a) purastâtin bs and in c he understands sa7&â=yâtâ (not -137), as enumerator," and nimisas as gen.. with asya. He also reads in d svaghnt, and quotes and expands Yâska's derivation of the word from soa + han. The verse is bhurij if we insist on reading vz instead of ¹va in d. Read 'va, or aksân goaghntva, or with Ppp. ?

6. What fetters (pâa) of thine, O Varuṇa, seven by seven, stand ¹ triply relaxed (vi-sâ), shining— let them all bind him that speaks Ś â untruth ; whoso is truth-speaking, let them let him go. : our sinântu, at beginning of c, is our emendation, obviously necessary; a few mss. (including our Bp.E.H.) have inântu, and the rest chin (our P,M, âhin-, doubtless â ; meant for ckin-), which SPP. accordingly retains; the comm. has ck7nartu, explaining; Ś5 it as for chindantu. Ppp's version of the verse is found with that of the half of vs. 4; it eu reads chinadya ; it also has saptasaptatis in a, and rusarâ rusantal at end of b; and

Ś its d is yas sabhyavâg ati tam syjami. The comm. also reads in b rugantas, which is, f

Ś as at iii. 28. I, an acceptable substitute for the inept rzg-; in b he apparently has visas, and takes it as fatra tatra badd=âs, while the true sense obviously is “laid open ready for

Sot use "; the = triply " he regards as alluding to the three kinds of fetter specified in vii. 83.

h 3 a, b. x 7. With a hundred fetters, O Varuṇa, do thou bridle (abk4i-dkâ) him;

let not the speaker of untruth escape thee, O men-watcher; let the 24 villain sit letting his belly fall [apart], like a hoopless vessel, being cut

¹4 round about. ³ 6 The two editions read in c graṅgayizvâ, with the majority of the mss. ; but nearly half ea (including our P.M. W.H.Op.) have (raṅsay-, and two of ours (K.Kp.) sra7gay-—all â tf of them misreadings for sraṅsay-, which the comm. gives (= jalodararogena srastan: (ch krtvâ). The disease called water-belly," to which c and d refer, is dropsy, Varuṇa's - g ¹ g punishment for sin. ] In â, SPP. reads abandâhâs with the comm., but against all his mss. and the majority of ours (P.p.m.M.W.0.Op. have -â%as), which have -âkrâs; as bandhra (i.e. banddhra, from bandh + tra) is so regular a formation that we have no (ed : right to reject it, even if it does not occur elsewhere. Ppp. puts varuna in a before gt : abki, omitting exam, thus rectifying the meter (which might also be done by omitting i the superfluous varupa) ; and it omits the 7 of -vâ7 in b. There is not a jagatr pada in the verse, and d becomes regularly z7isfubk by combining kâce 'va-. ( ¹ 8. The Varuṇa that is lengthwise (samâmyâ), that is crosswise (7- âmyâ); the Varuṇa that is of the same region (saṅzdegyâ), that is of a different region (videgyâ); the Varuṇa that is of the gods, and that is of men— ¹ . If the word vârupas, thrice repeated, were left out, there would remain a regular . Ś g gâyatrr; and the meaning would be greatly improved also; if we retain it, we must ( i either emend to varupa, vocative, or to wârunds 'of Vâruṇa,' i.e. this fetter,' or else we ¹ i must understand oâr unas as here strangely used in the sense of vârunâs : the comm.

( makes no difficulty of doing the last. Ppp. reads in a, yas samânyo ; in b, yag cyar-

¹ degyo (or cyari-) ; in 6, yo dâivyo varugo yas ca manusassa; and adds fvâṅs tv etâni 4 er prati muṅcâmy atra. ] For the first two epithets compare xviii. 4. 70; the next two are li variously understood by the translators ; they are rendered here in accordance with the comm. Though so differently defined by the Anukr. ef. ii. 3.6 n. J, the verse as it ¹ i stands is the same with vs. 9, namely 11 X3=33 syllables.

gs 9- With all those fetters I fasten (abi-sâ) thee, O so-and-so, of such- ¹ gx and-such a family, son of such-and-such a mother; and all of them I successively appoint for thee.

He [If the verse is regarded as metrical, with three padas (and it scans very fairly as a such), we ought to accent âsâz voc. of asââ ] at beginning of b. The comm. perhaps derstand gnu in c as independent, 474 (SPP. so holds). The last two verses are, as g I were, the practical application of vss. 6 and 7, and probably added later. ] As to the i ¹e vaming of the names, see Weber's note, p. 75-1 ;

docs.title: 17. Against various evils : with a plant
docs.text:
(Cukra.— caturviṅgarcar: trayari sâktinâm. apâmârgavanaspatidevatyam. ânugubham.]

Verses 1—6 are found as a hymn in Pâipp. v., and hymns 18 and rg follow it there, with some mixture of the verses. Vs. 8 is found separately in ii. Hymns 17-19 are called by the comm. Zvapantya ' of strewing.' They are used together by Kâug. (39.7), with fi. rr and iv. 40 and others, in the preparation of consecrated water to counteract hostile sorcery; and vs. ry. 5 is reckoned by the schol. (46.9, note) to the dukswapnanâgana gana.

Translated : Zimmer, p. 66; Grill, 37, 130; Griffith, i. r55 ; Bloomfeld, 69, 393; Weber, xviii. 73.

I. Thee, the mistress of remedies, O conquering one ()esâ), we take hold of ; I have made thee a thing of thousand-fold energy (-oiryâ) for every one, O herb.

Ppp. reads for b nâjesa "grntmake. We should expect in ec -v7ryâsz, and three of SPP's mss. (none of ours) so read ; but he has not ventured to admit it into his text; the comm. gives (yam, but explains as if yam (aparimitasamarthyayuktâm). The comm. regards the plant saṅadeor (name of various plants, including Sida cordifolia and rkombifolia, OB.) as addressed. He takes ujjese in b as dative, = jjetum.

2. The truly-conquering, the curse-repelling, the overcoming, the reverted one (punaṅsarâ)—all the herbs have I called together, saying may they (?) save us from this." = The last pâda is translated in accordance with the better reading of Ppp.: ato na paârayan iti. In b, Ppp. gives punaccarâa ; SPP. presents punajs-, in closer accord- : ance with the mss. than our puzass-. The comm. does not recognize the meaning (reverted ' (i.e. ' having reverted leaves or fruit ') as belonging to punahsarâ, but renders it as ⁴ repeatedly applied " (26k Tks pyena bakhutaravyâdhinivr ftaye saruti). He readsin a capathayopantm, and in c abhi (for akwi): and one or two of SPP's mss. support him each time ; our O.O0p. give addki, by a recent copyist's blunder ; the comm. supplies gacchanti for his sam-abkâ to belong to. The Anukr. takes no notice of the excess of two syllables in a.

3. She that hath cursed with cursing, that hath taken malignity as her root, that hath seized on [our] young to take [its] sap — let her eat [her own] off spring.

The verse is a repetition of i. 28. 3, and the comm. again, as there, reads 7âude at end of b. He notes that a full explanation has been already given, but yet allows himself to repeat it in brief ; this time he gives only mârchâpradam as the sense of mira. Ppp. (which has no version of i. 28) gives here, for c, 4, yâ vâ rathasya prâsare by ato chant u roasak. As i. 28. 3, the verse was properly called virârparhyâbrkatr. Correct the verse-number from 6 to 3 in the edition.

4. What [witchcraft] they have made for thee in the raw vessel (pârra), what they have made in the blue-red one, in raw flesh what witchcraft they have made —with that do thou smite the witcheraftmakers. ‘ The verse is nearly accordant with v.31. I below. Ppp. reads in b ya sâtre nir.

A raw vessel is one of unburnt clay (agakve mrtpâtre, comm.). The comm. defines : the blue-red one " as fire, blue with smoke, red with flame; and the “raw flesh " as tk that of a cock or other animal used for the purposes of the charm. The Z77yâ appears to be a concrete object into which an evil influence is conveyed by sorcery, and which 5 then, by depositing or burying, becomes a source of harm to those against whom the pc sorcery is directed (mantrâusadhââibhih atrok ptâakarin, comm. to iv. 18. 2). The comm. reads zvayâ in dâ, and first pronounces it used by substitution for twas, then fe retains it in its proper sense and makes jaki mean hanta"yâs: both are examples of fl his ordinary grammatical principles. The Anukr. ignores the metrical irregularity of — c reject yâr 2. ² Bloomfield, on the basis of Kâug., interprets it as a thread of blue

¹ and red; and this is confirmed by the Ppp. s7rre. J Ś 5. Evil-dreaming, evil-living, demon, monster (a5kvâ), hags, all the ill-named (f.), ill.-voiced— them we make disappear from us. ete Ppp. has in a dussvapnan: durjrvatar, and, for , 4, durvâcas sarvaṅ: durbhâtar: ⁴ : tam ito nâ-. A couple of our mss. (I.H.p.in.) read aṅk4ṅm in b. The comm. gives

Jtvatyam in a (with two of SPP's mss.), and (with our P.M.W.E.) asmin instead of

asmân in d. He first defines a5hvam simply as great," and then as a special kind ¹ of demon or demoniac (quoting RV. i. 185. 2) ; and the durpamnts as pâaâcts having various bad appellations, such as chedika and bkedika. The verse is repeated as

6. Death by hunger, death by thirst, kinelessness, childlessnessthrough thee, O off-wiper (zpâmaârgâ), we wipe off all that.

The translation implies the obvious emendation of znapadyâtân (p. anapaeâyâtarr)

in b to -2pazyâ-, which is read by the comm. and by three of SPP's mss. which follow I : him; SPP. very properly admits -gpatyâ- into his text (but forgets to emend his gaâatext thoroughly, and leaves in it the absurd division anapactyâtâm.) Weber, however, f discussing avaâya, Berliner S)., 1896, p. 272, defends the reading apadya-.] The comm. says nothing of the sudden change here from sakadevr to apamarga, which ( ought to be another plant (Achyranthes aspera: a weed found all over India, having ¹ el very long spikes of retrofiected flowers), but may possibly be used here as a synonym or appellation of the other. In his introduction, he speaks of âzrâha, apâmaârga, and sakadev as infused in the consecrated water.

7. Death by thirst, death by hunger, likewise defeat at dice— through thee, O off-wiper, we wipe off all that.

Ppp. omits this variation on vs. 6.

8. The off-wiper is indeed of all herbs the sole controller (vagir); i with it we wipe [off] what has befallen (âsṅiâta) thee ; then do thou go about free from disease. . ¹ Ppp. (in book ii.) has for b vâvâsâm eka it pati, combines in c my ima "sthitam, and reads at the end carah. Asthitam (also vi. 14. I and VS. vi. 15) has perhaps a : : more special sense than we are able to assign to it; the comm. paraphrases by kr tyadr- = : : bhir Bpatitan rogadâikan.

docs.title: 18. Against witchcraft : with a plant
docs.text:
[Cukra.— (etc. : see under hymn r7). 6. lrkatigarbṅâ.]

Found in Pâipp. v. (vs. 6 before 5). Used by Kâug. only in company with h. r7, as there explained.

Translated : Grill, 25, r31; Griffith, i. 156 ; Bloomfield, 7o, 396; Weber, xviii. 77.

I. The same light with the sun — night possesses the same with the day ; I make what is effective (sazyâ) for aid ; sapless be the makers (f.) [of witchcraft].

KFtvarts at the end borrows a special sense from its relationship with Ś72yâ a case of «reflected meaning "— see note to iii. r1. 8 . The construction in the first half-verse (if here rightly understood) is peculiarly intricate : samâm jyâtis is, as it were, cotrdinate with the samâ of samâvatt, as if it were samajyotismatt: i.e. “night has its light as good as the sun's or the day's." Or else jyâris (R.) is to be taken outright as “moonlight " (= later jyorsnâ). Ppp. begins with samâ bhâmis sṅ-, and has in c sabkya for satyam. One of our pada-mss. (Op.), like one of SPP's, divides in b sameâvalr,; the Ś comm. defines the word by of equal length " (samânâyâmâz) ; and Ertvaris by kar tana- (ras (taking it from 77 ' cut). In our text, the -sign has dropped out from under the &-sign in this word.

2. Whoso, O gods, having made witchcraft, shall take it to the house of one unknowing — let it, like a sucking (ââârṅ) calf to its mother, go back unto him.

The comm., with one or two of SPP's mss., reads ârâr instead of âârât in b ; dkârâs he defines by stznapânar: kxrvan. There is a redundant syllable in c unless we abbreviate iva to 'va.

3. Whoso, having made evil at home, desires to slay another with itnumerous stones make a loud crash when it (f.) is burned -

Ppp. is partly defaced in this verse ; and it gives us no aid in solving the difficulties of the second half. The discordance between the masculines yâs and pâpmânam in g a, b and the feminine 245yâm is perhaps best removed by supposing k74â to have i been mentally substituted for gâgman (the comm. supplies kr tyâyârm to tasyânz); Grill violently emends a7 in a to Zmâyam (sc. patryâm ¥), and thinks that this raw vessel. bursts noisily in pieces when burnt; R. conjectures that thick stones crack when the krtya is burnt, perhaps so as to wake the intended victim. The comm. paraphrases i ama by anukṅla (va sakha sthitak, i.e. an assistant or confederate, and reads in c. ângâhâayan drained " or made ineffective; the stones are produced by the countermagic, and are called on to do (%arikrati = punak-punaṅ knrvantr: a convenient i substitution of the imperative I) damage (pkaf=hkiṅsanam) to the kr fyâ-krt. The translation given above implies a threat of the destruction of the ky by burning and by ¹ stones tumbling crash (p4af for phas?) upon it. The harsh resolution k7t-4 makes i the verse a full anustubk. Bp. also has dugâhâyam. ] ²] Oxytone, not perispome. J ²

4. O thou of a thousand abodes (?-âkâman), do thou make them lie (?) crestless, neckless ; take back the witchcraft to him that made it, like a sweet-heart (277yâ) to a lover (priyâvant). Śâ

For vkikkan in a, Ppp. reads visâkhâr (our P.M.W.E. have uâṅsân, our Bp.LH. ' v4â5ân). In b, SPP. reports all his authorities as reading ¢âyayâ (p. wa); no such 4 form. has been noted among our mss. but Ppp. has câyâ iva; Benares ms. R., ckz-

¹ yayâ,; and T., ckayayâ ; in most mss. y and 2 are but imperfectly distinguished, and, : as some of SPP's authorities are oral, he is to be presumed right; and the translation implies ¢âyaya for the sa7dht, Prât. i. 17]. The comm. reads instead Ś5âyaya, from ¹d ksi (= ksayam prâpaya). He rehearses the series of diverse senses given by Yâska to ¹e âdhâman, and declares them all intended by the word in a. The verse he regards as : ¹ addressed to the sakadev. ( 5. I, with this herb, have spoiled all witchcrafts— what one they have : made in the field, what in the kine, or what in thy men (pârusṣa). 447 Ppp. reads in c and d the datives gobhyas and purusebhyas; the comm. explains tt purusesu as “in a place frequented by them " ; for vz re he reads ware 'in the wind.

A few of our mss. (P.M.W.) have adâdusan in b. The Anukr. takes no notice of er the deficiency of a syllable in d.

6. He who hath made hath not been able to make; he hath crushed a (cr) a foot, a finger ; he hath made what is excellent for us, but for him- Ś self a burning (âpana). ¹ ¹Ś The verse is repeated below as v. 31.11, but with a different last pada, which reads abkagâ bhâgavadbhyak. Ppp's version of a-b is yâ7#: cakâra na ga;âkha gagire ¹ pâdam aṅgulim (omitting kartum) , yam sc. krtyâm ? ] is a preferable reading. The ¹ comm. also has aṅgulim; our -rim is authenticated by the comment to Prât. i. 66. ⁴ Ppp's d reads as does our v. 31. 1 I â, but with ab4agâ for -gâ. The verse is metrically defined in the same way as here atv. 31. IT the Anukr. seems to scan it as 349: 8+8

(cf., for example, iii. 8. 4) ]; but 247 2urm is evidently as the accent of gag shows to be =

¹ reckoned to a, and the paâda-mss. so divide. |The suspicion is natural that a sâ has been lost between a4 and ¢agâka. So ca has been lost at iv. 5. 5 a (cf. RV. vil. 55. 6 a). . If we are right in restoring sâ, and if we pronounce cag7-¢ (as the Ppp. reading suggests), Ś i we should then scan rr+48: 848.—The accent of caâka can hardly be more than a blunder.— The comment to this verse seems to have failed of thorough revision at

W's hands.

7. Let the off-wiper wipe off the kṣerriyâ and whatever curse [there is] ; [wipe] off, forsooth, the sorceresses, off all the hags. r Ppp. reads in c -dkânyas, rectifying the meter. The comm. here defines kṣerriya as hereditary disease (Śserrari mâtâpitycar razz tarsaṅâ;âr).

8. Having wiped off the sorcerers, off all the hags, O off-wiper, with ¹ thee do we wipe off all that.

Ppp. is defaced in this verse. The comm. first explains againâyjya in a into an 1 imperative, apamyââki; but then, as an alternative, he allows it its own proper sense.

docs.title: 19. Against enemies: with a plant
docs.text:
[Cukra.— (etc. : see hymn 17). a. pathyâpaṅâti.]

; Found also, in connection with the two next preceding hymns, in Pâipp. v. Used by ¹ ¹ Kau: only in company with hymns 17 and 18, as described under h. 17. But vs, 2 is ¹ reckoned to the aṅkaya gaya, employed as battle-charms ; see Kang. 16. 8, note. Se ¹ Translated: Grill, 34, 132; Griffith, i. 157; Bloomfield, 71, 3973 Weber, xviii. 81.

1. Both art thou not relative-making, and now art thou kin-making; also do thou cut off (? â-c4id) the progeny of the witchcraft-maker, like a reed of the rainy season (vârsika).

Or, perhaps, ' a last year's reed ' (but comm., varsâsu bhavam). The first halfverse is very obscure, and the translation follows the text as closely as possible (Ppp. ; differs only by beginning nize 'vâ 'sy), understanding a-banâkukrt, and not abandhukr (which would be accented on -%77) ; possibly the sense is thou makest common cause with some and not with others.” The comm. takes -477 both times from 7 (cut' (which is not impossible) := kartaka or chedaka ; and he cites RV. iv. 4.5 ; « slaughter thou our foes, the related and the unrelated. Nagâm he explains as etatsarzjṅar succhedar truavigesam. The Anukr. seems to sanction abbreviation to 'va in d.

2. Thou art bespoken (?) by a Brahman, by Kaṇva son of Nyshad; thou goest like a brilliant army (?); there is no fear (Ś4ayâ) there where thou arrivest (gra-âp), O herb.

Ppp. has in a garâyukto "si, and this is very probably the true form of the word here used; the difficulty is that neither yuj nor vac is anywhere else found used with ¹ pari; prayukṅa employed ' ] is what we should expect. We have ⁴Kayva's plant" mentioned at vi. 52. 3. The imperfect meter of b (which the Anukr. fails to notice, as it does also the like deficiency in d) gives a degree of plausibility to Grill's suggestion that the pâda is intruded on an original anustubh. The pada-mss. waver between nârsadâna and nars- (our Bp. emends s to s; Op. is altered obscurely; D.K. haves), but s is certainly the true reading, as required by Prât. iv.83 ; SPP. has wrongly chosen y for his pada-text. The comm., with a couple of SPP's authorities that - follow him, reads reâs7mate in c (our P.M. W.E. have fvâim arr.) The mss., without any statable reason, accent âszi in d, and our edition follows them; SPP. strangely g gives &sti in saṅhkitâ-, but asti in pada-text. [Are not p2âryuktâ and par yuki ¹ alike awkward phonetic renderings of prâ-yuktâ ? Ct. Ppp. cacire (=gagr-â), iv. 18. 6; = and daâhire (= dadṅre, Roth, ZDMG. xlviii. 116). ] i

3. Thou goest to the head (âg7a) of the herbs, causing to shine (27) g upon [us] as it were with light ; also rescuer art thou of the simple ¹ (pâka), likewise slayer art thou of the demoniac. : Ppp. puts pâkasya before 7777 in c; the comm. paraphrases it with gakta"yaprajṅasya one whose wisdom ( Ś7a7ṅz) is yet to be matured '] durâalasya. Ś

4. When yonder, in the beginning, the gods by thee removed (nâs-k7). the Asuras, from thence, O herb, wast thou born, an off-wiper.

Ppp. has in b the older form akrnvata, and for c reads tasmad dhi tvam osaâhe agp-. The comm. takes adi in c as meaning upari vartamanak or gresthak san.

5. Splitting apart (v7-54âd), hundred-branched — «splitting apart" by name is thy father; in return (pratyâk), do thou split apart him who assails us.

Ppp. has sundry corruptions : vivindatr in a, vibinda in b, Zaṅz tvâ at end of t. The comm. omits v7 in c. Pâda c needs some such emendation as to 747: tu-ânm. â

6. The non-existent came into being (sam-bk7) from the earth; that goes to the sky, the great expanse (wâcas); let that, verily, fuming os abroad, come back thence on the maker. ² The translation implies the obvious emendation, made in our text, of 74d âyâm for el tâd yâm, which is read by all the mss. and by the comm., and retained in SPP's text, ee though in a note he approves our alteration ; it is only another example of mistaking an i ' abbreviated for a full reading (ây for its grammatical equivalent 42y : compare Li. 22. 1, Ś and Roth, ZDMG. xlviii. 104 ]). Ppp. reads in b brkat vacas; and it has for c ad it Ge waco vyadhṅmayat. The comm. gives bhâmyanm for yas in a, and vat for tat at begin- â Ś% ning of b. He renders asar by asatkalpan: krtyârâpan, or, alternatively, by acobha- ⁴ nar: krtyârṅpam. The accent -kâpâyat is contrary to all rule, and doubtless false; i MS. (i. 10. 20; p. I60. I) has âyât, which is correct. The general sense of the verse Śe is obscure ; but it appears to parallel the return of the charm upon its producer with the

action of water in exhaling from the earth and coming back as rain. â 7. Since thou hast come into being reverted (pratyâṅc), having ¹ reverted fruit, do thou repel (yu) from me all curses, [repel] very far Ś the deadly weapon.

; The verse is nearly repeated as vii. 65. 1. Ppp. has for c, d pratṅsky ty amun: kr tya- — krtar: jaki. The comm. reads in b pkala, vocative ; regarding, of course, the apamarga Ś plant as addressed. = 8. Protect me around with a hundred ; defend me with a thousand;

may the forceful (4gṅâ4) Indra, O lord of the plants, assign force (ojmân) 0 unto thee. I i Ppp. has for d bâadyo ¹jmânam i dadkuh. It can hardly be that the writer does v.

not use here ugrâ and ojmân as words felt to be related ; but the comm. gives for the

¹ former his standing and always repeated zâgṅrnabala, and paraphrases the other with gjasvitva.

docs.title: 20. To discover sorcerers : with an herb
docs.text:
¹ [MEY Eman. —navarcam. mâtynâmadâivatam. &nugtubham : I. svarây ; 9. bhuriy.] ¹ ft Found in Paipp. viii. (in the verse-order r—, 7, 6, 8, 9, 5). Reckoned by Kâug.

(8.25) to the câtanâni ; and by the schol. (8. 24, note) added to the sn âty nâmâni : with i good reason, if we may trust the Anukr. (which adds to what is given above : anena

mary nâmân ¹sadhim eva 'stâur ) ; but the comm. says nothing about it. The hymn is i used by itself (28. 7) to accompany the binding on of an amulet of sadampuṣpâ ‘ever

flowering ' (or, as the comm. and schol. say, 77âsandṅyz) in a healing ceremony (the

¹ comm. says, against (zakmagraka and the like).

Translated: Ludwig, p. 525 ; Grill, 2, 133; Griffith, i. 159; Bloomfield, 68, 398; ¹ â Weber, xviii. 84.—See also Hillebrandt, Veâa-chkrestomathie, p. 48.

Ś I. He (?) looks on, he looks toward, he looks away, he looks : the sky, i the atmosphere, then the earth— all that, O divine one (f.), he looks at.

Ppp. has the 2d sing. pagyasi all the five times, and it is an easier reading (adopted he by Grill in his translation), especially in d, unless we may emend âevi to dev; accord-

6 ing to the comm., the subject throughout is the wearer of the amulet, and the divine one, as is also indicated by Kâug,, is the sadampusga plant, a plant evidently having somere thing about it that resembles or suggests eyes. Ppp. reads z for r in c. [Read p74 for prâti in a? Pronounce dvântar- inc.

2. Three skies, three earths, and these six directions severally —by thee let me see all beings, O divine herb.

Ppp. has makt (for -7ṅ) instead of p7¢kak in b, and in the second half-verse, Zaza ¹har: sarvâ yaryna pagyâmi. Some of our mss. (P.M.) give pâsyâni in 4. Pâda a is redundant by a syllable, unless we pronounce g7hv?s. [For the triplicity, comm. cites RV. ii. 27.8 and AB. ii. r7 end. J

3. Of that heavenly eagle art thou the eye-pupil; thou here hast ascended the earth as a wearied bride (vadṅ?) a litter.

Ppp. puts digyasya after suparpasya. The ground of the comparisons made in the verse is altogether obscure, and the comm. casts no light upon them. Bloomfield discusses this vs., AJP. xvii. 402.

4. May the thousand-eyed god set it in my right hand ; with it do I see every one, both who is Ctdra and [who] Aryan.

Ppp. has kast' âdadar at end of b, and; for second half-verse, fato "kaṅ: sar var: pagyami adbhutan (sic) yac ca bhavyam. Pagyâni would be an acceptable emendation in c. The comm. (with one of SPP's mss.) reads tvayâ in c; he regards the ⁴god " in a as Indra..

5. Make manifest [thy] forms ; do not hide thyself away; then mayest thou, O thousand-eyed one, look upon the kimidâns.

Literally (in d) ‘meet with thy look." Ppp. begins c with evâ instead of azko, and ends d with pagyâmy âyata. The abbreviation in c of the stem -caksus to -caksu is one of those noted in the Prât. rules ii. 59 and iv. roo. d

6. Show me the sorcerers ; show the sorceresses ; show all the pââcâs: with this intent I take hold of (â-725k) thee, O herb.

For second half-verse, Ppp. has âpasprg eva tisthantam dargaya maâṅ: kimtâinant.

7. The eye of Kagyapa art thou, and of the four-eyed bitch; conceal thou not the pââcâ, like the sun gliding (sz2) in the clear sky (o7âkrâ).

That is, allow him to be no more concealed than the sun etc. Both editions read -akṣyâs at end of b, but it is against the authority of the mss., all of which (save two ¹ of SPP's which follow the comm. in giving the true reading) omit, as in numerous other cases, the y after the sibilant. The comm. regards Saramâ as referred to; and, in futile attempt at explaining her possession of four eyes, says etena pradhysyarvan: wktam. Cf. Weber, Berl. S3., 1895, p. 849, n. 3.) He explains the reference to eyes by the resemblance of the flowers of the plant in question; but this looks rather like a plausible guess than like a statement on any authority. Ppp. has for first half-verse kacyapasya caturaksas syaṅtyâg caturaksâ. The comm. derives okra from vi-idk, ¹ and glosses it with antariksa. The Anukr. appears to approve the abbreviation to 4 s«ryam 'va in c. Bloomfield thinks that kagyaṅa punningly suggests pacyaka seer,' and cites TA. i.8. 8, kagyapaṅ pagyako Śhavati yat sarovan paripagcyati.

8. L have seized (uâ-grabk) out of his shelter (paripâṇa) the sorcerer, the kimidtn; with it do I see every one, both Ctudra and Aryan.

Ppp. has in a, b2âṇaṅ: yarudhanat kimidinaṅ. The comm. makes tena refer here to yaruâkânam, and supplies graham to sarvam—evidently without reason. 1

9. Whichever flies through the atmosphere, and whichever creeps across the sky; whichever thinks the earth a refuge (nârkâ) — that pigâcâ do thou show forth.

Ppp. has for b bhomâ co ¹pasarpati, and in c divam for bhâmim.; and its â is tvaṅ picâcark dye kuru. The comm. (with a couple of SPP's mss.) has aâki- instead of az in b; he glosses nâtham with soaminam. The verse is not bhurij if we combine 3 ‘ntâr- in a. Correct the misprinted verse-number.

Here, at the end of the fourth ann vâka, with 5 hymns and 42 verses, the old Anukr. says arha kuryad dvadaga.

Here ends also the seventh grapâthaka.

docs.title: 21. Praise of the kine
docs.text:
[Brakman. —gavyam. trâigtubham. 2-4. jagati.]

This hymn is not found in Paipp., but it occurs in the Rig-Veda (vi. 28. I-75 vs. 8, in a different meter, is perhaps a later addition), and also in TB. (ii. 8. 811-12). Itis used by Kâug. (19. I), with i. 4-6 and others in a rite for ailing kine, and also (a1. 8 ff.) in one for the prosperity of kine, vs. 7 being specifically mentioned as repeated when they go forth to pasture ; vs. 7 appears further to be quoted at rg. 14, in a rite for the cow-stall; but the comm. declares two verses to be intended, and, if so, they must be vii. 75. I, 2, since there is here no following verse. In Vâit. (21. 24), in the agnistoma, the cows intended as sacrificial gifts are greeted with this hymn. The schol. (Kâug. 16. 8) reckons vs. 4 to the abkaya gapa. The comm. and Kegava's scholion to Kâug. 27.34 declare hymns 21-30 to be m7gâra-hymns (Kâug. 27.34; 9. I), but the name would seem properly to belong only to hymns 23-29, which form a related group, and are by the Anukr. ascribed to Mrgâra as author. 5

Translated : by RV. translators ; and Griffith, i. IGr ; Weber, xviii. 87.

I. The kine have come, and have done what is excellent; let them stay (sad) in the stall (gos7ṅâ) ; let them take pleasure with us ; may they be rich in progeny here, many-formed, milking for Indra many dawns. The other texts have no variants for this verse. The comm., after his wont, turns the two aorists in a into imperatives ; he renders ranayantn alternatively by ramayantu and ramantâm ; and he takes "dawns" as equivalent to " days " (âvasân). |Full many a morning yielding milk for Indra.' ]

2. To the sacrificer and singer, to the helpful one (?), Indra verily gives further, steals not what is his; increasing more and more the wealth of him, he sets the godly man (devayṅ) in an undivided domain Ckhilyâ)..

The other texts have in a the decidedly better reading g7 nate ca ciksari of which ours is simply a corruption ; the comm., heedless of the accent, takes our (7gate as a verb (=g7k prayacckati). In â they have the better accent âŚhinne and TB. reads EâI most of our mss. could be better understood as #4725 than as Eṅilyé; the comm. defines Śhila as apr akatar: sthanam, and khilya as tatrabkava; R. conjectures « stonewall" for 2kilya. All our mss., and part of SPP's, read mukkâyati in b. 23, They shall not be lost; no thief shall harm [them]; no hostile [person] shall dare attack their track (?); with whom he both sacrifices to the gods and gives, long verily with them does the kine-lord go in company.

Both the other texts* accent Śyârkis in b, as does one of our mss. (O.), and one of SPP's. Before this word TB. has 737 'nâ amitr6. The comm. explains gyazhis as : vyathâjanakam âyudham. The pada is very obscure as it stands. [An earlier draft of the translator's ms. reads: " Naganti, by its association, and its difference from nagyanti, must be meant as subjunctive (aor.), notwithstanding its ending." I am tempted to suggest nd (4 nagan; tâ (acc. pl. fem.) nâ dabhati râskaras.—BR., vi. 1438, take gyâthis as 'unbemerkt von,' with genitive, Zsa. But see Geldner's discussion of the combinations of gyâthis with â-dkrs, Ved. Stud. ii. 29.— Note that TV's âmâ rr (both ed's read so in the text and both have â- in the comm.) is neither am7zro nor amitrâ. ] In TB., the pratikas of vss. 3 and 4 stand in RV. order at ii. 8.8xr; but the vss. are given in full at ii. 4. 69.

4. No dust-raising horseman (?ârvan) reaches them; not unto the Ś slaughter-house (?) do they go; those kine of that sacrificing mortal roam over wide-going fearlessness.

RV. differs only by retaining the a of agnute in a, as do one or two of our mss. (O.K.) and half of SPP's; and its pada-text divides sari skrtactra in b, while the AV. pada-mss. (except our Op.) leave the word undivided (by an oversight, the AV. Index Verborum gives the RV. form). The comm. explains arvâ by kiṅsake uyâghradik, and -kakâra by udbhedaka ; also sar:skrtatra by mâṅsapâcaka (because viasitan ¹râyare pâlayari), quoting from an unknown source the line saṅskrtak syad vigasitak sam sky tatrag ca pâcakak. The comment to Prât. liv. 58 makes the word come from Ś the root 27. TB. ] also retains the a of acnute and it] has in 4d mâriyasya. In our printed text, the upper accent-mark in renâkakâto is over the wrong k. ¹

5. The kine [are] Bhaga ; Indra has seemed to me the kine; the kine; [are] the draught of first soma ; these kine— that, O people, [is] Indra; Ś with whatever heart [and] mind I seek Indra.

The translation implies in a the RV. reading ackân, of which our â4âf seems merely an unintelligent and unintelligible cortuption; TB. has instead acckâ¥, and our i O.K. give the same. Both the other texts add 47 after iṅâmi in d. The comm. translates in a “may Indra desire that there be kine for me." ] The latter part of c is i of course the well-known refrain of RV. ii. r2. J ¹

6. Ye, O kine, fatten whoever is lean; the unlovely (acrzrâ) one ye Ś make of good aspect ; ye make the house excellent, O ye of excellent i voice ; great is your vigor (vâyas) called in the assemblies (saâ4â). (

The RV. version agrees at all points with ours ; TB. accents Z) cam in a and has. i â re aclrlâm in b (its krpurhar is a misprint, as its commentary shows). The comm. reads ³ kr puta in c; sabhâsu in 4 he paraphrases with janasamuhesu.

7. Rich in progeny, shining in good pasture, drinking clear waters at a good watering-place—let not the thief master you, nor the evil-plotter ; let Rudra's weapon avoid you.

The translation of a follows our text, though the false accent rugântis (TB. has the same reading) shows that the word is only a corruption of the RV. reading râgântis 8 ⁴ cropping, grazing.' The comm., though reading rugantrs, renders it â pam bhaksa- : yantis. [The TB. comm. in both ed's reads râantis. ] Both the other texts have in a sâyâvasam, and at the end het? rudrâsya vrjyâR (TB. v7 Rjyar). With our c, d com- (rt pare also TS. i. I. I (differing only in the order of words in â ruârâsya kettk pâri s 6 vo vypaktu, which is metrically much better than our AV. order, albeit the RV. order is as good as that of TS. if we pronounce ruây-âsya J). The comm. supplies to agṅacaṅsas in c vyâghradir dustamygak. For kata, see Skt. Gram. Ś 615. ]

docs.title: 22. For the success and prosperity of a king
docs.text:
4 ⁴ [Pasistha (? Atharvan ? y.—âindram. tr âigtubham.] of Found in Pâipp. iii. (with vs. 3 before vs. 2), and most of it also in TB. (ii. 4. 77-9). : Used by Kâug. (14.24) in a rite for victory in battle (the editor of Kâug. regards the i next hymn also as included, but evidently by an error), and also in the ceremony of 4 consecration of a king (17.28) Weber, Râjasâya, p. 142 ]; and the comm. mistakenly Ś regards it as quoted at 72. 7, giving the pratika as nam indra, instead of imam Gr indram, as Kâug. really reads (xii. 2.47, evidently the verse intended). The Anukr.

spreads itself at very unusual length over the character of the hymn: imam indra ³4 vardhaye "li vasistha âinâran trâistubhar so 'tharoâ ksatriyâya râjṅe candramase prarhamabhik paṅcabhir niramitrikaranamukhyene 'nâram aprârthayad grâma- ¹ ga vâcvadi sarvaṅ: râjyopakaranar: ca tatak parâbhyâm antyâbhyâm indrarâpena ; svayam eva ksatriyar râjanaṅ: candramasam &isâa prapudad iti. Probably Vasistha ¹ 4 is the intended ysâ-name, and so 'tharwâ (one ms. szutk-) a misreading for something else. Śe Translated : Ludwig, p. 457; Zimmer, 165 ; Grill, 67, 135; Griffith, i. 162 ; Bloomi. field, 115, 404 ; Weber, xviii. o1.—CfŚ. Hillebrandt, Veda-ckxestomathie, p. 43.

I. Increase, O Indra, this Kshatriya for me ; make thou this man sole chief of the clans (v7) ; unman (nis-aks) all his enemies ; make them subject to him in the contests for preeminence.

The comm. (with one of SPP's mss.) has in b the strange reading wr sâm for vigâm.,; ¹. and it treats akan and uttaresu in d as two separate words. He takes a&spuṅi as from aks ‘attain ' (ak57 vyâp1ax), and so explains it (nirgatavyâptikân kur). lSee

Delbrtick's discussion, Gurupṅjâkâumudi, p. 48-9.) TB. combines a of this verse

(reading ksarrâyâuâin for am me) with b, c, 4 of our vs. 3. In our edition, an anusvâra is substituted for an accentmark over the syllable -zra- in d.

2. Portion thou this man in village, in horses, in kine ; unportion that pe man who is his enemy; let this king be the summit of authorities (ksarrâ);

O Indra, make every foe subject to him.

Ppp. elides the a of amitras in b, and in c has the better reading varsman at the

Ś summit,' which is also offered by the comm., and by three of SPP's mss. TB. has vârsmaṇ, but as first word of a very different half-verse, our iii. 4. 2 c, 4, which it adds bh to our first half-verse here to make a complete verse ; in a it has inâm & instead of

4 Ś nâm, and in b afr amâm instead of ni râm, thus rectifying the meter (the Anukr.

Ś takes no notice of the metrical irregularity of our b) ; and it leaves asya without accent : ⁴ at the end. Nearly half the mss. (including our P.M.W.I.K.) have in â (41777, and & : the comm. seems to understand cazrân, TB. combines yb 'mâtro, against the meter.

3. Let this man be riches-lord of riches; let this king be people-lord of people; in him, O Indra, put great splendors; destitute of splendor make thou his foe.

As noted above, TB. combines the last three pâdas of this verse with our 1 a; it reads asmat instead of asmitn at beginning of c. The comm. foolishly gives himself much vain trouble to prove that the epithets in a and b are not repetitious.

4. For him, O heaven-and-earth, milk ye much that is pleasant (vânâ), like two milch kine that yield the hot-draught (gkarmâ-) ; may this king be dear to Indra, dear to kine, herbs, cattle.

Ppp. combines Jughe "va in b, and has 547yas in c; and at the end it agrees with TB. in reading uzâ 'pâm for pacunâm. TB. further has asmâ in a, and -7âghe 'va dhenuk in b but see Prat. i. 82 n. ]; and it prefixes sâm to dukâthân. Probably it is the loss of that prefix or of some other that causes dukâarṅâm to stand in all the mss. without accent at the beginning of the pâda : an inadmissible anomaly, though read in both texts; we ought to have emended to Juhâzhâm. The comm. explains that gharma- in b signifies the pravargya. The meter requires the prefix.

5. I join to thee Indra who gives superiority (?uzzarâvanty, by whom men conquer, are not conquered ; who shall make thee sole chief of people (jâna), also uppermost of kings descended from Manu.

Ppp. reads in a fam uttarâvantam indra. TB. has in b jâyâsi and parâjâyâsat, and in the second half-verse sâ tvâ 'kar ekavrsabhâr svânâam âthe râjann utt-. The comm. explains uttarâvantam by aticayitotkarsavantar.

6. Superior [art] thou, inferior thy rivals, whosoever, O king, are thine opposing foes; sole chief, having Indra as companion, having conquered, bring thou in the enjoyments (b44jana) of them that play the foe. i

Ppp. has in a aâkare santv anye. TB. puts together a and c as first half of a verse to the other half of which our text has nothing corresponding ; and it reads (avysa for, ekavysâs. The comm. takes prati and gatravas in b as two independent words ; he paraphrases b4âjanâni by bhogasadhanani dkanâni.

7. Of lion-aspect, do thou devour (ad) all the clans (v7) ; of tigeraspect, do thou beat down the foes; sole chief, having Indra as com- â panion, having conquered, seize thou on (â-k4id) the enjoyments of. them that play the foe.

Ppp. has only the second half-verse, and reads for d cazrâyaram abki tiszhâ maṅân st Ś (our vii. 73. ro etc. : see under that verse). The whole verse is wanting in TB. The Ś comm., with one of SPP's mss., reads âpa for 4va in b. He paraphrases aââk7 (which a is a frequent expression for the action of a ruler upon his subjects) very properly by bhunksva ; and i khida, less acceptably, by âcckindhi.

docs.title: 23. Praise and prayer to Agni
docs.text:
Ś [My gâra.— sapta mygârasanyṅakânt suktâni nânâdevatyâni. rrâîggubhâni: gant 3. purastâjyotiymati ; 4. anugtubk ; 6. prastârapaṅnâti.]

Found," with the six hymns that follow, all together (but in the order 23, 25, 27, 26,

28, 29, 24), in Pâipp. iv. The seven are known by Kâug. (9. r) as the 77gâra hymns hn (also by the schol., as by the Anukr. ; that the comm. to h. ar gives the name to 2130 er was there remarked ; here he speaks of a heptad of hymns " as intended in 9. r); they ts are reckoned (9. r) to the ŚykhackântigaRa, and also (32. 27, note) to the aṅkoliṅga br gana; and they are employed in a healing rite (27.34). In Vait. the hymn accom- Śâ5t panies the kindling of the fire in the parvan sacrifices (2. rr), and vs. 4 is similarly re used (5.15) in the agnyâdheya. It was noted under the preceding hymn that the Se editor of Kâug. mistakenly regards this one as included in Kâug. 14. 24. The first and (e last verses of each ] of the m7 gâra hymns are given also by TS. (iv. 7. 15), MS. Ss (iii. 16. 5), and X. (xxii. 15) ; only the hymn to Bhava and Carva (our 28) is omitted, ¹² and, on the other hand, those texts have similar invocations to the Agvins and to all Ś the gods. And the comm. to our h. 24 quotes also TS. vil. 5. 22, where a mp gâresti . ¹ with ten oblations, to the divinities worshiped with the verses in question, is prescribed. ee 1 See further, as to this litany, Weber's note, p. 95 f.— The m7gâra-verses occur in 5 TS. and MS. at the very end of the kânâas (iv. and iii.) concerned. ] In the verse-

Translated : Griffith, i. 163 ; Weber, xviii. 94.

I. I reverence (man-u) first the forethoughtful (prâceras) Agni, him ¹e g of the five peoples, whom men kindle in many places ; we pray to him who hath entered (pra-vig) into clans after clans (27): let him free us He from distress. I ‘ Ppp. has in b paṅcaj-; the comm., pâṅcqvajṅasya, for which he gives three different interpretations, the last one making yajṅasya equivalent to janasya. Manve he paraphrases by janâmi. In a, MS. has am tânâam for prâcetasas ; for b, TS.MS. give yâm

¹ pâncajanyam bakâvah samindhâte and, for c, vkvasyân vit pravivigivânsan ¹ make. The absence of reduplication " (Sz. Gram. Ś 803 a) is doubtless due to

Ś the oft-repeated syllable 7 or wâ. The pratika is cited, MGS. i. 5.5 —cf. p. 145. I The Anukr., at the end of the descriptions of the seven hymns, says that all the verses ¹ contain —i.e. end with—an anustubh pada. Its definitions of the meters in detail are I too inaccurate to be worthy of attention throughout.
  1. As thou carriest the oblation, O Jâtavedas ; as, foreknowing, thou adaptest the sacrifice— so do thou convey to us favor from the gods:
let him free us from distress.

Ppp. offers no variants in vss. 2-4, but puts 4 next after i. The comm. takes Jeveg bhyas in c first as dative and then as ablative. th ee 3. Put to service at every course ( yâman), best carrier, sharer (4bhaga)

at every rite, Agni I praise, demon-slayer, sacrifice-increaser, offered to with ghee : let him free us from distress. 9 : All the mss. (and SPP. with them) make the division of the verse, with obvious ww impropriety, before instead of after agntm ve, being apparently led into the blunder by remembering the two words as beginning the Rig-Veda. The comm. gives the right division, as does also our edition by emendation. Nearly all the mss. (not our I.K.) read bâkigtham at end of a; both editions give wâk-, with the comm. The comm. paraphrases #bâagain by âbhaktayyam âsevyam evarmgunavigstanz. |The vs. scans as II+II : IZ+8=42. Even with the misdivision (11 +7 : 8843), it is no parastajjyotismatt (44)- 4

4. The well-born Jâtavedas, the mighty (vâ5727) Agni belonging to all men (vâigvânarâ), the carrier of oblations, we call on: let him free us from distress.

The verse, as already noticed, comes second in the Ppp. version of the hymn. The comm. explains vibhu as pervading " (uyâpaka).

5. With whom as ally the seers made [their] strength shine out; with whom they repelled the wiles of the Asuras ; with whom, Agni, Indra conquered the Paṇpis—let him free us from distress.

Ppp. makes in a the combination yena rs-, and reads in b iâyotayan; for the latter, the comm. (with two or three of SPP's mss.) gives wddyotayan ; a few of the mss. g (including our Bp.K.) have -fayan.

6. By whom the gods discovered the immortal ; by whom they made the herbs rich in honey; by whom the gods brought the heaven (svâr) — let him free us from distress.

The comm. takes ara in a as meaning the drink of immortality ; more probably it signifies immortality itself.

7. In whose direction [is] whatever shines forth (vi-ruc) here, what is born and to be born, all of it—I praise Agni, [as a] suppliant I call loudly on [him] — let him free us from distress.

TS. and MS. have a quite different first half-verse : yâsye 'dâm prâpân nimisâd yâd ¹ Śjati yâsya jarâm jânamaâanar: ca kâvalam. The comm. renders zârkitas first by; nâthamanaṅ, phalaṅ: kâmayamanaṅ, and then by nâthah svâmr serṅzjâto ';ya. ‘

docs.title: 24. Praise and prayer to Indra
docs.text:
[Mygâra.— (see h. 23). r=. cakvarigarbhâ purakcakvar:.]

Found in Pâipp. iv., with the other 77gâra hymns, and used by Kâug. only as one ¹ of the group (see under h. 23); its first and last verses occur in the same Black Yajur- Veda texts (do.). Translated : Griffith, i. 165 ; Weber, xviii. roo. Ś I. We reverence Indra; constantly do we reverence him; these praise:-hymns (st6ma) of the Vrtra-slayer have come unto me; he who goes to the call of the worshiper (dâcvâṅs), of the well-doer — let him free us from distress.

Ppp. has in a indrasya manve cagvad yasya manvwire, which is better, in both sense and meter. TS. and MS. (agreeing throughout) read fn ârasya manwve prathamâsya Pprâcetasal in a; in b, Zpa mâm upâ 'guk; and, in c, kâvam âpa gânta. The verse f is properly enough purajcakvari, but there is no reason why it should be called in Śer addition ¢akvarigarâha. ² 2. He who, having formidable arms, is repeller (2yayṅ) of the for- : midable ones (f.) ; who battered the strength of the Dânavas ; by whom re are conquered the rivers, by whom the kine— let him free us from distress. Hkh Ppp. has in a yo 'grapâm and omits yayus; and at end of b it reads Zsasâda. The St first pada is full of questionable points, and probably corrupt; the comm. explains ¹ : yuyus (though SPP. says in a note that his text reads yayus), and by yâvayitâa prrhak- 4 kartâ; to ugripâm he supplies carr usenânânt.

3. He who is filler of people (carsaṇt-), bull, heaven-finder (svarvâd);

for whom the pressing-stones proclaim [his] manliness ; whose is the . sacrifice with seven priests, most intoxicating—Ilet him free us from 4 distress. : Ppp. has carsant instead of vysabkas in a, and, for c, yasyâ 'dhvaryus saptakota ¹ mudicynt. The comm. renders carsaṇi- by manugya-.

4. Whose are cows (vagâ), bulls, oxen ; for whom, the heaven-finder, i sacrificial posts (soâru) are set up; for whom the bright (gukrâ) [soma]

purifies itself, adorned with sacred words (Śrâkma-)— let him free us from distress. : Ppp. has in c yasmiṅ cukras pravartate. The comm. explains vaga in a as « barren cow" (vandhyâ gank), and svaru as yṅpavataksanacakala, used for yâpa. I Cf. : RV. vi. 16.47.

5. He whose enjoyment (jâsti) the offerers of soma desire ; whom, possessed of arrows, men call on in the cattle-raid (gâwisti); on : whom depends song (?arkâ), on whom force—let him free us from distress.

Ppp. reads in b isuvantam. Prât. ii. 23 teaches the form of gawâsti. The comm.

explains arkas as arcanasââhanabhâto mantral stutacastrâadilaksanat.

6. He who was born first for the doing of deeds ; of whom first the

Ś heroism was noted ; by whom brandished (zâ-yam) the thunderbolt went at (abki-i) the dragon —let him free us from distress. (ee As in one or two other cases," the mss. have in a yajṅé instead of jajṅâ, but one or guy two of SPP's follow the comm., who reads jg7ṅé, as does also Ppp. ; and both of the ¹â editions give this. In b the comm., with three of SPP's authorities, gives 4nutadâham : in c he derives gyata from root yam, and renders it by akâstt ; we might emend to

¹abkyâyar6 "him and get a form from that root, which would yield a preferable sense.

I For the use of a2ki-² with vajra as subject and with acc., Whitney has noted the excellent parallel, RV. i.80. r2.] [So x. 10.18. I — 7. He who, controlling, leads together hosts (sagrâmâ) for fighting; “ who mingles (sam-sz7j) the possessions (pusyâ) of the two parties—I praise Indra, [as a] suppliant I call loudly on [him] : let him free us from distress.

Ppp. has in b pustyâ nas. TS. and MS. read in a (as does also the comm.) the sing. sa7kgrâmâm, and they put yudhe after vact ; at end of b they give rrayânâ instead of dvayâni. The comm. thinks doayânt to be stripurmsarmakant nâthunâni.

docs.title: 25. Praise and prayer to Vayu and Savitar
docs.text:
[37gâra.— (see h. 23). 3. aticakvarṅgardhâ jagatr; 7. patkyâbrkhati.]

Found in Pâipp. iv. (in the verse-order 1-3, 6, 5, 4, 7, and after our hymn 23). The Black Yajur-Veda texts (see under hymn 23) put their passages corresponding to our hymn 29 (to Mitra and Varuṇa) between these corresponding to our 24 and 25. For the use of the hymn as one of the m7gâra hymns in Kâug., see under hymn 23; the comm. further quotes it as employed by Naks. K. 18, in a cânz7 ceremony named vâya"yâ. The metrical irregularities are not worth the trouble of detailing.

Translated: Griffith, i. 166 ; Weber, xviii. ro.

I. Of Vâyu, of Savitar we reverence the counsels (vidâtka) : ye who enter and who defend what has life (â/manyânr); ye who have become ee encompassers of the all— do ye free us from distress.

TS. and MS. read bibhytâs (for viâthas) and râksatas in b, and TS. (abhṅvârus in c; and both have âgasas in the refrain. MS. further combines 7 tr in b, and has 74 ao r- in the refrain. The comm. is uncertain as to the sense of wâdârha. Geldner ‘ renders, "Wir gedenken des Bundes zwischen V. und S.," ZD MG. lii. 746: cf. Foy, KZ. xxxiv. 226. ] Doubtless it is a metrical consideration that causes the change from 3d to 2d person in the refrain of hymns 25, 26, and 28. [Grammar and meter favor restoration of the older and longer form paribkâva in c—see Lanman, JAOS. x.413.

2. Of whom are numbered the widths of the earth ; by whom the welkin (râjas) is made fast (yup) in the atmosphere ; whose progress no one soever has reached (anu-ag)— do ye free us from distress.

Ppp. has in a varimani parthioâ, which improves the meter ; also guszhitâm for; yupitam in b, and prayâm for grâyan in c. Yupiṅâm (perhaps ' smoothed out, spread i uniformly ' cf. Bloomfield AJP. xii. 418, 419 ]) the comm. explains by mârchita# sad ⁴ âhâryare. The pada-text divides in c pracâyâm, for which SPP., on the authority of only one of his mss., unaccountably substitutes graezyân (a number of our mss. give instead yân) of. BR. v. 1635.

3. In [conformity with] thy course (urazâ) people (jâna) go to rest; ¹ when thou art risen, they go forth, O thou of beauteous luster; ye, O Vâyu and Savitar, defend beings — do ye free us from distress.

Ppp. has yackatas for raksarkhas at end of c; the comm., with a couple of SPP's. mss., reads rakyatas ; and he paraphrases it, without a werd of remark, with pâlayatṅas.

4 Away from here, O Vâyu and Savitar, drive (siâ7) ye what is ill done, away the demons and Cimidâ ; for ye unite (sam-s77) [men] with refreshment (7774), with strength — do ye free us from distress.

Nearly all the mss. read in c szjârka (instead of -Ś4as). The comm., with two J ² or three of SPP's mss., reads samiâam (for ¢imidamr) in his text in b, but explains samidhâm (by sam diptarn krtyân ca); itâs in a he takes from root 7 and paraphrases Śṅ by gamayathas ? Emendation in a to duskftam, ' evil-doer,' would be acceptable ; the 40 Ś comm. takes it as accented (= asmadiyam gâpanm). kt 5. Let Savitar and Vayu engender (â-s7) in my body (tani) wealth, Śu prosperity, very propitious dexterity; do ye put here freedom from et yâṅgma, greatness ; do ye free us from distress. ¹ Tan? in b is translated as a locative because so regarded by the Prât. (under i. 74), ² as it is also by the comm. (= tanvâm, asmadiye carire) ; it might be nom. dual; or, yet ¹ better, it might be emended to fanâdaksâm. Ppp. reads aveyaksmarâr: suhasmasi ¹ 6 âhattam for c. The comm. paraphrases & suvarâm with prerayatâm prayacchatam. ¹ 6. O Savitar, Vayu, [give] forth favor in order to aid; ye cause to (f revel in the intoxicating jovial [soma]; hitherward from the height ( (pravâr) confirm ye of what is pleasant (vâmâ); do ye free us from ²r distress. ⁴ ¹ The strong ellipses in the first half-verse are filled by the comm. in accordance with er the translation. Ppp. reads in b maâdayetânt, and in c pravarâ ni yachatas. The ¹ comm. makes gravâtas (= prakarsavatas) cobrdinate with vâmâsya, qualifying dkanag i sya understood. Pischel, Ved. Stud. ii. 74, takes it as acc. pl. with vâmasya, ' streams Lr â of wâma, and compares râyâ âhârâ, vâsvo arpavâ, etc.— Render the subjunctive in b by ( cause ye ' etc. ?

7. The best blessings (âgâs) have come unto us in the domain (âkâman)

of the two gods; I praise god Savitar and Vâyu: do ye free us from distress. ² et v ² 35 I = = :

Ppp. combines to a7 "â50 in a. MS. reads tras for ââas ; for dhâman in b it . has âhârmas, and TS. dhârme; for c, both give stâṅmi vâyân savitârark nathits johavtmi ; and, as in vs. 1, MS. begins d with 73, and both end it with Śgasas.

The fifth annvâka ends here in the middle of the 77gâra group; it has 5 hymns and 35 verses ; and the old Anukr. says aparâ) paṅca.

docs.title: 26. Praise and prayer to heaven and earth
docs.text:
[Mrgâra.— (see h. 23). I. puro "ir jagati; 7. yâkvaragarbhâtimadkyejyoris.]

Found in Pâipp. iv. (in a somewhat different verse-order ¥), after our hymn 27. The other texts (see under hymn 23) have but one verse that represents the hymn, made up

¹ of parts of our vss. r and 7. As to the use of the mygâra hymns by Kâug., see under h: 23. In Vâit. (15. 13), this hymn (or vs. r) accompanies the offering to the udumbara Ś twig in the agnâsroma. Order, 1, 2, 4, 6, 3, 5, 7.

Translated : Griffith, i. 167; Weber, xviii. 106. a 1. I reverence you, O heaven-and-earth, ye well-nourishing ones (subkâjas), who, like-minded (sâceras) did spread out unmeasured intervals

ŚŚŚŚjana); since ye became foundations (pratisthâ) of good things, do ye

¹ free us from distress. a Ppp. omits the intrusive and meter-disturbing sâcetasâu (which, on account of its accent, is reckoned to b in the translation, as it is also by the pada-text) ; and, against rule, it combines in b ye Ś7ark-. The comm., with one of SPP's mss., reads apr athe- ²7m ; and TS.MS. have the same, followed by âmâtebhir Śjobhir ye pratisthe âbhavatân: : vâsânâm : they have of the verse only these two pâdas, used as part of a closing verse. The first half-verse is found also in the Nâigeya-â77âa of SV. (i. 623 a, b) : this reads mânye for manyéâ, accents subkâjasâu, omits (like Ppp.) sâcetasân, and ends with âmitam abht yâjanam ; its second half-verse is our 2 c, d.

2. Since ye became foundations of good things, ye much increased, divine, fortunate, wide-extended ones, O heaven-and-earth, be pleasant to me : do ye free us from distress.

Ppp. has in a Śabhṅvarkus (for âbhavatant). The comm., with a couple of SPP's mss., reads praviddhe (= sâtravat sarvajagadanupravidâke) in b. Asnoted under vs. I, SV. has (omitting me in c) the second half-verse, here carried on as refrain through vss. 3-6. [In c, scan Ś72kvr . siouE.]

3. I call upon the not-distressing, of excellent penance, wide, profound, a to be reverenced by poets : O heaven- etc. etc.

Possibly an antithesis is intended between the first two (doubtfully translated) epithets, both founded on zzp 'heat.' Ppp. has the better reading vâm for akam at end of a.

4. Ye who bear the immortal (ama), who the oblations ; who bear the streams (srozyâ), who human beings (manugyâ) : O heaven- etc. etc. : Ppp. puts b before a.

5. Ye who bear the ruddy [kine], who the forest-trees; ye within whom [are] all beings : O heaven- etc. etc. ¹ ¹ One or two of our mss. (H.I.), as the majority of SPP's, make at the beginning the s false combination yâ usr-. The comm. declares usriya a gonâman. ¹

6. Ye who gratify with sweet drink (7/4lz), who with ghee; without whom [men] can [do] nothing whatever : O heaven- etc. etc.

All the pada-mss. make in b the absurd division gaknncvântâ, as if the word were a Ś neut. pl. from the stem gaknuvânt. Ppp. has in a k777â2is. The comm. interprets k7lâla simply as anna. 0

7. This that scorches (abkhi-guc) me, or by whomsoever done, from : what is human, not divine— I praise heaven-and-earth, [as] a suppliant I call loudly on [them] : do ye free us from distress. ¹ ¹ The verse looks as if broken off in the middle, to allow addition of the regular close. Ppp. has at end of b the more manageable reading pauruseyan na dârvyam. TS. docs.text:
[Mygâra.— (see h. 23). I. dyyatijâgaragarbkâ bhurij.]

Found in Paipp. iv. (next after our h. 26), but having nothing correspondent to it in the Yajur-Veda texts. Having the same beginning (6âavâgcarvâz) as xi. 2.1, one cannot tell in many cases which of the two hymns is intended by a quotation in Kâug.; but according to the comm. (also to Kegava ; Dârila appears to think otherwise) this one is employed in a healing ceremony at 28. 8; it is also reckoned (26. I, note) to the ¹. ta kmanâṣana gana.

I. O Bhava-and-Carva, I reverence you, know ye that ; ye in whose direction is all that shines out (vâ-ruc) here, who lord it over these bipeds [and] quadrupeds : do ye free us from distress. ¹

Ppp. has, for b, yayor vârn: yad idan vitisthate ; our vâs makes this pada redundant. In c, some of the pada-mss. (including our Bp.) have sya (but asyâ, correctly, ¹ in 6 c). The expression in b corresponds with that in 23. 7 and vii. 25. 2. According it to the comm., the name Bhava signifies bkavaty asmar sarvan: jagad; and Garva,. Cruâari kinasti sarvam antakâle. ¹

2. Ye whose is whatever is on the way and afar ; who are known as best shooters among arrow-bearers ; who lord it etc. etc. ¹

Ppp. has vitarân for viditau (perhaps vigitaut) in b, and its c reads Śhavâgarvâu bhavatam me syonṅnu, which then continues to be (as in 26. 2-6) part of the refrain through vs. 6, taking the place of our c. The comm., with a couple of SPP's mss. has 7 isubhf tzu for 4am in b. He explains abkyadkve by samipaâe;e. Perhaps a means rather 'on whose way [is] even whatever is afar.' )

(including our Op.) corrupt further to stzvât, and the comm. to zem? (manufacturing for it two different, but equally absurd, explanations after his manner ef. Fest ¹ gruss an Rotk, p. 91 ). From whose deadly weapon no one soever escapes (apa-pad), Sl among gods and among men (mânuga) ; who lord it etc. etc. a Ppp. reads in a, b Śâ7 canâ 'ntar devesu uta. / — 6. Whoso is witchcraft-maker, root-cutter (?), sorcerer, down on him

I. I go about with the Rudras, the Vasus, I with the Adityas and the All-gods ; I bear Mitra-and-Varuna both, I Indra-and-Agni, I both s I There is in this verse no variant from the RV. text. docs.title: 33. To Agni: for release from evil
docs.text:
[Brakman. —aglarcam. pâpmanyam ; 3gneyam. gâyatram.]

Found in Pâipp. iv. Is RV. i. 97, without a variant except in the last verse; occurs also in TA. (vi. iI. I). Reckoned by Kâug. (9.2) to the Śykackânti gana, and also (30. 17, note) to the papma gana ; used, under the name of aṅâgṅa, in a ceremony of expiation for seeing ill-omened sights (42. 22), in a women's ceremony for preventing Il undesirable love and the like (36. 22), and in the after funeral ceremonies (82. 4).

Translated : by the RV. translators; and Griffith, i. 175 ; Weber, xviii. 134. — Cf. also Lanman, Skt. Reader, p. 363.

I. Gleaming (guc) away our evil (aghâ), O Agni, gleam thou wealth unto [us] : gleaming away our evil.

This first verse is found a second time in TA. (vi. ro. 1). The refrain is a mechanical repetition of r a, having no connection of meaning with any of the verses. The comm. It explains âpa cocucar by nagyatu, and & cugugdht by samyddhan: kuru. TA. reads cugudhyâ in both places in both editions.

2. With desire of pleasant fields, of welfare, of good things, we sacri- ( fice— gleaming away our evil— i

3. In order that the most excellent of them, and in order that our. patrons (s7rf) — gleaming away our evil—

4. In order that thy patrons, O Agni; in order [namely] that we may be propagated for thee with progeny — gleaming away our evil— i

5. As of the powerful Agni the lusters (bkân²) go forth in every i direction — gleaming away our evil.

These four verses are (rejecting the intrusive refrain) one connected sentence: the Ś ² prâ's in vss. 3 and 4 repeat by anticipation the jâyemahi prâ of vs. 4 b; ⁴we" are, in ⁴ fact, Agni's s7râ's, since we depute him to sacrifice for us, just as our sârz's procure us,. the priests ; and our progeny is to increase and spread like the brighmess of the fire. Gr TA. spoils the connection by putting vs. 5 before vs. 4; and the sense, by reading sârâyas for bhânâwvas in 5 b. Ppp. has jâyemake in 4 b. One of our padâa-mss. (Cp.) ¹ agrees with the RV. pada-text in dividing sugarusyâ in = a (the rest read suogatuyṅ). ¹

6. For, O thou that facest in every direction, thou art [our] encompasser on all sides : gleaming away our evil.

7. Our haters, O thou that facest in every direction, do thou make us pass over as with a boat : gleaming away our evil. i

8. Do thou pass us over unto well-being, as [over] a river with a boat: gleaming away our evil.

Ppp. agrees with RV. [and TA. ] in reading nâuâyâ (which implies stnâhum ¹va) instead of nâvâ at end of a; and our O. has the same.

docs.title: 34. Extolling a certain rice-mess offering
docs.text:
. I [Atharvan.—agtarcam. trakmâsyâudanain. trâigtubham : 4. bkuriy ; 5.3-av. 7p. kti ; 6. 52. atigakoari; 7. bhurikgakvart ; 8. jagati.] Śâ Found in Pâipp. vi. Used in Kâug. (66. 6), in the sava sacrifices, with the braṅma- ; syâudana sava, to accompany the making of pools and channels in the rice-mess, filling RE them with juices (rasa), and setting on the ground, with szrz and water, knob-bearing bo plants as specified in the text. Doubtless it is on account of this treatment that the rice- ¹ mess in question is called vâszârin ' out-strewn, expanded.' ( Translated : Muir, OST. v. 307 (vss. 2-4) ; Ludwig, p. 437; Griffith, i. 176; Weber,

I. The Śrâkman [is] its head, the Ś7ââr its back, the vâmadevyâ the ( belly of the rice-mess ; the meters [are] the (two) sides (wings ?), truth its pe mouth; the vâ57774n [is] a sacrifice born out of fervor (iâpas).

Ppp. reads giras in a, and its d is uâ)â yajṅas tapaso 'âhi jâtak. The comm.

explains brakman as signifying here the rathantara sâman, and also satya in c as Ś¹ «the saman so called; or else the highest brakman "; vistârin he makes to mean Ct vistiryamâṇâvayava. el 2. Boneless, purified, cleansed with the purifier, bright (gâcz), they go to a bright world ; Jâtavedas burns not away their virile member; in the heavenly (svazgâ) world much women-folk is theirs. ¹ Ppp. makes pâtâs and cuddkâs exchange places in a; and there is confusion in its ne text. The comm. explains anasthâas by na vidyate asthyupalaksitar Sâtkâugikaṅ ¹ cariram e3am, and strainam by stripân: samuho bhogartham ; the they" are the per-

formers of the sawa sacrifice. The Anukr. does not notice the redundancy of a ce syllable in c.
