3. Whoso cook the visiârin rice-mess, ruin (â4oarti) fastens not on them at any time; [such a one] stays (as) with Yama, goes to the gods, revels ¹ with the soma-drinking (somyâ) Gandharvas.

Ppp. has kutas for kadâ in b, and szumyâis in d. The pada-text writes 4vartâṅ without division, yet the comment to Prat. iii. 46 quotes the word as exemplifying the

; combination of final a and initial 7; the comm. understands and explains it as a-varzti somya he paraphrases with somârka. The metrical irregularities (11 +12: Io +II=44)

are ignored by the Anukr.

4. Whoso cook the vigtârin rice-mess, them Yama robs not of their seed ; becoming chariot-owner, [such a one] goes about upon a chariotroad ; becoming winged, he goes all across the skies.

6 Ppp. has in c ratkâyân iyare. In the metrical definition, the Anukr. seems confused

¹ here ; but vs. 4 appears to be intended.

¹ Ś 5s This, extended, is of sacrifices the best carrier; having cooked the ye vistârin, one has entered the sky; the bulb-bearing lotus spreads

Ś (sam-tan), the bisa, (âlṅka, (âphaka, mulâli: let all these streams (âṅârâ) g come unto thee, swelling honeyedly in the heavenly (svargâ) world; let complete (sâmanta) lotus-ponds approach thee.

The mss. (with the exception, doubtless accidental, of our PK.) all read Śâ4isthas at end of a, and this SPP. retains, while our text makes the obviously called-for emendation to wâk- ; the comm. has wak-. The things mentioned in c, d appear to be edible parts of water-lilies : the bulbous roots, leaf-stems, and radical fibres, which in some l species, as the Nymphaca esculenta, are savory, and which are eaten somewhat like aspar- ¹ agus. That they should be viewed as special gifts to the pious indicates quite primitive conditions, and suggests a region abounding in standing waters. Either the pools and channels of Kâug. are founded on these specifications, or they are original and intended to be emblematic of such products. The ṅumuda is the N. esculenta (kâirava, comm.); i and the comm. explains bisa (he reads visa) as the root-bulb of the padma (Nehembium speciosum) cf. Lanman, JAOS. xix, 2d half, p. 151 Ś.], ¢âl74a as that of atpala (a Nymphaea), capkaka as a hoof(capha)-shaped water-plant, and mulâlz as = mpatṇ. ¹ Caphaka occurs also at ApCS. ix. 14. 14, where it seems to signify an edible plant or i fruit, perhaps a water-nut. Ppp. differs widely from our text: it begins ga yajṅo vitato bakhistho vigtara pakwo die-; it omits c and d; for e and f it has our 7 a, b with ² variants : see under 7; then follow our e and f (8, upa . . . saman?âṇ, is wanting), with = variants : er3s tvâ kulyâ upa yanti vivahâ, and svadhayâ for maâkumat. But our c and d are found further on as parts of vs. 7, with pundartkam for ânârkarn, and he calṅkham and gapakhas. It is doubtless by an oversight that SPP. has in b, in both saṅzhilâ and pada, the false accent d7uâm (but our O. also gives it). The verse lacks ¹ one syllable of being a full k777 (So syllables). The comm. ends vs. 5 with mulâlt, and ee begins vs. 6 with the following refrain.

6. Having pools of ghee, having slopes of honey, having strong drink (sârâ) for water, filled with milk (Ś57râ), with water, with curds —let all Ś these etc. etc. ¹

Ppp. agrees in a, b with our text (we should expect rather madhuku2yâs); but for Ś Ś the refrain it has elas tvan: ralpâ upa yanti vivatas svarge loke svadhayâ mâda- genes yantri (the remaining pâda again wanting, as in vs. 5). The refrain appears much ¹ hs more in place with this verse than in vs. 5. The comm., as already indicated, makes its a vs. 6 of our 6 a, b, preceded by the refrain of vs. 54 the refrain of our vs. 6 it omits altogether. The sârâ seems most probably to have been a kind of beer or ale so Roth : not distilled liquor, as Zimmer, p. 280, suggests . A full atiaṅwvarr (6o) calls for two more syllables.

7. Four vessels (kumbhâ), four-fold, I give, filled with milk, with water, with curds —let all these etc. etc.

Ppp. had the first two pâdas, as noted above, in its vs. 5, reading for a carus kum 6byân: I carurâdhâ dadari ; its vs. 7 is our 5 c, 4 (with the variants already given) together with the last two pâadas of the refrain, reading svadhayâ for madkumat in the former pada, o and 7a for rvâ in the latter. The comm. (with one or two of SPP's mss. that follow him) has dadkâmi in a.

8. This rice-mess I deposit in the Brâhmans, the wâgârin, world-conquering, heaven-going (svargâ); let it not be destroyed (ksi) for me, ¹ swelling with svadṅâ ; be it a cow of all forms, milking my desire. ¹ f : Several of our mss. (P.M.W.E.) combine in d dkenâs kâm-. Ppp. has for a imam ² odanam pacasi miraddhaâhâno; in b, lokajitiyart svargyam (the comm. also has the de. better reading svargyam); in c, ksesta sadasigyamâṇa ; for 8, vivarnpa kâmadughz g âhenur astu me. docs.text:

Not found in Pâipp. Not used individually by Kâug., but only as one of the cz12nani (8. 25). Our mss. of the Anukr. do not contain the expected definition of the hymn as one of ten stanzas (dagarcam). ³] The Berlin Anukr. reads szzyanjasanm. J i

Translated : Ludwig, p. 526; Grill, 3, 136; Griffith, i.1r79; Bloomfield, 35, 407; Ś : Weber, xviii. 41. Ś

I. Them let him of real force burn forth — Agni Vâigvânara, the bull; whoso shall abuse and seek to harm us, likewise whoso shall play the niggard toward us. Ś

The comm. paraphrases durasyât with dustan ivâ "carer: asmâsv aviâyarnanaṇ: : 2 dosam udbkavayer. The Prat. (iii. 18) allows both 7 and 7 in denominatives like arâzây-, , 2 and its comment quotes this word as example of the former.

All the mss. read in a ââpsaz, which is accordingly retained by SPP. ; our edition emends to âsat to agree with vs. r c; the comm. also has Jipsâz ; and it is favored by the c4par of the parallel expression in vi. 37.3. With the second half-verse compare 4

2. By thee do we expel (caf) the Apsarases, the Gandharvas; O goat- ¹ horned one, drive the demon ; make all disappear by [thy] smell.

Let the Apsarases go to the stream, to the loud (?) down-blowing of ¹ the waters : Guggulâ, Pilâ, Naladi, Aukṣagandhi, Pramandani : so go ( 3 away, ye Apsarases ; ye have been recognized. i ¹ I See Weber's note and reference to Rumpelstilzchen. 7ârâ in bis rendered cross- Ś ing"; but as this sense is found nowhere else, it seems safer to take the word as the adjective, common later; the comm. glosses it with ²ârayâtâaran, a worthless etymological guess. [In the prior draft, W. notes the suggestions concerning awacvasârn given by ¹he BR. i. 490 and OB. i. 126 and implying ava = 'away'; but rejects them. ] . : 4. Where [are] the acvatthâs, the nyagrâdṅas, great trees, with crests . £4 thither go away, ye Apsarases ; ye have been recognized.

The division and numbering in our edition of this verse and the two next following is i faulty, owing to the unclearness of the mss. first used ; the correct division, agreeing Śâ with the Anukr., is given by SPP., and our translation follows it and makes clear what J it is ]; vss. 3-5 all end with the refrain tâ¢ pâre 'fz- etc., and this, with the number 4, Si : needs to be added in our text after (ikhanâgtnak. i 5. Where [are] your swings, green and whitish ; where cymbals [and] ¹ 6 lutes sound together — thither go away, ye Apsarases; ye have been ft recognized.. I Change the number 4 to 5 at the end of the first line of p. 74 of the edition. ] The

8. Terrible are Indra's missiles (ker), a hundred spears of iron ; with them let him push out the oblation-eating, 4vakâ-eating Gandharvas. y

Half our mss., and the large majority of SPP's, read at the end of this verse ryata 4 both editions give satu, as in the next verse. A7aṅâ is defined as a certain grass-lke 4 marsh-plant, Blyxa octandra, the same with ¢âivala or gâivâla ; the comm. defines it. as jaloparisthâl (âivalavicesâak, but attempts no explanation of why the Gandharvas 1 should be supposed to eat it. He reads in b cazaprstis (one feels tempted to emend rather to gazâbkystrs), and in c abhikradan (for haviradzn). The Anukr. takes no . g notice of the redundant syllable in c (also in 9 c). ¹

9. Terrible are Indra's missiles, a hundred spears of gold ; with them ¹ let him push out the oblation-eating, 4vakâ-cating Gandharvas. ( This very slightly varied repetition of vs. 8 is wanting in Ppp. All the mss. have ¹ ¹ rsatu at the end here. 0 ro. All our pada-mss. read in b jyotayaomâmakân as a compound, and it seems very g & strange that SPP. gives in both forms of text jyotaya mâamakân, as two independent ¹ words, and reports nothing different as found in any of his authorities; it is perhaps an : oversight on his part. Either reading being plainly untranslatable, the rendering given ¹ = : implies emendation to jyotayamâanakân, as the simplest and most probable alteration ; i several cases of such expansions of a participle in mâna by an added -ka occur Skz. Bloomfield's note , one of them (pravartamânakâ) even in RV. ¹ Ppp. reads as follows : avakâcar: abhicâco bicchi âyatayamânakâr: : gandharvân sarvan ogadhe kruu tasvaparâyaṇal ; this supports the proposed reading in its most essential feature, -maâna- for -mâma-, and further favors the version of the comm., gyoz- 0 for jyor-. R., in the Festgruss an Bâhtlingk (p. 97), had ingeniously conjectured the i word as a name for the will-o-the-wisp, deriving it from jyotaya mâm give me light, ¹ I by an added suffix -aka. The comm. paraphrases by matsambandhino ganâharvân ¹ udakesu prakâacaya. Ct. Whitney, Festgruss an Rotk, p. 91; also note to ii. 3. I.

II. One as it were a dog, one as it were an ape, a boy all hairy—having Ś become as it were dear to see, the Gandharva fastens upon (sac) women ;. him we make disappear from here by [our] mighty (vizyâvant) incantation. I In our edition, strâyam at the end of d is a misprint for strâyas, which all the mss. ¹ have, with no avasâna-mark following, though distinctly called for by the sense, and therefore supplied by us; Ppp., however, reads striyanz, with sqjate before it; and it ¹ omits the last pada, f: which omission would furnish an excuse for the absence of inter- 0 ¹ punction after strâyas.

12. Your wives, verily, are the Apsarases ; O Gandharvas, ye are fh ¹ [their] husbands ; run away, O immortal ones; fasten not on mortals.; All the pada-mss. commit in c the palpable error of dividing gkâvatamariyâ(k) into i dhâvata : martyâṇ, as if the 2 which follows âkâvat- were one of the common prolongations of a final vowel in sa7kâtâ ; the comm., however, understands arnar yak,; and SPP. admits this by emendation into his padâa-text. docs.title: 38. For luck in gambling : by aid of an Apsaras
docs.text:
[Bâdarâyapi.— duidevatyam. &nugtubham : 3. 6:.3-av. jagatr; 5. bhurigatyasti ; 6. tri|tubk;

7. 3-29. 5p. anugutgarbhâ purauparigâjyotismatt jagatr.)

This and the two following hymns are not found in Pâipp. Kâug. uses it (doubtless only the first four verses) in a ceremony (41.13) for success in gambling. Verses 5are called kar&ipravâdâs and used (21. 11) in a rite for the prosperity of kine, and also (66.13) in the saa sacrifices, with a kar kr as sava ; and they are reckoned (19. I, note) to the pu3tika mantras. The comm. attempts no explanation of the mutual relation of the two apparently unconnected parts of the hymn; but Weber, in his note to verse 7, suggests a connection |. [As to Bâdarâyaṇi, see introd. to h. 40. ]

Translated : Muir, OST. v. 430 (vss. I-34); Ludwig, p. 454; Grill, 71 (vss. 1-3), 140; Griffith, i. 183 ; Bloomfield, 149, 412; Weber, xviii. 147.

I. The up-shooting, all-conquering, successfully-playing Apsaras, that wins (7) the winnings in the pool (? glâha)— that Apsaras I call on here.

The form apsarâ, instead of apsarâs, is used throughout this hymn ; the comm. regards it as a specialized name for the Apsaras in this character or office: dyṅtakriya- âJhidevatâm apsarojatyam. Udbhindarim is paraphrased by panabandhena dhanasyo ¹dbhedanar kurvatim, as if it were the causative participle. The technical terms of the game are only doubtfully translated, our knowledge of its method being insufficient; glâha is taken as the receptacle, of whatever kind, in which the stakes are deposited ; the comm. explains it thus : grkyate paṇabandhena kalpyata iti dyṅtakriyâjeyo (mss. ayo) 'rtho glakak.

2. The distributing (vi-ci), on-strewing (2-47), successfully-playing Apsaras, that seizes (grak) the winnings in the pool—that Apsaras I call. on here.

The comm. explains the first two epithets respectively by collecting " (taking v7 as intensive) and scattering."

3. She who dances about with the dice (? 4ya), taking to herself the winning from the pool—let her, trying to gain (?) for us the winnings, obtain the stake (?prakâ) by magic (mâyâ); let her come to us rich in milk; let them not conquer from us this riches.

The wholly anomalous sâazt in c is here translated, in accordance with the current understanding of it, as somehow coming from the root saz or sâ l i.e., as if it were for the normal sâ57-s-arz : considering that the consonant of the root sz happens to coincide with the sibilant which is characteristic of the desiderative, we might be tempted to put sEsâni : sa: : stksant : sak (Skt. Gram. 1030 a), but for the accent ]; the comm. reads instead cesanti (= avagesayantzy. The comm. further has in b Zdadkânas (explained as = adadhana: so SPP's K. reads), and in prakân (= prakantavyân aksâan: a. false etymology and worthless interpretation). He explains gyâs as ekâdayak paṅcasar kkyânta aksaviesâk. He divides our vss. 35 into four verses of four pâadas each, without any regard to the connection of sense, thus giving the hymn eight verses ; among our mss. also (SPP. reports nothing of the kind from his) there is more or less discord- â ance in regard to the verse-division, and some of them agree with the comm. [Our sṅsart appears in W's Index Verborum, p. 382, at the very end of the “unclassified residuum " of AV. material, —

4. She who delights (pra-mad) in the dice (257), bringing (5kz) pain f and anger —the rejoicing, the delighting one : that Apsaras I call on here.

The translation implies retention of 54krati at end of b, read by all the mss. and by the comm., and retained by SPP., and the emendation instead in a to y& 'ksâsu pramsdate, which is metrically better, makes better connection, and has the support of the comm., with one or two J of SPP's authorities. SPP's note to Śââratz, "so read ( except by K. who follows Sâyaṇa," is unintelligible, since the latter has also â4))ratl. ¹ I Delete the accent mark under uve. ] ¹

5. They who (f.) go about (saw-car) after the rays of the sun, or who "go about after [its] beams (mârâci) ; of whom the mighty (? vâjtnivant) ¹ bull from afar moves around (pari-i) at once all the worlds, defending — let him come unto us, enjoying this libation, together with the atmosphere, he the mighty one.

According to the comm., the "they who " and "of whom " in a and c are the Apsa- Ś rases, this being apparently to him the tie of connection between the two divisions of i the hymn ; and vâjini is the dawn, and vâjinrvant the sun : all of which is very ques- i tionable, at least. SPP. reads in d paryâtti, with, as he states, the majority of his mss., ¹ but with only two of ours; the comm. has paryeri, and it is also thus quoted by the comment to Prat. iv. 81. SPP. further leaves the final 7 of sârvân unassimilated before f lokân, for the wholly insufficient reason that nearly all his mss. so read; the point is one i that requires to be regulated by the prescriptions of general grammar and of the Prât., i without heed to the carelessness of scribes. The passage is even one of those quoted g under Prat. ii. 35 as an example of assimilation. The metrical definition of the Anukr. Ś T— is inaccurate, and perhaps corrupt; the verse (12-11: I24 II: XI + II=68) should be g specified as of 6 pâdas and 3 avasânas, like vs. 3; it is not bkurij; and for atyasti the :; I London, not the Berlin ms. ] reads jagatyasti. One is tempted to suspect the syllable ¹ sazk- in a. Pronounce yâsarsabhâ in c. g ‘

6. Together with the atmosphere, O mighty one; defend thou here ¹ 2 the Zarkâ calf, O vigorous one (vâjâ7); here are abundant drops (siokâ) ¹ = for thee ; come hitherward ; this is thy kark7; here be thy mind. ²

The comm. reads in a vâjinrvân, as in 5 f; in b he has Zarkin varsân (and one of SPP's mss. gives karṅâin); and, in 4, namas instead of manas, and SPP. reports three of his four pada-mss. as also having nâmas. The comm. explains kzrṅr as karkavarṅa or cubhra. The minor Pet. Lex. suggests the emendation of vazsâm to vagân in this verse and the next. Three of SPP's mss. and one of ours (O.) separate karkt ikâ in san kâtâ in d. The Anukr. ignores the deficiency of a syllable in b.

7. Together with the atmosphere, O mighty one ; defend thou here the karkt calf, O vigorous one ; this is fodder ; this is the pen; here we bind ¹ (ni-bandk) the calf; according to name we master you : hail l ¹ The comm., with one of SPP's oral authorities, has again varzsân in b, and also ¹ vatsan in d (this time, with our P.M.W.E.). Kâug. (21. 11) quotes c and â, with the direction to do “as directed in the text"; the comm. Kegava ] explains that a rope is to be prepared with twelve ties (d2man) ; and that with c fodder is to be offered to the kine, and with d the calves are to be tied to the rope. If this is correct, the reading would ¹ seem to be properly varzsân in all cases, and perhaps Śz7ky&(k) varsân in 6b and 7b i

(thus filling out the meter). The mss. add (as directed by the Anukr.) a second avasânadf sign after badhutmak, and SPP. retains it. The verse (11410: 848: ro=47) falls Ś55 4 short of a full jagarr by the amount of the deficiency in b. II think ZarZyks, as a ¹ genitive sing. fem., ought to be oxytone (JAOS. x. 385) ; but ZarZyâs, pronounced i kar kto, might be better. ]

docs.text:

(vii. 5.23). The hymn is used by Kaug. au in the parvan sacrifices (5. 8) with the saz nati offerings, and vss. g and ro earlier in ¹Ś the same ceremonies with two so-called pwrastâaddkhomas (3. 16) ; also the hymn again sd in the rites (59. 16) for satisfaction of desires. On the earth they paid reverence (sam-nam) to Agni; he throve of (rdk) ; as on earth they paid reverence to Agni, so let the reverencers pay reverence to me. The metrical ¹ â definitions of the Anukr. for vss. i-8 are of no value; the odd verses vary from 34 to 37

Ś syllables, and the even from 38 to 40. We might have expected the epithet t7yavasâna Ś (3-a.) to be applied to the even. ² 2. Earth [is] milch-cow; of her Agni [is] calf; let her, with Agni as se calf, milk for me food (7), refreshment, [my] desire, life-time first, progeny, prosperity, wealth : hail ( ¹ ; There is in TS. nothing to correspond to our vss. 2, 4, 6, 8. Our edition combines

‘ âyus pr-, because required by Prat. ii. 75 ; but the mss., except one of SPP's, have ¹ ; ; âyuk pr-, which SPP. retains.

3. In the atmosphere they paid reverence to Vayu; he throve; as in the atmosphere they paid reverence to Vâyu, so let the reverencers pay

¹ reverence to me.

Ś TS. has a corresponding passage, in the form as given above.

Ś 4. The atmosphere is milch-cow ; of her Vâyu is calf; let her, with Ś“e Vayu as calf, milk for me etc. etc.

¹ The comm. has ta3ya ' of it (i.e. the atmosphere), instead of zzṣyas.

od 5. In the sky they paid reverence to Aditya; he throve; as in the sky - " : : they paid reverence to Aditya, so let the reverencers pay reverence tome. The corresponding TS. passage has sârya instead of ââṅyd.

6. The sky is milch-cow; of her Aditya is calf; let her, with Aditya as calf, milk for me etc. etc.

In the edition, sâ is misprinted for sâ.

7. In the quarters they paid reverence to the moon (caznârâ) ; it throve; as in the quarters they paid reverence to the moon, so let the reverencers pay reverence to me.

In TS., the asterisms (nâksatra) are here connected with the moon ; and there d follow similar passages respecting Varuna with the waters, and several other divinities.

8. The quarters are milch-cows ; of them the moon is calf ; let them, with the moon as calf, milk for me etc. etc.

Both editions read Jdukâm in this verse, as in vss. 2, 4, 6, following the authority of : nearly all the mss. ; only our H.D. have the true reading, dukrâm, which ought to have ¹ : been adopted in our text.

9. Agni moves (car), entered into the fire, son of the seers, protector a against imprecation ; with homage-paying, with homage, I make offering er ¹ to thee; let us not make falsely the share of the gods. a

That is (a), ' Agni is continually to be found in the fire.' Three of SPP's authorities Ś read mânasâ in c, thus ridding the verse of an objectionable repetition; but both editions i give nâmasaâ, which the comm. also has. In d our edition has karmabhâgdânm, following ¹ our pada-mss. (which read karmacbhâgâm) ; but SPP. has correctly, with his mss. and ¹ the comm. (=â kârsma), karma bhâgâm. More or less of the verse is found in Ś several other texts : thus, in VS. (v. 4) only a, b, ending b with abhṅastipâva ; in MS.. : (. 2. 7), with adhîrajâ esâṅ at end of b, a wholly different c, and, for â, mâ devânar yRyupama bhâgadhâyam ; in MB. (ii. 2. 12), only a, b, with b ending as in MS; in TS. ¹ (. 3.72), the whole verse, b ending like MS., c beginning with svâ=âkṅtya brâhmapa, ¹ and d ending with mithuyâ kar bhâgadhâyam ; in TB. (ii. 7.15), the whole, beginning with uyâghrd yâm agnarn car-, and ending b with 57 ayâm, its c and â agreeing Ś 5 throughout with ours ; in ACS. (viii. 14.4), the whole, but ending b ³ like MS. and TS., ¹ 5 and having for c, 4 tasmâi jukhomi havisâa ghytena ma devânam momuhad bhâgadhe- ¹ yam; in Ppp., the whole verse, just as in ACS., except that a ends with grawistâ and ² that â has yâyavad for momukad and (unless mân is a slip of Roth's pen) mar; for mz J. See Bloomfield's discussion of mithuyâ kr, IDMG. xlviii. 556. ] The meter i i (10411 : I24 I I=44) is irregular, but the Anukr. takes no notice of it. *] The Calcutta ed. has awirâja esak, misprint for adki-.

ro. Purified with the heart, with the mind, O Jâtavedas— knowing all the ways (vayâna), O god ; seven mouths are thine, O Jâtavedas; to them 1 I make offering — do thou enjoy the oblation. % Pârâns in a can only qualify kauyâm in 4: compare RV. iv. 58. 6'b, antâr krdâ - mânasâ payâmanak. The pada-text makes one of its frequent blunders by resolving in c saptâsyâni into saptâ : Zgyani instead of into saptâ : âsyâni, the designation of the accent in sazzkhitâ being the same in both cases, according to its usual method. SPP. i accepts the blunder, reading #syar.

It is impossible to see why these two concluding. verses should have been added to ¹ the hymn.

docs.text:

(vyazk) away ; I smite them back with the reverter (pratisarâ). ss ; Pratisara, the comm. says, means gratimukham nivartata âbhicârikar karma gent ¹nena ; and jukvari means komenâa 'sman abhicaranti. The analogous formula in the

¹ Here, again, part of our mss. (E.I.H.), and nearly all SPP's, give the false accent bkwmâm ; both editions read bkâmim. The other texts associate Aditi with this gy quarter," or "the quarter here," as they style it.

This, the eighth and concluding anuvâka of the book, has 5 hymns and 47 verses ; ² the quotation from the old Anukr. is saptadaca 'ntyak, to which is added jagarcavacca. a

Here ends also the ninth grapâtkaṅa.

One of our mss. (I.) sums up the content of the book as 323 verses; the true number is 324. Observe that the last vs. of hymn 2o is numbered 7 when it should be 9-1 i Book V.

Anukramaṇi assumes 8 verses as the normal length of a hymn of this book (see p. 142); but there are only two such hymns

(“hymns " 9 and ro, both prose l). In fact,

There are in this book, 2 4 zz 6 5 3 3 3 2 I hymns,

Much and variously used by Kâug., but in situations that have nothing to do with the meaning of the hymn, and cast no light upon its difficulties: g â thus, it is employed with the following hymn in a battle-rite (15. I), for victory; and ¹ the two hymns together again in a ceremony (22. r) for welfare, while hymns 1 to 3 g i (and v. 1. 3 separately) are reckoned ro. r, note to the pustika mantras; vs. 1 alone g (with vi. 17 and another) appears in a ceremony (35. 12) against abortion ; vss. 2-9, in

one (35. r3 ff.) for the benefit of a person seized by jambha ; vs. 3 is further applied i in a charm (21. 12) for good-fortune in regard to clothing, vs. 4, in a women's rite

(34. 20) for winning a husband ; vs. 5 (with iii. 30, vi. 64, etc.) in a rite (12. 5) for 4 g harmony ; vs. 6, in the nuptial ceremonies (76. 21), on marking seven lines to the north of of the fire, and again (79. 1), with an offering at the beginning of the fourth-day observi ances ; vs. 7, in a remedial rite (28. r2) for one in misery (amar), giving him a portion, ¹ ; and again, in the ceremony against false accusation (46. 1), with vii. 43; vs. 8 in a rite Ś ¹ oe i for prosperity (21. 15), on occasion of the division of an inheritance ; and vs. 9, later gee (21.17) in the last-mentioned ceremony.

Sn The hymn is intentionally and most successfully obscure, and the translation given is

4 in great part mechanical, not professing any real understanding of the sense. It is very Ś probable that the text is considerably corrupted ; and one cannot avoid the impression — : also that the lines are more or less disconnected, and artificially combined.

Ge ² Translated : Ludwig, p. 394; Griffith, i. 187 ; Weber, xviii. r37.

1. He who came to (4-547) the womb (yâṅi) with a special sacred text (dhaṅmantra), of immortal spirit (-âsu), increasing, of good birth, of unharmed spirit, shining like the days — Trita the maintainer maintained three (z74, neuter).

The Pet. Lexx. render yâhaṅmantra by lacking speech "; Ludwig, by "of distinguished meditation." Ae "va (p. âhâeiva) is perhaps rather to be understood as âhahoiva. 2. He who first attained to (â-sad) the ordinances (âhârman) makes ¹ thence many wondrous forms; eager (? dkâsyṅ) he first entered the a womb (yânî), he who understood (â-ciz) speech unspoken.

In b the translation follows Ppp., which reads krnute for -use ; Ppp. also has a differ ent c, yag ca yonin prathamâ "vivea ; and it ends â with anucitan: yigâya.

3. He who left (ric) [his] body to thy heat (gâka), flows the gold; his [men] are bright (crâci) after; there they (two) assume (ââ) immortal i names; let the clans (v7) send garments for us.

The first pâida might equally mean « he who left thy body (self) to the heat." Inb, g ee ksârar might equally be pres. pple. qualifying kfranyam. W. have asmat, but doubtless only by the not infrequent error of substituting â7 i for 2), and our understanding of the sense is too defective to justify emendations; Ppp., d however, has asi. Inc, Ppp. reads arra dadhrse 'mrt-. The Kâug. use of the verse appears to be derived only from the occurrence of vâstrâṇi in â.

4. When these formerly went further forth, approaching each unfading seat —the poet of the dry (? gusâ), the two licking mothers—do ye (two) ¹ send for the sister (fâmt) a capable (âkiâzya) spouse.

The translation is, of course, simple nonsense. None of our J mss. accent gus in a ; P.M. accent pâruyânt before it; one (T:) combines -nzo juryâm in b. 4

5. This great homage, verily, to thee, O broad-going one, do I a poet make with poesy (kâṇya) ; when the two (m.), going united (sazmyâṅc) i against the earth ((5â), [then] increase here the (two) great bank-wheeled (? r6dhacakra) ones (f.).

⁴ Bank-wheeled," i.e. rolling on between their banks. Juz in our text (beginning of c) is a misprint for yâr. Prat. iii. 4 determines 7; ii. 97 determines s7 ; vâavydhâte (p. vav-) is by iii. 13. The Kâug. use of the verse seems suggested simply by samyâṅcâu. The irregular verse (9-11 : II FI2=43) is very imperfectly defined by the Anukr. Seven bourns (naryâdâ)y did the poets fashion; unto one of these verily went one distressed ; in the nest of the nearest (zpamdâ) community â (? âyâ) stood the pillar (skambhâ), at the release (visargâ) of the roads, in the supports (dkarâṇa). i k The verse is a RV. one, from a mystic and obscure hymn (x. 5.6) ; RV. puts 77 after Ś51 Śkâm in b, and in c accents upamâsya niâé, which alone is acceptable; all our mss. al give âpamasya, which our edition follows ; and all save one (D.) read nZge without Ś accent, which we emended to nige. Ppp. gives in b (Zsâm anekâm, and omits, probably 4 by an oversight, the second half-verse. The life of mankind is compared to a race-

; track, on which the gods have marked many (seven) stations ; each generation (yuga) Śâ reaches only one such goal, getting as far as the place where the next begins; there its Gan road terminates." R. 4 7. Also, of immortal spirit, vowed (? vrâta), I go performing ; spirit, fa i soul, of the body then (? 747) with kine (? sumdââgu) ; and either the I mighty one (gakrâ) assigns treasure, or as the oblation-giver pursues pp. (? sac) with refreshment. (x This verse and vs. 5] 4? are the most utterly hopeless of the hymn ; even the conjectures of the comm. respecting them would be welcome. Ludwig renders sumâdgu by 2 « erfreut gegangen." For b, Ppp. reads asnrâs putas svadkayâ samaâgu ; in c, vâ ² jyestho ratna. Vâ in c in our text is a misprint for 272. The verse lacks oply one Śh syllable of being a full f751ubk, and that deficiency might be made up by reading either : Ś Ś cakrâs or râtnar as trisyllabic.. [A barytone urâza is unknown elsewhere.

¹² 8. Also son prays (? 7g) father for dominion ; they called for well-being him of the chief bourn (?); may they see now, O Varuṇa, those that are ¹ ¹ Ee thy shapes (vistkâ) ; mayest thou make wondrous forms of the one much rolling hither. ¹ The translation implies emendation in b to the compound jyesthâmaryâdarm,* i.e. thim I ¹ . who has received the best domain.' In â our âvârwytatas is for the -rvrar--of all the l ⁴ c, d are augmentless forms, and may, of course, be rendered indicatively. Ppp. begins mss. ; it can hardly be that the text of this pada is not further corrupt. The verbs in " i the verse with puzro vâ yat pit-, and ends b with svaszi. ¹ and half." The second pada is properly jagari. ¥] No ms. has -ââm. 1 9. Half with half milk thou mixest (? pz) ; with half, O Asura (?), thou i increasest [thy] vehemence (?). We have increased the helpful (cagmâya)

which Ppp. has, instead of the vocative gusma, and asura, again with Ppp. (perhaps

docs.text:
[(Brhaddiva Atharvan.— navakam. vârupam. trâgubham : 9. bkurik parâtiâgatâ.]

Found also in Pâipp. v. It is a RV. hymn (x. 120); and the first three verses occur in other texts. For the use of the hymn with its predecessor in Kâug. 15. I and 22. r and rg. I, note, see above, under h. 1; it is further applied, with vil. 1, in a 2â7ya rite (59. 17), with worship of Indra and Agni. The various verses appear also as follows vs. 3, in a rite for prosperity (21. 21) ; vs. 4, with vi. r3 in a battle-rite (15.6) ; vs. 5 in g a similar rite (15.8) ; vs. 6, in another (15.9), and yet again, with vi. 125, and vii. 3 etc.,; as the king and his charioteer mount a new chariot (15.11); vs. 7, next after vs. 3 (21. 23), with the holding of a light on the summit of an anthill; and vs. 8 in a ¹ women's rite 34. 21 J, next after v. 1. 4—all artificial uses, having no relation to the texts quoted in them.

Translated : by the RV. translators ; and Griffith, i. 189; Weber, xviii. 164. i

I. That verily was the chief among beings whence was born the formidable one, of bright manliness; as soon as born, he dissolves [his]. foes, when all [his] aids (ma) revel after him. ==

RV. reads in d 4nu yâr vigve mâdanty kmak, and all the other texts (SV. ii. 833; ⁴ VS. xxxiii. 80 5 AA. I. 3.4) agree with it. The Anukr. ignores the considerable metrical ees irregularities. i

2. Increasing with might (câoas), he of much force, a foe, assigns (â7â) fear to the barbarian, winning (n.) both what breathes not out and what breathes out ; brought forward (n.), they resound together for thee in the revelings.

Sense and connection are extremely obscure ; but all the texts (SV. i. 834; AA. as above) agree throughout. Prâbhṇ 77, of course, might be loc. sing. of 47. Sâsṅz inc ¹ Ś is (with Grassmann) rendered as if it were sâsnis. Ś er

3. In thee they mingle skill abundantly, when they twice, thrice Ś i become [thine] aids ; unite thou with sweet (svâdâ7) what is sweeter than he sweet ; mayest thou fight against yonder honey with honey (nâdṅu).

RV. differs only by reading vr #janti vâoe at end of a; and SV. (ii.Ś35) and AA. (as above) agree with it throughout; as does also Ppp. ; TS. (iii. 5. 107) begins d with i âra 7 57, and ends it with yodṅ7, which looks like a more original reading. I Cf. Geldner, Ved. Sâgg, ii. ro.q,.

4. If now after thee that conquerest riches in contest after contest (râṇa) the devout ones (vâpra) revel, more forcible, O vehement one, extend thou what is stanch; let not the ill-conditioned Kagokas damage thee. ¹

RV. begins a with 47 cid Jkt tvâ, and b with mâde-made ; in c it reads (with Ppp.) âhrsno for gusmin, and at the end of the verse yatudhâna durevâṅ ; Ppp. has instead âureva yaruâhanark. ¹

5. By thee do we prevail in the contests, looking forward to many ¹ 4 things to be fought [for]; I stir up thy weapons with spells (vâcas) ; I 4 sharpen up thy powers (vâyas) with incantation (Śrâhman). : i RV. and Ppp. have no variants. ¹ 6. Thou didst set that down in the lower and the higher, in what ot abode (duronâ) thou didst aid with aid; cause ye to stand there the ¹ moving mother; from it send ye many exploits. uk RV. and Ppp. put the verse after our 7. Ppp. has no variants; RV. reads in a Ś² : âuaram pâran ca, and, for c, 4d, marâra sthapayase Jigatnṅ âta inosi kârvarâ Śc purkṇi : a quite different, but little less obscure version of the text : " Indra checks the br revolution of the sky, in order to gain time for his deeds.” R.

‘ 7. Praise thou fully, O summit, the many-tracked, skilful (? fŚkvan), ¹ most active (i7â) Aptya of the Aptyas ; may he look on with might, he i of much force ; may he overpower the counterpart of the earth. ŚŚe The RV. version is different throughout : stusâyyam purnvârpasam F(hvam inâtamam Ce âptyâm aptyânam : â darsate (âvasâ saptâ dânan prâ saksate pratimânani bhṅri; and pc Ś with this Ppp. agrees. The translation follows our text servilely, as it may be called, ge save in the obviously unavoidable emendation of 2ptâm to Zptyâm in b; O. is our only ms. ean that reads zpâyân. The verse is far too irregular to be let pass as merely a trâ5tubk.

8. These incantations (brâkman) may Brihaddiva, foremost heavenwinner, make, a strain (câ5â) for Indra; he rules, an autocrat, over the great stall (gorrâ) ; may he, quick (? târa), rich in fervor, send (?) all.

2 The fourth pâda is attempted to be rendered literally from our text, although this is i plainly a gross corruption of the RV. text: âârag ca vâvâ avrnod âpa svâk. RV. has i also before it svarâjas, and in a vivakti for krpavat. Ppp. agrees with RV. through- 5 out. Swvarsâs (p. svajosâṇ) is prescribed by Prat. ii. 49.

9- So hath the great Brihaddiva Atharvan spoken of his own self

(tan?) [as of] Indra ; the two blameless, mother-growing sisters— [men]

both impel them with might (gâvas) and increase them. i ¹ : The second half-verse seems again a corruption of the RV. version, which has plurals

Ś instead of duals in c, and omits the meter-disturbing ene (p. ene â7) in 4. Ppp. again agrees with RV. ; but in b it has zaum for tanvam. Our text should give, with the others, mâtar kvar- in c; all the mss. have it. [The vs. is svar) rather than 4277).

I. Be splendor mine, O Agni, in rival invocations (vi4avâ) ; may we, kindling thee, adorn ourselves ; let the four directions bow to me ; with ¹ thee as overseer may we conquer the fighters.

The other texts (with MS. i. 4. r) have no variants in this verse. Ppp. appears to read prathema for pusema in b..

2. O Agni, pushing back the fury of our adversaries, do thou, our : keeper (gopâ), protect us about on all sides ; let our abusers (âurasyi) go away downwards ; among themselves (amâ) let the intent of them awaking be. lost. rr

RV. reads at the end kâme asmiân, and Ppp. agrees with it, also TS. TS. has further 8 ndrâvantas in b, and in c, strangely enough, 77 gopâm, as two separate words. ee

RV. and TS. read yajantu and kavyâ (for i577) in a, and, for 4, v4ve devâso âdhs vocarṅ nak (but TS. me). Ppp. agrees with our text except for ending with mam 2a.

Ye six divine wide ones, make wide [space] for us; all ye gods, wrong that is hateful find us. ¹ revel here; let not a portent find us, nor an imprecation; let not the Ś Only the first half-verse is RV. material, forming its vs. 5 with our 7 c, 4; the latter i : half-verse we have had already as i. zo. ¹ perous (pustâ) for our progeny and for ourselves (fanṅ); let us not be : ¹ deserted (4) by progeny nor selves ; let us not be made subject to the be hater, O king Soma. Śeṅ All the mss. accent at the beginning ṅsrâs ; our text emends to t4sras. The second half-verse, as above noted, goes with our 6 a, b to make one verse in RV. and TS. ; and = : also in Ppp., which has the variant dkanena for tanâbhis in c. For the present verse, rege Ppp. agrees in the first half with our text, only reading me for nas; for second half it Ś 4 has : man: visas sammanaso yusantân pitryarn: ksatranm prta janâre asmâar. The ² eg Anukr. ignores the extra syllable in a. . 8. Let the bull (makisâ) of wide expanse grant us protection, having . ¹ much food (-Ś5²), [he] the much-invoked in this invocation; do thou be

gracious unto our progeny, O thou of the bay horses ; O Indra, harm us not, do not abandon us.

. RV. and TS. read yan sad at end of a, and mydaya at end of c (also our O.) ; at end i of b, RV. and Ppp. have -k577, while TS. agrees with our text. In d the pada-text has.

ririsak, by Prat. iv. 86. The Anukr. takes no notice of the two redundant syllables in a.

docs.title: 7. Against niggardliness and its effects
docs.text:
[âtharvan (7). — dagakam. lakudevatyam (I=3, 6-I0. arâtiyṅs ; 4, 5. sârasvatyân). ânuṣtn- Ś ; bham : I. virâdgarbhâ prastârapaṅkti ; 4. pathyâbyhatr ; 6. prastârapanâti.] v Not found in Pâipp. Used by Kâug. in the niry tikarman (18. 14), with an offering of rice-grains ; and, with iii. 20 and vii. 1, in a rite for good-fortune (41.8) ; while the a schol. also adds it to vi. 7 (46. 4, note), in removing obstacles to sacrifice ; of separate verses, vs. 5 (schol., vss. 5-10) appears, with vii. 57, in a ceremony (46. 6) for the 4 : success of requests. Vaâit. has the hymn (or vs. 1) in the agnicayana (28. 19), with the vantoṅhana rite ; further, vs. 6 in the parvan sacrifices (3. 2), with an oblation to " Ś Indra and Agni; and vs. 7 at the agnigioma (12. 10) in expiation of a forbidden utterance. The fourth pada lacks a syllable. ¹ ee

It seems as if nagnâ bobhuvarr were the equivalent of makânagnt bhavantr ' becom- Ś es ing a wanton,' the intensive element being shifted from the adjective to the verb. The — pada-text reads svapnayâ, by Prat. iv. 30. &.

I. With fuel of vâkaṅkata do thou carry the sacrificial butter to the gods ; O Agni, make them revel here; let all come to my call.

2. O Indra, come to my call; this will I do; that hear thou; let these over-runners (? atisarâ) of Indra's bring to pass (sam-nam) my Ś design ; by them may we be equal to (ak) heroism, O Jâtavedas, self-controller.

. ; Brahmân : probably performer of an incantation. Ppp. reads abkibkṅtaye in b.

Udvâcana is heard of nowhere else, and the name looks so improbable that the Pet. Lexx. conjecture zâdvâṅcana ; Ppp. has instead adwâtana ; it puts this verse at the end of the hymn. The redundancy of d is passed without notice by the Anukr.

docs.title: 11. [Dialogue between] Varuna and Atharvan
docs.text:
Ś ¹ Ś¹âtharvan.—ckâdarakam. vârupam. trâigubham : I. Śhurâ ; 3. paṅkti; 6. 52. atiakvarr;

i ec

Ś â Found also in Pâipp. vifi. It is used by Kâug. only once, and in a connection which

casts no light upon it, namely at 12. 1, in a rite for general welfare (one eats a dish of nmilkrice cooked on a fire of mââṅnaka-sticks). It is not quoted at all by Vait. The ¹ ¹" interpretation in detail is difficult and far from certain.

Translated : Muir, OST. i.2 396; Griffith, i.zo3 ; Weber, xviii. 2or.— Treated by Roth, Ueber den A V., p. 9; also by R. Garbe, Wissenschaytliche Monatsâlitzer, K6nigsberg, 1879, no. r.— A note in lead-pencil shows that Whitney meant to rewrite his ms. of this hymn. But the reader may consult the recent detailed comment of Weber.— Weber assigns vss. 1-3, 6, 8, and ro b, c, d to Varuṇa ; and 4, 5, 7, 9, and ro a to Atharvan. Varuṇa has a mind to take back the cow which he gave to Atharvan, but gives up his intention at the request of Atharvan. Further reference to this legend seems to be made at vii. ro4. i. ¥] Possibly the copy from which this is set is a second i draft. J '

I. How unto the great Asura didst thou speak here? how, with shining manliness, unto the yellow (4âri) father ? having given, O Varuṇa, a spotted [cow] as sacrificial fee, thou hast with the mind intended (? cits) re-bestowal (?). i

The second half-verse is probably meant as what was spoken." The translation of. d implies Aufrecht's acute emendation (in Muir) of the reading to punarmaghatvdâm. The sense of punarmagha is very doubtful : Roth “ greedy"; Muir (Aufrecht) « to take Ś her back," and « revoking " ; neither seems to belong properly to the word, which ought Ś to mean something like (bountiful in return ': i.e. Varuṇa is expected to give back to 2 Atharvan the cow the latter has presented to him (or another and better one). One . se might conjecture in c vârupe ' to Varuṇa,' and understand câkits as 'impute' or ' expect. Ś Roth regards the verse as spoken by Varuṇa ; Muir, by Atharvan; the former is more acceptable. Ppp. begins karhâ diva asurâya bravâmaṇṅ karhâ, and reads pr(nz) inc. ¹ IR. takes kâr7 as 'wrathful.'

2. Not at pleasure am I a re-bestower ; for examination (?) do I drive home this spotted [cow] ; by what poesy (kâuya) now, O Atharvan, [art] thou [poet]? by what that is produced (jârâ) art thou jâtâvedas ? ef

The rendering of b implies the necessary and obvious emendation of sânz cake es (P.M. W. -k5ve) to sanrcâkse, infinitive. Kâmena seems taken adverbially, = 42m7ya, ¹ kâmam, kṅmaâr ; the god is not to be moved to counter-liberality by the mere desire of his ¹ g worshiper, but challenges the latter's claim on him. Jâṅaveâas, lit. ' having for posses- 3 sion whatever is produced (or born),' ¢all-possessor' B.P.M. accent Ghar van in c; one might emend to 474areâ : 'in virtue of what poetic merit art thou Atharvan? The i ¹ verse belongs of course to Varuna. Ppp. reads in b szṅpyccki and wpâjet. ¹

3. I verily am profound by poesy ; verily by what is produced I am ¹ Jjâtâvedas ; not barbarian (ââsâ), not Aryan, by his might, damageth (27) the course which I shall maintain.

Muir ascribes the verse to Atharvan; Roth, better, to Varuga ; the god asserts that it is he himself to whom wisdom and possession belong ; his worshiper is comparatively nothing. Ppp. begins with sarvasar: and reads mahitvar: in , and kanigya at the end. The Prat. (iv. 96) establishes the long 7 of mzṅâya as a padâa-reading. The Anukr. absurdly calls the verse a a7 kti, although it is an evident z-â57ubk, not less regular than ) a great proportion of the verses so called. [The se in c is easier rendered in German d than in English. J Ś

4. None else than thou is more poet, nor by wisdom (meâṅâ) more wise (dkṅra), O Varuṇa, self-ruling one (svadkâvant); thou knowest all gy these beings ; even that wily man (7âna) now is afraid of thee. : Ppp. reads in a vedṅâ anu (for medhâyâ), and has at end of b the more antique 59 form svadâhâvas; as second half-verse it gives : (vam aṅga viva janmani vertha v4 matan na (uj jano man bibkâyaṇ. SHE 5. Since thou verily, O self-ruling Varuṇa, knowest all births, O well. or conducting one —is there anything else beyond the welkin (râas)? is there anything below what is beyond, O unerring one (? amura) ? ¹t The version given implies that k72 is interrog. particle in c, d, as best suits the ¹ â answer in the next verse : else, ' what other is beyond ' etc. Aura in b is understood Ś as am7ra, as required by the meter: cf. v. I. 9. Ppp. again reads svaâkâvas in a; a and, in b and further, janma craddkhadant te kin: mena rajasas pare 'sti kim avarena ( avaram asṅra. The majority of mss. (B.P.M.H.s.m.O. etc. ; only E.I.LH.p.m.K. have ast) accent âsti at end of c. For the combination enâ parâs = beyond,' in 3d pada, ² see BR. iv. 494. I suggest for d, (Is there (274m) (anything behind, 4varam, i.e.) 4 Ś anything beyond that (enâ, substantive pronoun) which is beyond (pârena)?' I 6. There is one other thing beyond the welkin ; there is something, ¹ Ś" hard to attain, hitherward from what is beyond : this I Varuṇa, knowing it, proclaim to thee. Be the paṇâ's of degraded speech ; let the barba- : rians creep (sz) downward to the earth.

The translation implies emendation of varuna to vâru nak in c, which seems necessary, as the verse evidently belongs in Varuga's mouth ; both Roth and Muir so understand it. In d is implied aâkhâvacasas, which all the mss. read; alteration to -varcasas ‘ might be welcome, but is hardly called for. Ppp. is considerably different; it reads & ya ekam enâ rajasas pare 'sti pare kena âṅââakhyar: tyajan yat : tat tue acchovacasas ¹ : âasâ ya upa sarpantu riprâ. The meter of a would be rectified by omitting the super-eH fluous enâ ; that of b, by a like omission (which the Pâipp. text also favors), or, so far as the meaning is concerned, better by reading enṅ pârepa dur- etc. The description of the verse by the Anukr. as an aṅâakvari ( nough it still lacks one syllable of sixty) (: helps to authenticate the text as the mss. present it. . " g Whitney, on the revision, would doubtless have made clear his views as to b. Both ¹ sense and meter indicate that the enâ in a and the enâ in b are intrusions; they have

; 'blundered in from 5 c. Omitting them, I render: ⁴ There is one other thing beyond the gg welkin ; [and,] beyond [that] one thing, [is] something hard to get at (durpâcar cit) al [if you start] from this side [of them].'] ] I understand tat toe acckovacasas to mean merely that Ppp. reads rue for tz and acchovacasas for adkovacasaṅ — not that it omits ¹ the rest from ze to nzâ:r.

7. Since thou verily, O Varuṇa, speakest many reproachful things among (as to?) re-bestowers, do not thou, I pray, belong to (aâki-bk7) ¹ ee such gaṇts ; let not people call thee ungenerous (arâdhâs).

: The rendering implies emendation of 5474 to bkâs at end of c, which is made also by

Roth and Muir. The pada is corrupt in Pâipp. v : 8. Let not people call me ungenerous ; I give thee back the spotted [cow], O singer; come thou mightily (câc75his) to every song of praise (stotrâ) of mine, among all human regions (77).

Roth's suggested emendation of âiky7 at the end to vikZṣi ' settlers, tribes,' accepted by Muir, is unquestionably'an improvement of the text; Ppp. has unfortunately a different ¹ reading : 2 yâht janesu antar devesu manusesu riprâa. Diksu is read in Prat. iv. 34 c. i

9. Let uplifted (aa-yam) songs of praise of thee come, among all human i regions. Give now to me what thou hast not given me; thou art my suitable comrade of seven steps ;— -

That is, apparently, ready to go seven steps (or any indefinite distance) with me. Roth suggests as an improved reading #âattas ‘hast taken from me ' in c, and Muir so renders. Both words are alike, and equally, wrong grammatically, using the passive ¹ pple in the sense of an active ; 4daztam âsti would be correct, and at this Ppp. perhaps f points : dehi tar makyarn: yadi latoam asti yadyo nas saptapadak sakkâ sak. Ppp. i also begins with ya te stotrâni bandhanâni yani, and apparently has âiksu in b. i ro. Of us two, O Varuṇa, [there is] the same connection, the same ³ birth (77). 7

I know that which is of us two this same birth; I give that which I have not given thee ; I am thy suitable comrade of seven steps ;— gs

It seems necessary to divide this verse between the two speakers, and doubtless ¹ Roth's assignment of only the first pâda to Atharvan is better than Muir's of the first v EES half-verse. With Roth's division the #âu is called for in a as in b, and Roth's emendation to samânâ bândkhus, though it is read by Ppp. (whose testimony on such a pointis i of little value), is hardly acceptable ; better samâ nau. Ppp. reads also, for b, vada te vâitad vada: sama jak; and, for c, dadami tubkyar: yadi tarvan: ast; and it Ś omits d. The translation implies 42zrtam âsti as in 9.

II. A god, bestower of vigor on a singing god ; a sage (vâgra), of good ee wisdom for a praising sage. ee

Since thou, O self-ruling Varuna, hast generated father Atharvan, con- i nection of the gods, for him do thou make well-extolled generosity; our i i comrade art thou, and highest connection. g.

The first line is here (with Muir, and Zimmer, p. 205) taken as belonging to Varuṇa's reply given in the preceding verse. We must emend at the end either to ¹ paramâg ca or to bândhu. All the mss. leave stxvale in b unaccented, as if it were a verb-form. Ppp. reads svadkâvarn: in c, vigvaâevam at end of â, urvâyus kruuht ¹ prag- in e, and, for f, sakkhâ no sti varunag ca bandkuk. The Anukr. makes no account of the extra syllable in e. In b, the vertical over su is gone. |Pâdas cf are ¥ not part of the dialogue. J ¹

docs.title: 12. Apri-hymn : to various divinities
docs.text:
Lâṅgiras.— ekâdagar cam. trâi5tubkam. jâtavedasam. 3.paṅkti.) ¹

This is a RV. hymn (x. 110), and found also in VS. (xxix. 25-6, 28-36), MS. (iv. I3. 3, 5), and TB. (iii. 6. 3), with almost no variants from the RV. text. Paâipp. ll does not contain it. Kaug. applies it (45. 8: but the pratika, simply szmiââhas, might ¹ designate any one of several other verses in the text) in the vagâcamana ceremony, to accompany the offering of the omentum; and in the parvan sacrifices (=. 36) occurs a pâda resembling 2 b. In Vaâit. (ro. rr: the pratika is unambiguous) it goes with the et prayâya offerings in the pacutandla. ¹ Translated : by the RV. translators ; and Griffith, i. 205 ; Weber, xviii. 207.— See : Weber's general remarks ; and compare hymn 27, below.

I. Kindled this day in the home of man (mânus), thou, a god, O Jâta- ¹ vedas, dost sacrifice to the gods ; and do thou bring [them], understanding it, O thou of friendly might ; thou art a forethoughtful messenger, ob post. ¹Ś ³ The only variant in this verse is that MS. omits the peculiar and problematic accent a of vâha in c.

2. O Tantinapat (son of thyself?), do thou, anointing with honey

(mâdku) the roads that go to righteousness (7ââ), sweeten them, O well- ¹r tongued one; prospering (dk) with prayers (kz) the devotions (mân- Se mas) and the sacrifice, put (7) thou also among the gods our service

; The mss. accent, without assignable reason, svaâdâyâ in b, but the edition emends to . svadaya, in agreement with the other texts. ry The three Yajus-texts insert between this verse and the next an alternative invocation

to Narâgafsa (RV. vii. 2. 2).

3. Making oblation do thou, O Agni, to be praised and to be greeted,

come in accord with the Vasus. Thou art invoker (4677) of the gods, O ¹ youthful one (? yakovâ) ; do thou, sent forth, skilled sacrificer (yâ;zyâṅs), sacrifice to them.

Hjâhvâna in a is perhaps to be understood as passive (= Ś4uta), ‘receiving oblation.' There are no variants. The Anukr. absurdly calls this verse a gaṅâti, because, I by omitting resolutions of semivowels etc., it is capable of being read as jo syllables. rE The Anukr's of RV. and VS. both reckon it as tristubh.

4. The forward Śarkâs, through the fore-region of the earth, is wreathed

¹ on this dawn (vâstu), at the beginning (âgra) of the days; it spreads out

2 abroad more widely, pleasant to the gods, to Aditi. I ¹ ¹ (Forward and fore-region,' i.e. ‘eastward ' and east. All our mss. read v7 yase

¹ in b, but the edition makes the necessary emendation to -ze, in accordance with the four i Ś : other texts, and the translation given implies ze.

¹ 5. Expansive let them open (vi-gri) widely, like wives adorned for

² their husbands ; ye great, divine, all-furthering doors, be ye favorable to ¹ ( the advance of the gods.

Our pada-text divides the last word as suprâyanâ}, while the RV. pada has supra:

Ho ayanâṅ, the meter appears to indicate that suprayâṇâj is the true original reading.

6. Let Dawn and Night, dripping (? susoay-), worshipful, close, sit down here in the lair (yâni) — the two heavenly, great, well-shining i women, putting on beauty (cr7) with bright adornment. d

The other texts differ from ours only by accenting #pâke. [ The comment to Prat. ii. or cites suyvay as a case of reduplication; and BR. vii. 1142 connect it with su g (impel.' But see Weber.— He renders # by Heran.'

7. The (two) invokers of the gods, first, well-voiced, shaping (m2) the sacrifice for man (mânus) to sacrifice, urging forward at the councils (vidâtha) the (two) singers (kârâ), pointing out forward light through the fore region.

There are no variants. Griffith, after Mahidhara, takes the «light as the â4avaniya fire.

8. Unto our sacrifice let Bhârati come quickly, let Idâ, taking note here in human fashion ; let the three goddesses, well-working, sit upon I this pleasant barkis — [also] Sarasvatl. . &

The translation implies in d the reading sârasvatz, given by RV. VS. MS. ; TSB. rs I both ed's, Bibl. Ind. and Poona supports AV. in reading -7k, which, however, can ¹ ee hardly be anything but a blunder. The four other texts have at the end sadantu. All i Śa our mss. have manugyâr in b and so have all SPP's authorities J, and this form is ¹; authenticated by Prat. iv. 65, the comment explaining how it is derived from mzanuzgyavar. As being, therefore, the indubitable AV. reading, it should not have been ¹ ee altered in our edition to -soâ7, to conform with the four other texts, even though i doubtless a corruption of -swâr. SPP. also alters it.] [In c, correct âzwir to âevâr..

9. To him, god Tvashtar, who adorned (27) with forms these two generatresses, heaven-and-earth, [and] all existences, do thou today, ¹ O invoker, sent forth, skilled sacrificer, sacrifice here, understanding it. en

There are no variants. a ro. In thy way (tmânyâ) anointing them, pour thou down upon (upa- gr ava-syj) the track of the gods the oblations in due season; let the forest- ¹ tree, the queller (camitâr), god Agni, relish (sead) the oblation with honey, with ghee.

Forest-tree,' doubtless a big name for the sacrificial post. That the ‘queller' is a separate personage is shown by the plural number of the following verb. [E. Sieg discusses pârhas, Guruptjakaumudi, 97 ff. ; later, Oldenberg, ZDMG. lv. Goz. g

II. At once, when born, he determined (visnâ) the sacrifice; Agni became foremost of the gods; at the direction of this invoker, at the voice of righteousness (774), let the gods eat the oblation made with

The other texts read in ec the nearly equivalent praâââ. 1 : hail 1"

docs.title: 13. Against snakes' poison
docs.text:
[Garutman.— ekâdagarcam. takgakadevatyam. jâgatam : 2. âstârapankti ; 4, 7) 8. anugubh; ¹â 5. tristubh ; 6. pathyâpaṅkti ; 9. bhurij ; ro, rr. nicyd gâyatrr.] : Found (except vs. r) also in Pâipp. viii. (in the verse-order 3, 2, 4, 6, 5, 7-11). It ( is not quoted in Vaâit. ; but in Kâug. 29. I-14 all the verses are brought in in their 4 order, in connection with a ceremony for healing poison-wounds ; verse r (or the hymn) Gt is also used at 48. 9, in a witchcraft rite. [The London Anukr., in 6 places and for 7 ¹ Ś poison-hymns, gives Garutmâ (not -mân) as rye. I ⁴ : Translated : Griffith, i. 208 ; Bloomfield, 27, 425 ; Weber, xviii. 2rI. ¹ I. Since Varuṇa, poet of heaven, hath given [them] to me, with for- 4 midable spells (vâcas) do I dissolve thy poison ; what is dug, undug, and e attached (saktâ) have I seized; like drink (44) on a waste hath thy poison been wasted (wi-as). ¹ The epithets in c are of obscure application : probably buried in the flesh by the Śâe bite, or unburied but clinging. Gi ⁴ 2. What waterless poison is thine, that of thine have I seized in Ge these ; I seize thy midmost, thine upmost juice (râsa); also may thy lowest then disappear for fright. . Ge g ⁴ These in b is fem. (etâsu) ; doubtless 'waters' is to be supplied. Ppp. reads in a i padakam (for apod-), and in b ta t76hir. Yâz ta in a in our edition is a misprint for ¹ : yâr re. Kaug. (29.2) calls the verse grakaṇi. |For necar, see Skt. Gram. § 847 end,

¹ and § 854 b.

3. A bull [is] my cry, like thunder through the cloud (7âbkas) ; with thy formidable spell do I then drive it off (544%) for thee; I have i seized that juice of his with men}? ]; like light out of darkness let the ee sun arise. ¹ ⁴ ¹ One is tempted to emend nâbkasâ in a to -sas or -sânm, ' the thunder of the clouds.

Ppp. reads zzm (which is better) vacasa bâdhâitu te in b, grabkis for the strange ig nybhis Weber, 'krâftig' in c, and jyotise "va tamaso 'dayartu sâryak in 4. The i of

( iva is uncounted in the meter of d. Kaug. calls the verse prasarjani.

â 4. With sight I smite thy sight ; with poison I smite thy poison; die,

O snake, do not live; let thy poison go back against thee. ¹ : ¹ : All the mss. [including SPP's read Śkes at beginning of c, but our edition makes. ¹ the necessary emendation to âke. Ppp. has for a Śalena te balark hanmi its b is

Ś ² wholly corrupt; for c etc. it reads rsana kanmâ te vidam ahe marista ma jivi praty i . anveta va visa. As for d— the later Hindus thought that snake poison did not ⁴ ae hurt a snake; cf. Indische Spriche, 3ooI. But see the interesting experiments of Sir a Joseph Fayrer, in his Thanatophidia of India, London, 1874, p. 74-5. My colleague, gc Dr. Theobald Smith, Professor of Comparative Pathology, has most kindly examined for me the recent literature concerning the auto-toxic action of snake.venoms. The evi- Ge ay dence is not conclusive as yet, but points to the immunity of snakes to snake-poison.— fhe Cf. vii. 88, below. ances

5. O Kirâtan, O spotted one, O grass-haunter (?), O brown one! listen ye to me, O black serpents, offensive ones stand ye not upon the track l (?siâmân) of my comrade ; calling out (â-râvay), rest quiet in poison. d

It is hardly possible to avoid emending stzmânam in c to stkâmânam ' station ' or s7âmânam ' course,' from sz ‘run '— but not quotable J; Ppp. is very corrupt in c, i d, but seems to intend no variants. It reads wpatarni Śabkrav in a; our babkra is by Ś Prât. i. 81, and this passage is quoted in the comment on that rule. It further mutilates; to asâtalikâ in b. The accents in our text and SPP's ] on âsitâs and âlikâs are against all rule, and doubtless to be regarded as misreadings ; the translation implies their i absence. In c correct to sâkhyuh (accent-sign lost over 2). A number of our j mss. (P.M.H.I.O.) Land five of SPP's read miâ5é for vigé in â (and nâmise 'at a wink' would be an acceptable emendation) ; M.W. end with rabhadkvam. l Griffith identifies. kâirâta with karait, the Hindustâni name (now well known in the Occident) of an i awfully venomous little serpent. This would be most interesting, if certain ; but friend Grierson writes me that it is improbable on phonetic grounds. We should expect in Hind. 22ra. J =

6. Of the Timatan (?) black serpent, of the brown, and of the water- (1 less, of the altogether powerful (?), I relax the fury, as the bow-string of Ś ee a bow; I release as it were chariots.

The translation is as if the reading at end of c were manyṅm* The paâareading in c is sâarrâa-sakâsya, according to Prat. iii. 23. Ppp. has fzyimârasya in a, and in c upodakasya ' water-haunting,' which is better. Whitney would doubtless have revised this carefully. The divergences of the translators reflect the uncertainties of the exegesis. 'I slacken as it were the cars of the wrath of etc.— Griffith. tI release te (thee) from the fury of ' etc.— Bloomfield. (Des Asita . . des Manyu Streitwagen gleichsam spanne [ich ] mir ab' or 'die Streitwagen des Grimmes des Asita' etc.— Weber. For â, ' as the string from off (40a) the bow.'] * Ppp. reads manyunm.

[Mayobhṅ.— agâdacakam. Śrakmaâjâyâdevatyam. ânuṣtubkham : I—6. trigebh.]

Ppp. reads -karas and -Śhuvas in c, and : apas in d. The first pâda is properly jagarz, though the Anukr. takes no notice of the fact.

2. King Soma first gave (pra-yam) back the Brahman's wife, not Gat bearing enmity ; he who went after [her] was Varuṇa, Mitra; Agni, ¹ invoker, conducted [her] hither, seizing her hand.

To be seized by the hand indeed is the pledge (?ââkâ) of her, if one a has said [she is] the Brahman's wife"; she stood not to be sent forth for i a messenger : so is made safe (gupitâ) the kingdom of the Kshatriya. The misfortune, descending (avapad) upon the village, of which ¹ they say this is a star with disheveled hair" —as such, the Brahman's wife burns up the kingdom, where hath gone forth a hare (?gagâ) accom- ¹ panied with meteors (z2kuṣt-). t ¹ That is, such apparent portents are really the woman, that has been misused. 4 service ; he becomes one limb of the gods ; by him Brihaspati discovered the wife, conducted by Soma, like the sacrificial spoon, O gods. ¹ ¹ In d RV. hâs the doubtless better reading devâs, cas the gods [discovered] the sacriar ¹ ³ ficial spoon.' ¹ ee led away; she makes (â%z) discomfort (durâkâ) in the highest firmament

W., which often agree in a misreading) give 4panârâ (instead of 74-) in c, and this is to be regarded as the proper AV. text, and is implied in the i translation ; our edition reads #pan-, with RV. The Anukr. does not notice the deficient syllable in a (unless we are to syllabize br-âk-, which is very harsh). Ppp. combines Śrâkmaṇe "va in a, and puts the verse at i the end of the hymn. i

RV. has utâ instead of the repeated adadus in b; and it gives the better reading krnvânâs in c. And in both points Ppp. agrees with it but with zo for nas]. i rr. 9. The Brahmans have sharp arrows, have missiles ; what volley if Ś (cara"yṅ) they hurl, it is not in vain ; pursuing (anu-kâ) with fervor and with fury, they split him down even from afar.

Ppp. has z zzya at the end, instead of exam. Pâda b is of course jagatr. i ro. They that ruled, a thousand, and were ten hundreds, those Viitahavyas, having devoured the cow of the Brahman, perished (parâ-bh7). ¹

rr. The cow herself, being slain, pulled down those Vâitahavyas, who cooked the last she-goat of Kesaraprabandh3 (?). ¹

The second half-verse is totally defaced in Ppp. The pada-text reads in d caramae a âjâm ; the accent is anomalous, and the sense unacceptable ; Ludwig's translation, i ue ¹ ¹ « letztgeboren," implying emendation to carama-jâm, suggests a welcome improvement ¹ of the text. docs.text:

The mss. make awkward work of writing 4sauvânâs ; nearly all have ksupie- only Bp.² ;rpue-, and E. ksuw-; but there cannot well be any question as to the true reading. 2. Like a lion hath thundered the wooden one, stretched (vâ-âarâF), like a bull roaring at a longing cow; virile (vfyan) [art] thou, impotent thy rivals ; Indra-like [is] thy vehemence (gâṣma), overpowering hostile plotters.

The translation implies emendation to wâcâtâs in b, as made in our edition ; the mss. vâsitâm. All the sarṅhiâta-mss. (after their usual custom: see my Sk. G7. 232) abbreviate in a to -#7â2ruw-, and many of them (P.M.W.E.H.O.) have the misreading -nidkruo-. The pada-text does not divide âruvâyak, but the case is quoted in the comment to Prat. iv. 3. Found (vidânâ) suddenly (sâhasz) like a bull in a herd, do thou, seeking kine, bellow (rz) at [them], winning booty; pierce thou with : pain the heart of our adversaries ; let our foes, leaving their villages, go urged forth (pra-cyṅ).

Ppp. reads in a yâthan: saha sa-, and in c viâdhi. The Anukr. notes no irregularity in the verse, although d is clearly a jagarrpâda, and to resolve vidk7a in c is contrary to all analogy. 4. Wholly conquering the fighters, shrill-crying, do thou, seizing those that are to be seized, look abroad on many sides ; respond (? â-gz7), O drum, devout, to the voice of the gods; bring the possession of our foes.

Vedhâs is as superfluous to the sense in c as it is redundant in meter. The Anukr. takes no notice of the irregularity, nor of the deficiency in a (777% ua- being very harsh, and not found in RV.). The pada-text reads gF kya) in b ; pF tanâs is apparently to be understood with it. The voice of the gods (or of heaven, Jâfwr) is apparently the thunder.

5. Hearing the uttered (gra-yam) voice of the drum speaking, let the woman, suppliant, noise-wakened, run to her son, seizing his hand — our enemy, frightened in the conflict of deadly weapons.

One might conjecture in a grayatâm ' of [us] advancing. This verse and 6 and 9 are really the only regular f7457u5ks of the hymn.

6. Mayest thou first (pâroa), O drum, speak forth thy voice ; on the back of earth speak thou, shining (ruc) ; opening wide the jaws (jaŚk) on the army of our enemies, speak thou clearly, O drum, pleasantly (szṅâtâvaâ). Ś That is, ‘what is pleasant to us,' apparently. P#rva in a might also mean ¢in front, ( in our van.' Ppp. reads in a, b visakasva catrân: vada laku rocamânatk ; and it makes the second half-verse exchange places with 8 c, d. : V 7. Let there be noise between these two firmaments (nâbhas); sever- ¹ ally let thy sounds (âkvant) go swiftly ; roar at [them], thunder, truculent (?), resounding (glokak}t) unto the victory of our friends, a good partizan. 70 Mitra in mitratṅrya has to be taken as subjective instead of objective genitive. Itis ŚŚ only with difficulty (iantu ?) that b can be made metrically complete unless we read (4a ( for fe]. Ppp. reads at the end ¢raâdṅr. Bloomfield discusses uzpâpâna, AJP. xâ. 441. ] ¹ 8. Made by devices (gk), may it speak forth its voice; excite thou Śâr the weapons of the warriors ; allied with Indra, call in the warriors ; by y friends smite mightily down the enemies. Sat ⁴ By devices ': ie., apparently, with art. Emendation of vadari to vadâsi in a is sal Ś very desirable ; Ppp. has the 2d pers. Śkarasva instead ; and, as noted above, it substi- ⁴ eg tutes our 6 c, d for the second half-verse. There is a syllable lacking in a. a 9. A vociferating herald (?pravadâ), with bold army, making proclaim in many places, sounding through the villages, winning advantage, knowing the ways, do thou distribute (vi-4r) fame to many in the [battle] of two kings. ⁴ The verse seems to relate to the proclamation of victory and of the desert of those ¹ ¹ to whom it is due : see Roth, Festgruss an Bâkthngk, p. 99. Ppp. reads prasraveṇo for pravads in a, and b54aja for kara in 4d. For vayâna, Pischel, Ved. Stud. i. 297. ro. Aiming at advantage, conquering good things, very powerful, ¹ conquering a host, thou art sharpened by bŚrâhman; as the pressing- Gr stone on the [soma-] stalks in the press, do thou, O drum, dance on ¹ [their] possession, seeking booty (gauyân). . Ś The translation implies emendation of gauyâm (read by all our mss.) in d to ga"yân, ⁴ Ś as made in our edited text; but gazyâm vedas might perhaps mean their possession in or Ś kine. Prat. ii. 62 prescribes creyaṅkeras (not wask-). Bp. alone reads ââkr 7} in c, ¹ : which Pet. Lexx. prefer; aâyis is, to be sure, superfluous beside grâwâ, and can hardly Ś be translated. Ppp. has, for b, mâtraṅ daâhânas ruisito vigpagcit; and it reads adhz el (not "7kṅ7) in d. The first pada is defective, unless we make the violent resolution gr-e- 0 at the beginning ; in the third we have to read 'va or '7r7} J. Er 11. Overpowering foes, overpowering and putting down, overpower- . ing hostile plotters, seeking kine, overpowering, up-shooting, bring forth thy voice as a speaker (vâgwoâṅ) his discourse (mântra) ; speak up force t (?45) here in order to the conquering of the host. ¹ 2 Sâṅgran- in our text is a misprint for sâṅgrâm-. Ppp. offers no variants. The Ś4 words gatrâsâr and azsâz (both unchanged in pada-text) fall under Prat. ii. 82; iii. 1 a iv. 70. Gavâsaṇa (p. goe4saṇalk) is by Prat. ii. 23. The second pada is defective by 2 one syllable.

12. Stirring (-yu) the unstirred, going oftenest into contests, con- i quering scorners, going in front, unsubduable, made safe by Indra, noting counsels ()oidârâa), burning the hearts of our adversaries, go; thou quickly.

The abbreviated combination kyâyo- for kyââyo- has led here, as at i. 22. I, to the pada-reading kredyâtanak in 4. The defective meter of a (which is not to be honestly removed by resolving cy into c) makes the reading suspicious (perhaps sam âdane ?). i Ppp. has prtanâsât for puractâ in b, and kZpras for gupras in c. The metrical structure is very irregular, though the right number of syllables can be if forced out, if the divisions of pâdas be overridden ; the Anukr. takes no heed. Read in c mâtrân in our text (an accent-sign lost over 777). i

Let the drums, with bow-string noises, yell toward all (yâs) the ² quarters —the armies of our enemies going conquered in troops. â : Or jyâghoṣâs (as indicated by its accent) is independent noun, the noises of the ² bow-strings.' Various points in this verse are very doubtful; in a, a vocative vâgaâa seems much more probable, if only a suitable meaning could be found for it; and, if so, one may suspect the same character in Śk7riyâvaya (perhaps bhuryâvaya ' painful,' connected with Zor) ; the translation is mechanical, and follows the traditional text, since emendation yields so little satisfaction. Ppp. reads vakada for vi gada. In nistâkvarim is doubtless to be seen a word-play on tzkman, but the sense is only conjectural ; the word is quoted as an example under Prat. ii. 85.

7. O fever, go to the Mâjavants, or to the Balhikas, further off ; seek the wanton Ctdra woman; her, O fever, do thou shake up a bit (72).

Some of our mss. (O.R.K.) read #47s in d, as if the word were t4n instead of tn. Ppp. has giriṅz gaccha girâjâa st râutena mâyuso gra) ; dasin yityuccha prapharvyar: 137s ta kman nt "va dhunuki.

' Thy connection,' i.e. ' those with whom thou hast a right to meddle '; 'fields,' i.e. c territories ': d, these territories here belong to some one else.” Pada b is corrupt in Ppp. ; for â, it reads "zyaksetrâni vâyasâam, and it has further on this verse : nârkavindân nârvidalan nâdiyarn rvatukâvatin : praia ni takmane brṅmo 'nyaksetr an: vE yumaâanz. The pada-reading in c is prasârthak ; prâ-ar- would better suit the meaning given, (ready to set out,' lit. ‘having an object in front' (comm. to PB. xi. 1.6, prakarsena iyarti gacchalr ti prârtho 'nagvân ry. Ppp. begins with yas for yat, and leaves azko unelided in a. Most of our mss. have ¹7bki sma in d.

rI. Do not thou make them thy companions —the Śalâsa, the cough, the adyugâ (?) ; come not back hitherward from there: for that, O fever, I appeal to thee.

Zimmer (who translates vss. ro-12, at pp. 381-5) understands zâyugâ in b as 'sich anschliessend '; Ludwig as 'angestrengt,' qualifying kâsâm as adjective ; perhaps it means hiccough'; balâsa may be 'expectoration.' 12. O fever, together with thy brother the 2alâsaz [and] thy sister the 4 cough, together with thy cousin the scab (pâmân), go to yon foreign people.

Ppp. begins with this verse a new hymn, and has, for c, 6, apârz bhkrâtrâty vyena nagye "to marayanmm abhi. Read in our text at end of b sâṅâ (an accent-sign slipped out of place). Without note of variants, SPP. gives pagmâ in both texts instead of our i pâmnâ, and our H. reads pâgmânâ. In spite of the possibility of taking gâgsaâ as instrumental (cf. draghmâ, ram“, JAOS. x. 533), we must deem gânznâ the true reading and pâpmâ a blunder, due perhaps to the frequent collocation gapmân bhrâzryya,. ' AB. etc. ] Ś

The fever of the third day, of two days out of three, the constant, and the autumnal, the cold, the hot, that of the hot season, that of the rainy season, do thou cause to disappear. 4 ( In a the intermittent phases of the disease, of course, are referred to. The gada-text divides sadamedâmn in b, perhaps lit. 'ever-binding.' Pâda c lacks a syllable; the y Anukr. takes no notice of it; we might add ca at the end. Ppp. has in b Xâyanar ¹ instead of câradam ; and in c vigvagâradarm instead of (ar râram.

The translation implies in c the easy emendation to grâyan (pra-isyaṅ) ; the ¹ Ś accent and pada-reading (pracegyân) view the word as future from gra-i; the translators SSS assume -gyânt, and reach no acceptable sense. The comm. to Prât. ii. rr correctly e; quotes the case as one of the assimilation of final 2 to initial 7 The Anukr. this time takes no notice of the extra syllable in c if we should read 77a instead of 'va. docs.title: 24. To various gods as overlords
docs.text:
( [4tharoan.—saptadaakarn. braṅmakarmâtmadevatyam. atigâkvaram : I-I]. 4p. ati4akvari;;

II. gakvart ; X5-r7. 3-2 (15, I6. bh urig alijagati ; 7. Vir Gy (akvarz).]

I Not metrical. ] In Pâipp. xv. is found a corresponding piece, but one differing con- d siderably in detail ; it contains counterparts to our vss. I, 2, 4, 7-12, I4, I5, I, but not at all in the same order, and interspersed with nine other verses of similar tenor (1. mitrah prekivyâṇ ; 6. vasus samvatsarasya; 7. samvarsara [iṅnâm; 1. visnuṇ Ś parvatânâm ; Y2. tuastâ râpaRâm ; 5. sanudâro nadtnâm ; v6. parjanya osadkmzrm,; ¹ SE ¹7. br kaspatir dzvânâm ; 18. prajâpatik prajanâm)y. Similar passages occur also in kl other texts : thus, in TS. iii. 4. 5 (and the part corresponding to our 15-17 is repeated ¹; again, with slight variations, at iv. 3.32; and the same part, with variations, is found five times as a refrain in MS. ii. 7. 20), in PGS. i. 5. ro (which closely follows TS. iii. ¹ 4.5), and in CCS. iv. ro. I, 3 (with nothing corresponding to vss. r5-r7). The hymn is ¹ used by Kâug. in a royal coronation (17. 30), in the nuptial ceremonies (78. r1), and in — the Gjyarantra (137. 42). And many of the verses appear also in Vaâit., with oblations ‘ to the various divinities mentioned, in different ceremonies : thus, in the Zgrayana, vs. 7 (8.7); in the caturmâsyâni, vss. 1-3, 6, 7 (8. 13), 4.(8. 22), 9 (9. 27); in the agnâstoma, vss. 8 (19.2), 5 (19.3), II (19. II).

Translated : Griffith, i.228 ; Weber, xviii. 260. — Cf. Weber's Râjastya, Berliner AP. 1893, p. 142. ¹

I. Savitar (‘the impeller ') is overlord of impulses; let him favor (a2) me, in this worship (5râkhmaṇ), in this rite (kârman), in this representation

(purodhâ), in this firm-standing, in this intent, in this design, in this benediction (7s), in this invocation of the gods: hail! ¹ ¹ This is the tenth item in Ppp. ; TS. (with PGS.) and CCS. have the same. The Ppp. : order of actions is different, and includes fewer members : brakman, karman, purodṅz, ¹ âevakati, Bkâti, âgis (âgisas so ¹ twice svâkâ); TS. and PGS. give brâhman, ksatrâ, 5 acts, puroâhâ, kârman, devâhṅti; MS., brâhman, purodhâ, kârman, Śâs, devâhuti; I CCS., brakman, kyatra, harman, â;is, pratisthâ, devakuti. The Anukr. text is in part & confused and doubtful, and the inaccuracies of its metrical definitions of the parts of the (i hymn are not worth tracing out and noting. In our edition, the accent mark under the : first syllable of Zk7zyâm is a misprint, and to be removed. f : 2. Agni is overlord of forest-trees ; let him favor etc. etc. i : This is the eighth item in Ppp. In TS. and PGS., Agni is made lord of beings i (Phṅrâ); in CCS., of the earth.
  1. Heaven-and-earth are overlords of givers; let them favor etc. etc. ¹ ¹ Literally, care overladies' (47kipatnr). Neither Ppp. nor the other texts have any- Ś i thing corresponding to this verse. As in a number of other similar cases, the mss.

g p g we make very awkward work of writing the 77 of dârFpâm, the majority (Bp.P.M.W.H.E.T.)

giving instead re, one (I.) Ś7, one (K.) 77, and a few (O.D.R.) correctly 77; the edited text has wrongly 7a. ¹ 4. Varuṇa is overlord of the waters ; let him favor etc. etc.

This item stands second in Ppp. ; TS. has it also; but in CCS., Varuṇa is addressed as overlord of ordinances (âharma).

5. Mitra-and-Varuṇa are overlords of rain ; let them favor etc. etc. 4 a This item is wanting in all the other texts. The mss: all read v7 Ś2yâ 'dhipe (p. vrstyâ : ââhip-), the error doubtless originating in a double saṅzdki, such as is extremely frequent in Ppp.

6. The Maruts are overlords of the mountains ; let them favor etc. etc.

According to Ppp. (11) and TS., Vishṇu is overlord of the mountains; TS. sets the â Maruts over the troops ( gana), and CCS. gives them no place. ¹ ¹ 7. Soma is overlord of plants ; let him favor etc. etc.

Ś In Ppp. (74) Soma is overlord of milks (payasâm); in TS. and CCS., of herbs.

8. Vayu is overlord of the atmosphere; let him favor etc. etc.

¹ Here Ppp. (3) and the other texts give the same overlordship.

¹ 9. The sun (sya) is overlord of sights (or eyes : eâksus) ; let him favor etc. etc.

In Ppp. (4), the sun is called overlord of heaven (â7v); and so also in TS.; but

CCS. sets him over the asterisms.

¹ ro. The moon is overlord of asterisms; let him favor etc. etc.

This item comes fifth in Ppp.; TS. has it also; in CCS. the moon is not mentioned, a : while the asterisms, as noted above, are put under the sun.

11. Indra is overlord of heaven; let him favor etc. etc.

In Ppp. (9) Indra is overlord of acts or rites (Śâ4rman); in TS. and CCS., of chiefs (esthâ).

12. The father of the Maruts is overlord of cattle ; let him favor etc. etc.

In Ppp. (13) and in TS., this overlordship is ascribed, equivalently, to Rudra; it is wanting in CCS. fl

13. Death is overlord of creatures (prâjâ) ; let him favor etc. etc.

In Ppp. (18) it is Prajâpati instead of death ; and so also in CCS.; TS. has nothing corresponding.

This item is number 19 in Ppp. ; but in CCS. it is wanting; and in TS. Yama is set over the earth. Here, again, the reading pitrenâm is found in one ms. (Bp.). Additional items in TS. are bf haspârir brâhmanaṅ, mitrâṅ satyânarm (CCS. the same), samudrâh srotyânâam, ânnar sâmrâjyanam, tvâsta rEpâpnant (CCS. tv. sarmidhârz i râpaRant) ; CCS. has only those already given.

Is. The upper (pâra) Fathers—let them favor etc. etc. Ee

The translation implies emendation to zazâs at the beginning of vs. 17, as the sense seems to require, and as the other texts suggest. (iii. 4. 5: and PGS.), pttaral ¹ as pitamahâh pare 'vare tâtâs tatamahâ ihâ ma etc.; TS. iv. 3. 33, pitârah pitamakâṅ pâre vare té naj etc., with which MS. agrees. Two of our mss. Ludwig understands the last epithet as meaning belonging to us both," which is not impossible ; Weber, der doppelt schafft'; it is literally ' possessing what is of both. docs.title: 26. Accompanying a sacrifice
docs.text:

I, in a ceremony of consecration of a new house, and given x in the paddhati (see note to Kaug. ro. r) among the pustika mantras. Used in Vâit. ¹ 16. 6 in counteracting an enemy's soma-offering (agnistoma) ; and vs. 12 a, bin 19. 4, also in the agnistoma, with a cup for the Agvins. Neither treatise teaches us anything. whatever as to the real meaning of the hymn. The matter is in considerable part i metrical, though in part also too irregular to be so called. ¹
