I. The sacrificial formulas (yâjus) at the sacrifice, the fuel, haill let Agni, foreknowing, here join for you.

Or tjoin (yj) you.' Join" is probably used in the sense of (duly use or apply' i (Ludwig, "anwenden "). The verse is plainly composed of two f2â5125k pâdas, but the Anukr. refuses to resolve szâkâ, and so reckons only 21 syllables.

2. Let the heavenly impeller (savâtâr), the bull (makiṣâ), foreknowing,

Ppp. reads, after prajanan, yajṅe sayujas svâkhâ. The Anukr., in this and many of beat the following verses, simply counts 2o syllables (6777. bratz), without heeding the fact : i that each contains a Zâ57ubkh pâda. : 3. Let Indra, foreknowing, at this sacrifice join songs and revels ll (kthâmadâ), the well-joined ones (?): hail Lo Ppp. reads and combines sayṅjas so-. The mechanical definition of the Anukr.

implies a division into 774-8 syllables. There is some blundering of the mss. over ( i ukthamadâni, B. appearing to read ukya-m-, and P.W. uktâm-. Suyṅjas, here and in ¹ vss. 7-11, may be genitive ' of the well-joined one; it does not agree in gender with 4 : the nouns that precede [ aside from Zo J. ( 4. The directions (prâisâ) at the sacrifice, the notices (nivid) : hail Ś taught by the wives, carry ye here, joined. ² ; Ppp. reads prâisa nividâ priyo yajunsi ci tar etc. ¹ 5. The meters (c4ândas) at the sacrifice, O Maruts : haill as a mother ¹ her son, fill ye here, joined.

The meter and its treatment by the Anukr. are the same as in the case of vs. I. ¹ 6. Here hath come Aditi, with 2arkâs, with sprinkling [waters], extending the sacrifice : hail : A perfectly good pair of frâsfubh padas.

7. Let Vishṇu join variously the fervors (44pas) at this sacrifice, the well-joined ones: hail l

Ppp. again gives sayujas so-. i 8. Let Tvashtar now join variously the forms at this sacrifice, the well-joined ones: hail!

All the sa7khitâ mss. read râpâ asmiân, as in our text, the pada-text having r#pâṇ ‘ Ppp, on the other hand, gives baṅuâhâ virâpa 'smin. Probablyit is a case of anoma- ¹ lous saṅâki (with hiatus), which should have been included in Prat. iii. 34 (see the note to that rule); but one may also conjecture that the true reading is Śakudhâ ¹ ¹nurâpak. kt 9. Let Bhaga join now for him the blessings (4s); at this sacrifice let him, foreknowing, join the welljoined ones: hail ¹ Ppp. combines asmâ 'smin, and reads sayujas, as above. The Anukr. evidently ¹e reckons three padas, of rr +78 syllables.

ro. Let Soma join variously the milks (pâyas), at this sacrifice, the welljoined ones: hail i 11. Let Indra join variously the heroisms, at this sacrifice, the welljoined ones : hail

12. O Agvins, come ye hitherward with worship (ârâhman), with vâsar-utterance increasing the sacrifice. O Brihaspati, come hitherward with worship ; this sacrifice [is] heaven (svâr) here for the sacrificer hail

Ppp. has instead, for d, yajṅan: vaya svaritaṅ yajamânâya âhekhi suâhâ. The Anukr. would have us read the last pada as 15 syllables, and calls the verse a Jjagatr because amounting to 48 syllables, though the first three pâdas are regularly fristubâ. d

With this hymn ends the fifth znuvâka, of 5 hymns and 69 verses; the Anukr. cita- 4 tion is navâa "paraj ; and Bp.D. add further agara saste navâ para (Bp. -rar ca ca ¹nuvâkak).

docs.title: 27. Apri-hymn : to various divinities
docs.text:
[Brakman. —dvâdacakam. &gneyam. I. byhatigarbhâ tristubh ; a. 2-6. simnâm bhuriganustubk ; 3. 2:9. Gri bykatr ; 4. 2:9. sâmni bhurighy hati ; 5. 2-6. sâmnr trigtubh ; 6. 22.

virây nama gâyarri ; 7. 2-p. sâmni brkati (imâ [2—y ?] ekâvasânâk); 8. samstârapaṅkti ; 9. 6:6. anugtubgarbhâ parâtiagati ; ro-ra. purangṇik.]

This peculiar and half-metrical Z57Fhymn occurs also in several Yajur-Veda texts namely, in VS. (xxvii. i1—=22), in TS. (iv. I. 8), and in MS. (ii. 12. 6) ; further, in K. (xviii. 17), and (acc. to Schroeder's note) in Kap.S. The versions in VS. and TS. agree very closely throughout, in readings and in division; there is in all the verses a more or ¹ less imperfect metrical structure, of three zriszubk-like pâdas to a verse. MS. also in general agrees with these, but has an inserted passage in its vs. 5 which dislocates the - division of vss. 2-4. Ppp. has the same hymn in ix, and follows pretty closely the Ś Se Yajus-version. In our text the proper division is thrown into great confusion, and there rT are many readings which are obviously mere corruptions. The Anukr. supports our mss. at all points. The division of VS. and TS., as being necessary to any understand- : ing of the hymn, is noted in brackets in the translation below.

The hymn is not used as an zp7Fhymn in the liturgical literature, but is quoted in l Kâug. (23.7) in the ceremony of consecration of a new house, and again (45.8), in the vagâcamana rite, to accompany (with the kindred hymn v. r2) an offering of the omen- ; tum of a cow; while (19. 1, note) the padâkati reckons it among the puṣtika mantras. ⁴ ¹ Vss. r and 2 (with the division as in our text) are used by Vait. (10.13, 12) in the pagubandha ceremony. a ¹ Translated : Ludwig, p. 434; Griffith, i. 232:— Weber, xviii. 269, gives a general es : introductory comment to the hymn, but leaves it, on account of ' the numerous mis- ³ ¹ divisions and corruptions of this, its Atharvan version," untranslated. Cf. hymn 12 of et this book.

I. Uplifted becomes his fuel, uplifted the bright burnings of Agni, ¹ most brilliant ; of beautiful aspect, with his son, —J2.] son of himself ¹ (tânânâpâr), âsura, many-handed,— Ś

All the Yajur-Veda texts agree in ending the verse with the third pada, and in reading at the end suprârikasya sânâh ; of this our text is a palpable corruption, and appar-. ently made after the addition to this verse of the following pâda, in order to help their g connection. Ppp. also has -kasya sânos, and at the end of a bkavantu ; it and the Yajus-texts read vivâvedas instead of ³âṅripanis. The description of the verse by the Anukr. if we pronounce ârdhuâ in a] is correct, counting the second pâda as of 9 syllables. [ : z [2 b]. A god among gods, the god anoints the roads with honey ¹ (mâdhu), with ghee. ¹ The end of this verse is the proper end of vs. 2; MS., however, adds to it the first tt pâda of our 3; and it reads for a devâ devebhyo devayânan. In b, VS.MS. have anaktu; TS., 4 'nakti; and VS. TS. set the avasâna-mark next before pazââs. ¹ 3. With honey he attains the sacrifice, pleased, the praised of men (nârâgâṅsa), Agni the well-doing, the heavenly impeller (savârâr), having all choice things. ed All the other texts, including Ppp., read in a pr7nânâs, of which our p7ââ- is doubt- : less to be regarded as a blundering corruption. VS. TS. have before it zaksase ; and, F² Ś in b, agne, with interpunction after it; Ppp. omits agne (or agnik) ; MS. adds as third â pâda the first pada of our and the other texts' vs. 4. Our pada-text rightly divides the if verse into three padas ro: 8: 9 J, though the Anukr. acknowledges only two. 4. Here he cometh with might (gâvas) unto the various ghees, praising, he the carrier, with homage,— ² Ś It needs the first part of the next verse to end off this, and the other texts so divide. “ They have also the much easier reading ghz téna for ghy tâ cit; Ppp. gives gh tena râe . vaknir namasâa 'gnin sruco etc. (adding 5 a). VS. TS. have a single interpunction ¹ after nâmasâ ; MS. makes its verse out of our 4 b and j a, b, with interpunction after 5 a. [VS.TS.MS. accent 7znâ.

5 [4 c]. Agni, unto the spoons, at the sacrifices (zâ7varâ), the profferings (7a2yâj). [5.] May he sacrifice his greatness, Agni's,— tl The Yajus-texts have at the beginning agnâm (also Ppp. : see under vs. 4), and later prayârsu (which the TS. pada-text divides prayârosu ; ours gives pracyâksu). MS's , verse is made of ours with our 4 b prefixed.

6 [5 bl. [He] crossing (?) among pleasant profferings ; both the Vasus stood and the greater bestower of good (uâs).

This whole verse in our text is corrupt, and the translation, of course, only a mechanical one. The Yajus-texts have sâ zn (TS. I) manârâ suprayâsak (TS. mandrâsu ² i rayâsak : this variation shows how uncertain the tradition was as to the sense of the i passage) ; and MS. makes here the insertion spoken of above, reading suprayâsa stâriman : barbâso mitrâmakâj ; all then finish the verse with vâsug céristho vasuâhâi tamag ca. Ppp. is spoiled, but appears to read at the beginning svenamindrask. The I makers of our texts perhaps understood -âââtaras as plural of -7haty ; the paâadivision vasuedhâtaras is specially prescribed by Prat. iv. 45. The metrical definition i concerns only the number of syllables : 8+12=20. Ppp. ends with -7ztamag ca. ] be ¹ 7.16]. The heavenly doors all defend always after his course (vrazâ) — ² This verse is doubtless corrupt in its second half; the Yajus-texts, and also Ppp., 1 read instead vratâ dadante agnâṅ (Ppp. 'gneṅ); and MS. has before it w4vâ, and I Ppp. wived. The Anukr. ignores the evident fristubh character of a.

8 [6 c]. Lording it with Agni's domain of wide expansion, [7.] dripping, worshipful, close, let dawn and night favor this our inviolable (? adkvarâ)

sacrifice.

The other texts (including Ppp.) read -wyacasas, omit agnâs and read pâtyamânâs in a; and they have an entirely different b, namely Ś¢ asya yâsane divye nâ yénâu ; what our text substitutes was found as v. rz. 6 a above. The Anukr. name for the meter, samstarapankri, is wholly misapplied, since it has to be read as r2+ 11: 847.

9 [8]. O heavenly invokers, sing ye unto our uplifted sacrifice (adkvarâ) with Agni's tongue ; sing in order to our successful offering. [9.] Let the three goddesses sit upon this ba7kts, Idâ, Sarasvati, Bharati, the great, besung.

We have here two complete verses combined into one; but the division goes on after this correspondingly in all the texts. The three Yajus-texts, and Ppp., begin with J2tzya kotâra (the accent kâ?âras in our version is against all rule), and MS. inserts inzâm y after zrdhvâm in a; for b, c they read (ner jihvâm abhi (but MS. jikvâ "5ht) gr uttam 4 Śrnutâm nak svistim (MS. -fam) ; further on they have saâantu for tan: (but MS. instead syonâm); near the end, VS.TS. put maht after bhârarz; MS. has a sign of interpunction after malt; Ppp. reads makâbhârati. The pâda tisrâ devir etc. is the same with RV. iii. 4. 8 4 (which reads sadantu). The definition of the Anukr. fits the meter very badly ; the pada-text notes only 5 padas, nor is a division into 6 well possible ; they would count rr +948 : rx +14=53, mechanically a bhurig atijagati. to. That wonderful seminal fluid (zrâpam) of ours, abounding in food, = O god Tvashtar, abundance of wealth, release thou the navel of it. i=

The other texts (including Ppp.) omit deva and read toâsya (but MS. fuâstar), add- Śe5 ing after it suvâzyam ¥; all also have at the end asmâ instead of the senseless z5yâ, and all but MS. have gyarn for gya; their mark of interpunction is set after suvâ7y an (or before 7âyâs). Compare also RV. ii. 40. 4; iii. 4.9. Our Bp. reads in a, by an oversight, 4dṅhum (emended in Bp. to 4âŚhutam); but D.K. have ârebhutarmn as pada-text. This and the two following verses have small right to be called pzrazsniṅ ; this one counts 11: 8-+7=26 syllables. Read at the end in our text asyâ (an accent-sign slipped out of place). Ś But TS. suvâram. i

11. O forest-tree, let thou loose, bestowing ; let Agni [as] quellr willingly sweeten the oblation for the gods. ¹ te

Ppp. reads sumanâ for tmanâ ; also, at the end, s#ââyati, with the Yajus texts. The latter also have (except MS.) âzvâsn for devebkyas, and after it they all put their mark of interpunction. The Yajus and Ppp. version of the last pada is identical with ¹ RV. iii. 4. ro b save that RV. has (awâs]. This ⁴puranspik" counts II : 9+7=27 syllables.

12. O Agni, haill make thou, O Jâtavedas, the sacrifice for Indra; let all the gods enjoy this oblation.

The Yajus-texts put the pause in its proper place before vvz. For yajṅdm, TS. VS. read kaṇyâm, and MS. has devâbhyas ; Ppp. has Śââgam. This puraunspik" counts (if we divide the last two pâdas as indicated in the pada-text) 11 : 9-+7=27 syllables.

docs.title: 28. With an amulet of three metals : for safety etc
docs.text:
⁴ [A har van. — caturdacarcam. trivydâevatyam (agnyâdin mantroktân devân samprârthya trivy- : : tam astâur). trâi|tubham : 6. 5p. atigakvari ; J, 9, Io, ra. kakummatyanugtubkh ; 13. puraugpîṅ.]

The second half of r is prose. ] Found also (except vs. z and vss. 12-14) in ¹ Paipp. ii. Used by Kâug. twice, in company with i.g and i. 35, in a ceremony (11. 19) b ; for obtaining one's desires and in one (52. 20) for winning splendor; and vss. I, I2-I4 t¹ in one (58. ro, 11) for gaining length of life. ¹ Translated : Ludwig, p. 387; Griffith, i. 234; Weber, xviii. 271. ¹ I. Nine breaths with nine he combines (? sam-maâ), in order to length I of life for a hundred autumns; in the yellow (kârita), three; in silver, three ; in iron (?âyas), three— enveloped with fervor. ¹ Yellow,' doubtless 'gold.' Ppp. reads râjasâ for tapasâ in d. The second halfverse can hardly be called anything but prose, though the Anukr. takes it as good âstubh ² meter. It appears doubtful whether this verse belongs with the rest, and whether the nine prâpagrakas, or the nine verses of the 777 stoma, are not rather intended in it. 4 2. Fire, sun, moon, earth, waters, sky, atmosphere, directions, and ¹ quarters, they of the seasons in concord with the seasons —let them rescue (pâray) me by this triple one. & The verse, as was noted above, is wanting in Ppp. One and another ms., here as gt later, reads 7 vFz. To fill out the meter of c we have to make the harsh and unusual ¹ resolution of the first â of ârzavas.

3. Let three abundances (pâsa) resort to the triple one; let Pâshan g anoint it with milk, with ghee; affluence of food, affluence of man

(pâruṣa), affluence of cattle—Ilet these resort hither. Ppp. reads in a trâvytag ; in c aṅyasya, and bkâuma both times (247- in 4). We need ¹Ś in a to resolve 77-gyaṅ.

4. O Adityas, sprinkle this man well with good (vâsz); O Agni, do thou, thyself increasing, increase him ; unite him, O Indra, with heroism; let the prospering triple one resort to him. Ś ¹ Ppp. has, for c, 6, yasmin trivye chetâan pusayispur imam etc. (our c). Our mss. 9 vary at the end between posayâspî and -nâṅ, the majority having -74 (only B.O.I. -77);

our text should be emended to -zâ4. But SPP. reads -74 and notes no variants. Ś The Anrnkz., as usual, does not note that a is a jaga?i pâda.

5. Let earth, the all-bearing, protect thee with the yellow one; let ¹ ‘ Agni rescue [thee] in accord with the iron; let the silver one (ârjuna), in ¹ â concord with the plants, bestow (242) on thee dexterity, with favoring i i Ppp. reads in c virudbhis te arjuno saṅ-. The meter is like that of verse 4.

6. Triply born by birth [is] this gold: one was Agni's dearest; one

fell away of Soma when injured ; one they call the seed of devout waters;

ee let that triple gold be thine in order to life-time.

Instead of veâkâsâm in d, a much easier reading would be vedṅâsas nom. (as tacitly emended by Ludwig) ; and this is favored by Ppp., which has vedaso rerâ "hus; it further gives in e rrivytâstu ve. With bed compare TB. i. I. 38. The name atâakvarz given to the verse by the Anukr. demands Go syllables, but only 57 (I 1+ I 1+ I2 : II +12) can be fairly counted.

7. Triple life-time of Jamadagni, Kagyapa's triple life-time, sight of the immortal (amâta) triply, three life-times have I made for thee.

Ppp. reads âyâyusam ; and, at the end, nas kyâht for te "karam. JUB. iv.3. I has this version: triyâyusaṅ kagyapasya jamadagnes triyâyusam : (râzy amytasya puspani trip ayunsi me "kruok ; and several of the Grhya-Sutras (CGS. i. 28 ; HGS. i.9.6 ; IMP. ii. 7.2; MGS. i. r. 24 (cf. p. 150) ]; MB. i. 6.8) give the frst half-verse, with a different ending ; also VS. iii. 62. GGS. ii. 9. 21 gives the prar7ka. ] There is no reason for calling the meter kakummzatr.

8. When the three eagles (szparnâ) went with the triple one, becoming, mighty ones (cakrâ), a single syllable, they bore back death along with (sâkâm) the immortal, warding off (antar-dkâ) all difficulties.

¢ Warding off,' literally ' interposing [something between] themselves [and]; ' along with,' doubtless = ' by means of ' (cf. vii. 53. 1 : xii. 2. 29). Single syllable,' or ' the one; indissoluble ': probably the syllable on is intended. I

9. From the sky let the yellow one protect thee; from the midst let Ś the silver one protect thee; from the earth let that made of iron protect = [thee]; this [man] hath gone forward to strongholds of the gods. d

Ppp. combines at the end pur 'yam. This verse also is called kz Eummatri by the = Anukr. without any reason. d ro. These [are] three strongholds of the gods; let them defend thee on all sides ; bearing these, do thou, possessing splendor, become superior to them that hate thee. ‘ It needs only the usual resolution zu-âm in c to make this verse a regular an uszubk. ¹ = 11. The stronghold of the gods, deathless (am7a) gold, what god se first bound on in the beginning, to him I pay homage, [my] ten extended [fingers]; let him approve my binding-on the triple one. ²

Ppp. has at the end â7vy14 vadkena. The translation implies in â the reading manyarâm, which is given in our edition, though against part of the mss., that read i i manyantam. Let him (or it) assent to my binding-on,' dative infinitive,

12. Let Aryaman fasten (c72) thee on, let Ptushan, let Brihaspati; : what is the name of the day-born one, therewith we fasten thee over. : For the obscure third pada compare iii. 14. I. The verse is a regular grnustubk, if b is properly read, as & p75 7 bFhaspâriṅ (so the pada-text). This and the two following verses, which are not found in Ppp., seem to be independent of what precedes.

13. Thee with the seasons, with them of the seasons ; thee unto lifetime, unto splendor ; with the brilliancy of the year —with that we make Ś : [thee] of closed jaw (? sârkhanṇ). ¹ hn, Say

The verse is repeated as xix. 37. 4 in our ed. ; but SPP's repeats iii. ro. ro instead. It is found also in HGS. i. iI. 2, with 27 omitted at the ead of b, and, for c, 4, saṅṅva-- Śsarasya âhâyasa tena sann anu grhpâsi this gives us no help toward understanding the obscure last pada; the translation implies emendation to sâ7#âṅanuz, and understands the verse as directed against involuntary opening of the jaws (âvaricatio. maxiâllae inferioris) : cf. viii. 1. 16. The Anukr. foolishly calls the verse a puransṇik.

14. Snatched (ṅp) out of ghee, anointed over with honey, fixing the earth, unmoved, rescuing, splitting [our] rivals, and putting them down, do thou ascend me in order to great good-fortune.

The verse agrees nearly with xix. 33.2. The mss. read Śkindânt (p. bhindân) for bhindâr in c. A corresponding verse is found in a RV. kṅiâla to x. 128 : ghrtâd ulhegtam madhumat suvarpan dhanarmjayark dharunan: dhârayisnu : ruak sapatnar adhkarâṅg ca krnvad i roka mam makate saubhagâya. Given also by von Schroeder, Tâṅbinger Katha-kss., p. 36.

docs.title: 29. To Agni: against demons
docs.text:
[Câtana. —paṅcadacar cam. jâtavedasam uta mantroktadevatâ kam. trâ:gtubkam : 3. 3:6. virân:

nâma gâyatri ; 5. purotijagali virâgjagati ; Iz—I5. anugtubk (rz. bhkuriy ; ¹

I4. 4.9. par âby kati kakummatr).]

Found also (except vss. ro, rr) in Pâipp. xiii. No notice is taken in Vâit. of any part of the hymn; but in Kâug. 8.25 it is reckoned among the câzana hymns, or as. belonging in the câtana gaṇa, and two or three of its verses (2-4) are separately quoted, as will be pointed out below.

Translated : Ludwig, p. 526 ; Griffith, i. 236 ; Weber, xviii. 277. ³

I. Joined in front, carry thou, O Jâtavedas ; know this, O Agni, as. [it is] being done ; thou art a physician (547547), a maker of remedy (bhesajâ) ; by thee may we gain cow, horse, man (pâruṣa).

That is (b), take notice of this rite performed in thine honor. The verse is found also in HGS. i. 2. 18, which in a puts (as does Ppp.) purastât at the end, inserts in b karma after vidâṅâ, and reads in d gâ acvan purusan. Kaug. (3. 16) quotes the verse, in company with several others, at a certain libation in the parvan ceremonies.

2. So, O Agni, Jatavedas, do thou do this, in concord with all the gods : he who hath played [against] us, whosoever hath devoured (gkas) us, that this enclosure of his may fall.

The sense of c appears to be ' whoever hath pillaged us in or by play.' The sense of the imprecation in d is obscure. Ppp. reads as follows : tvam for tar in a; for b, c rena vidvan kavisz yavisthak: pigâco 'syatamo dideva; sya in 4; and, as e (or as 3 a), yo ya tad eva yatamo jaghâsi. Kâug. 47.9 quotes the verse (the scholiast says, vss. 2, 3) as accompanying the offering of portions of sacrificial butter in witchcraft ceremonies. The Prat, in ii. 77, prescribes the combination -âkâ pâr- in d. Haplography for ‘ya yatamo : cf. 4 c.]

3. That this enclosure of his may fall, so, O Agni, Jatavedas, do thou do that, in concord with all the gods.

Ppp. reads yathâ somasya paridhis patâtik tatha foam agne.

4. Pierce thou into his eyes, pierce into his heart, bore into his tongue, destroy (pra-m7) his teeth ; whatsoever pigâcâ hath devoured of him, that one, O Agni, youngest [god], do thou crush back.

Ppp. reads for a moksâan na viddhi by dayarn: na viddhi and piâco syatamo in c, and yavisthas in d. Kâug. (25.24) quotes the verse in a remedial ceremony.

5. What of him is taken [or] taken apart, what is borne away, what. soever of himself is devoured by the pâcâcâs, that, O Agni, do thou,; knowing, bring again ; into his body we send flesh [and] spirit (âs7).

Ppp. reads for 4 carire prânam asum erayâ san: syjema. The Anukr. defines the d meter correctly, according to its methods.

6. In raw, in well-cooked, in mixed (? cabâla), in ripe, what pigâcâ hath injured (dambk) me in the partaking—that let the pâgâcâs atone for (? vi-yâtay) with self [and] progeny ; be this man free from disease.

Ppp. has for a our 8 a (reading rua for m7), and for 8 a yâme sap. qavale vip. ; 1 further, for b odane manthe diva ota leke ; and here and in the verses that follow, it varies between dadambha and didambṅa.

7. In milk (k57râ), in stirabout whoever hath injured me, who in ² grain growing uncultivated —in the partaking [thereof] —that let the pigâcâs etc. etc. 2%

Ppp. reads in a kyzre tvâ mâṅse, and in b pacye. y ee

8. In the drinking of waters whatever flesh-eater hath injured me ¹ lying (47) in the lair (gâyanaâ) of the familiar demons (yât4) — that let fl the picâcâs etc. etc.

We are tempted to emend (with Ludwig) câyânam to ¢âyânas at end of b. Ppp. reads ( here, in a, b, nearly our 6 a, b, a with the three variants given above, and b with Zmam for yo ma, and with "cane ; and it adds our ro c, d instead of the refrain.

9. By day, by night, whatever flesh-eater hath injured me lying in the i lair of the familiar demons —that let the pâgâcâs etc. etc. era

Ppp. reads rvâ for ma in a, and in b skravyâad yarug cayare piâcak : ud agne don ; Se prthak : cruthky apy enarn: dehi niryter upasthe. In c of the refrain of all these verses i Ś is a syllable lacking, unless we make a harsh and unusual resolutiorr. ‘ ro. The flesh-eating, bloody (rudkhirâ), mind-slaying pigâcâ do thou slay, O Agni, Jatavedas ; let the vigorous Indra slay him with the ² thunderbolt; let bold Soma cut [off] his head. ¹

The Anukr. takes no notice of the lacking syllables in b and c, the latter of which, indeed, is easily made up for by resolving vâjr-e-na. Ś ir. deliverance (upâraṇa) do I put forward (puro-âkâ), in order to this man's ¹ being unharmed. ¹ With b compare viii. i. 8 b, which appears to give the clew to the meaning ; pâraṇa Ś is the action-noun to wâpâray (viii. 1. 17-19; 2.9). docs.title: 31. Against witchcraft
docs.text:
[Cukra.— dvâdagarcam. kyty3dṅsapadevatyam. ânugubham : Ix. br katrgarbââ; (i 12. pathyṅir hati] ² Not found (except vs. 12) in Pâipp. Not noticed in Vâit. The hymn is reckoned ge (as belonging in the Śr2yâ gaṇa or krty2pratikaraya gaṇa (see note to Kâug. 39. 7), and it is quoted with several other hymns in Kâug. 39. 7, in a ceremony for counteracting ¹ : magic.

Sha Translated : Griffith, i241; Bloomfield, 76, 456 ; Weber, xviii. 284.

I. What [witchcraft] they have made for thee in a raw vessel, what they have made in one of mixed grains; in raw flesh what witchcraft they have made —I take that back again. That is, doubtless, 'back to its maker ': cf. iv. 18. 4; and, for the whole verse, iv. 17. 4. The Anukr. makes no account of the redundant syllable inc.

2. What [witchcraft] they have made for thee in a cock, or what in a kurâra-wearing goat; in a ewe what witchcraft they have made—I take j that back again. ¹

Geldner discusses Zurira 'horn,' Ved. Stud. i. 130. i

3. What [witchcraft] they have made for thee in the one-hoofed, in the one with teeth in both jaws, among cattle; in a donkey what witchcraft they have made —I take that back again.

4. What [witchcraft] they have made for thee in a rootless [plant], or [what] secret spell (? valagâ) in a narâci; in thy field what witchcraft â they have made — I take that back again.

The pada-text does not divide valagân. ee

5. What [witchcraft] they have made for thee in the householder's fire, also, malevolent (dug), in the eastern fire; in the dwelling what 72727 witchcraft they have made — I take that back again.

What [witchcraft] they have made for thee in the army (sâzâ), what they have made in arrow-and-weapon ; in the drum what witchcraft they i have made —I take that back again. ¹ es

To make the meter complete in the two preceding verses, we need to make the unusual resolution wya-am at end of a. ec

The indefinite 'seat' may be used for dwelling, or for place of sacrifice." The i ; Anukr. takes no notice of the metrical irregularities in a, b.

9. What [witchcraft] they have made for thee in the human-bone, and : what in the destroying (? sâmkasuka) fire, [what] dimming, out-burning, a flesh-eating one —I take that back again.

⁴ Human-bone ' (if not a corrupt reading) is perhaps an epithet of the funeral fire = the fire which leaves of the human body nothing but fragments of bone.' 10. He hath brought it by what was not the road; we send it forth from here by the road ; he unwise, O men, hath brought [it] together, Ś out of thoughtlessness, for the wise (âk7ra). I ; The translation implies the reading maryâṅ : dhtrebhyak : in c, instead of maryâo Ś â;rebhyaṅ, as given by the pada-mss. ; the emendation is suggested by BR. v. 1668; but of. maryadhâatrya (maryâ kl âhâtrya ?) in MS. i. 4.8 (p. 56, l. 18). He who hath made hath not been able to make ; he hath crushed ¹ a foot, a finger ; he, fortuneless, hath made what is excellent for us [who ¹ are] fortunate ones. ¹ The first three pâdas are identical with iv. 18. 6 ac, and our d here is read by Ppp. Ś in that hymn but with aṅkagâ for Ś4]. rz. The witchcraft-maker, spell-hider, root-possessor, worthy of cursa gf ing—let Indra smite him with his great deadly weapon ; let Agni pierce . hifa with a hurled [arrow]. ¹ This verse is found in Ppp. i., where, for c, d, is read : inâras tu sarvâṇṅs tan hantu (; sattvaghnena bhavam iva. Ś The last or sixth anuvâka contains 5 hymns and 7o verses; the old Anukr. says: ¹ ¹ sasthe tu navâai "ka ca para ru sasthe. docs.title: 6.1 Book VI
docs.text: I The sixth book consists mainly of hymns of 3 verses. It is divided into thirteen anuvâka-groups, which have ten hymns each, except the third, seventh, eleventh, and twelfth groups, 4 which have eleven hymns each, and the thirteenth, which has eighteen. It thus contains one hundred and forty-two hymns: 4 and of these, one hundred and twenty-two have 3 verses each; twelve have 4 verses each ; and eight have 5 verses each. On account of the intrinsic interest, the variety, and the convenient length of the hymns of this book, they have been favorite subjects of translation and comment. Over half of them (79) have been translated by Ludwig in his Der Rigveda, vol. iii. (Die Mantra-btteratur); over half of them (74) also by Bloomfield in Sacred Books of the East, vol. xiii.; over a third (1—s0) by = Dr. Carl A. Florenz in Bezzenberger's Beitrâge aur Kunde der a Indogermanischen Spracken, vol. xii. 249—314; and nearly a quar- 5% ter (34) by Grill in his Hundert Lieder.) ¹ The hymns of 4 verses are hymns 16, 17, 38, 63, 76, 83, 84, 107, III, I21, I28, and — 130. The hymns of 5 verses are hymns 34, 108, 122, 123, I32, I33, I38, and r39. At the beginning of its treatment of this book, the Anukramaṇi calls it the " book of : % hymns of 3 verses " or Ścasṅktakângâa, and adds that "that number is the norm": tatra trcaprakytir itarâ vikytir iti. The possibilities of critical reduction to this ¹ “ norm " are frequently illustrated among the twenty hymns just cited. Thus the ¹ eo reduction may be effected by omission of some of the refrains and combination of the i 04 remainders, as in hymns 38, 107, I30 (this the commentator actually so reduces). HESŚ Again, the intrusions are sometimes indicated by the meter, as in hymns III, 123. Or, Ś again, they are indicated by their absence in other versions : thus hymns 16, 17, 34, i Ś 63, 83, 108, and r28 consist in fact of only 3 verses in the Pâippalâda text. — For the sequence of the books with reference to the normal lengths of their hymns, see the ¹ table on p. exlviii. See p. cli, end..

docs.text:

Sing at evening; sing greatly; put clearly, O son of Atharvan; ¹ Ś5 praise god Savitar. 46 4 All the mss.— and SPP., following them —put the avzsâna-mark after Jkeṅ7, thus Śr falsely dividing the irregular gâyatrt into two pâdas r2: 12 J; hence, of course, they accent Śtharvaṇa ; and most of the pada-mss. the young, of unhateful speech, very propitious. ¹ Again all the mss. spoil the structure of the verse by putting the division-mark after sanṅk. In both verses, SPP's text follows the mss., while ours emends in accordance on with the true sense—which is now further supported by the other text, and by Ppp. 7 ft An easier reading is offered by ACS., namely ram un stuky antaksindhur sunuṅ: ¹ satyasya yuvânam : adro- Indra is called “son of truth " in RV. viii. 58 (69). 4; the descriptions of the verse suit Savitar ill. RV. ix. 78. 2; the varieties of reading show that the pâada was virtually unintelligible to the text-makers. docs.text:
Found also in Pâipp. xix. (in the order 1, 3, 2). The second verse is used by Kâug. (29.27) in a remedial rite against demons, while partaking of a rice-mess boiled over birds' nests. Vaâit. (16.13) has the hymn in the agnisfoma, when the soma is tuned into the large wooden vessel.

I. For Indra, O priests, press the soma, and add the water; [Indra] who shall hear the praiser's words and my call.

Or, (the words and call of me the praiser.' With b compare RV. vii. 32.6 d. Ppp.; has, for b, c, (rnotanâ tu dhâvata : stotriyarn: havaṅ crpava” âhavan: tu nak. Ppp. reads roâ for yam in a. The comm. takes andṅasas as nom. pl., explaining it Ś by annabhṅras. ¹

docs.text:

docs.text:

Ś Pp y g y t Brahmaṇaspati ; with sons, with brothers, let Aditi now protect our hard ¹ to surpass [and] saving power. e5 The verse is found also in SV. 3. Unto knowledge (? 2k), O Agvins, do ye aid us; make wide for us, O wide-goer, unremitting; O heaven, father, repel whatever misfortune.

The beginning of the verse is probably corrupt, but Ppp. gives no various reading, merely prefixing deva toagtar (apparently out of 3.3): compare RV. i. 117. 23 b, v40â âhtyo agvina prâvatam me. In c, the great majority of mss., which SPP. follows, have the true accent gyâṇs (i.e. 24âus, the word requiring to be pronounced as two syllables see my Skz. Gram. 314 b); exceptions among our mss. are only Bp. and I. Several of our saṅkîtz-mss. have i before pâtar (viz. P.M.E.H.). The meter lacks a syllable in a.; Correct the ed. to gyâṅs.]

docs.title: 5. For some one's exaltation
docs.text:
[4rharvan.— âindrâgnam. ânugubham : 2. bhuri.]

Found also in Pâipp. xix., and in VS. (xvii. 50-52) TS. (iv. 6.37), MS. (il. ro. 3). Used in Kâug. (4.9) in the parvan sacrifice, with an oblation to Agni; and again (59. 7), with vi.6 and vii. 91, by one desiring a village ; and for success in traffic, see under vi. 1. In Vâit. (29. 15) the hymn accompanies the laying on of fuel in the agnicayana, and vs. 2, in the parvan sacrifice (2.145 3. 3), two offerings to Indra; for the use in Vaâit. 16. 9, see under vi. 3. The comm. further points out vs. 2 as addressed to Indra ¹ in the Naks. K. 14. g

Translated : Ludwig, p. 431; Florenz, 254 or 6; Griffith, i. 247.

I. Lead him up higher, O Agni, [thou] to whom oblations of ghee are re made ; unite him with splendor, and make him abundant with progeny.

VS. TS. have in a the later form ut1arâm. In b, ghrténa presents the rare case of an i acṅ instrumental dependent on a vocative, and ought, like a genitive in the like construction, to be unaccented ; it is so in all the three Yajus texts. Ppp. reads ghrzebkir Zhutal. ¹ VS. TS. exchange 1 c and 2 c; and TS. has dhânena ca for bak: kydâṅi at the end. Ppp. has, for 4, devanân: bhâgadha asar (cf. TS, 2 4). This first verse otcurs also in Ap. vi. 24. 8, which has, for a, ud asmâṅ uttarân naya, agrees with VS. and TS. in c, and reads (aṅân in d.

2. O Indra, put this man far forward ; may he be controler of his i fellows ; unite him with abundance of wealth; conduct him unto life i ²e (jroâtu), unto old age.

In a, VS.TS. have again pratarâm ; VS. MS. have naya for Eyâhi; for c (as already noted), VS. TS. have our 1 c; for 4, MS. has devebhyo bhâgadâ asat, VS. and TS. nearly the same, VS. substituting devânâm, and TS. -ââ ; Ppp. has, for â, our r d. The meter of d might be rectified by abbreviating jrvâtave to -zvâi (a form found in; MS.CB. and Ap.), or by emending it to jroâtum. lh

3. In whose house we make oblation, him, O Agni, do thou increase; ¹ him may Soma bless, and this Brahmanaspati. i

The three Yajus texts have, in a, kurmâs for kypmâs, and VS. MS. (with Ppp.) put kavis after grk4. In c, all three have devâ âdhi bravan (but MS. Śruvan). The last half-verse occurs below, as 87.3 c,d (corresponding to RV. x. 173. 3 etc.).;

docs.title: 6. Against enemies
docs.text:
¹ Found also in Pâipp. xix. For the use of the hymn by Kâug. 59.7, see under the 4 preceding hymn ; by Kâug. 50. 13, see under vi. r ; by Vâit. 16. 9, see under vi. 3. (6 Translated : Ludwig, p. 430; Florenz, 255 or 7; Griffith, i. 247. ¹ ge I. Whatever godless one, O Brahmaṇaspati, plots against us—every such one mayest thou make subject to me the sacrificer, the soma-presser. ²4 Ppp. has abkidâsari at end of b.

2. Whatever ill-famed one, O Soma, shall aim at us of good fame, smite upon his face with the thunderbolt ; may he go. away crushed Ś (sam-pis).

Notwithstanding the direct antithesis with Jdujṅgcânsa, all the mss. in a read susaṅgt ¹ ¹ nas; both editions emend to sugazstnas, which is also read by Ppp., and by the com- i (er mentary. Whoever, O Soma, shall assail us, of the same kindred and also .a stranger — draw (77) away his strength, like the great sky, even now (?).

Ppp. reads, in a, ye na soma 'bhidâsatak. The verse is RV. x. 33. 5, which reads indra for soma in a, 4va for âpa in c, and ââha tmânâ at the end. For this last, the vadâhatmânâ (not divided in the pada-text) of all the AV. mss. seems merely an unintelligent corruption (altered in our text to vaâka tmânâ). The comm., however, naturally makes no difficulty of understanding it as = vaâkâtmana (explaining it b

Y ] g ) g y acanirâpena) and as qualifying âyudhena understood. docs.title: 7. For blessings
docs.text:
¹- [4 harvan.— sâumyam : 3. vâivadevi. gâyarram ; I. nicyt.]

Found also in Pâipp. xix. The hymn appears in Kâug. (46. 4) as a help in removing ¹ obstacles to sacrifice, or an expiation for sacrificing for an improper person ; and it is vy reckoned (note to 25. 36) to the svastyayana gaṇa5 for its use by so. 13, see under vi. 5 Translated : Florenz, 256 or 8; Griffith, i. 248. ¹ ¹ I. By what road, O Soma, Aditi or friends go, not hostile, by that do thou come to us with aid. â5 ¹ ¹ The comm. understands mâ7râs 'friends' to mean ⁴Aditi's twelve sons, Mitra etc."; ¹ ¹ i.e. as the equivalent of zââtyâs, which is not impossible. |The description as nic? . 3. By what, O gods, ye did repel (or) the mights of the Asuras, by that do ye yield refuge unto us.

Ppp. begins with yâni, and has correspondingly tebkâs for tena in c. docs.title: 8. To win a woman's love
docs.text:
[ Jamadagni.— kâmâtmadâinatam. patkyâpaṅkti.]

Not found in Pâipp. Used by Kâug. (35. 21), in the rites concerning women, with vi.g and 102 and ii. 30, for bringing a woman under one's control. 5

Translated : Weber, Jad. Stud. (1862) v. 261; Florenz, 257 or 9; Guill, 54, 158; Griffith, i. 248 ; Bloomfield, roo, 459.

I. As the creeper (45ujâ) has completely embraced the tree, so do thou embrace me —that thou mayest be one loving me, that thou mayest & be one not going away from me. i s

The refrain of the hymn is found twice above, at the end of i. 34. 55 ii. 30. 1. SPP. here again, in opposition to his mss., gives the pada-reading âpacgâṅ in e. The Anukr. ee % takes no notice of the metrical deficiency of a but see note to 7. 1.

2. As the eagle, flying forth, beats down his wings upon the earth, so Ś do I beat down thy mind —that thou etc. etc.

The comparison here is a strikingly ineffective one, and the attempts of the trans- ¹ lators to give it aptness are to no purpose..

3. As the sun goeth at once about heaven-and-earth here, so do I go about thy mind —that thou etc. etc. a

Part of SPP's mss. read paryatti in b. The comm. gives cigâram ' swiftly ' as the SE meaning of saâyas.

docs.title: 9. To win a woman's love
docs.text:
[famadagni.— kâmâtmadâivatam. ânugubham.]

Found also in Pâipp., but in ii. (not in xix., like the hymns that precede and follow). ²l Used by Kâug. (35. 21) with the preceding hymn, for the same purpose.

Translated : Weber, Ind. Stud. v. 264 7 Florenz, 258 or ro; Griffith, i. 249; Bloom- ¹ field, ror, 459.

1. Want (vâṅck) thou the body of me, the feet ; want the eyes ; want the thighs; let the eyes, the hair of thee, lusting after me, dry up with love. Ś

Ppp. puts tanvânm (not -am) after pâdân in a, reads vâccha in b, begins c with ak5o, adds ogzhâu after kegâs, and ends with âgyarâm. Read aksyâi in c in our text (an ¹ accent-sign omitted over the zx). Delbrtick, Vergleickende Syntax, i. 386, joins mâm with mena : so Gregoire, KZ. xxxv. 83.

2. I make thee cling to my arm, cling to my heart; that thou mayest 4 be in my power, mayest come unto my intent. ¹ : The second half-verse is the same with iii. 25. 5 c, d, and nearly so with i. 34.2 c, d ¹ i Let. vi. 42. 3, note]. Ppp. reads, for a, b, mai tvâ âṅsanimygan: kpomi krâaya- ¹ sprgam ; and begins c with mame 'd apa kr-. ¹ 3. They whose navel is a licking, in [whose] heart is made concilia- ¹ tion —let the kine, mothers of ghee, conciliate her yonder to me. ¹ The comm. reads ans in d, and so is able to understand yâsâam at the beginning as relating to "women " understood, and not to gâvas; and he explains âréhanam by ¹ ¹ 5 âsvâdanityam 'something to be enjoyed by tasting.' The obscure and difficult first pâda is perhaps corrupt.

docs.title: 10. Greeting to divinities etc. of the three spheres
docs.text:
[Canitâti.— nânâdevatyam : I. 3gneyr, 2. vâyavyâ, 3. sâuryâ. I. samnr trigtubk, 2. prââpatyâ 5 45 brhati, 3. stmni byhart.] ¹ : : This prose hymn is not found in Pâipp. In Kâug. (9. 3, 5), it is quoted after each i (anti gana, to accompany a pouring out of water three times (â7 (rik pratyâsiṅcati Ś the comm. does not notice this use); and again (12. 3), it is prescribed in all rites for get success ; being further (note to 8.23) reckoned to the vâstu gana. Ś Translated : Florenz, 258 or Io; Griffith, i. 249. ²t I. To earth, to hearing, to the forest-trees—to Agni [their] overlord, " hail

It is not easy to read 22 syllables in the verse. 2. To breath, to the atmosphere, to the birds — to Vayu [their] overlord, hail l ¹ It is strange that in this verse the sphere is placed after the human faculty. ¹ 3. To the sky, to sight, to the asterisms —to Strya [their] overlord, hail l tl The first anuvâka, of ro hymns and 30 verses, ends here. The quotation is simply ¹ ¹Ś pratkama (or -mâ): see under the next anuvâga.

docs.title: 11. For birth of sons
docs.text:
( ¹ [Prajâpatik.— retodevatyam uta mantroktadevatyam. â&nugubharm.) 4 g The hymn is found also in Pâipp. xix. Accompanies in Kâug. (35.8) a rite for ¹ conception of a male child (pu savana); fire is generated between gai and agvatrka, : and is variously applied to the woman.

Translated : Weber, v. 264 ; Ludwig, p. 477; Zimmer, p. 319; Florenz, 260 or 12;

Griffith, i. 250; Bloomfield, 97, 46. ts I. The acvatthâ [has] mounted upon the gam? there is made the pe generation of a male; that verily is the obtainment of a son; that we bring into women.

Some of SPP's mss. read, with the comm., puṅsâvanam in b. Ppp. combines agvarthâ "ru- in a, and for c, d has tad eva tasya bhesajan yar strigv 3haranti tam, ⁴ that is the remedy of this—namely, that they pur this into women.

2. In the male, indeed, grows (Ś47) the seed; that is poured along into the woman ; that verily is the obtainment of a son; that Prajâpati said.

Several of our mss. (Bp.P.M.W.E.H.) read gâ7:st at the begiming. CGS. has (i. 19) a nearly corresponding verse : pursi vai puruse retas tar striyâm anu Śiṅcatu : i tatkâ tad abravid dhâta tal prajapatir abravit.

3. Prajâpati, Anumati, Sinivâli hath shaped ; may he put elsewhere woman-birth ; but may he put here a male. 9

Ppp. has in c risâyam ' triple birth ' (or for sârâsṅyam 2). Two of the Prat. rules (ii. 88, iv. 83) mention szââsâyam (p. strâtsâyam). CGS. has for this verse also a correspondent (i. 19): prajapatir uy adadkar savitr vy akalpayat : strigâyan: anyânt sv (anyâsv Ś) â dadkat pumâṅsam â dadkâd ika.

docs.title: 12. Against the poison of snakes
docs.text:
[Garutman. — taksakadâivatam. â&nugtubkam.]

Found also in Pâipp. xix. Used by Kaâug. (29.28) in a remedial rite against the poison of serpents. i Sṅ

Translated : Ludwig, p. 5o1 ; Florenz, 262 or r4; Griffith, i.250; Bloomfield, 28, 461. — See Bergaigne-Henry, Manuel, p. 149. i

I. I have gone about the race of snakes, as the sun about the sky, as ⁴ night about living creatures other than the swan (kaṅsâ); thereby do I ward off thy poison.

It would appear from this that the Zaṅsa is regarded as exempt from the dominion of night, doubtless as remaining awake: cf. Pliny, Vaz. Hâst. x. 23. But Ppp. reads, in c, 6, 7âtrân jagad (vân ni dhvaṅsad avâadir imaṅ: visam. The comm. reads and : Se explains janim agama in b ; and in c derives Zaṅsa from root kan, and makes it mean i — the soul (âtman), to which alone poison does not penetrate! The Anukr. does not ¹ heed the redundant syllable in c. Ppp. combines ak7nâm, without elision. ]

2. What was known of old by priests (brakimâi), what by seers, what by gods ; what is (Ś47tâ), is to be, that has a mouth—t therewith do I ward off thy poison. i

Ppp. has uditam for viditam in b, and âsunvatr at end of c. The comm. explains âsanvat to mean asyayuktar: : leno 'ccâryamanamantrasakitain. â

3. With honey I mix (prc) the streams ; the rugged (? pârvata) mouns tains [are] honey; honey is the Pârusṇz, the Cââlâ; weal be to thy ¹ : mouth, weal to thy heart. : The comm. reads at the beginning madhv a prṅce ; he takes the streams for the i Ganges etc., the mountains (pârvata) for the Himâlaya etc. and the hills (gâr7) for their foot-hills ; the garuṣpṇt for the great river of that name, and (7564/7 as adj., ‘rich in water-grass ' (câṅvâla): all these are to pour on (â sâcantu) poison-removing honey. The Ppp. text is quite different : abhi nâ prksa nadyas parvatâi ‘va girayo madkhu madhu pr|(r (pala samaste ‘stu cane hydaya. Perhaps paruspr signifies here an eddying ' brook, and (75774 a pool ' rich in water-plants.' [ Considering that the effect of snake-bite upon heart and blood must have been well known to even the most unlettered Hindu, I am tempted to suggest emendation of aszâ to asnâ.] In R. and W's ed., correct nadyâg to nadyârk.

docs.title: 13. To the instruments and ministers of death
docs.text:
[Atharvan (svastyayanakâma). —mârtyalvalm. ânugtubham.]

Found also in Pâipp. xix. The hymn is variously employed by Kâug. : in a rite for victory (14. 25), with iii. 26, 27; and again (15. 6), similarly, in favor of a Vâigya ; in the preparation of the house-fire (72. r3), with an offering; four times in the chapter of portents : once (104. 3) when Brahmans quarrel; again (105. 1) when images play pranks ; yet again (113.3) when a cow suckles an ox (these three in company with i.19); once more (123. 1), when animals touch sacred things ; and it is further reckoned (note to 25. 36) to the svastyayana gana.

Translated : Florenz, 264 or 16; Griffith, i. 251.

I. Homage to the weapons (vadkâ) of the gods; homage to the weapons of kings; likewise the weapons that are of the Vâicyas—to them of thine, O death, be homage.

Ppp. has viâvânâm in c.

2. Homage to thy benediction ; homage to thy malediction ; homage to thy favor, O death; this homage to thy disfavor.

Ppp. omits the first half-verse, doubtless by accident. The comm. takes the datives in a and b as nomina agentis.

3. Homage to thy sorcerers ; homage to thy remedies ; homage to thy roots, O death ; this homage to the Brahmans.

docs.title: 14. Against the balâsa
docs.text:
[Bab krupingala (?).— balâsadevatyam. ânuggubham.]

Occurs also in Pâipp. xix. Used by Kâug. (29. 30) in a remedial rite against catarrh (cles man), with variously administering prepared water to the patient.

Translated : Florenz, 265 or 175 Griffith, i. 252 ; Bloomfield, 8, 463; vs. 1 also by Grohmann, Jad. Stud. ix. 397, with an excursus on the balâsa.

I. The bone-dissolving, joint-dissolving, settled (âstkita) heart disease, all the balâsa, cause thou to disappear, that is seated in the limbs and in the joints.

SPP, adopts in a the saṅhirâ-reading parusraṅsâm (p. parulhesraṅsânz), with nearly all his mss, and with the comm. The majority also of our mss. not E.O. ] omit the but the Prat. authorizes no such abbreviation, and the point is one in regard to which the usage of the mss., however seemingly accordant, is not to be trusted. Ppp. reads, in c, nis ky âṅt for nâaya. The comm. takes the two words in a as names of disorders, ² which is perhaps preferable, and regards them as occasioned by phlegm (cleyman); balâsa he defines as kâsacvâsârmaka glsmaroga. |For âsthita, see note to iv. 17. 8.1 ¹ I Delete the accent-sign over -sz7 in c.

2. The Śalâsa of him that has balâsa I destroy like a mugkarâ; I cut its bond like the root of a gourd.

The accent rvârvâs is noted in the commentary to Prat. iii. Go ; Ppp. reads uloâkro yaYkâ. The comm. defines uruâr7 as ' the fruit of the karkafr' (Cucumis utilissimus) anc explains the comparison to be with the stem of this fruit, which becomes loosened of itself when ripe : cf. xiv. 1. 17. Ppp. and the comm. read puskaram in b. Ppp. also has krnomâ instead of ksinomi, a preferable reading (BR. pronounce ksinomi false; but nz-forms of this root occur in Brâhmaṇa and Sttra; ak nomi, however, would be better in place). [See BR. v. 1348 and 838. ] (

3. Fly out forth from here, O balâsa, like a young âusgâ; then, like the [last] year's bulrush, scud away, innocuous to heroes. . Ppp. has, for b, suparpo vasarer (va l cf. RV. i. 25. 4 ] ' like a bird from its nest ': a ; much easier reading. The comm. explains Zuniga as an ordinary adjective, 'swiftgoing,' and, instead of (inka, reads cucuka "a wild animal so called." For c, 4, Ppp. has adhe ‘ta ioâ 'hano 'padrâky avâiraha. The comm. reads (as that is izâs , pple of root 7, for #as in c. The Anukr. appears to sanction the contraction ie va in c.

docs.title: 15. For superiority
docs.text:
[Uddâlaka. —vânaspatyam. ânugtubham.]

Found also in Pâipp. xix. Kaâug. applies (19.26) in a rite for prosperity, with : ²Ś% vi. 42. 3, using an amulet of barley. It is also reckoned (note to 19. 1) to the pustika : ‘ mantras.

Translated : Florenz, 267 or 19; Griffith, i. 252.

1. Thou art the highest of herbs; of thee the trees are subjects ' Ś4 (upasti); let him be our subject who assails us. ¹

The verse is RV. x. 97. 23 (with which VS. xii. ror precisely agrees), which has, for Ś a, toâm uttamâ sy osadhe, and accents âpastayas ṅpastis. Ppp. elides the z of asi in a, and in c, 4 has upastir asmâkan bkṅyâad yo 'smân. The comm. regards the palâca ¹ are : tree as addressed. ¹

2. Whoever, both kindred and not of kin, assails us, of them may I be highest, as this one of trees.

The Ppp. version of i. 19. 4 a, b is (as pointed out at that place) nearly our a, b here. ¹ In this verse Ppp. reads samb- and asamb-, and its c is sambanâhṅr sarvâṅs vin rea.

3. As of herbs soma is made highest of oblations, as the tâlâgâ of trees, [so] may I be highest. 1

Ppp. reads, for b, , uttaman kavir ucyare (which is better): yavâ tuam Śiva vyksanâm. The comm. has palâ3ga in c. If talâca is a good reading, it may mean the same ¹ as (alṅâa (Flacourtia catapkracta). ¹

docs.title: 16. To various plants (?)
docs.text:
caturycam. I. nicrt 3-p- Śâyatri; 3. byhatigarbhâ kakummaty anugtubk ; 4. 32. pravigṅâ.]

Found also in Pâipp. xix. Appears in Kâug. (30. I), in a healing rite, explained as intended for disease of the eyes, with various use of mustard plant. Verse 4 is quoted alone later (51. I5), in a rite explained by Keg. simply as one for welfare, by the comm. as for welfare in connection with food (aṅnasvastyayana): and the comm. reads in Kâug. anna- (not âla-) bhesajam ; the three ¢alâṅjâlâgrâyâ of 51. 16 the comm. explains as sasyawallrs.

The whole hymn is totally obscure ; that it relates to a disease of the eyes, as assumed by the native comment, there appears no good reason to believe.

Translated : Florenz, 268 or zo; Griffith, i. 253 (see his notes); Bloomfield, 30, 464.

1. O âbayu, non-âbayu I thy juice is sharp (Śgrâ), O âbayn I unto thy broth do we eat.

The hymn is unintelligible, and the translation only mechanical. Ppp. and the comm. read zv-, anâe- in a, b (Ppp. combining #grâ "v-); and the comm. derives the words from the verbal stem Zuaya, with suffix 7, and renders (being eaten' (aâyamana), 'not being eaten ' (aâhaksyamâṇa), understanding 'mustard' (sarsapa) to be addressed. Ppp. has, for c, ya te karmam agimaki and, in a, elides 'ṅâvayo ].

2. V7hâlka by name is thy father, madâvarz (intoxicated) by name is thy mother ; for thou art he, not thyself, thou that didst consume thyself.

SPP. reads in a vikâklas. The translation of the second half-verse implies the altered division and accentuation of c that is made in our edition ; the mss. read sâ hina (not divided in pada-text) tvâm asi; and SPP. follows them. Ppp. has for c gevas tvam asi (its d is like ours), but it omits a, b, and, on the other hand, adds at the end babhrug ca babhrukarnag ca nilakalacâlâcavas paccâ. The comm. reads wihaṅla for vikhalka (which is supported by the commentary to Prat. i. 46) in a, and regards 47 na as two words in c. The verse as it stands (849: 648=31) is very improperly passed as a simple anustubk. An âsi between 47 and nâ would mend the meter of c if such stuff were worth mending.

3. O 77uvilikâ, quiet down; this racket hath quieted down; both the brown and the brown-eared one : go away, O nirâla

It is perhaps by a misprint that SPP. reads âva : ²aya (for i) in the pada-text of a (though our D. has also 7-). To the comm., (7uwilikâ is the name of a pâcaâct that produces disease ; ââlaba, a kind of disease of the eyes; âaṅ4ru and babhrukarpa, causes of disease ; and nâ7âla, also a disease. The translation implies the emendation of ntr âla to nirâla Ppp. has a peculiar text: fâulike "ve 'layâ 'vâ imâîlavâilâi thas toâm âkutin: jusâno manasâ svâhâ ; but part of this belongs perhaps to the following piece. [The Anukr. scans as 8-9: 8:6.) *] Comm. reads nirâla ; R. bas nr &ala, and T. has ntlâcala. Comm. has further aââzhi : 4: Alasâlz art thou first; sââṅjâlâ art thou after; nṅlâgalasâla. This verse is wanting in Pâipp. (save so far as its last word is found in that version obs: 2). The comm, understands the three obscure words it contains to be names of a ; ²e i : en ³ grain-creepers (sasyavallr); he gives the second the slightly different form calâṅjâla. d The comment to Prat. iv. ro7 quotes alasâlâ 'si as instancing the indispensableness of the pada-text to a student; but what good it does him in this instance is quite unclear. Our Bp. gives the third pada thus: ntlagalasâl 7 nîlâgalasâla. The verse is capable g of being read as 847: 6.

docs.title: 17. Against premature birth
docs.text:
[Atharvan.— catury cam. garbhadyṅhanadevatyam. &nugtubham.] y

Found, except vs. I (in the order 4, 2, 3), in Pâipp. xix. Used by Kâug. (35.12) in the rite for securing the foetus against abortion. i

Translated : Ludwig, p. 477 ; Florenz, 269 or 21; Griffith, i. 254; Bloomfield, 98, 467.

I. As this great earth receives the embryo of existences, so let thine ¹ embryo be maintained, in order to birth after pregnancy.

The comm. reads anusâtram for ânu sâtum. The first half-verse has already I occurred, as v.25. 2 a, b where the note gives the parallel passages The comment to Prat. ii. ro3 notes the non-lingualization of the s of sâtum after 4nu—which is wholly superfluous unless it read ânusâtunn.

2. As this great earth maintains these forest-trees, so let thine etc. a etc..

Ppp. begins yathe lyam urvr prthivi, and reads, in c, 4, garbha anu and suvitave. 4 Ś
