docs.title: 18. Against jealousy
docs.text:
[A tharoan (?).— irsyâvinâzanadevatyam. ânuâtubharm.] eu

Found also in Pâipp. xix. Used by Kâug. (36. 25), with vii. 45 and 74. 3, in a rite 5 against jealousy. ¹ ee ' Translated : Weber, Ind. Stud. v. 235; Ludwig, p. 514 ; Florenz, 270 or 22; Grill, 28, r59; Griffith, I. 254; Bloomfield, ro6, 467.

I. The first blast of jealousy, and the one after the first, the fire, the heat of the heart — this we extinguish for thee. Ś

Ppp. has readings in part better : for b, madhyamâm aâkamâm uta; for agnim in c, satya; at end, nir mantrayâmake. The comm. explains âkrâjim by vegayuktân: v gatim.

2. As the earth [is] dead-minded, more dead-minded than a dead man, ( and as [is] the mind of one who has died, so of the jealous man the mind [be] dead. : Feeling " would be in this verse an acceptable equivalent for zzanas tmind.' el Ś 3. That fluttering mind (manaskâ) that has found place in (crizâ)

thy heart —from it I set free thy jealousy, like the hot vapor from a bag of skin. The translation implies at the end the emendation (first proposed in BR.) of the apparently senseless nytes into âftes, which the comm. reads, and which SPP. has accordingly admitted into his text; the result of fermentation, escaping when the Ś 46 vessel is opened, is apparently intended. Ppp., however, has zy es, although it gives ŚŚ sundry various readings (in part mere corruptions): for a, yad yan me by di srukaṅr; : ( in b, prathayispukam ; in c, tar te rigyâmi mu-. The comm. divides b into manas ¹ hf kam patayispu kam.

docs.title: 19. For ceremonial purification
docs.text:
. [Camtâri.— nânâdevatyam uta cindramasam. gâyatram : I. anugtubh.] ¹ : i Found also in Pâipp. xix. Translated by Ludwig (p. 431). Quite various use is Ś ŚÎf made of this hymn in the sâzras. In Kaâug. it is included (9. 2) in the Śrkackânts ⁴ ; gana; it is associated (as are vi. 23, 24, 51, 57, 59, 61, 62) with i. 4-6 etc. in a rite for 2. good fortune (4I. 14); it appears in the savaya)ṅâas (66. 16), with the pavitra sava; 4 and the comm. declares it and vi. 51, 62 to be intended by pawitrâis at 61. 5, also in 3 the sawayajṅa chapter. In Vâit. it accompanies a purifying rite (11. 10) in the agn'- Ś stoma, and (with vi. 69 etc.) the pouring out of the surâ in the s7utrâmaṇr ceremony Ś Ś 130.13 J; and vs. 2 in the aguyadheya (6. 11), with an offering to Agni pavamaâna. ¹ 6 Translated : Ludwig, p. 431; Florenz, 272 or 24; Griffith, i. 255.

I. Let the god-folk purify me; let men (mdânu) purify me with prayer uh (dk%); let all beings purify me; let the purifying one purify me. Ppp. reads at the end mâm. The verse is found in sundry other texts, with considerable varieties of reading : the first pâda is the same in all (only RV. has mâm); in the second, RV. (ix. 67. 27) has vâsawas for mânavas, while VS. (xix. 39) reads ¹ mânasâ dhiyas, and TB. (i. 4. 8²) and MS. (iii. II. 10) agree with AV.; in the third,

VS. agrees with AV., and MS. differs only by giving Ś4nrâ ma, while TB. has v4va âyâvak, and RV. vkve. devâk punitâ ma; the fourth is omitted in TB., and RV.VS. Ś have jâtavedak puntht ma, while MS. differs only by punâkt. The readings of K. ¹ i (xxxviii. 2) I have not. The comm. explains âkiyâ in a by buddhyâ karmaRâ vâ, and fe : pavamaânas in d as either wind or soma. He (2. Let the purifying one purify me, in order to activity, dexterity, life, ¹ ks likewise unharmedness. ¹ : : Ppp. arranges a as punâtu ma pavamanaR. It gives, for c, yok ca suryaṅz ârge ¹ (cf. our i. 6. 3 and xii. 2. 18), and this is also the reading of MS. (ib.), which alone of ¹ ¹ all the other texts has a correspondent to this verse.

3. With both, O divine impeller (sawitâr), with purifier and with y impulse, do thou purify us in order to seeing. ¹ ( rt This verse is found in all the texts that have vs. I. RV. (ix. 67. 25) VS. (xix. 43) Hi have, for c, mâm punthi vigvâtak, and MS. (as above) the same save punâkhi,; TB. v ² ee (i. 4.82) gives instead idâm brâhma punimake. v

docs.title: 20. Against fever (takmân)
docs.text:
[BhrgUargiras.—yaksmanâ anadâioatam. I. atâagalr ; 2. kakummat prastârapanktip

3. sataṅpankrij.]

Only the last verse is found in Paipp., in book xiii. Appears in Kâug. (30.7) ina remedial rite for bilious fever, and is reckoned (note to 26. 1) to the takm anâgana gaza.

Translated : Grohmann, Jad. Stud. ix. 384, 393 ; Ludwig, p. 511 ; Zimmer, p. 380; Florenz, 273 or 25; Griffith, i. 255 ; Bloomfield, 3, 468.

I. Of him as of burning fire goeth the vehemence (?); likewise, as it were, shall he crying out go away from me ; some other one than us let the ill-behaved one seek ; homage be to the heat-weaponed fever.

The translation given implies the easy emendation of gusmâ as to gâsmas, which eases the meter," and helps the sense out of a notable difficulty. The comm. and the translators understand (perhaps preferably) mattâs in b as pple of mad, instead of quasi-ablative of the pronoun za, as here rendered ( he flees, crying like a madman," R.). The comm. takes avratas as intended for an accusative, -fam. The verse is really a. jagarr with one redundant syllable in a. ¥] The metrical difficulty is in the prior part of a; the cadence of a is equally good with cusmâṇas or with câsmas.

2. Homage to Rudra, homage be to the fever, homage to king Varuna, the brilliant (roâs7mant), homage to the sky, homage to the earth, homage to the herbs.

The Anukr. scans the verse as rz +12: 9+6 = 39 syllables.

3. Thou here who, scorching greatly, dost make all forms yellow—to thee here, the ruddy, the brown, the woody fakmân, do I pay homage. Ppp. reads, in a, râras for yas; its c, d are arunâya babkrave tapurmaghavâya name stu takmane. The comm. understands vânyâya in â as gerundive of root van = saṅseuyâya: perhaps 'of the forest, i.e., having no business in the village. The verse (9411: 9+12) is too irregular for the metrical definition given cf. vif. 2.21 J.

The second gnuvâka ends here, having ro hymns and 32 verses, and the quotation from the old Anukr. is simply âvitiyân, which ought to combine with the prarkama of the first aṅuvâka —only one does not see how, as the two are not equal in number of verses.

docs.title: 21. To healing plants
docs.text:
[Cartâti.— cândramasam. ânugubham.]

Found also in Pâipp. 1. Used by Kâug. (30.8) in a remedial rite for growth of hair.

Translated : Florenz, 275 or 27; Grill, 50, 160 ; Griffith, i. 256 ; Bloomfield, 30, 470.— See also Bergaigne-Henry, Manuel, p. 150.

I. These three earths (27thivâ) that there are —of them earth (Śk2m7) is the highest ; from off their skin have I seized a remedy.

Ppp. elides the initial a of aka in c, and its â is sam u jagrabka bhesajam. See Griffith's note. J ⁴ Ś 2. Thou art the most excellent of remedies, the best of plants ; as Soma, lord (? bkâga) in the night-watches (yâma), like Varuṇa among the gods. : The comm. takes yâma in the sense here given (akorârrabhâgesu sââkyesu), and ¹ ¹ Soma as 'moon,' which is doubtless true ; but he renders b4agas by 'and the sun.'

Ppp. exchanges the place of 'remedies' and tplants,' and reads yaj7as for somas in c. ¹ The Anukr. appears to authorize b4age 'va in c. 3. O ye wealthy (revânt) ones, doing no violence, desirous to bestow ¹ ud ye desire to bestow; both are ye hair-fasteners, and also hair-increasers. if ⁴ Ppp. exchanges the place of -âṅkants and -vardkants, and reads the equivalent fol sâsâsantis for sigasavas. Anadhyṣyâs in a would seem a better reading. The Anukr. Ś overlooks the deficiency in a; insertion of szkâ after revaris would rectify it.

docs.title: 22. To the Maruts
docs.text:
gŚ : [Carntâti.— âdityararmidevatyalm). mârutam. trâigubham : 2. 42. bhurigjagari.] ¹Ś Found also in Pâipp. xix. Used by Kâug. (30. 11) in a remedial rite against protu- , ¹ i berant belly etc. Keg. and the comm. read further in the rule the pratika sasrugts of ŚŚṇt hymn 23, and detail a second lengthy process in the same rite as performed with the two.

Hymns 22—24 are also explained as among the apâṅ saktâni (7. 14 and note). In ² Vâit. (9. 5) this hymn appears in the câturmâsya sacrifice as addressed to the playing (rigin) Maruts. Translated : Ludwig, p. 463 vss. i-2 ] ; Florenz, 276 or 28; Griffith, i. 256. 4 I. Black the down-track, the yellow eagles, clothing themselves in Śe waters, fly up to the sky; they have come hither from the seat of righteousness (r¹â); then, forsooth, with ghee they deluged the earth. Ś The verse comes from the mystic and obscure hymn RV. i. 164 (vs. 47), and is found i again twice below (ix. ro. 22, which see; xiii. 3.9). It is also found in several of the a Black Yajus texts : TS. (iii. r. rr), MS. (iv.12. 5), K. (x6. 9, I3). RV.MS. end with ¹Śâ 2rthivi uy Śdyare TS. has âsitavarpâs (for krspârr niyânam) in a, mâhas (for (eke apâs) in b, sâdanâni krtvâ in c, and, for 4, 4d 7 prthivt ghytair uy âdyare. Ppp. agrees with RV.MS. at the end of the verse, and it combines, in its frequent way, suparpâ po. 2. Ye make the waters rich in milk, the herbs propitious, when ye bo bestir yourselves, O golden-backed Maruts; do ye lavish (p7n2) both susel tenance and good-will there, where, O manly Maruts, ye pour honey. ¹ Ll The first, third, and fourth pâadas are found as b, c, d of a verse in TS. iii. I. IIS; ¹ ( . TS. reads krṅuta (as does also Ppp.), and it omits crvṅs 5 it also has, with the comm., ¹ It ¹ pinvatka in c (which is better). Ppp. further reads yams for civâs, and ejati for -14â ; i

Vand siṅcata for -7kâ.

3. Water-swimming [are] the Maruts; send ye that rain which shall ( ¹ Ś¹â fill all the hollows; the glâṅâ shall bestir itself, like a girl that is thrust, 4 ¹ Ś 5 thrusting the u, like wife with husband. 1 T (4 . .. 1 ¹ The text of this verse is hopelessly corrupt, and all attempts to make connected sense of the second half must apparently be (like that of Pischel in Ved. S7ud. i. 81 5.) forced ² ¹ and unsuccessful. Baunack, KZ. xxxv. 532, may also be consulted. ] The version of it presented in TS. (iii. r. 1x9) rather sets off its difficulties than gives any help in solying them. It makes marutas vocative in a, and the comm. also understands the word as vocative, not heeding its accent; the preferable reading would be âdapruto marutas, both vocative. The comm. then takes fn together with wdâprâtas as qualifying meghân ' clouds ' understood. Ppp., with the majority of SPP's authorities and some of ours (P.M.), reads udaplhirtas. Then tâ7 (pada-text tân) is read by all the author ties in both texts, although the sense necessarily requires (as in our translation is assumed) 4m, as antecedent to yâ. But here, again, all the gada-texts have yâṇ, which completes their confusion. TS. has, for b, the wholly different and doubtless secondary phrase vystinz ye vigve mariâto junânti, making of the line 'O Maruts, send those water-swimming ones who, [namely] all the Maruts, hasten the rain." The comm. f 5 understands yz, but then also v4w3â, as neut. pl. (vr 7hiyavâdisasyânt), while all our padâa-texts have correctly wâwâj ; the comm. then is obliged to supply a cz ' and ' after nivâtas. In c, 4, TS. reads krâcati for ejati, gâraa for giâhâ, perum for rus, and tuRjanâ for tundanâ (some of the mss., including our O. D.R., have tudanâ); the comm. also has zz7janâ, but gaklâ (so printed ; but it should doubtless be gaZṅâ, i since he derives it from root garṅ ' chide ' : one of our mss. (W.) and three of SPP's have gâlkz) instead of glâkâ or gârdâ, he translates it ' thunder.' These changes on glâkha and ru, at least, are plainly no real variations of reading, but blind blunders over an unintelligible text. Ppp. is corrupt and hardly legible : perhaps ye jakâti ktaknz kanye "va dunnonar dunnâma patye "va jâyam. R. suggests that the line cd belongs 1 & to a gambling hymn, and that we are to read glakas and #rurm, a comparison being E Ś made between the shaking of the dice-holder and the agitatio of a female at the coitus. d

docs.title: 23. To the waters : for blessings
docs.text:
[Cartâti (?).— abdevatyam. &nugtubkam : a. 3. Śâyatri; 3.paroszik.] g SHER

Found also in Pâipp. xix. Reckoned by Kâug. (9. 2) to the ;rkackânti gana, and ³e also (note to 7.14) to the apâsz su ktani ; and again (41. 14), with yi. rg etc., used in a ; - rite for good fortune : as to its combination (30. r1) with the preceding hymn, see that hymn. In Vâit. (4. 14) it accompanies in the parvan sacrifices the pouring out of water. ¹

Translated : Ludwig, p. 431; Florenz, 278 or 305 Griffith, i. 257. i

I. Flowing on, devoted to it; by day and by night flowing on; I, of 5 desirable activity, call upon the heavenly waters. . ²

The verse is found as a ila or appendix to RV. x. 9, as vs. ro of that hymn. . Śe²] It reads there, in a, t4dapasas, which is an obvious and called-for emendation of our text, and assumed in our translation; in c, -Ś7atṅs, which is also an improvement (our P. has it, but apparently only by an accident); and, for â, â devtr vase huve. Ppp. has, for d, akṅpo devir upa bruve. The first pâda lacks a syllable, unless we resolve ¹ sa-sy-u-. ¹

2. Let them release here the worked-in waters of the ceremony for. conducting forward; let them at once make [them] to go.

The translation implies emendation of âpas in a to apâs, or else the use of the former ¹ as accusative, as in more than one other passage. O's, lit. 'woven in ': ie. brought in as part of the ceremony. But the comm. reads 714s, and explains it as = saṅz2atâs or ²-04 : avicchedena pravahantyak. In a, b, the reading of Ppp. appears to be like ours ; but ee in c it has bhavantu etave. Ct. v.23. 1 for Ś12s. ] ¹ 5 3. In the impulse (savâ) of the divine impeller (savitâr) let men do their [sacred] work; weal to us be the waters, the herbs propitious.

Ppp. reads krpvanti in b. Here, to preserve the balance of forms, apâs has to be : understood as nominative.

docs.title: 24. To the waters : for blessings
docs.text:
⁴ [Cartâti (?). — abdevatyam. ânugubham.] ¹ Found also in Pâipp. xix. Reckoned in Kâug. (9.2) to the brhackânti gapa, and ; l (note to 7. 14) to the apân: sṅkiâni ; used in a rite for good-fortune (41.14) with Ś¹ vi. 19 etc.: see under rg; and also (30. 13) in a healing ceremony for heartburn, eŚ dropsy, etc. 4 Translated : Florenz, 279 or 31; Grill, 13, 61; Griffith, i. 258 ; Bloomfield, r2, 471.

I. They flow forth from the snowy (mountain); in the Indus somewhere [is their] gathering; may the heavenly waters give to me that ¹l remedy for heart-burn. Ś.f Ppp. reads, for a, b, kimavatak prasravaras tâs sindkum upagackarak. In â, the true reading is of course 47 dâyo-, and SPP. so reads, though doubtless against his mss. Ś 6. as certainly against all ours; it is a very rare thing to find the full form written in such a case (and hence the pada-text blunder ²-âyota in i. 22. ). 2. Whatever hath burnt (â-dyut) in my eyes, and what in my heels, my front feet ; may the waters remove all that —they of physicians the ¹ most excellent physicians. a The collocation of suffering parts in a, b is very odd ; Ppp. seems to read for a, . yad aksibhyâm âd-, and, for b, parsuibhyân kydayena ca ; for 8, tasty ristam ivâ (5 ¹nasak. One or two of our mss. (P.H.) agree with some of SPP's in reading karat at end of c; and two of his have 7; before it. The pada-division subkhisakelama is (er taught in Prat. iv. 46. 3. Ye whose spouse is the Indus, whose king is the Indus, all ye streams that are —give us the remedy for this ; for that would we enjoy you. Ppp. exchanges the place of the two epithets in a. The comm. reads stzna at end ; et of b. Before szkâna most of our mss. retain the final â, as usual ; SPP. does not note be ¹ i anything as to his authorities.

docs.title: 25. For relief from pains (?) in neck and shoulders
docs.text:
be : [Cunajepa. — mantroktamanyâl ai loinâ anadevatyam. ânugtutham.] ¹ Found also in Paâipp. xix. Used in Kâug. (30.14) in a healing rite against gangage malas, with kindling fifty-five paracu (comm., (7) leaves by chips.

Translated : Kuhn, KZ. xii. r30 (with Germanic parallels); Florenz, 280 or 32;

Griffith, 1.258; Bloomfield, rg, 472 (cf. AIP. xi. 323).

r. Both the five and the fifty that gather against those of the napelet them all disappear from here, like the noises (? vâkâ) of the apacits.

Mânyâs etc. may of course as well be nom., and the comm. so understands them, supplying gandamaâlâs ' pimples, swellings ' for them to agree with ; 2547 would then be left without object, or with indefinite object, 'one,' understood. The comm. renders vâkâs by vacaniyâ dosâṇ, and takes apacttân as accus. fem. pple: Śas blameworthy faults leave an honored woman "I Under VS. xvii. 57, the comm. renders vâṅâs by vâEkyan. : 2. Both the seven and the seventy that gather against those of the neck — let them all etc. etc.

Part of the mss. (including our DR.) accent saptâ at the beginning, and SPP. with good reason adopts that in his text.

3. Both the nine and the ninety that gather against those of the shoulders—let them all etc. etc.

Ppp., in these verses, exchanges the numbers of r and 3, omits yâs every time in a, and combines manyâ "bhi, grâioyâ 'bhi, skanda bi.

docs.title: 26. Against evil
docs.text:
[Brakman.— pâpmadevat kam. ânngubham.] ; Found also in Pâipp. xix. Used in Kâug. (30.17) in a healing rite against all diseases ; and reckoned (note to 26. r) to the Zakmanâcana gapa. The comm. finds it quoted also in the Nakṣ. K. (15), in a ceremony against niryi.

Translated : Florenz, 282 or 34; Griffith, i. 259 ; Bloomfeld, 163, 473.

I. Let me go, O evil (pâpmân); being in control, mayest thou be : gracious to us; set me uninjured in the world of the excellent, O evil.

All the mss. leave pâpman unaccented at beginning of â, and SPP. follows them. The second pada occurred above as v. 22.9 b. Ppp. rectifies the defective meter of c, by reading a ma bhadresu dkâmasv atve dk-. The comm. gives san instead of sar in b. The Anukr. overlooks the deficiency of two syllables.

2. Thou who, O evil, dost not leave us, thee here do we leave ; along at the turning apart of the ways, let evil go after another. The comm. understands anu"yâeartane as one word in c. Ppp. exchanges the place of 2 c, 4d and 3 a, b, reading, for the former, patho uya wyâwartane nis papma roan: suvâmasi ; land it has ma for na in a.

3. Elsewhere than [with] us let the thousand-eyed immortal one make its home; whomsoever we may hate, him let it come upon (74); and whom we hate, just him do thou smite..

Ppp., as above noted, has the first half of this verse as its a c, , reading corruptly nyzcya : for ny ucyatu ; its version of c, d is yo no dvesti tan gacka yar dvismas tar: jahi. ³ The comm. renders ny ucyatn by nitarâi gacchatu.

docs.title: 27. Against birds of ill omen
docs.text:
[Br gu. —yâmyam uta nâirytam. jâgatam : a. trégtubk.]

Found also in Pâipp. xix. With. 28.1 and 29. 1, it constitutes RV. x. 165. MGS. ii. 17. 1 a—e is made up of our vi. 27, parts of 29.1 and 28.3, and 8, 1: see also the pratrkas in Knauer's Index. ] Hymns 27, 28, and 29 are employed together in Kâug. (46. 7) against birds of ill omen (the comm. to AV. reads patatribhyas for patitebkyas of the edition of Kâug.).

Translated : Florenz, 282 or 34; Griffith, i. 259 ; Bloomfield, 166, 474.

I. Seeking what, O gods, the sent dove, messenger of perdition, hath come hither, to it will we sing praises, make removal ; weal be [it] to our bipeds, weal to our quadrupeds.

RV. has precisely the same text in this verse. Ppp. begins with âeways k-. Some of the mss. (including our P.M. W.T.) read nâṅkytinz in c. The verse lacks two syllables of being a full jagatt.

2. Propitious to us be the sent dove, harmless, O gods, the hawk (cakunâ) [sent] to our house; for let the inspired (vâpra) Agni enjoy our oblation, let the winged missile avoid us.

Ppp. agrees with RV. in the better reading grṅâsu (for grhânm nak) at end of b. ] One suspects that « hawk " may be too specific. ]

3. May the winged missile not harm us; it maketh its track on the hearth, in the fire-holder ; propitious be it unto our kine and men; let not the dove, O gods, injure us here.

The form asârt (p. astrt #7) is quoted under Prat. i. 74 as an example of a locative in 7 (pragrhya); RV. has the less primitive form âṣ7rvâm ; the comm. explains it by uyaprayâam aranyânyam. For c, 4, RV. has a slightly different text: ¢âr no gebhyag ca prrngebhyac ca stu mâ no hiṅsid ihâ devah kapâtah. The AV. version spoils the meter of c, but the Anukr. does not heed. this.

docs.title: 28. Against birds of ill omen etc
docs.text:
[BkygUL.— YEMyam ula n&irytam. trâigtubham : 2. anugtubh ; 3. jagatr.)

All the verses found also in Pâipp., but not together ; I. occurs after the preceding hymn in xix. ; 3. at a later point in xix. ; 2. in x.; and there is no internal connection perceptible among them. Used by Kâug., with the preceding and the following hymn, against birds of ill omen (46. 7); and vs. 2 is especially quoted as accompanying the leading of a cow [and] fire three times around the house. ] Vss. r and 3 occur at MGS. i. r7. 1 —see under h. 27.

Translated : Florenz, 285 or 375 Griffith, i. 260.

I. With the praise-verse (7c) drive ye the dove forth (pranâdam); reveling in food (4) we lead a cow about, breaking up tracks hard to go in; leaving us (our ?) sustenance shall it fly forth, swift-flying. Pranâdam, lit. with forth-driving,' a quasi gerundial cognate accusative. RV. (x. 165. 5) has nayadhvam at end of b, a better reading. In Ppp., b, c are omitted. For c, RV. has saṅyopâyanto duritâni vioâ. In â, both RV. and Ppp. (also the comm.) end with p74 patâar pâristhak, of which our reading can only be a corruption; Bârhisthal (p. pârhisthak) indicates a confusion with parkhiesthâ the non-division and accent also point to pâristhak as tue reading Ppp. has ivan for kitvâ aa.

2. These have taken fire about; these have led the cow about; they have gained themselves fame (crâvas) among the gods — who shall venture to attack them?

The RV. has the same verse at x. 155. 5 (also VS., xxxVv. 18, precisely the same text with RV.), reading, for a, b, pârz 'mâ gâm anesata pâry agnim akysata. Ppp. trans poses a and b and reads pary agnim aharyata (a false form). The aryata of our text is plainly nothing but a corruption ; and part of the. mss. (including our P.M. W.I.) have instead arâsata or artsata ; K. risaru.

3. He who first attained (â-sad) the slope [of heaven], spying out the road for many, who is master of these bipeds, who of the quadrupeds — to that Yama, to death, be homage.

With the former half-verse is to be compared RV. x. 14. I a, b: gareyivânsan pravâto makir 4nu b. p. anupaspacânâm (which is AV. xviii. 1. 49 a, b); â is the last pâda also of RV. x. 165. 4 (of which a, b are found here in 29.1); c is nearly equal to RV. x. 121. 3 C (our iv. 2. I c; xiii. 3:24 c). Ppp. follows RV. in c in putting ke before asya (reading ṅay asya). Our pada-text accents asyâ : Śe; in RV. also asyâ is accented. The verse lacks two syllables of being a full jzgarz. Pischel discusses the verse, Ved. Stud. i. 73: cf. 66. ] Ppp. has pravatâsasâda.

docs.title: 29. Against birds of ill omen
docs.text:
[Bhr gu. —yâmyam uta nâirytam. bârhatam : I, 2. virâunâmagâyatri ; 3. y-av. 7p. virâgaṣti.]

Not found in Pâipp. Used by Kâug. (46. 7) with the two preceding hymns.

Translated : Florenz, 287 or 39 ; Griffith, i. 260 ; Bloomfield, 166, 475.

I. Them yonder let the winged missile come upon ; what the owl utters, [be] that to no purpose, or that the dove makes its track (aââ) at the fire.

The second and third pâdas are RV. x. 165. 4 a, b (we had d in the last verse of the preceding hymn); RV. omits 7 in c; its addition damages the meter of the pâda, but the Anukr. overlooks this. Pâdas b,c also occur at MGS. ii. 17. 1 d—cf. under h. 2. 2. Thy two messengers, O perdition, that come hither, not sent forth or sent forth, to our house —for the dove and owl be this no place.

The comm. reads ezâu for etâs in a; he renders âpadam by anâ;rayabhṅtan.

3. May it fly hither in order to nou-destruction of heroes ; may it settle (7-sad) here in order to abundance of heroes ; turned away, do thou speak away, toward a distant stretch (? sa7tvât); so that in Yama's house they may look upon thee [as] sapless, may look upon [thee as] empty (âbhṅka).

The sense would favor the accent dvâirahatya in a; and avṅakatyâyâaz, which the comm. reads, would be a further improvement. The comm. also has papadâyat at end of a, and, for c, parâm eva parâvatam. He explains abhṅ kan by agatavantasn. At the end of e, grââ ought, of course, to be grṅ2 ; but most of the mss. (all of ours that are noted) have gr4â, and SPP. also has admitted it into his text. As to Yama's house. cf. Hillebrandt, Ved. Mythol., i. 512. For câkacân, see Gram. § Ioo8 b.

docs.title: 30. To the cami plant : for benefit to the hair
docs.text:
[Eparâabhrava.—câmyam. jâgatam : 2. trigubh ; 3. 42. kakummaty anugtubṅ.]

Found also in Pâipp. xix. Verse 1 is wholly unconnected in meaning with the others, nor do these clearly belong together. Used by Kâug. (66.15) in the sawayajâas, at a sava called paunalgila ( paunasira, comm.); and vs. 2 (2 and 3, comm.) in a remedial rite (31. I).

Translated : Ludwig, p. 512; Florenz, 288 or 4o; Griffith, i. 261.— See also Bergaigne-Henry, Manuel, p. 151.

I. This barley, combined with honey, the gods plowed much on the Sârasvati, in behalf of Manu (?); Indra, of a hundred abilities, was furrow-master; the liberal (? sudânu) Maruts were the plowmen.

Ppp. has this verse only by citation of its pratika, as if it had occurred earlier ; but it has not been found elsewhere in the text. It occurs also in TB. (ii. 4.87; exactly repeated in APCS. vi. 30.20 ; PGS. iii. 1. 6), MB. ii. 1.16, and K. (xiii. r5). The TB. version begins with ezâm un tyâm mâdk- (so MB. also), and it gives in b sârasvatyâs and manâv: cf. manâv âdhi, RV. viii. 61. 2; ix. 63-8 ; 65.16; and the translation follows this reading ; MB. has vanâva carkrdki. The comm., too, though he reads maṇââ, explains it by manuṣyâjârzn. In a, he has saṅyitam (for samyutam). He explains acarkrsus by krtavantas, as if it came from root 471 SPP. reads mapnâi, without note of variant.

2. The intoxication that is thine, with loosened hair, with disheveled hair, wherewith thou makest a man to be laughed at — far from thee do I wrench [out] other woods; do thou, O gamâ, grow up with a hundred twigs.

Even the lines of this verse seem unrelated. Ppp. has, in a, made vikeco yo vikegyo and its c, d are entirely different: Śhrâpaghno varivṅnaâ janitvar: tasya te prajayas suvâami kegam. SPP. reads catâvakâ in â, with a part of the mss. (including our P.MK.Kp.). The comm. explains u7k5i by vygcâmi; but its connection and form, in the obscurity of the verse, are doubtful. W. Foy discusses root 777, KZ. xxxiv. 241 ff., and this vs. at p. 244. ] R. writes: " The fruit of the ga7, the pod or kernels, is regarded (Caraka, p. 182, l. 6) as injurious to the hair; and from the designation kegcamathant in Râjan. 8.33 is to be inferred that it makes the hair fall out. But nothing is said of an intoxicating effect. To the two trees usually identified with cam?, Prosopis spicigera and Mimosa suma, belongs neither the one nor the other effect. Nor is either ' of great leaves." [ The Dhanvantariya Nighaṇtu, p. 188 of the Poona ed., also speaks of amr as kegahantrz and of its fruit as kecanâacana.

3. O thou of great leaves, blessed one, rain-increased, righteous! as a mother to her sons, be thou gracious to the hair, O gant.

It is possible to read sixteen syllables out of the second half-verse (accenting then m7ââ), but the description of the Anukr. implies 84-8: 846=30 syllables as does also the position of the avasâna-mark, which is put after mz ga i Ppp. eases the situation by (inserting nas before cami in â; it also reads #râhvasvapne (for varsavyâdhe) in b.

docs.title: 31. At rising of the sun (or moon)
docs.text:
[Uparibabkrava. —gavyam. gâyatram.]

Found also in Pâipp. xix., as in RV. (x. 189. I-3), SV. (ii. 726-8), VS. (iii. 6-8), TS. (i. 5.39), K. (vil. 13), MS. (i. 6.1). Used by Kâug. (66.14) in the savayajṅas, with a spotted cow as sava. And by Vâit. in the agnyadheya ceremony (6. 3), as the sacrificer approaches the âkavantya fire; and again in the sattra (33. 28), spoken by the Brahman-priest to the kolar, after the mânasastotra. Also in i. 631-3 = Nâigeyacâkha v. 46-8.

Translated : as RV. hymn, by Max Miiller, ZDMG. ix. (1855), p- XI ; Geldner, Sâebenzig Lieder des RV, 1875, p. 57; Ludwig, number r6o ; Grassmann, ii. 433; and as AV. hymn, by Florenz, 289 or 41; Griffith, i. 262.

I. Hither hath stridden this spotted steer, hath sat upon his mother in the east, and going forward to his father, the heaven (suâr).

All the texts agree in this verse, except that TS, has âsanat and gṅnak in b, while Ppp. has prayat in c. It seems to be a description of the rising of a heavenly body, — the comm. and the translators say, the sun; but the epithet " spotted," and the number thirty in the third verse point rather to the moon. The mother " is of course the earth, upon which it seems to rest a moment.

2. He moves between the shining spaces, from the breath of this outbreathing [universe]; the bull (Gnakisâ) hath looked forth unto the heaven (svâr).

RV. (with which, through the whole hymn, SV. and VS. entirely agree) reads (as does TS.) apâanatt (p. apasanatt) at end of b; in c, it reads ââam for svââ. TS. inverts the order of a and b, and has the same c as our text ; on the other hand, MS. has our b, but arpave (for rocanâ) in a, and a wholly peculiar c: grâri wâm skro âhabhik. Ppp. has (nearly as TS.), for a, b, yasya prapâad apanatly antag carati rocanaṅ; and Jivam (with RV.) at the end. The sense of the verse is very obscure, made so by the unintelligible second pada ; Roth suggests apânati as 3d singular J, with 7zocanâ stars as subject : ⁴ They die at his breath ": but this teems with difficulties. [In Geldner's note, anati was taken as 3d plural. ] Our P.M.IR.T.K,, and all SPP's authorities, separate rocanâ asyâ in sa7hîta (the pada-text reading -#7), and SPP. has accordingly, properly enough, adopted it in his text: see the note to Prat. iii. 34. Ppp. also has uyâkkyan. J

3. Thirty domains (dkâman) he rules over; voice, the bird, hath set up, to meet the day with the lights of morning.

This translation is one of despair, and of no value, like the others that are given of the verse. Taken by itself, the first pada is well enough, and seems most naturally (as noted above) to refer to the thirty days of the moon's synodical revolution, or spaces of the sky traversed by it in them; to understand it of the thirty divisions of the day (mukâria) looks like an anachronism ; and thirty gods (Ludwig) is wholly senseless. LRoth observes : Ushas, in returning to her point of departure, traverses thirty yejanas (RV. i. 123. 8): the path of the light around the world thus appears to be divided into thirty stages. ] The variety of reading of the texts indicates, as in many other like cases, the perplexity of the text-makers. RY. (with SV.VS.) has, for b, vâ% patamgâya Jhtyare ; TS. and MS. have patargâya, but TS. follows it with (riye, and MS. with hṅyate. Ppp. reads gâya su (riyat. In c, RV. (etc.) reads â4a, particle, for âhas, and the comm. does the same ; TS. gives, for the whole pâda, prâty asya vaka dyubhtk while MS. substitutes our 2 c, in its RV. version, having given its wholly independent version of this as 2 c (see above); Ppp. has at end âivi. In a, MS. reads tâ7câddhâma, as compound ; the other texts (and three of SPP's authorities) have triṅgââd dhâma y (the pada-reading is dhâma). Both TS. and MS., it may be added, put vs. 3 before 2. y

With this hymn ends the third zzuvâka, of rr hymns and 33 verses ; the extracted { item of Anukr. is simply â72ya (see end of the next annvâka).

docs.title: 32. Against demons
docs.text:
lr, 2. Câtana ; 3. Atharvan. —agnidâivatam. rtrâṅtubham : a. prastârapaṅkti.]

The first two verses found also in Pâipp. xix.* Kâug. has the hymn (or vss. 1, 2) in a remedial rite against demons (31. 3); the fire is circumambulated three times, and a cake is offered ; and it is reckoned (note to 8.25) to the câzana gaṅa. Verse 3 is by itself reckoned (note to 16.8) to the abkaya gaya, and also (note to 25. 36) to the svastyayana gapa. Ppp. then has a third verse, whose a= vi. 45. 1 a, and whose b is ¹ corrupt. Roth's note seems incomplete.

Translated : Florenz, 291 or 43; Griffith, i. 262 ; Bloomfield, 36, 475.

I. Within the flame, pray, make ye this sorcerer-destroying libation with ghee ; from afar, O Agni, do thou burn against the demons; mayest thou not be hot toward our houses.

Our mss. (so far as noted) and nearly all SPP's, accent jukutâ in a ; but his text, as well as ours, emends to jukutâ. The comm. understands at the beginning antar dave ¹ as two separate words ; and that is a preferable, and probably the true, reading. The gen. 4 in d is peculiar ; we should expect with it f7apaâti, in impers. sense : ¹ may there be no sickness befalling our houses.' Ppp. reads gkrtaṅ: nal at end of b; and, for d, mz ¹smâkan vasṅ pa tiipantkṅ. The verse (10+ 10: I2+ II =43) is ill-defined as a mere z7âstubh.

2. Rudra hath crushed (gr) your necks, O pââcâs ; let him crush in (agi-cr) your ribs, O sorcerers ; the plant of universal power hath made you go to Yama.

A few of SPP's authorities (also the Anukr., in citing the verse) read agar? in a. Some of our mss. accent pââcâṅ at end of a (P.M.I.p.m.), and yâtudhznâk (P.M I.); all the pada-mss. absurdly have vâwâtahovrryâ)ṅ at end of c. Ppp. has, for a, b, ar vo vo grivây acaris piâaca vo pa cruâty agniky and in d it gives mytyunâ for yamena. I The verbal forms with suspicious 77" in the AV. (carâis etc., asaparyââr: cf. Gram. 88 555 , 9o4 b, 1068 a) have been treated by Bloomfield, ZDMG. xlviii. 574 ff., and B5htlingk, ibidem, liv. 510 ff. Cf. also note to xviii. 3. 40. J

3. Fearlessness, O Mitra-and-Varuṇa, be ours here ; drive ye backward the devourers with your gleam ; let them not find a knower, nor a foundation (pratisthâ); mutually destroying one another let them go unto death. The verse occurs also in AGS. (ifi. ro. 1), which has, in a, b, -nâ makyam astv aris ⁴ carrnn dahatau pratiya ; inc, vindantu yy in 9, (hindâanâs. The latter half-verse is rane found again as iil. 8.21 c,d. Pâda a has a redundant syllable unheeded by the Anukr.

docs.title: 33. Praise to Indra
docs.text:
[Jâtikâyana.— indradâivatam. gâyatram : 2. anugtubṅ.]

Found also in Pâipp. xix., and in AA. (v. 2. 1) and CCS. (xviii. 3.2); and the first verse, in the Nâigeya supplement to SV. i. (i. 35 or SV. i. 588). Kaâug. quotes, in the section relating to house-building, marking cattle, etc., with the simple direction iy âyojanâanâm agyayak (23.17); the schol. and the comm. declare it to relate to the rite for success in plowing (475ikarman); the details of the process described by them have nothing to do with the expressions of the Atharvan text. Again, it appears in a i kâmya ceremony (59. 18), with vii. 2, 6, etc. (by a sarvaphalakâma, comm.); and the comm. holds it to be intended (ro6. 1, 8) in the portent-rite for the collision of plows. It is further reckoned (note to rg. r) to the pustika mantras.

Translated : Florenz, 293 or 45; Griffith, i. 263.

I. Of whom the welkin (râ7as) here [is] the allies, [who] thrusts (?) people, the wood, the heaven —great [is] Indra's gladness.

This is a mechanical version, not pretending to sense; the verse appears to be too corrupt for anything else. The other texts bring plenty of variants, but no real improvements of reading. All agree in c; also in yâsye 'dâm at the beginning of a; between, SV. has ârâjo yâjas tnje jâne vânan: svâk; AA. has arâias tâjo yṅjo vânari sâhak; CCS. has gia ârujas tujo yujo balaṅ: sakak. Ppp. reads inte janaṅ svak, and, for the rest of 1 and 2, indrasya nâagnikecavak vrsânar âkrṣadas cavas pura yarkâ dhistinah indrag ca rantyan: makat. The comm. explains fuje by tojan3ya catr ipâr hiṅsanâya, takes yâjas as a verb = saṅmnadâhar: karoti, vânanz as vananiyan, svâr as susthu praptavyam, etc.: all the purest nonsense.

2. [He is] not to be dared against; [his] might, dared, dares daring against [others]; as, of old, his fame [was] unwavering, Indra's might [is] not to be dared against. : The (provisional) translation given implies emendation of text, in a, d, to ââ%7se, in b, to ky sâpârn: dkrsitâm, and, in c, to 'uyarkt. AA's version of the whole is 7nâ dhr3a 2 dadharsa dââhkrsEpân dhrsitâr câvaṅ: purâ yâdâ nn âtioyâthtr tnârasya âkyṣital sâhak. LCt. iv. 21. 3 and note, and Geldner, Ved. Stud. Ś. 29. ] CCS. has nothing cor responding to the second half-line; for the first, it reads anâdhr|tan vipanyayr ag : ¹âhysa adadharsayâ: âkysânan: âhyyitan gavak. The reading of Ppp. was given i ; under vs. 1. The comm. has wyatki in c. ¹ 3. Let him give us that wide wealth, of reddish (pâcâ7ga-) aspect; : Indra [is] most powerful lord among the people. i

Ppp., also the comm., and one of our MSS. (H.) read dadkhâtu in a, and AA. and CCS. and the comm. have âm for tân; Ppp. gives no instead; instead of arṅm in b, ¹ CCS. has puru, and AA. repeats rayân. In ec, both AA. and CCS. read favastamas; : the comm., tuvittamas. Our tuvistamas is vouched for by two rules of the Praâti-. câkhya, iii. 96 and iv. 59. Further, the comm. in b reads -saâ7(am: That the verse is Ś : uspik and not gâyarri appears not to be noted in the Anukr. I CCS. omits 7 at the end.

docs.title: 34. Praise and prayer to Agni
docs.text:
[Câtana.— paṅcarcam. 1 agnidâtvatam. gâyatram.]

Only vss. I, 3, 4 found in Pâipp. xix. It is also a RV. hymn, x. 187 (with exchange ¹ Śâ of place between vss. 2 and 3); in other texts is found only the last verse. As in the &ŚŚ case of certain previous hymns with a refrain, one may conjecture that, with omission ¹ ¹ of the refrain, and combination of the remaining parts of verses, it was made into or i g viewed as three verses ; but the case is a much less probable one than those we have Ś¹ had above. docs.title: 35. Prayer to Agni Vâigvânara
docs.text:
Cl LX âugika. — vigvânaradâivatam. gâyarram.]

Found also in Pâipp. xix., and in the Crâuta-Sâtras of Agvalâyana (vil. rr. 4) and

Câṅkhâyana (x. 9-17); the first verse, further, in VS. and MS. This hymn and the

one following are called by Kâug. (31. 5) wâṅwânariya, and used in a general remedial rite ; and verse 35. 2 is reckoned (note to 32.27) to the aṅṅoliṅga gana. In Vâit., hymn 35 appears alone in the agnicayana (29.5), with i. 21 and vil. 84, accompanying the covering of the first courses of bricks. = 4 Translated : Florenz, 295 or 475 Griffith, i. 264.

El ² ¹ ²

I. Let Vâigvânara, for our aid, come forth hither from the distance — Agni, unto our good praises.

ACS. has this verse precisely as in our text, and so has VS. at xviii. 72 land CCS. has the gratika, a, but VS. xxvi. 8 has again the first two pâdas, with agnâr ukthâna. vâhasa (see under the next verse) for third; and MS. iii. 16.4 has the latter version, with the further variant of 24 prâ (i.e, doubtless, #27 7 prâ) at the end of a. Ppp. has the bad reading ârâyâ pra; it further exchanges the third pâdas of 1 and 2, i and reads as 2 c wpe ma) sustutizk mama.

2. Vâigvânara, our ally (sâ7âs), hath come unto this our offering— i Agni, at our songs, in our distresses.

The two Sutras have for c agnir ukthena vwâkasâ (found in VS. MS. in combination with r a, b); Ppp., as also noticed above, has for c our I c. The translation given implies that 4ṅkasu (which is read by all the mss. without exception, and is quoted so in the commentary to Prât. iv. 32) is the same with the usual â7ṅâaṅsu; no stem ârṅkhan ¹ is found anywhere else ; the comm. foolishly explains it by abkâgantauyesu, adj to i ukthesu. The translation, moreover, represents the pada-text reading of âgamatin a as 4: agamat; but it seems altogether likely that the true meaning is : gaat 'may he come.'

3. May Vâigvânara shape the praise and song of the Afigirases; may he extend to them brightness (dyumnâ) [and] heaven (svâr).

Of the two Sttras, CCS. supports our czklpar (comm. cakypar) in sense by reading jŚanat; ACS. has the better reading câkanat ' take pleasure in' ACS. also has aṅgirobkyas in a (both preserve the a of aṅg-) ; Ppp. has no aṅgirobkis. In b, Ppp. and CCS. have yajṅam for uktham ; ACS. has stoma for -masm, and in c omits a (if it is not a misprint); Ppp. has pra instead of a7 su.

docs.title: 36. In praise of Agni
docs.text:
[Atharvan (svastyayanakâmaRk).— âgneyam. gâyatram.]

Found also, imperfect, in Pâipp. xix., and in other texts, as SV. (ii. 1038-60), etc., 4 mentioned under the several verses. For the use of the hymn with its predecessor by Kâug. (31.5), see under the latter.

The Sâman version, as also that in VS. (xxvi.6), in MS. (iv. r1. I), and ACS. ¹ (viii. ro. 3), is precisely accordant with ours ; that in CCS. (iii. 3. 5) has kz um instead of gharmâm in c. ¹

docs.title: 37. Against curses
docs.text:
: g : (ALrharvan (svastyayanakâmaṅ).— cândyamasam. â&nugtubham.] Found also in Paâipp. xx. Quoted by Kâug. (48.23) in a witchcraft ceremony Śl ¹ (against the effect of an opponent's sorcery, comm.), with giving a pale lump (Śânâan:

pagum : the comm. explains it as a lump of white dirt) to a dog; and vs. 3 is, doubt- Ś Vn less correctly, regarded by the comm. as intended at 43. 37 (the prarzka would equally . ¹ designate vii. 59), with the laying on of fuel from a tree struck by lightning. docs.text:

Found also in Paâipp. ii. (in the order 1, 2, 4, 3); and in TB. ii. 7. 7¹- (in the order I, 4, 2, 3) and K. xxxvi. 15 (in the order 3, 2, I, 4). This hymn and its successor are employed together by Kaâug. (13. 3-6) in a rite for glory, with the navel-hairs of sundry creatures cf. Weber, Râjasâya, p. 99, n. 3 J, and splinters of ten kinds of trees; and f they are reckoned to both varcasya ganas (notes to 12. ro and 13.1). They are d further included [ 139. I5 with several others (i. 30; iv. 30, etc.) in a rite (called wisarjana, comm.) in the ceremony of entering on Vedic study.

I. What brilliancy (rvâsi) is in lion, in tiger, and what in adder, in fire, in the Brahman, what in the sun: the fortunate goddess that gave birth to Indra—let her come to us, in union with splendor.

Ppp. reads vavarâha for jajâna in c, and sa ² nâi "tu in d. TB. has in the refrain & gan (or & gan) for at za.

2. What brilliancy is in elephant, in leopard, what in gold, in waters, in kine, what in men (gi rusa): the fortunate goddess etc. etc.

Ppp. and TB. agree in reading âgvesu purusesn gâsu in b.

3. In chariot, in dice, in the bull's strength (24a), in wind, in raingod, in Varuṇa's vehemence (câṣma): the fortunate goddess etc. etc.

Ppp. inverts the order of wâze and parjânye in b; TB. and comm. Jread e77athâsya in a.

4. In a noble (r7janyâ), in the drum, in the drawn [arrow], in the horse's vigor, in man's roar (?): the fortunate goddess etc. etc.

Ppp. and TB. agree in prefixing yâ at the beginning of the verse, and TB. has i krândye for vâje in b, while Ppp. has, for b, rvigir agve mâyârk stanayitna gesu ya. M3yâ is not properly used of p#rusa 'man,' and the expression is obscure and doubtful. The comm. takes Zyatâyam as = ârââyamânâyâm and qualifying dunâubkhâai l For the meaning here assigned to it, see note to vi. 65. 1. ] In this hymn, again, it appears as if the equivalence to three verses were recognized, the refrain of vss. 2, 3 being left out of account. But the Anukr. acknowledges four verses, and each of the four has its refrain in TB.

I. Let fearlessness, O heaven-and-earth, be here for us; let Soma,

Savitar, make us fearlessness; be the wide atmosphere fearlessness for

docs.title: 41. To various divinities
docs.text:
[Brahkman.— bahudâivatam uta cândramasam. ânuggubham : I. Śhury; 3. trâgubkh.]

Not found in Pâipp., nor, so far as observed, in any other text. Used by Kaâug. (54. 11), with ii. r5, in the godâna ceremony, as the youth is made to eat a properly cooked dish of big rice (makâvriṅî).

Translated : Florenz, 301 or 53; Griffith, i. 266.

I. To mind, to thought, to device (44), to design, and to intention, ⁴ to opinion (matt), to instruction (grutzâ), to sight, would we pay worship i with oblation. f

The meter in b would be rectified by reading #k41yâi. In his note toi. 1. I, W. took i ruta here as ' sense of hearing.'

2. To expiration, to perspiration (uyânâ), to breath the much nourishing, to Sarasvati the wide extending, would we pay worship with y ation.

3. Let not the seers who are of the gods leave us, who are self (anṅ)- protecting, self-born of our self; O immortal ones, attach yourselves to us mortals ; grant life-time (âyus) in order to our further living.

With the first line is to be compared AB. ii. 27. 7 : rsayo dâivyâsas tanâpEvRnas tanvas tapojak (Florenz). Tuna (lit. 'body') 'self' apparently refers throughout to ourselves. This verse is translated by Muir, OST. v. 296. (Ar kâsisur Fsayo datviz nak would make good meter. docs.text:
[I Śkṅrguaṅgiras (parasparanmcittâiṅikaranaṅ).— manyudevatyam. &nustubham : r, 2. bkur(.]

Found also, with considerable variation, in Paipp. xix. Used by Kâug. (36. 28-30), in the section of rites concerning women, for the appeasement of anger: with vs. 1, one takes a stone on seeing the angry person ; with vs. 2 one sets it down toward the same; 1 with vs. 3 one spits upon it (z5hkinisthrvati : the text would suggest rather abkiâtiszhati). ¹ The hymn is reckoned also (note to 26. 1) to the tzkmanâcana gana. In Vâjt (12. 13) it is employed in the agnistoma in case of an outbreak of anger.

Translated : Ludwig, p. 515; Florenz, 302 or 54; Grill, 29, 162; Griffith, 1.267; ( Bloomfield, 136, 479.

I. As the string from the bow, do I relax (ava-tan) fury from thy i heart, that, becoming like-minded, we (two) may hold together (sac) like friends. ¹

The Ppp. version is in many points different : ava jyâm iva âhanvina; cusmaṇz tanomi te kydah : adhâ sammanasâu bhutvâ sakhike "va sacâvake. The first halfverse occurs at MP. ii. 22. 3, with kyâas transferred to the beginning of bj] also in. HGS. (. 15.3), with dkanvinas (like Ppp), and with ky das transferred as in MP. J, and with gym for jyâm. In this verse and the next, the Anukr. does not allow the abbreviation "oa after sâkkh2yau. y

2. We (two) will hold together like friends ; I relax thy fury; we cast in thy fury under a stone that is heavy.

Perhaps better thy fury that is heavy '; but the version of Ppp. with the comm. ] decidedly supports the translation as given: acmanâ manyun gurwṇa pi ai dadkmasi. Ppp's version of a, b is this : vi te manyur nayâmasi [ cf. MP. ii. 22.2 ] sakkike 'va sacâuakâi.

1I do not see why prâpadâa may not here be rendered by toe.'] Ppp. reads, for b, parsuibkyam prapadâabhyâm ; and, for c, 4, parâ te dastyâm vadhaṅ: parâ manyur suvâmi te. The second half-verse recurs at the end of the next hymn. Pâda d is a stock-phrase : see i. 34.2; iii. 25. 5; vi. 9.25 43.3.

docs.text:
[(As 42.) —manyugamanadevatâkam. &nugtubham.]

Found also in Pâipp. xix. In Kâug. (36.32), the hymn appears, next after hymn i 42, in a rite for appeasement of anger, darb)a being treated as an amulet (? osadkhivar)..

Translated : Florenz, 303 or 55; Grill, 30, 162; Griffith, i. 267; Bloomfield, 137, 480.

I. This darbkâ [is] fury-removing, both for one's own man and for a stranger ; and this is called a fury-removing fury-appeaser of fury.

The translation implies the emendation of vimanyukasya in c to -kag ca (as proposed ³ by Grill, ând virtually by Florenz). Ppp. supports the change, reading vimanyako % manyugamano 'stu me ; it has vimanyakas also in a.

2. This that is many-rooted, [that] reaches down (ava-stââ) to the sea, the âarbhâ, arisen out of the earth, is called a fury-appeaser.

Ppp. reads, in b, prthiuyâm ‘in the earth,' instead of samudyâm ' to the sea'; end of c, and â, nisthitas sa ce 'stu vimanyakak. The Anukr. takes no notice of the y deficiency of a syllable in a.

3. We conduct away the offense (? garâṇi) of thy jaws, away that of thy mouth, that thou mayest not speak uncontrolled, mayest come unto my intent.

The last half-verse is a repetition of vi. 42. 3 c, 4 which see]; it is wanting in Ppp. perhaps as result of a lacuna. Most of the mss. have the false reading mâkṅyâan in b, but SPP. also emends to -7, being supported by the comm. The latter explains carânim by kiṅsâhetubhurârir kroâhabhivyanjikâam dhamanim.

docs.title: 44. For cessation of a disease
docs.text:
[I Fâvâmitra.— mantrokadvvatyam uta vânaspaiyam. ânugtubham : 3. 3:6. mahGtyhati.]

I Partly prose —vs. 3.1 The verses 1, 2, are found also in Pâipp., I a, b in iii.; 16, d and 2 in xix. Used in Kâug. (31.6) in a remedial rite against slander (apavâda; but the text of. Bloomfield, p. Ślv. l reads apavârz), with help of a self-shed cow-horn properly prepared.

Translated : Ludwig, p. 509; Florenz, 304 or 56; Griffith, i. 268; Bloomfield, ro, 481.— Cf. Bergaigne-Henry, Manuel, p. 151; Zimmer, p. 390.

I. The heaven hath stood ; the earth hath stood; all this living world hath stood ; the trees have stood, sleeping erect; may this disease of thine stand.

The peculiar epithet Zrâdhwasvapna was applied by Ppp. to a tree also in its version of 30.3, above. "Stand," i.e. come to a standstill." ]

2. What hundred remedies are thine, and [what] thousand, assembled — [with them thou art] the most excellent remedy for flux, the best effacer of disease. i

Ppp. has yar for yâ in a, and sambkytani (for -gatâant) in b; instead of c, it reads tesâm asi vam urtamam anâsrâva saroganam* (= ii. 3.2 c, 4); in â9, ska. The k Ppp. reading, and ii. 3. 2, suggest supplying rather tof them' than ' with them ' between I the half-verses. The comm. understands a, b as addressed to the patient (uyâdṅita). g ¥] Intending, presumably, anâsrâvam aroganar.

3. Rudra's urine art thou, the navel of the immortal (amFta) ; vigâṇakâ (‘horny') by name art thou, arisen from the root of the Fathers, an effacer of the vârikrta.

This prose-stanza is reckoned by the Anukr. as if metrical. Vârtârta, like vâtrkarâ, is too doubtful to render; its derivation from vâra 'wind' is extremely unsatisfactory, and Zimmer's connection of vâfa with our “wound " etc. is also questionable ; the; i. comm. understands vârr kytanâcant (var: = âsrâvasya rogasya cosayirrry. The name visanakâ points to some use of a horn, such as is indicated in the Kâucika (sva- i yaṅsrasta gogrṅga ' a self-shed cow-horn'). [Note that the epithet deciduous " (svayansrasta) corroborates the etymology of visâna as set forth by W. at iii. 7. I, ¹ note. ] The verse (746: 8 + 8-7) does not at all agree with the description of the i Anukr.

I. Go far away, O mind-evill why utterest (cas) thou things unuttered? Go away; I desire thee not; do thou frequent (sanz-cara) trees, woods; Ś in houses, in kine [is] my mind.

I. Thou who art not alive, not dead, immortal-embryo of the gods art thou, O sleep; Varunâni is thy mother, Yama thy father; Araru by name art thou.

Ppp. reads yamas pita. The mss. are much at variance as to two points in this

verse : whether asi or âsi after garbkâs, and whether ârarus or arârus. As regards the former, they are nearly equally divided ; both printed texts give asi, which is doubtau ⁴ ..¹ ².

We know thy place of birth (janttra), O sleep; thou art son of the gods' sisters (;âmî), agent of Yama ; end-maker art thou; death art thou ; so, O sleep, do we comprehend thee here; do thou, O sleep, protect us from evil-dreaming. 3. As a sixteenth, as an eighth, as a [whole] debt they bring together, so do we bring together all evil-dreaming for him who hates us.

'Eighth' ¹ is literally hoof (capṅâ), from the eight hoofs of cattle etc. The sixteenth or eighth is possibly the interest. docs.text:
[ARgiras (?).— âgneyam ; 2. vâivadevi; 3. sâudhanvanâ. trâigubham.] I

Found also in Pâipp. xix. and in TS. (iii. I. 9-2), and KCS. Not used by Kâug.; appears in Vâit. (21. 7) in the agnisfoma, with vi. 48 and ix. I. 11-3, at the szva nas.

I. Let Agni at the morning libation (sâwana) protect us, he that belongs to all men (vââuvânarâ), all-maker, all-wealful ; let him, the l purifier, set us in property (ârâviga); may we be long-lived, provided i with draughts.

Ppp. ends b with garkikyd vigvakystik, and TS. has mahinâ, KCS. (ix. 3. 21) maṅrnâṇy, and MS. (i. 3.36) vigvagrts, for vivakFt; all have drâvipam (for ae) in c; and 4 MS. reads p7âtâ} sâvanât in a. Neither Ppp. nor TS. nor KCS. (ix. 14. 17) have any variant in this verse.

3. This third libation [is] of the poets (Zavâ), who rightfully (zâna) ¹ sent out the bowl; let those Sâudhanvanas, who have attained heaven, conduct our happy-offering unto what is better. ²

That is (a), of the Ribhus, one of whose merits, leading to the conferral of immortality upon them, was their service to the ceremonial in connection with the libational ¹ bowl, which they made four. [For this the comm. gives ample citations, e.g. RV. i. 161.2.) Ppp. combines, in c, szuâdhanvanâ 'my ta "nacânas, and ends the verse with ² nayâtha. docs.title: 70. To attach a cow to her calf
docs.text:
[A ânkâyana.— âghnyam. jâgutarm.]

Not found in Pâipp. Used by Kâug. (41. 18) in a rite for producing mutual attach- : ment between cow and calf. : Translated : Grill, 65, 165; Griffith, i. 283; Bloomfield, 144, 493. g

I. As flesh, as strong-drink, as dice on the gambling-board ; as of a lustful man the mind is fastened (ui-han) on a woman — so let thy mind, O inviolable one (agṅnyâ), be fastened on thy calf.

The verses are six-pada jagatr (6x 8=48). [ The stanza is wrongly numbered. ]

2. As the elephant strains foot with foot of the she-elephant; as of a : ¹ lustful man etc. etc. ( The obscure first line is with intention rendered obscurely; the Petersburg Lexicon conjectures hastens after, step with step, which then Grill follows. The comm. takes : ¹ ¹ : uâynje as = unnamayati, "bends up, for love (premṇâ), her foot with his foot." be 3. As the felly (pradât), as the rim (upadht), as the nave upon the ¹ felly ; as of a lustful man etc. etc. I See p. xcii. ] ¹ â The first line is again obscure, both in its internal relations and in its relation to the Ś Eâ¹ refrain (in this resembling r a, b). BR. define wpadki as 'the part of the wheel ee between the felly and nave,' but this ought to be arâs ' the spokes ': the comm. explains ¹ ¹t it as (the circle, bound together by the felly, that is the binder together of the spokes i (nemisambadâhak arânâr sambandhako valayak)—i.e. a sort of rim inside the felly.

ŚŚ Probably a solid wheel, without spokes, is had in view. We should expect some other ² preposition than aâkâ ' on' to express the relation of the nave to the felly.

docs.title: 72. For virile power
docs.text:
(âLtharvângiras.—cepo 'rkadevatyam. ânustubham : I. jagati ; 3. bhu7ij.],

Found also in Paipp. xx. Used by Kâug. (40. 16, 17) in a rite for sexual vigor, with an amulet. The arZa-thread spoken of in 16 may find its explanation in the peculiarity reported by Roxburgh (Flora Inâica, ii. 31): "A fine sort of silky flax is in some parts prepared from the bark of the young shoots."

Translated : Griffith, i. 474. —CtŚ. iv. 4; vi. ror.

I. As the black snake spreads himself at pleasure, making wondrous forms (vâpus), by the Asura's magic (mâyâ), so let this arkâ suddenly make thy member altogether correspondent (? sâṅsamaka), limb with limb.

The comm. reads sitas instead of asitâs in a, and explains it as 'a man that is bound. He takes arka as 'an amulet of arka-tree' (Calotropis gigantea, of which various medicinal use is made). In â he reads sa7 samagam and paraphrases the latter with cof like going ' (samanagamana). The Petersburg Lexicon conjectures for sânzsanzaka joined to one another.' The verse is mixed z7¹57ubk and jagarr. g

2. As the member of the (ayâdara is made big by the wind —as great as is the member of the pârasvant, so great let thy member grow. ig

What creature the parasvant is is unknown (Pet. Lex. "perhaps the wild ass"); the r7yâdara is yet more obscure, being mentioned only here. The comm. reads (âyodarantz, i and defines the fzyodara as (a kind of animal '; the b4a of sthṅlabka he takes as representing a verbal root : stââulyena bhâsamânanm. i

3. As much of a limb as is that of the pârasvant, that of the elephant, and that of the ass—as great as of the vigorous (vâj7) horse, so great let thy member grow.

The comm. reads and explains yâvad aṅgiṅanm at the beginning as two independent words ; the metrical irregularity, as well as the anomalousness of the word as a derivative and compound, suggest emendation to yâvad âṅgam (aṅgam = pasas). Cf. Pischel,. Ved. Stud. i. 83, with reference to the ass. ;

The seventh anuvâka, having 11 hymns and 34 verses, ends here; and the mss. quote the old Anukr. to this effect : cazâsybhir adkikas tu saptamaṇ Śyât.

docs.text:
[htharvan. — sâmmanasyam. mantroktanânâdevatyam. trâstubham : I, 3. 5.ur.]

Found also in Pâipp. xix. (with the verse-order I, 3,2). This hymn with iii. 12, vi. 93, xii. I, is reckoned by Kâug. to the vâsiospatyâni (8. 23) or the vâstn gaza; and it ¹ [ and the following hymn, with others (12. 5), to the sâmmanasyâri; also, by the schol. : ¹ (note to Ig. I), to the pustika mantras; and vs. 3 (so comm. : not vii. 6o. 7] by itself : (23. 6) in the ceremony of entering a new house. ¹ Translated : Griffith, i284; Bloomfield, 135; 494.

I. Let Varuṇa come here, Soma, Agni; let Brihaspati with the Vasus come here ; come ye together, [his] fellows, all of you, like-minded, unto the fortune of this stern corrector (ugrâ cetry).

Ppp. reads abk7- instead of wpa- in c, and has at the end sŚjârâs. The comm. explains certy as " one who properly understands the distinction of what is to be done and what is not to be done"; in this word cif seems to take the value of 7 or cây y ‘one who notes and visits or requites.'

2. The vehemence (gâsma) that is within your hearts, the design that has entered into your mind—that I frustrate with the oblation, the ghee; in me, O [my] fellows, be your satisfaction (ramâri).

Intended to restrain intending emigrants, apparently ; as also vs.3. All the mss., and both editions with them, read 74 at the beginning of c, although it is unquestionably an error for 7m, referring to &kṅtân, as the comm. correctly reads and understands. Only one ms. (our Bp.²) has sriwayâami, all the rest crrw-, or its phonetic product, ckrFe- ; but SPP. quite unaccountably (against the sense, and against the use of Vsrz, which has no causative conjugation quotable before the Lalita-Vistara) adopts stvqyami from the comm. (= parasparasambadâdhân karomi): Ppp. has crevayâmi and in â (as in 1 d) sŚjâatâs. The Anukr. should have noted the verse as zârz. [Read y6 v6 sti in a? ]

3. Be ye just here; go not away from us; let Pâshan make [it] pathless for you in the distance; let the lord of the dwelling (vâstu) call aloud after you; in me, O [my] fellows, be your satisfaction.

Ppp. has, in a, e ha yâta m7 pa, at the beginning; it rectifies the meter of b by omitting vas; in c, it reads (yam akvan for johavitn; in â, it again has sujâtâs.

docs.title: 74. For harmony
docs.text:
LAtharvan.— (as above.) ânugtubham : 3. trigrubh, tripâmadevatyâ.]

Found also in Pâipp. xix. (in the verse-order 2, 1, 3). Reckoned by Kâug. (12. 5), with the preceding hymn and others, to the szmmanasyâni.

Translated : Griffith, i. 285 ; Bloomfield, r35, 495.

1. Together let your bodies be mixed (prc), together your minds, together your courses ; together hath this Brahmaṇaspati, together hath Bhaga made you come.

Ppp. has, for 4, somaṅ sar: spareayâru man. The comm. renders sampreyantâm by parasparanuragena samsyjyantân.

2. Concurrence of the mind for you, also concurrence of the heart, also what of Bhaga is wearied (grâniâ)— therewith I make you concur.

Ppp. has, in 4, sani jRUpayâati mam. It is one of the most peculiar and unaccountable of the occasional peculiarities of the pada-text that in d it reads sâmejRapayânmti, combining the preposition with the verb, though the former has the accent. Of all the mss. noted, only one of SPP's has the usual reading * Crântâm in c seems an impossible reading, but even Ppp. gives nothing else. The comm. explains it as 'toil-born penance ' (cramajanitar¹ lapaky. Emendation to cântam 'tranquillized,' ie. rtanquillity, would be very easy, and tolerably satisfactory. ] Whitney's collation certainly notes also D.Kp. as reading sâm : jṅapayâmi ; probably his eye rested on the sam oR dpanam of b (which in his collation-book stands just above the sâmojRapayami of â), when he wrote the above statement. I suspect that the avagraha of sâmsjṅapayâami has blundered in from the samcjṅâpanarm of a and b by a similar mistake of the scribes. Ct. the pada reading ṅpas;ekima at vi. 114. 2.

3. As the Adityas, severe (ugrâ), not bearing enmity, united with the Vasus, with the Maruts, so, O three-named one, not bearing enmity, do thou make these people here like-minded.

Ppp. reads, in a, vasavas instead of vasubhis, and, in c, 9, yamânan imar jana sammanasan kypu tvam, which is better in so far as it makes ak72- adjunct of the object rather than of the subject in the sentence; our text desiderates ¢krpzyarnânan. The verse is found also in TS. (ii. I. 113), which has, in b, marââdbhr rudrâṇ (our reading seems a corruption of this) samâjânatâ 'bht ; and, in c, d, yamâna vkve devâp sâmanaso bhavantu. A god tripâman appears to be met with only in this verse; the one meant is probably Agni, as conjectured by BR., and also explained by the comm.

docs.title: 75. To eject a rival
docs.text:
[Katandha (saparnaksayakâmaṅ). — mantroktadevatyam ; Gindram. ânugubharm : 3.64. jagati.]

Found also in Pâipp. xix. (with the verse-order 1, 3, 2); and in TB. (iii. 3. 113-4) and Ap. (iii. 14.2). LTB. and Ap. agree with Paâipp. in the verse-order and several other points. ] Used by Kâug. (47. 10) in a rite of sorcery ; and again similarly (48. 29-31), with strewing of âdzrbha grass.

Translated : Ludwig, p. 373 ; Grill, 22, 165 ; Griffith, i. 28 5; Bloomfield, 92, 495.

r. I thrust yon man out of home, the rival who fights [us], with the oblation of ejectment ; Indra hath demolished him.

One of our mss. (0.) reads at the end also here (ct. 66. 2, above and note to 32.2 J) waraiz. Ppp., also TB.Ap., have nirâ- at the beginning of c; and TB. Ap. have nam in d (the two agree in every point through the hymn). Ppp. parâgart, as at 66.2.

2. Let Indra, Vritra-slayer, thrust him to the most distant distance, whence he shall not come back, through constant years (sââ).

Ppp. TB. Ap. read rug for tâm in a, and TB.Ap. nayaru for nudatn in b, while Ppp. has, for b, indro devo aciklpar all three have -yasi at end of c.

3. Let him go [beyond] three distances; let him go beyond the five peoples; let him go beyond the three shining spaces, whence he shall not come back, through constant years, so long as the sun shall be in the sky.

Instead of â, TB. Ap. have three times 744, and they omit padas d, e; RV. (viii. 32. 22 a, b) agrees with them in pâdas a, b. Ppp. reads anu for ati at end of b, and has, for c, the corrupt ²4a ca tua tu rocanâ; it omits â, e, like the other texts. The pada-text ‘ reads rocanâ (not -nâj), maintaining the usual and proper gender of the word, although, being qualified by tâsrâs, it is apparently taken here as feminine, and should be rocanaâ. The mark of punctuation added after d in our edition is not in the mss.; it was heedlessly introduced in going through the press; and the accent of cagvartbhyas is misprinted.

docs.title: 76. For a ksatriya's security from death
docs.text:
[Kabandha.— caturycam. sâmtapanâgneyam. ânugtubham : 3. kakummari.]

Found also in Pâipp. xix. Used by Kâug. (50. 4), with i. 26, 27 and vi. 3, by one desirous of success in conquest, and for other like purposes.

Translated : Ludwig, p. 459; Griffith, i. 286.

I. They who sit about him, who pile on [fuel] in order to beholding [him] —let Agni, fully kindled, with his tongues arise out of [their] heart.

The sense is somewhat obscure. In b, câksase probably (that he may become conspicuous '; the comm. very strangely renders it for injury (4âṅsâyâî) and regards the “they " as demons and the like. Ppp. begins yene 'daṅz par-, and elides the a of agnir in c.

2. Of the heating (? sâmtapanâ) Agni I take hold of the track (? padâ), in order to length of life (4yzs)— out of whose mouth the soothsayer (addhârt) sees the smoke arising.

Ppp. reads, for c, d, dharur yasya pagyata mama dyantag critak, corrupt. The comm. explains pada as either ‘place ' (stkâna) or ' sound ' (cabda).

3. He wno knoweth the fuel of him, piled on by the kṣatriya— he setteth not the foot (paââ) in detriment unto death.

Ppp. elides the initial z of asya in a, and begins c ma vihvare. To the comm. abkikvâra is ' a roundabout crooked cause of meeting death.

Not found in Pâipp. Used by Kâug. (4o. 18) in a rite for sexual vigor, after vi. 72. i . Translated : Griffith, i. 474. —Ct. iv. 43 vi. 2.

I. Play thou the bull, blow, increase and spread; let thy member increase limb by limb; with it smite the woman. The comm, takes yaya and aṅgam in c as two separate words, and many of SPP's saṅzhitâ mss. accent yârhâ 'gâm. According to the comm., the amulet of arka-wood is the remedy here used. Cf. also the Bower Manuscriât, ed. Hoernle, Part I., p. 5, ( a loka 6o, and p. 17, where pomegranate rind and mustard oil take the place of ara.

RE (2. Wherewith they invigorate one who is lean, wherewith they incite ki) one who is ill — with that, O Brahmanaspati, make thou his member taut like a bow.

Our Bp. reads vâjayânti in a. The second half-verse is nearly a repetition of iv. 4.6 c, d. The comm. reads vagam for kya in a.

3. I make thy member taut, like a bowstring on a bow; mount, as it were a stag a doe, unrelaxingly always.

This verse is a repetition of iv. 4.7. The Anukr. passes unnoticed the abbreviated a both here and in vs. 2.

docs.title: 102. To win a woman
docs.text:
[Jamadagni (abkisammanaskâmak).— Śvinam. &nustubkam.]

Found also in Paâipp. xix. Used by Kâug. (35.21) in a rite concerning women, with vi. 8, 9, etc., for reducing to one's will. Verse 3 is also reckoned (r9. r, note) to the pustika mantras.

Translated : Weber, Ind. Stud. v. 243 ; Grill, 54, 169; Griffith, i. 301; Bloomfield, ror, rz.

I. As this draft-horse (vâkâ), O Agvins, comes together and moves together [with his mate], so unto me let thy mind come together and move together.

The comm. paraphrases vâkas with sugiksito ‘¢vak, ' a well-trained horse,' but regards the driver (vâkaka) as the unexpressed object |? or adjunct ] of the verbswhich is also possible.

2. I drag along (â-Ś4id) thy mind, as a king-horse a side-mare (?); like grass cut by a whirlwind, let thy mind twine itself to me.

Some of SPP's authorities give p75thyâm in b; but in general the mss. cannot be relied on to distinguish szy and s74y. The Pet. Lex. understands the word with 7, but the minor Pet. Lex. with in the sense here given, which Grill (following Roth) accepts. I Cf. W's note to xviii. 4. ro. ] The comm. explains the word as ca7kubaddham [a mare] tied to a stake (to the pole of the chariot?) râj7gva as agvagrestha, and khidâmi as madabkimukham utkhanamy unmâulayâmy âvarjayâmi. The reading ma in c, which our edition wrongly accepts, is that of only two of our mss. (Bp. Bp). I Read therefore (Fam. J The comm. explains resmar as regako vâtyâtmako vâyuk. Ppp. ends b with 7 52V3 M0 9yak-

3. Of ointment, of madâgha, of kâstha, and of nard, by the hands of Bhaga, I bring up quick a means of subjection.

The construction of the genitives in the first half-verse is obscure. The comm. makes them depend on anurodhanam, and so also Grill. They are perhaps rather the means by which the anurodhana (= anulepana, comm.) or gaining to one's purposes of the desired person is to be brought about, and so are co6rdinate with Bhkagasya, the latter's 'hands ' taking the place of the ‘means ' or ' aid" which would have better suited them. Z7urâs in c is possibly genitive, ' of quick' (or powerful) Bhaga (so the comm. = tvaramâṇasya). Ppp. reads (as in other places) madhugasya in a; the comm. madâdkughasya. Ppp. has also 2 for uâ in d. Several of our mss. (P.M.I.O.T.) accent ânu râdk-, and so do six of SPP's authorities.

The tenth anuvâaka, of ro hymns and 3o verses, ends here ; the quoted Anukr. says ‘ simply âagama. ; Here ends also the fourteenth prapârhaṅa.

docs.title: 105. To get rid of cough
docs.text:
[Unmocana.— kâsâdevatyam. â&nuggubharn.)

Not found in Pâipp. except 2 a, b in xix. Employed by Kâug. (31.27) in a remedial rite against cough and catarrh.

Translated : Ludwig, p. 510; Zimmer, p. 385; Griffith, i. 302 ; Bloomfield, 8, 513.— Ct. Hillebrandt, Veda-ckrestomathie, p. 5o.

I. As the mind with mind-aims flies away swiftly, so do thou, O cough, fly forth, after the forth-driving (?) of the mind.

The comm. paraphrases manasketâis with manasâ buddhivy ty ketyamanâir JRâyamanâir gṅrasthâir visayâik ; and the obscure pravâyyar with pragantavyan: avadhin.

2. As the wellsharpened arrow flies away swiftly, so do thou, O cough, fly forth, after the stretch (?) of the earth.

The comm. explains sa# vat by sam katagradeca, which at least shows his perplexity.

3. As the sun's rays fly away swiftly, so do thou, O cough, fly forth, after the outflow of the ocean.

In all these verses, all the authorities anomalously accent the vocative, kâse , our edition makes the called-for emendation to ase; SPP. reads kâse.

docs.title: 106. Against fire in the house
docs.text:
[Pramocana.— durvâcâlâdevatyam. ânugtubham.)

Found also in Pâipp. xix. (with the verse-order 2, I, 3). Kâug. employs the hymn (52. 5) in a rite for welfare, to prevent conflagration of the house : a hole is made inside, and water conducted into it, etc. And vss. 3, 2 appear in Vâit. (29.13), with others, in the agnizayana, in the rite of drawing a frog, water-plant, and reed over the site of the fire-altar.

Translated : Ludwig, Der Rigveda, iv. 422 ; Grill, 63, r7o ; Bloomfield, AJP. xi. 347, or JAOS. xv. p. xiii (= PAOS., Oct. 1890) ; Griffith, i. 303 ; and again, Bloomfield, SBE. xiii. 147, 514.

I. In thy course hither, [thy] course away, let the flowery J%roâ grow; either let a fountain spring up there, or a pond rich in lotuses. ; The verse corresponds to RV. x. 142. 8; where, however, the words in b are all plural, and c, â read thus : kradâg ca pungâriknni samudyâsya grhâ imé. SPP. against the majority of his authorities, strangely adopts in his text the RV. version of b; it is read also by the comm., and apparently by Ppp. ; we have noted only one of ¹ our mss. as having puspintR (O.s.m.). The comm. says : anena 'gnikrtabadkasya ¹yantâbhâvah prarihitak.

2. This is the down-course of the waters, the abode (wivâana) of the ocean ; in the midst of a pool are our houses : turn thy faces away.

The first halfverse is RV. x. 142.7 a, b (also VS. xvii. 7 a, b; TS. iv.6. 13; MS. ii. 10. I), without variation. The last pada is by the comm. regarded as addressed to : Ś the fire (one of whose common epithets is vi varomukha ' having faces in every direc- Eh tion '); perhaps rather ' the points of thine arrows ': cf. VS. xvi. 53. ¹ 3. With a fetal envelop of snow, O house, do we envelop thee; for

Śâlt ¹ the envelop to be avakârâpena câivâlena. Ppp. combines bhuve ‘gnir.

docs.title: 108. For wisdom
docs.text:
[Câunaka.— paṅcarcam. medhâdcvatyam : 4. ogneyi. ânugtubham ; 2. urobyhatr;

by Pâipp. xix. has vss. I, 2, 5, thus reducing the hymn to the norm of this book. Found used in Kâug. (To. 20), with vi. 53 so the comm. : but Dârila understands xii. r. 53 as intended , in the meâhâjanana ceremony ; and also (57. 28) in the upanayana, with wora ¹ ship of Agni. : ¹ Translated: Muir, i. 255 ; Griffith, i. 304.

I. Do thou, O wisdom (zedkâ), come first to us, with kine, with horses, thou with the sun's rays ; thou art worshipful to us.

The comm. explains medhâ as crutadhâraasâamarthyar apini dev, and finds in c an elliptical comparison (zptopamâ): "as the rays of the sun quickly pervade the whole world, so come to us with own capacities able to pervade all subjects."

2. I call first, unto the aid of the gods, wisdom filled with Śrâhman, quickened by brâhman, praised by seers, drunk of (?) by Vedic students.

Ppp. omits brakmajâtâm in b, without rectifying the meter, which can only be saved by leaving out the superfluous prathamâm in a. It avoids, in c, the doubtful prapztam by reading instead pranikitâm ; and it has avasâ (for avase a ?) vrpe in d. Prâpitâam should perhaps be understood as coming from pra-pz or pra-gyâ; the comm. takes it alternatively * both ways, paraphrasing it with either sevitâm or pravarâhitânz. The Anukr. reckons â(rakmaṇvaton to b (so do the pada-mss.), and passes without notice the deficiency of a syllable in a; in fact, prathamâm is intruded, and the verse otherwise a good anugtubk. That is, he refers it to pâati by sevitâm and to pz or 4yâ by pravardhitam.

3. The wisdom that the Ribhus know, the wisdom that the Asuras know, the excellent wisdom that the seers know — that do we cause to enter into me.

It is the intrusion of b4adrâm in c that spoils the anustubk, but does not make a regular Śr4ats.

4. The wisdom that the being-making seers, possessed of wisdom, know — with that wisdom do thou make me today, O Agni, possessed of wisdom.

Many of the mss. (including our P.M.H.I.K.O.) leave vidas unaccented at the end of b. The second half-verse is VS. xxxii. 14.c, d (which has kuru for Erp); [so also RV. kkila to x. I51 J.

5. Wisdom at evening, wisdom in the morning, wisdom about noon, wisdom by the sun's rays, by the spell (vâas), do we make enter into us.

Ppp. is corrupt in c, d : meâhânk suryeno 'âyato dkṅrapâ wla stvama.

docs.title: 110. For a child born at an unlucky time
docs.text:
¹ (1 [AL tharvan.— âgneyam. (trâigtubham :: Ir. paṅkâi.] ar This hymn is not found in Pâipp. Kaâug. (46.25) applies it for the benefit of a child born under an inauspicious asterism.

of I. Since, an ancient one, to be praised at the sacrifices, thou sittest

¹ as kâtar both of old and recent—do thou, O Agni, both gratify thine own self, and bestow (â-yaj) good fortune on us.

The verse is RV. viii. 11. Io (also TA. x. 169). Our text has several bad readings, which are corrected in the other version : 47 in a should be kan, satsi should be sârsi, i and pip7âyasva should be p7ây- (TA. has, in a, pratnâsi, which its comm. explains by . vistârayasi ): this last the comm. also reads, but renders it Zjyâdikaviyâ paraya. The el verse is not at all a paṅkri, although capable of being read as 4o syllables.

Ś 2. Born in fyesthaghnt, in Yama's two Unfasteners (vicir) — do thou protect him from the Uprooter (mâlabârhaṇa); may he conduct him nn across all difficulties unto long life, of a hundred autumns.

; The consecutiveness of the verse is very defective, inasmuch as (born (jârâs, nom.) — in a can hardly be understood otherwise than of the child, while Agni is addressed in b, and spoken of in third person in c, 4. Three asterisms are here and in 112] referred to, all in our constellation Scorpio: Antares or Cor Scorpionis (either alone or with s, 7) is usually called jyesthâ ' oldest, but also (more anciently ?), as an asterism of ill omen, jyesthaghnt ' she that slays the oldest"; mâ7la ' root, also in the same manner 7 âlabar kant or -na, lit. t root-wrencher,' is the tail, or in the tail, of which the terminal star-pair, or the sting (A v), has the specific name vic tâ%. See note to ii. 8.1. ] The comm. takes yamasya as belonging to m7labarkanât. By a misprint, our text begins with jyâi- (read jye-). See TB. â. 5. 28. ]

3. On the tiger day hath been born the hero, asterism-born, being born rich in heroes ; let him not, increasing, slay his father ; let him not harm his mother that gave him birth.
