docs.title: 111. For relief from insanity
docs.text:
Lâtharvan. — caturycam. âgneyam. ânugtubham : I. parânustup trigubh.] i This hymn, like the preceding, is wanting in Pâipp. Kaug. (3. 24) reckons it as one of the marty namani (with ii. 2 and viii. 6) ; and the comm. quotes a remedial rite against demons (26. 29-32) as an example of their use.

Translated: Ludwig, p. 512; Zimmer, p. 393; Grill, 21, r 70 ; Griffith, i. 306 ; Bloomfield, 32, 518.— Ct. Hillebrandt, Veda-ckrestomatkie, p. jo.

I. Free thou this man for me, O Agni, who here bound, well-restrained, cries loudly ; thenceforth shall he make for thee a portion, when he shall be uncrazed.

Nearly all our mss., and the great majority of SPP's, have the false accent azâs at beginning of e; both editions give â/as. The comm. reads yazha for yadâ in 4d. The comm. paraphrases suyaras by susthu niyamito nirudâhaprasarak san. Pâda b has a redundant syllable.

2. Let Agni quiet [it] down for thee, if thy mind is excited (vâ-yu); I, knowing, make a remedy, that thou mayest be uncrazed.

The comm. reads udyaran: (= grahavikâreno 'âbhrântam) instead of uâdyutam in b.

3. Crazed from sin against the gods, crazed from a demon — I, know. ing, make a remedy, when he shall be uncrazed.

A few of the authorities (including our O.) accent yââa in d ; yârṅâ would be a preferable reading. Bloomfield, "sin of the gods," AJP. xvii. 433, JAOS., etc. ]

4. May the Apsarases give thee again, may Indra again, may Bhaga again ; may all the gods give thee again, that thou mayest be uncrazed.

The saṅzkirâ reading in a and c would, of course, equally admit of fz : aduk 'have ¹ given thee," and this would be an equally acceptable meaning; the comm. so understands ! and interprets. In our text, read gunas at beginning of c (the sign for z dropped out).

The difference of meter tends to point out vs. r as an alien addition by which this ¹ hymn has been increased beyond the norm of the book.

docs.title: 112. For expiation of oversiaughing
docs.text:
[Atharvan.— âgneyam. trâistubham.]

Found also-in Pâipp. xix. (vs. 3 in i.). Used by Kâug. (46. 26), with vi. rr3, in a spell to expiate the offense of parZoitei ' overslaughing,' or the marriage of a younger before an elder brother see Zimmer, p. 315.

Translated : Ludwig, p. 469; Grill, 15, 171; Griffith, i.306; Bloomfield, AJP. xvii. 437 (elaborate discussion, p. 430 ff.), or JAOS. xvi. p.cxxii (= PAOS., March, 1894); SBE. xiii. 164, 521.

I. Let not this one, O Agni, slay the oldest of them; protect him from uprooting ; do thou, foreknowing, unfasten the bonds of the seizure (grâki); let all the gods assent to thee.

The allusions in this verse to the same trio of asterisms that were mentioned in rro. 2 are very evident. According to the comm., Ś this one" in a is the pariwitta which he takes quite wrongly as the overslaugher — see comm. to vs. 3 a]. Ppp. reads g777a nas at end of c, and has, for 4, pitâapurrân mataraṅ muṅca sarvân (our 2 â).

2. Do thou, O Agni, loosen up the bonds of them, the three with which they three were tied up; do thou, foreknowing, unfasten the bonds of the seizure; free all— father, son, mother.

The comm. reads urtkitâs for utsitâs in b; the word is, strangely, not divided into ²rositâk in the pada-text, which non-division would be proper treatment for ṅ1t4717s, and part of the mss. (including our H.I.O.) read #âhâtâs. The second half-verse is wanting in Ppp. (save as d.is found in it as 1 d: see above).

3. With what bonds the overslaughed one is bound apart, applied and tied up on each limb — let them be released, for they are releasers ; wipe off difficulties, O Pâshan, on the embryo-slayer.

The comm. again commits the violence of understanding pârâvittas in a as if it were pariverta ' the overslaugher.' The participles in b are nom. sing. masc., applying to the bound person. The comm. again reads 7tkitas, again supported by a few mss. (including our H.I.), and the gada-text again has ârsitak, undivided. All our mss. save one (K.), and all but one of SPP's, read rz (without accent) in c; the translation given implies the emendation to 74, which is made in SPP's text, also on the authority of the comm. After it, SPP. reads mucyantâm, with, as he claims, all but one of his authorities ; of ours, only D.Kp.T. have it, and K. mucyatâm, all the rest muṅcantâm, as in our text. In Ppp., this verse is found in i., in this form : ebkis pâcâiF mudusâu patir nibadâkhak pareparârpito aṅge-aṅge vi te cytyantârt vicyrtar: ki santi etc. (â as in our text).

docs.text:

docs.text:
[Xâucika.—mantroktadevatyam. I. jagatl ; 2. panṅti ; 3. trigtubk.]

Translated : Ludwig, p. 442; Grill, 72, 173; Griffith, i. 311 ; Bloomfield, 165, 529. : 1. If (yât) atmosphere, earth, and sky, if father or mother we have injured (4iṅs), may this householder's-fire lead us up from that to the world of the well-done.

The first half-verse is found, without variation, in a number of other texts: in TS. (i. 8.53), TB. (ii. 7. 124), TA. (ii. 6. 28), MS. (i. 10.3), ACS. (ii. 7. 11) ; they do not agree entirely in the second half which they put in place of ours. Ppp. agrees with some of them, reading agnir ma tasmad enaso garkapatyak pramuṅcatu. Only bis really Ek Jagat.

2. May mother earth, Aditi our birthplace, brother atmosphere, [save] us from imprecation ; may our father heaven be weal to us from paternal [guilt] ; having gone to my relatives (jâm?), let me not fall down from [their ?] world.

The verse is found alse in TA. (ii. 6. 29), which reads at end of a âbkâasta énah; and, in c, 4, bhavâsi jâmt mitvâ (jâantm itvâ ?) mâ vivitst lokân : the variants are of the kind that seem to show that the text was unintelligible to the text-makers, and that we are excusable in finding it extremely obscure. Ppp. brings no help. Our translation implies in b abkâastyâs, but the pada reading is abkhtecastyâ, as if instr. ; the comm. understands -Zyâs. Our pada mss. also leave zz2 unaccented in d. Ludwig and Grill supply lokâr to pitryât : " from the paternal world." The comm. divides alternatively jâmi my toa and jamim rtvâ. The verse is a good fristubh, though capable of being contracted to 4o syllables. ²] Grill reports a Ppp. reading rrâza for bhrâta, although I do not find it in Roth's collations. Might it represent a (rârv antâriksam ?]

3. Where the well-hearted, the well-doing revel, having abandoned disease of their own selves, not lame with their limbs, undamaged in heaven (svargâ)— there may we see [our] parents and sons.

I The first half we had at iii. 28. 5. ] The verse corresponds to TA. ii. 6. 2¹e, which reads mâdante at end of a, tanvân svâyam at end of b, aclouâṅgair (so Ppp. also) in c (also âk7tâs, but this is doubtless a misprint the Poona ed. reads in fact âhruṅas f), and gitâran ca putrâm at the end. The comm. reads Zanwâs in b, with part of the mss. (including our P.M.1.O.), and agropâs in c. |For the substance of the vs., cf. Weber, 85. 1894, p- 775 ]

docs.title: 121. For release from evil
docs.text:
[Xâucika.— [caturycam.] mantroktadevatyam. I, a. trigtubh ; 3,4. anugtubk.]

Found also in Pâipp. xvi. For vss. 3, 4, cf. v. Schroeder, Zwei Hss., p. 15, Tâbinger Katha-kss., p. 75.) Used by Kâug. (52. 3) with vi. 63 and 84, in a rite for release from various bonds ; and with the whole znuwâka —see under h. rr4.

Translated : Ludwig, p. 442; Zimmer, p. 182 (3 vss.) ; Griffith, i. 311.

I. An untier, do thou untie off us the fetters that are highest, lowest, that are Varuṇa's ; remove (nis-s7) from us evil-dreaming [and] difficulty; then may we go to the world of the well-done.

Viâṇa (p. viesânz) is doubtless (antler ' here, as at iii. 7. 1, 2 which see] (though neither Kâug. nor the schol. nor our comm. make mention of such an article as used = here); but it was necessary to render it etymologically, to bring out the word-play between it and u7 gya ; the comm. treats it as a participle (= vimuṅcarr), disregarding, as usual, the accent (really vâ-sâ + ana VSk2. Gram. § 11350 CJ). The second pada is the same with vil. 83. 4 bh. The proper readings in c are (see note to Prat. ii. 86) dussvdpryam and nâsyva, which the mss. almost without exception * abbreviate to dusvagp- and nâyva, just as they abbreviate dazroâ to datvâ, or, in vs. 2 a, râjjvâm to râjvâam (see my Skz. G7. 232). SPP. here gives in bis szṅ hi â-text at soa, with all his authorities ; our text has a4 sua, with only one of ours (0.) : doubtless the true metrical form is at Suwa 'smât. Cf. Roth, ZD MG. xviii. 119, note. Ppp. lacks our second halfverse, having instead 2 a, b. ¥] That is, if we take the occurrences of the words as a whole in AV. ] Ś : :;

2. If (yât) thou art bound in wood, and if in a rope; if thou art bound ¹ in the earth, and if by a spell (24:)—may this householder's-fire lead us ¹ up from that to the world of the well-done.

The second half-verse here is the same with rzo. r c, 4, and seems uncomected with the first half. Ppp. reads, in a, 4âzrunâ and raja, and omits the second half-verse, ¹ Ś thus reducing the hymn to three verses, the norm of the book. ¹

3. Arisen are the two blessed stars named the Unfasteners ; let them bestow here of immortality (am71a); let the releaser of the bound advance.

The first half-verse is the same with ii. 8. 1 a, b; compare also iii.7. 4 a, b. The verse corresponds to TA. ii. 6. rs, which has, for a, am? AV. iil. 7.4, am# ye suthâge ( âṅvt, and, in 9, erâd for prat tu.

4. Go thou apart ; make room ; mayest thou free the bound one from the bond ; like a young fallen out of the womb, do thou dwell along all roads..

A corresponding verse is found in TA. (ii. 6. 1), which has, for a, vf jihtrsva bkân ky dhi,* and, at the end, 4nu soa (also parhâs after sârvân). Ppp. reads atthe end anu gacka, and this is what the comm. gives as paraphrase of 42u ksiya. The Anukr. seems te to authorize the contraction yonye 'va in c. In ec, yânes for y6nyâs. J k

docs.title: 122. With an offering for offspring
docs.text:
[Bkr gu. —paṅcarcam. vâicvakarmaṇam. trâ stubham g,5. jagarṇ].

Verses 2, 3 are found in Pâipp. xvi. [For vss. 13, cf. v. Schroeder, Zwe7 Hss., . Pp. 15, Tâbinger Katha-kss., pp. 75-76.] It appears in Kâug., with the hymn next fol- Ś lowing," in the savayajṅas (63. 29), accompanying the offering of saṅzsthâtahomas; and 4 g the comm. regards vs. 5 (instead of xi. i. 27, which has the same p7uatzka) as intended at Ś r 63. 4, in the same ceremonies, with distribution of water for washing the priests' hands. ⁴ Vâit. (22. 23) has both hymns in the agnistoma, with vil. 41. 2, as recited by the sacrificer.. I For the whole zzuvâka, see under h. 114. ] And with x. 9.26. ] Ś

Translated : Ludwig, p. 432; Griffith, i. 312. ¹

I. This portion I, knowing, make over [to thee], O Vigvakarman, first-born of right; by us [is it] given, beyond old age ; along an unbroken ( line may we pass (77) together. ¹ The connection in this verse is obscure ; prarhamajâs 'first-born' in b can only ; qualify I " grammatically ; doubtless it should be vocative, belonging to Vigvakarman. The comm. connects daztam directly with bkâgam, which he explains by pakvan anna: havirbhâgant vi. The second half-verse corresponds to TA. fi. 6. 1s c, d (in immediate connection with the two preceding verses of our text also), which differs only by reading ¹ at the end carema ; and this the comm. also reads. The first half-verse in TA. is as follows : sâ prajanân prâtigrbhntta vidvân prajâpari prarhumajâ rtâsya ; and Ppp. ¹ apparently intends a similar reading ; it has za7 prajanan iy ekâ, as if the verse had occurred earlier in the text; but it has not been found.

2. Some pass along the extended line, of whom what is the Fathers' [was] given in course (? 4yanena) ; some, without relatives, giving, bestowing — if they be able to give, that is very heaven. ¹ The TA. (ii. 6. 26) has this verse also, with variants: ânu sârcaranti for taranti 4 (besides the preceding 4x) in a, &yanavat at end of b, yâcchat at end of c (Ppp. has g yachan), caknuvâṅsas" for c(tksan and esam for cvâ in d. Both comm's understand ‘ ¹ rrâm ' debt with pâtryam, and abandhin (which appears to be used adverbially) as ¹Ś equivalent to aṅandhavas: though without descendants, they too reach heaven as ¹ ¹ ¹ reward of their gifts. Ppp. has also ze for cer in 4. The Calc. ed. seems to have i Cl caṅnâvâṅsâk so- Does it intend ca&nâvân (or caknâvân —see Gram. § jor) sâ so-? ²

3. Take ye (both) hold after, take hold together after; to this world they that have faith attach themselves (sac); what cooked [offering] of te , yours is served up in the fire, combine ye, O husband and wife, in order to the guarding of it. â 4 The verse is found in TA. (ii. 6. 27), with great differences of text: azu- is omitted ŚŚ at the beginning ; anu, second time in a, is accented, ânu ; b is samânâm pântham ¹¹ avatho gh tena ; purtâm for pakuâr is read (also by Ppp.), and yâd inserted before ere agnai, in cx; â is tâsmai gâtrâye 'hâ jâyâpati sânm rabhetham. The reading purtâm is Hl i against our understanding pakvâm of the body prepared by fire for the other world. a ² The comm. explains pârivistam by praksipram, the TA. comm. by pariprâgitam, both ‘ i ' apparently taking it from root vig. The verse is found repeated, with a different begini ning, as xii. 3.7. It is too irregular to be called a simple 775725k. *] Thus rectifying

its meter. ¹ 4. The great sacrifice, as it goes, with mind, I ascend after, with fervor

(?1âpas), of like origin ; being called upon, O Agni, may we, beyond old eh age, revel in joint reveling in the third firmament. Ś The connection of mânasâ, in a, is probably with anvârohâmi, that of 4pasâ is pos- Se sibly with sâyonis ; but the comm. understands connected with the sacrifice in virtue Ś of penance "; he guesses two different interpretations of the half-verse. Some of our mss. (lr (P.M.H.p.m.O.) make in c the combination âpakṅtâ 'gne which the meter demands. Ś : Neither this verse nor the next save its a] has anything of a jagarr character.

5. These cleansed, purified, worshipful maidens I seat in separate succession in the hands of the priests (brakmân) ; with what desire I now pour you on, let Indra here with the Maruts grant me that.

k The verse occurs again, with a slight variation at the end, as xi. r. 27, and, with much ¹ more important differences, as x. 9.27. In the latter verse, instead of the figurative;

appellation maidens," we have the divine waters (fem.) " themselves addressed.;

docs.title: 123. For the success of an offering
docs.text:
a : IBkrg].—paṅcarcam. uvâicvadevam. trâigubham : 3. 2-p. sâmny anugubk ; 4. I-av. 2-p. prâ-

¹ jâparyâ bhurig anugtubk.] f

[Partly prose, 3 and 4. ] This hymn and the one following are not found in Paipp. i a Its uses by Kâug. and Vait. with hymn 122 are explained under that hymn. And vss.

¹ 3=5 appear also in Vâit. (2. 135), at the parvan sacrifice, in the ceremony of gravaraṇa. f (For the whole anuvâka, see under h. 114. ³ Ś i Translated : Muir, v. 293 (vss. 2, 4,5); Ludwig, p. 302; Griffith, i. 313. ŚhŚ

2 Seat

I. This one, O ye associates (?sadkâstha), I deliver to you, whom Jatavedas shall carry [as] a treasure; the sacrificer follows after well-being ; him do ye recognize in the highest firmament.

The verse is found also in VS. (xviii. 59) and K. (xl. 13). VS. reads, in a, saâhastha and ze (for vas); in b, it puts gevadhim after auâhatz ; in c, it reads a. yajRâpatir vo âtra. The comm. explains saâkhasthâs as meaning ' the gods' (saka tisthanty ekatra svarge loke sthâne yajamânena saka nivasanty.

2. Recognize ye him in the highest firmament; ye divine associates, ye know [his] world there; the sacrificer follows after well-being; make ye what he has offered and bestowed plain for him.

This verse is found with the preceding in VS. (xviii. 60) and K. (xl. 13), and also in TB. (iil. 7. 133-4), but with considerable variants : at the beginning, e247 janâtha (TB. Jantar) par-; in b, TB. vFṅas for das, both VS. and TB. sadk- unaccented, which is better, but VS. vida, which is bad, and both râpâm asya (for lokâm âira), which gives a better sense ; for c, both yâd agâchar pathtbhir devayânâis; in d, both iszâp arte, and VS. krnavârka, but TB. kr nuat, both without sa.

3. O gods! O Fathers ! O Fathers! O gods I who I am, he am I.

The comm., with his usual carelessness of accent, takes the vocatives here for nominatives. Some of SPP's authorities (also our O.s.m.) omit the accent of the first asi.

4. He do I cook, he do I give, he do I offer; [as] he, let me not be parted from what is given.

That is, from my gifts, or their reward. The comm. counts and explains these two quasi-verses, 3 and 4, as one. But the Anukr. reckons this hymn (as it reckoned the preceding one) as one of five verses (paṅcarca), and SPP's edition as well as ours so divides. ]'As that one, I cook ' etc. would be an equally accurate translation, and the English of it is not so harsh.

5. In the firmament, O king, stand firm ; there let this stand firm; know of what we have bestowed, O king; do thou, O god, be well-willing.

The comm. understands the addresses of this verse as made to Soma, which is very questionable ; and the « this" of b to be the ââpârtdâm, which (or dattâm, vs. 4) is right. It must be by a corruption of the text that the Anukr. does not define the verse as an anustubk.

docs.title: 124. Against evil influence of a sky-drop
docs.text:
[âtharvan (nirrtyapasaranakâmaR). — mantroktadevatyam uta divyâpyan. trâigubharm.]

This hymn, like the preceding, is not found in Pâipp. It is employed by Kaâug. (46. 41) in an expiatory rite for the portent of drops of rain from a clear sky. In Vait. (12.7) it is used in the aguistoma when one has spoken in sleep; and vs. 3 separately (11.9), in the same ceremony, when the man who is being consecrated is anointed. |For the whole anuwâka, see under h. r14.

Translated : Ludwig, p. 498 ; Griffith, i. 314.

I. From the sky now, from the great atmosphere, a drop of water hath fallen upon me with essence (7âsâ); with Indra's power, with milk, Ś O Agni, [may] I [be joined], with the meters, with offerings, with the deed of the well-doing. Ś The verse is found also in HGS. i. 16. 6, with sundry variants : ma for mâm in a; ( apatac chivâya at end of b; in c, d, manasa ham & gam brakmanâa guptak sukyta ¹ g ¹ ¹ krtena; these are in some respects improvements, especially in relieving the embaras- ² ¹ i sing lack of a verb in our second half-verse. The comm. paraphrases antariksâr by; ¹ ul âkâgan nirmeghât, and supplies saṅigaccheya (as in the translation). It is a little ; ¹ : Ś strange that the fall of water out of the air upon one is so uncanny and must be atoned ² d for (Zkâcodakaplâavanadosac anti). i ; 2. If from a tree it hath fallen upon [me], that is fruit; if from the

L atmosphere, that is merely Vâyu; on whatever part of my body, and what : ¹ ¹ part of my garment, it hath touched, let the waters thrust perdition away. I eh This verse also is found with the preceding in HGS. ; which in a reads vy ksâgrad abhya- : a patat and omits ta; and in b reads yad v7 for yadi and fat for sa; for c, it has yatrâ are vrksas tanuvâi yatra vâsak, and in d 5â2dkantâm instead of nudantu. The comm. : l paraphrases the end of b thus : vâyvâtmaka eva na 'smâkar: dosâya. The third pada

Ś is really jagatr.

3. A fragrant ointment, a success is that; gold, splendor, just purify- ¹ ing is that. All purifiers [are] stretched out from us; let not perdition pass that, nor the niggard. ( : That is, the uncanny drop is all these fine things. The comm. renders pârrimam in b by cuddhikaram.; and aâki in c by ⁴ above." The second pâda is redundant by a syllable. ‘ With this ends the twelfth anuvâka, of 11 hyrns and 38 verses ; the old Anukr. q ¹ says astatriṅgo dvâdagak.

docs.title: 125. To the war-chariot : for its success
docs.text:
¹ LA thar van. — vânaspatyam. (râigubkam : 2. jagati.] ¹ Found also in Pâipp. xv. (in the verse-order 2, 3, I). This hymn and the next are six successive verses of RV. (vi. 47. 26-31), and also of VS. (xxix. 52—57), TS. (iv. 6. 65-7), ¹ E ¹ and MS. (iii. 16. 3). In Kâug. (15. 11) it and not xii. 3.33 ] is used in a battle-rite, He with vii. 3, 110, and other passages, as the king mounts a new chariot (at Kâvug. 10. 24 and 13.6 it is ix. r. r that is intended so SPP's ed. of the comm. to iii. 16 ], not vs. 2 of this hymn). In Vaâit. (6.8), vss. 3 and 1 are quoted in the agnyâdkâya, accompanying the sacrificial gift of a chariot ; and the hymn (or vs. 1), in the saṅtra (34. 15), as the king 1 mounts a chariot.

Translated : by the RV. translators ; and, as AV. hymn, by Ludwig again, p. 4593

¹ Griffith, i. 314.— See also Bergaigne-Henry, Manuel, p. 155.

I. O forest-treel stout-limbed verily mayest thou become, our com-

panion, furtherer, rich in heroes; thou art fastened together with kine ; be thou stout ; let him who mounts thee conquer things conquerable.

d ; There is no difference of reading among all the versions of this verse. GB. (i. 2. 21)

Ś quotes its pratika and so does MGS. at i.x3. 55 of. p. 155 J; MB. (i. 7. 16) has the whole verse. Kine," as often elsewhere, means the products of cattle, here the strips of ces cowhide ; and tree" the thing made of its wood l ef. i. 2. 3, note Gk

2. Forth from heaven, from earth [is its] force brought up; forth from forest-trees [is its] power brought hither; to the force of the waters, brought forth hither by the kine, to Indra's thunderbolt, the chariot, do thou sacrifice with oblation.

Or all the nouns (force " and power " in a, b as well) are to be taken as accusatives with yaja ' sacrifice to." Ppp. reads zbâr tar: at end of a, and parisambhy rar: in b. All the other versions have the better reading âuvytam at end of c; and so has the comm, followed by three of SPP's mss.; and it is accordingly adopted in SPP's text. MS. reads vy tam also in b, and antâriksar instead of âja âdbhytan: in a. TS.VS. have â7vâṅ p- at the beginning. The comm. refers to TS. vi. I. 34 as authority for identifying the chariot with Indra's thunderbolt.

3. Indra's force, the Maruts' front (ân7ka), Mitra's embryo, Varuṇa's navel—do thou, enjoying this oblation-giving of ours, O divine chariot, accept the oblations.

All the other versions have vâjras for âjas in a, and Ppp. agrees with them. All, too (not Ppp.), combine sâ 'mân: at beginning of c, against the requirement of the meter. The GB. quotes (i. 2. 21) the pratika of this verse in its form as given by our text. 1 PPD. has dkaruṇasya for vâr- in b.

docs.title: 126. To the ârum : for success against the foe
docs.text:
LA4tkarvan. — vEnaspatyadundubkidevatyam. bhuriktrâistubham : 3. purobykati virâggarbhâ trigtubk.] Found also in Pâipp. xv." (but I c, d and 2 a, b are wanting, probably by an error of the copyist), and in the same other texts as the preceding hymn (RV.VS. TS. MS. : in MS. the three verses are not in consecution with those of 125). Applied by Kâug. (16.1) in a battle rite, with v. zo, as the drums and other musical instruments of war, : duly prepared, are sounded thrice and handed to those who are to play them. Vit. (34. IT) has it (also with v. 20) in the same ceremony as the preceding hymn, as the drum-heads are drawn on. ] Seems to be an error for Pâipp. vii.

Translated : by the RV. translators ; and Griffith, i. 315.— See also Bergaigne-Henry, Manuel, p. 156.

I. Blast thou unto heaven and earth ; in many places let them win for thee the scattered living creatures (jâgat); do thou, O drum, allied with Indra [and] the gods, drive away our foes further than far.

The second pada is translated according to the reading of our text, whose vznvatânz, however, can hardly be otherwise than a corruption of the zzanutârn of the other texts; Ppp. has instead sunutâm, which is yet worse ; the comm. has vanutâm. MS. has, in d, rât for durât.

2. Resound thou at [them]; mayest thou assign strength [and] force to us; thunder against [them], forcing off difficulties; drive, O drum, misfortune away from here; Indra's fist art thou; be stout.

The other texts have, in b, at} staniki for abht sfana, and, in c, profâa for sedha, and the plural duchânas (save TS., which gives -2â), in pada-text -nzn).

3. Conquer thou those yonder ; let these here conquer; let the drum speak loud vâvad- ] [and] clear ; let our horse-winged heroes fly together; let our chariot-men, O Indra, conquer.

All the other texts have, for a, & 'mkr aja pratyâvartaye 'mâṅ, and vâvaditi at end of b; in c, for patantu, câranti (but MS. cârantu); while Ppp. reads patayanti. Amṅṅ before jaya doubtless means amân, and is so translated above ; but the pada-text under- ¹ stands it as amâm, and the comm. supplies carrusenâm. The Anukr. contracts the first pâda into 9 syllables.

docs.title: 127. Against various diseases : with a wooden amulet
docs.text:
[BkrgUvagiras.— oânaspatyam uta yaksmanâcanadevatyam. ânugtubham : 3. 3-a. 6-4. jagatr.]

This hymn is not found in Pâipp. Kaâug. applies it (26. 33-39), with ii. 7, 25; vi. 83, 109; viii. 7, in a healing rite against various diseases (with this hymn specially the person treated is to be smeared by means of a splinter of palâga, ib. 34; and the head of one seized by Varuṇa is to be anointed, ib. 39); and it is reckoned (note to 26. I) to the fa kmanâgcana gaṇa.

Translated : Zimmer, p. 386 (with comment on the diseases) ; Griffith, i. 315 ; Bloomfield, 40, 530.—See also Grohmann, Ind. Stud. ix. 396 ff.

I. Of the vidradhâ, of the red balâsa, O forest-tree, of the visâlpaka, O herb, do thou not leave even a bit (? pigitâ).

Or lŚhitasya may be a separate disease (so rendered by Zimmer : the comm. takes it as either “red " or [a disease of] the blood"). The form wâsâlpaka is given here on the strength of SPP's authorities (among which living repeaters of the text are included), and of the comm., which derives it from root szp (vividhar sarpari), with substitution of I for 7 ; no manuscript is to be trusted to distinguish Jpa and lya, and, as the word is unknown save in this hymn and in ix. 8 and xix. 44, there was nothing to show which was the true reading. The comm. takes caruraṅgnlapalâc avr ksa to be the tree addressed, and vidradka as vidaranactlo vranavigesak ; also pita as nidanabhârart dusian maâṅsam ; and balâsa as kâsacvâasââi. |Our P.M. E.I.O.R.K. combine wisâlpakasyosadhc in saṅzkirâ in c; and this SPP. adopts in his text, and reports nothing to the contrary from his authorities. ]

2. The two testicles that are thine, O ba2âsa, laid away in thine armpit (? kâksay—I know the remedy for that, the czpṅdru, a looking-upon.

By a blundering confusion of c and g in transcription, in our text and in the Index Verborum founded upon it, the form (ṅp7ââru instead of cr has been adopted for this verse. The comm. reads czpadru, and calls it “a kind of tree having this name "; perhaps crpââu is the true form. We should have expected rather #pa- or âpâ than âpagran in b (= apakrstam âcritâu; and kakge = bâhumule, comm). [" Testicles": perhaps swellings of the axillary ⁴glands." ]

3. The visâlpaka that is of the limbs, that is of the ears, that is in the eyes—we eject the visâlaka, the vidradkâ, the heart-disease; we impel. away downward that unknown yâksma. 8

docs.title: 128. For auspicious time : with dung-smoke
docs.text:
[Atharvâṅgiras (naksatrarâjânar: candramasam astâut).— caturycam. sâumyam ; akadkâmadevatyam. ânustubham.]

Except the third verse, this hymn occurs also in Pâipp. xix. Besides the ceremony reported under vs. r, Kâug. has the hymn (50. 13) in a general rite for good fortune, with vi. I, 3-7, 59, etc. etc.; and also, in the chapter of portents (roo. 3), in an expiatory ceremony on occasion of an eclipse of the moon (somagrakaṇa, comm); vs. 3, too, is specially quoted in the as7akâ ceremony (138.8), as accompanying a nineteenth [oblation 7].

Translated : Weber, Omina und Portenta (1858), p. 363 ; Zimmer, p. 353 ; Griffith, i. 316 ; Bloomfield, 16o, 532.— Bloomfield bad already treated it at length, AJP. vii. 484 ff, and JAOS. xiii. p. cxxxiii (= PAOS., Oct. 1886). A pencilled note on Whitney's ms. shows that he considered the propriety of rewriting the tranŚlation and comment for vi. 128,

I. When the asterisms made the gakadkâma their king, they bestowed on him auspicious (54adyâ-) day, saying " This shall be [his] royalty."

Cakadhtma (with irregular but not unparalleled accent: see my Skz. Gr. § 1267 b) means primarily ' dung-smoke,' i.e. smoke arising from burning dung (or else the vapor from fresh dung). According to the comm., it signifies here the fire from which such smoke arises, and then, on account of inseparability from that, a Brahman "; and he quotes TS. v. 2, 8r-2 : “a Brahman is indeed this Agni Vâigvânara." The Kaâugika- Sttra, in a passage (50.15, 16) also quoted by the comm., says that, with this hymn, having laid balls of dung on the joints of a Brahman friend, one asks dung-smoke, «what sort of day today?" He (of course, the Brahman ) answers « propitious, very favorable." ' Prof. Bloomfield takes gakaâkṅma to be out-and-out the title of a Brahman, " weather-prophet " ; but this seems not to follow from the Stra, also not from the Anukr., and least of all from the hymn. The Pâipp. version differs considerably from ours (but nearly agrees with one in an appendix to the Nakgatra-kalpa : see Bloomfield, AIP. vii. 485) : it reads yad râzjâanaṅz cakadkâman naksarrâṇy aky pura : Śhadrakam asmâi prâ 'yachan taro rastram ajâyata. The accentof âsâr ind is not explained by any known rule. So Kegava to Kâug. so. 16.

2. Auspicious day ours at noon, auspicious day be ours at evening, auspicious day ours in the morning of the days ; be night auspicious day for us.

docs.text:

docs.text:

If we consider the facts 4 Śr set forth in the paragraphs introductory to the foregoing books

: so it speaks of book vii. as the eṅa-rca-sṅkta-kânga. Presumably, therefore, we are to i Ś regard the r-versed hymn as the norm " of the book, although the 2-versed hymn is undeniably « prevalent.” ] See p. exlix.

I The book is divided into ten anuvâka-groups. These, with the number of hymns in each group and the number of verses in each group, are here given:

; — Anuvâka: r ; 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 10

Total, 286 verses. The Old Anukramaṇt seems to take zo verses as the norm of the ie : anuvâka. The Paris codex, P., in this book numbers the verses through each anuvâka

Ś% without separating the hymns. The commentator divides the anuvâkas into hymns © (¹ : (from two to four in each anuvâka), which Ś hymns," however, are nothing more than — mechanical decads of verses with an overplus or shortage in the last decad " when the total is not a multiple of ten: thus, anuvâka 1 has three hymns, of ro + ro +8=28 verses; 2 has two hymns, of ro + 13=23 verses ; 3 has three hymns, of 9+ 1011 =30 verses; 4 has three hymns, of ro+ 10+ 10=30 verses ; and so on. His anxvâka endings coin, cide throughout with those of the Berlin edition, save that vii. 23 is reckoned by him (and P.) to anuvâka 2 instead of 3, thus making for 2 and 3 his verse-totals 23 and 30 instead of 22 and 31 (as the Old Anukramaṇi gives them) and spoiling the count of his first decad " in 3. (Note that vii. 23 is a gakta-verse.) His decad "divisions cut in two our hymns 26, 45, 54, 68, 72, 76, 79, 97, and 109.

[It should here be mentioned that the Bombay edition, following the Major Anukramaṇî, counts hymns 6, 45, 68, 72, and 76 each as two hymns. From vii. 6. 3 to the end of the book, accordingly, Whitney gives a double numeration of the hymns: first the numeration of the Berlin edition, and then, in parenthesis, the numeration of the Bombay edition. As against the former, the latter involves a plus of one from vii. 6. 3 to vii. 45. I; a plus of two from vii. 45. 2 to vii. 68. 2; a plus of three from vii. 68. 3 to vii. 72. 2; a plus of four from vii. 72. 3 to vii. 76. 4; and a plus of five from vii. 76. 5 to the ead. Finally it may be noted that vii. 54. 2 is reckoned (forwards) to vii. 55, but that this does not affect the hymn-numbers save for the verse concerned. The book, like some of those preceding, begins with mystic, obscure, and un-Atharvanic material. The comm. has no idea what it means, and sets forth his ignorance at immense length, giving about five quarto pages of exposition to this first hymn, with wholly discordant alternative explanations. Later they are worked into the ordinary classification of Vasus, Rudras, etc. ; and what was formerly a serious religious problem, a hierarchy conceived as possible before the now-accepted gods (something like the pre-Olympians with the Greeks), has become an empty name." The comm. has instead mai 'syami, eo explaining it as = ma gamâyâmi Virtually all the authorities, too, leave than A ² unaccented (two out of fourteen of SPP's and our R.Ś.m. ltkan) ; this both editions & i emend. [The Anukr. seems to scan as It +8: 7 + 8=34. cH I The squatting posture in making water is, I believe, general with the natives of India ¹ to this day. So Hesiod, orks and Days, 727 : u9e ârr ṅeMow rerpappâvos Śp6bs He Sue. &âpevos krh. Ct. xiii. I. 56 and my note. (4 Here ends the ninth anuwâka, of 12 hymns and z1 verses : the old Anukr. says fu navamo dvadaca and efavinga.

docs.title: 103 (108). For betterment
docs.text:
⁴ ¹ ( % [Brahman — âtmadâioatam. trâigtubham.]

Found also in Pâipp. xx. Used by Kâug. (59. 19) with hymn 17 etc. (see under 17). ee Translated: Ludwig, p. 269; Henry, 41, 116; Griffith, i. 378. — Cf. Bloomfield,

1 I. What Kshatriya, seeking betterment, shall lead us up out of al ¹ this reproachful hate — who that desires sacrifice, or who that desires pe bestowal? who wins long life-time among the gods?

docs.title: 105 (110). An exhortation to holy life
docs.text:
: Vâvharvan.—mantroktadezatyay:. ânugtubhanm.] . eo : ot =.
